t: Has Machine Learning for Systems Reached an Inflection Point?
th: ML-for-systems adoption trajectory
pb: It is unclear whether ML-for-systems research has reached a tipping point analogous to AlexNet in 2012, where ML transitions from one of many competing approaches to the dominant methodology. The paper investigates whether systems research has arrived at or is approaching that inflection point.
me: The paper is a position/vision paper that surveys the trajectory of ML-for-systems research across sub-domains (scheduling, compilers, storage, networking, etc.), comparing their adoption curves to known ML inflection points in other fields. It evaluates evidence of maturation indicators such as production deployments, benchmark standardization, and displacement of handcrafted heuristics.
nv: Frames ML-for-systems progress as an inflection-point analysis, drawing a structured parallel to AlexNet's transformation of computer vision to assess readiness and remaining barriers.
tg: ml-for-systems, survey, position-paper, systems-research, inflection-point

t: Voyager: Input-Adaptive Algebraic Transformations for High-Performance Graph Neural Networks
th: Input-adaptive GNN execution optimization
pb: GNN execution performance is bottlenecked by irregular memory access patterns and low compute utilization, and algebraic transformations (operator reordering, operator fusion) that work well for dense DNNs fail to generalize across diverse and dynamically varying graph structures. Existing transformation strategies are applied statically and cannot adapt to per-input graph topology variations.
me: Voyager applies input-adaptive algebraic transformations that select or compose operator reordering and fusion strategies at runtime based on the structural properties of the incoming graph (e.g., degree distribution, density, sparsity patterns). It profiles lightweight graph statistics to guide transformation selection and generates optimized execution plans per input, avoiding the single static plan that prior compilers assume.
nv: Runtime input-adaptive selection of algebraic transformations (operator reordering and fusion) based on live graph topology statistics, enabling GNN-specific optimization that generalizes across structurally diverse inputs.
tg: gnn, algebraic-transformation, operator-fusion, input-adaptive, compiler

t: Early Termination for Hyperdimensional Computing Using Inferential Statistics
th: Statistically guaranteed early termination for HDC
pb: Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) inference can be terminated early to reduce computation, but existing heuristic early-termination methods lack statistical guarantees and may either unacceptably degrade classification accuracy or terminate inference later than necessary. There is no principled, statistically grounded method for HDC early termination.
me: The paper applies inferential statistics (hypothesis testing) to HDC classification to derive a principled early-termination criterion. Rather than using a heuristic threshold, it formulates the termination decision as a statistical test on the similarity scores of HDC class hypervectors, computing confidence bounds and stopping inference when the test rejects ambiguity with the required statistical confidence. This allows provable accuracy-loss bounds while minimizing wasted computation.
nv: First application of formal inferential statistics (hypothesis testing with provable confidence bounds) to govern early termination in hyperdimensional computing classifiers.
tg: hyperdimensional-computing, early-termination, inferential-statistics, edge-inference, approximation

t: Mint: Cost-Efficient Tracing with All Requests Collection via Commonality and Variability Analysis
th: All-requests distributed tracing via commonality-variability decomposition
pb: Distributed tracing systems face a fundamental tension between preserving essential trace information and reducing the massive volume of traces generated in production. The prevailing '1 or 0' binary sampling strategy either retains a full trace or discards it entirely, which fails to efficiently capture structural commonality across traces while still recording meaningful variability.
me: Mint decomposes traces into a commonality skeleton shared across structurally similar requests and per-request variability deltas that capture deviations. It collects all requests but stores only the variability delta relative to the common template, reducing storage volume while preserving full per-request observability. A commonality and variability analysis pass extracts templates offline or incrementally from the trace stream.
nv: Replacing binary trace sampling with a commonality-variability decomposition that retains full-request coverage at drastically reduced storage cost.
tg: distributed-tracing, observability, sampling, commonality-variability, cost-efficiency

t: EXIST: Enabling Extremely Efficient Intra-Service Tracing Observability in Datacenters
th: Ultra-low-overhead intra-service tracing for datacenters
pb: Intra-service application-level tracing imposes 5-10% average runtime overhead on traced applications (up to 18% worst case), making it impractical for continuous deployment in shared, stressed datacenters where sub-percent-level overhead is required for practical observability.
me: EXIST redesigns the intra-service tracing pipeline to achieve per-mille-level overhead through a combination of: extremely lightweight instrumentation hooks that avoid expensive context-switching or synchronization, asynchronous off-path trace collection and encoding that decouples tracing cost from the critical path, and selective event compression that preserves causality chains while discarding redundant intermediate events. The specific mechanism targets eliminating redundant data copies and reducing synchronization in the trace record path.
nv: A holistic intra-service tracing system redesigned from instrumentation to collection to achieve per-mille-level overhead, roughly 10-50x lower than existing schemes, while maintaining full causal observability.
mx: other: overhead reduced from 5-10% (up to 18% worst case) to per-mille level
tg: distributed-tracing, observability, intra-service, overhead-reduction, datacenter

t: TempGraph: An Efficient Chain-driven Temporal Graph Computing Framework on the GPU
th: GPU temporal graph execution via chain decomposition and GAC model
pb: Temporal graph path problems require vertices to be processed sequentially along time-dependent chains, creating inherently poor parallelism and slow convergence that prevents existing GPU solutions from utilizing the massive thread-level parallelism and high memory bandwidth of modern GPUs.
me: TempGraph transforms the temporal graph into disjoint time-dependent chains that expose temporal dependencies explicitly, then employs a Generate-Activate-Compute (GAC) execution model to decouple temporal dependencies between different chains by maintaining a set of shortcut references. This allows multiple chains to be processed concurrently by massive GPU thread pools while shortcut maintenance handles cross-chain dependency resolution, enabling fast convergence and high parallelism.
nv: The Generate-Activate-Compute model with inter-chain shortcut references that breaks temporal dependencies across disjoint chains, enabling concurrent GPU execution of temporally-coupled graph workloads.
mx: speedup: 3.0-16.2x over GPU baselines; 33.9-368.9x over TeGraph CPU baseline
tg: temporal-graph, gpu, graph-analytics, parallelism, chain-driven

t: AnyKey: A Key-Value SSD for All Workload Types
th: Workload-agnostic KV-SSD metadata management
pb: Existing Key-Value SSD (KV-SSD) designs are optimized only for workloads where values are much larger than keys; when key sizes are relatively large (an unexplored but real workload class), the expanded key metadata causes significantly degraded performance and potentially unbounded metadata growth.
me: AnyKey redesigns the KV-SSD metadata management architecture to prevent metadata size from scaling with key size. It introduces a metadata-bounded key representation that separates key identity from the full key payload, storing only fixed-size key references (hashes or compact descriptors) in the primary metadata structures while managing full key payloads separately. This ensures metadata overhead remains bounded regardless of key size distribution.
nv: A metadata-bounded KV-SSD architecture that decouples key metadata size from actual key size, enabling uniform performance across both small-key and large-key workload types.
tg: kv-ssd, storage, key-value, metadata-management, workload-diversity

t: PipeLLM: Fast and Confidential Large Language Model Services with Speculative Pipelined Encryption
th: Speculative pipelined encryption for confidential LLM serving on GPU TEEs
pb: Confidential GPU computing (e.g., NVIDIA H100 TEE) protects outsourced LLM inference through data encryption, but the encryption module imposes up to 52.8% throughput reduction for OPT-30B and 88.2% for OPT-66B due to synchronous encryption latency on the critical path.
me: PipeLLM overlaps GPU computation with encryption through pipelining, analogously to CPU instruction pipelining. The key challenge is that the encryption module does not know which data to encrypt until the GPU requests it, so PipeLLM introduces speculative pipelined encryption: it predicts the next data requiring encryption by analyzing LLM serving patterns (token generation sequences, KV-cache access patterns), pre-emptively encrypting predicted data ahead of GPU demand. A low-cost pipeline relinquishing mechanism handles mispredictions by falling back without correctness violation.
nv: Speculative prediction of encryption targets based on LLM serving patterns, enabling pipelined overlap of GPU computation and confidential encryption to nearly eliminate encryption latency on the critical path.
mx: speedup: reduces throughput overhead from 52.8-88.2% down to <19.6% vs. vLLM/PEFT/FlexGen (non-confidential baselines)
tg: confidential-computing, llm-inference, gpu-tee, speculative-execution, encryption-pipeline

t: Cascade: A Dependency-aware Efficient Training Framework for Temporal Graph Neural Network
th: Dependency-aware large-batch training for temporal graph neural networks
pb: TGNN training is severely constrained by temporal dependencies between input events: large batches improve parallelism but cause infrequent node memory updates leading to stale information and accuracy degradation, forcing small-batch training with high latency and underutilized hardware.
me: Cascade uses a topology-aware scheduler that packs as many spatially-independent events as possible into the same batch, then leverages inter-node memory similarity to identify 'stabilized' nodes whose memories have converged sufficiently to safely break temporal dependencies. This similarity-based dependency breaking allows temporally-independent events to be included in larger batches. An adaptive update frequency mechanism based on runtime feedback further reduces redundant memory updates, achieving 2.3x average (up to 5.1x) speedup without accuracy loss.
nv: Similarity-based temporal dependency breaking that identifies stabilized nodes whose memory states can be safely treated as independent, enabling large-batch TGNN training without sacrificing accuracy.
mx: speedup: 2.3x average, up to 5.1x over prior TGNN training frameworks
tg: temporal-gnn, training-efficiency, dependency-analysis, batch-scheduling, memory-freshness

t: OS2G: A High-Performance DPU Offloading Architecture for GPU-based Deep Learning with Object Storage
th: DPU-to-GPU direct data path for deep learning object storage
pb: Object storage for deep learning workloads imposes intensive CPU processing overhead and causes redundant data movements (DPU->host->GPU), consuming host resources and creating a data ingestion bottleneck that limits GPU utilization during training.
me: OS2G introduces a DPU offloading architecture that establishes a direct DPU-to-GPU data path, bypassing the host CPU entirely for object storage data delivery. It redesigns the object storage client to run on the DPU and exploits GPU-Direct or equivalent RDMA mechanisms to transfer data directly from the DPU's network interface into GPU memory. OS2G includes a DPU-side data processing pipeline (decompression, format conversion) to prepare DL-ready tensors before they enter GPU memory, eliminating the host CPU from the critical data path.
nv: End-to-end DPU-to-GPU direct data path for object storage in DL clusters that eliminates host CPU involvement and redundant data copies from the storage ingestion pipeline.
tg: dpu, object-storage, gpu, data-ingestion, near-data-processing

t: Velosiraptor: Code Synthesis for Memory Translation
th: Automated synthesis of OS memory translation code from hardware specifications
pb: OS code for configuring hardware memory translation and protection mechanisms must be manually adapted for each new hardware design, a repetitive and error-prone process that can introduce security-critical bugs breaking isolation guarantees for untrusted applications.
me: Velosiraptor synthesizes correct-by-construction OS memory translation code from a hardware-description specification of the translation/protection hardware. It takes a formal hardware model (specifying translation table formats, field semantics, and configuration operations) as input and automatically generates the OS driver code that correctly configures the hardware. The synthesis process uses a component library of translation operations and a constraint solver or template-based code generator to produce verified, hardware-specific configuration routines without manual coding.
nv: Automated code synthesis of OS memory translation drivers from formal hardware specifications, replacing error-prone manual adaptation with correct-by-construction code generation.
tg: memory-translation, code-synthesis, os-security, hardware-verification, compiler

t: Cooperative Graceful Degradation in Containerized Clouds
th: Cooperative graceful degradation for containerized cloud resilience
pb: Cloud operators lack a mechanism to automatically perform graceful degradation of applications during failures or capacity crunch while simultaneously satisfying application availability requirements and operator infrastructure objectives.
me: Phoenix uses criticality tags on containers to distinguish critical from non-critical services, then applies diagonal scaling—turning off non-critical containers during capacity crunch to free resources for critical services. A Kubernetes-atop controller implements this cooperative graceful degradation by jointly optimizing for both application-defined criticality constraints and operator-level infrastructure objectives. Phoenix handles failures in a cluster of 100,000 nodes within 10 seconds.
nv: Diagonal scaling: a cooperative degradation primitive that leverages application-supplied criticality tags to selectively deactivate non-critical containers, maximizing critical service availability during large-scale failures.
mx: other: critical service availability improved up to 2x during large-scale failures; handles 100K node cluster failures within 10 seconds
tg: cloud-resilience, graceful-degradation, kubernetes, containerization, fault-tolerance

t: PartIR: Composing SPMD Partitioning Strategies for Machine Learning
th: composable SPMD partitioning for distributed ML training
pb: Training large neural networks requires combining multiple parallelization strategies (data, model, and optimizer sharding), but existing systems make it difficult to compose, verify, and reason about these strategies in a predictable way. The tight coupling of partitioning strategies with ML implementation code makes it hard to experiment with or automatically derive optimal sharding plans.
me: PartIR provides a schedule-like API that incrementally rewrites a neural network's intermediate representation (IR) after each applied partitioning strategy. Each strategy (data parallelism, tensor/model parallelism, optimizer sharding) is expressed as a composable, declarative transformation on the IR. The system is hardware-and-runtime agnostic and follows well-defined general rewriting rules so each step is independently verifiable. Simulators and users can check the strategy's effect after each incremental rewrite.
nv: Decoupling partitioning strategies from ML implementation via an incremental IR-rewriting schedule API that allows predictable, verifiable composition of arbitrary SPMD sharding strategies.
mx: other: demonstrated on large model training with predictable, composable partitioning
tg: spmd, partitioning, parallelism, compiler-ir, distributed-training, sharding

t: CXLfork: Fast Remote Fork over CXL Fabrics
th: CXL-enabled zero-copy remote process cloning for serverless scale-out
pb: Remote process cloning across cluster nodes incurs high serialization and copying overhead, creating large cold-start latency for serverless functions and other scale-out workloads. Traditional fork() semantics do not map efficiently to distributed shared memory environments like CXL-attached memory.
me: CXLfork implements a remote fork interface that uses CXL-attached shared memory to achieve near-zero-serialization, zero-copy process cloning across nodes. It stores process state (pages, metadata) in globally-shared CXL memory for cluster-wide deduplication, so cloning a process on a remote node avoids transferring state over the network. Fine-grained tiering between local DRAM and CXL memory is supported, allowing hot pages to remain local while cold/shared pages reside in CXL memory. CXL-porter builds on top of CXLfork as an efficient horizontal autoscaler for serverless functions.
nv: Using CXL-attached globally-shared memory for cluster-wide process-state deduplication to achieve near-local-fork latency for remote process cloning.
mx: speedup: 2.26x over state-of-practice restore latency on average · other: 87% reduction in local memory consumption on average
tg: cxl, remote-fork, shared-memory, serverless, process-cloning, interconnect

t: Necro-reaper: Pruning away Dead Memory Traffic in Warehouse-Scale Computers
th: software-hardware co-design to eliminate dead memory traffic in warehouse-scale computers
pb: A significant fraction of memory traffic in warehouse-scale computers (WSC) is unnecessary: it consists of writebacks of deallocated (dead) heap data and fetches of uninitialized data, neither of which carries useful information. Short-lived heap allocations larger than a cache line—common in WSC—exacerbate this problem.
me: Necro-reaper is a software/hardware co-design that introduces new ISA instructions to let the hardware skip unnecessary dead memory traffic without requiring hardware-level tracking of live/dead data. A profile-guided compiler analyzes allocation lifetimes and annotates call sites with the new instructions. A customized memory allocator extends these annotations to inform the hardware at deallocation time. The approach leverages WSC's existing vertical integration (shared hardware, OS, compiler, and allocator stack) to make the analysis and insertion of instructions practical.
nv: New ISA instructions that allow software (compiler + allocator) to signal dead heap regions to hardware, eliminating unnecessary writebacks and uninitialized-data fetches without hardware tracking.
mx: speedup: 6% geomean IPC increase across 10 WSC workloads · other: 26% geomean memory traffic reduction
tg: dead-traffic, memory-bandwidth, wsc, isa-extensions, compiler, heap-allocation

t: Extended User Interrupts (xUI): Fast and Flexible Notification without Polling
th: hardware extensions for fast user-space interrupt notification without polling
pb: Intel's existing User Interrupt (UIPI) mechanism for fast user-space notification has correctness and performance limitations that prevent it from matching shared-memory polling latency while maintaining the efficiency of asynchronous notification. Current designs lack support for preemption in user-level runtimes, kernel-bypass timers, and efficient interrupt forwarding to accelerators.
me: xUI extends Intel's UIPI model with four hardware mechanisms: (1) tracked interrupts that allow senders to know when an interrupt was delivered, (2) hardware safepoints that let user-level runtimes implement preemption without kernel involvement, (3) a kernel-bypass timer for deadline-driven scheduling, and (4) interrupt forwarding to route notifications directly to accelerators (modeled on Intel's DSA). The design is modeled and evaluated in gem5 full-system simulation, measuring end-to-end latency for three distinct use cases.
nv: Hardware safepoints that enable user-level runtime preemption without kernel involvement, combined with interrupt forwarding to accelerators, all built on an extended user-interrupt model.
mx: other: performance of shared-memory polling with efficiency of asynchronous notification
tg: user-interrupts, notification, kernel-bypass, preemption, accelerator, uipi

t: Efficient Lossless Compression of Scientific Floating-Point Data on CPUs and GPUs
th: high-throughput lossless floating-point compression for CPUs and GPUs
pb: Scientific datasets are growing faster than storage and interconnect bandwidth, making data compression essential, but existing lossless compressors for floating-point data are either fast or achieve good compression ratios—rarely both simultaneously on both CPUs and GPUs.
me: The paper presents four new lossless compression algorithms specifically designed for single- and double-precision IEEE 754 floating-point data. The algorithms are fully compatible between CPUs and GPUs, enabling the same bitstream to be produced/consumed on either platform. Implementations exploit bit-level patterns in floating-point exponent and mantissa fields to achieve high compression ratios, and are tuned for SIMD/SIMT parallelism to maximize throughput on both CPU vector units and GPU streaming multiprocessors. Evaluated against 18 compressors from the literature on SDRBench scientific datasets.
nv: Four floating-point-specific lossless compression algorithms that are simultaneously CPU/GPU bitstream-compatible and achieve best-in-class throughput (>500 GB/s on RTX 4090) without sacrificing compression ratio.
mx: other: compress+decompress >500 GB/s on RTX 4090; outperforms most of 18 compared compressors in ratio and throughput
tg: compression, floating-point, scientific-data, gpu, cpu, throughput

t: Rethinking Java Performance Analysis
th: methodological soundness of Java performance benchmarking
pb: Java performance benchmarks and evaluation methodologies have drifted out of alignment with modern workloads and system behavior, undermining the reliability of empirical performance research built on them. Maintaining representative benchmarks and sound methodologies is difficult given the pace of language and system evolution.
me: The paper conducts a critical examination of existing Java benchmarks and performance analysis methodologies, identifying gaps between benchmark behavior and real-world Java application characteristics. It analyzes warm-up effects, JIT compilation artifacts, and measurement pitfalls specific to managed-language runtimes, then proposes methodological improvements and guidelines for representative evaluation.
nv: A systematic critique and re-grounding of Java performance analysis methodology, identifying how managed-runtime artifacts (JIT warm-up, GC) invalidate common measurement practices.
mx: other: methodology critique; no single headline number
tg: benchmarking, java, methodology, jit, runtime, managed-languages

t: Einsum Trees: An Abstraction for Optimizing the Execution of Tensor Expressions
th: global tensor data-layout optimization via Einsum Tree IR
pb: Optimizing the execution of multi-operand einsum tensor expressions requires co-optimizing both the contraction path (order of binary contractions) and the data layout of intermediate tensors, but these two problems have been studied in isolation, leading to suboptimal global execution performance.
me: The paper introduces Einsum Tree IR, an intermediate representation that captures a full contraction path as a tree structure, enabling global optimization of tensor data layouts across all intermediate binary contractions simultaneously rather than locally per contraction. Given a contraction path (computed by existing algorithms), Einsum Tree IR applies global data-layout optimization to minimize data movement and improve cache utilization. The resulting optimized sequences of binary contractions are executed on general-purpose server CPUs (Arm and x86) using existing optimized BLAS/tensor kernels.
nv: Einsum Tree IR: a global intermediate representation for jointly optimizing tensor data layouts across an entire multi-contraction path, rather than optimizing each binary contraction independently.
mx: other: improved overall einsum execution times vs. locally optimized contraction paths on Arm and x86
tg: einsum, tensor-contraction, compiler-ir, data-layout, cpu, memory-optimization

t: Faster Chaitin-like Register Allocation via Grammatical Decompositions of Control-Flow Graphs
th: parameterized register allocation via CFG treewidth decomposition
pb: Register allocation via graph coloring (Chaitin-style) is NP-hard in general, but practical compilers rely on heuristics that do not exploit the sparse, structured nature of real program control-flow graphs (CFGs). This leads to suboptimal allocation or unnecessary spills in programs with structured control flow.
me: The paper formalizes the sparsity of structured program CFGs using graph-theoretic parameters (treewidth, pathwidth) and introduces a grammatical decomposition—parsing the CFG into a tree decomposition. Register allocation is then solved efficiently via dynamic programming on this tree decomposition, yielding a parameterized algorithm whose complexity scales with the treewidth of the CFG rather than graph size alone. This exploits the observation that real programs' CFGs have small treewidth, making previously intractable exact or near-exact coloring feasible.
nv: Leveraging grammatical (tree) decompositions of CFGs to design faster parameterized register allocation algorithms that exploit the bounded treewidth of structured program control flow.
mx: other: faster parameterized register allocation via treewidth-bounded CFG decomposition
tg: register-allocation, compiler, graph-coloring, treewidth, cfg, parameterized-algorithms

t: MoC-System: Efficient Fault Tolerance for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Model Training
th: sparse-activation-aware fault tolerance for MoE LLM training
pb: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs have model parameter counts far exceeding dense models of equivalent compute cost, making checkpoint-based fault tolerance extremely expensive in terms of checkpoint size, write bandwidth, and recovery time for distributed training at >10k node scale.
me: MoC-System exploits the sparse activation pattern of MoE models: only a subset of experts is activated per token, so most expert parameters are not updated in any given training step. The system uses a Model-on-Checkpoint (MoC) approach that selectively checkpoints only the experts that were actually updated (activated) during a training step, avoiding checkpointing dormant expert parameters. This is combined with distributed checkpoint orchestration to overlap checkpoint I/O with forward/backward computation and expert-parallel sharding to minimize per-node checkpoint volume.
nv: Exploiting MoE sparse activation to checkpoint only updated (active) experts per step, drastically reducing checkpoint size and I/O without sacrificing fault recovery correctness.
mx: other: reduced checkpoint overhead for MoE models; specific numbers not in abstract
tg: fault-tolerance, checkpoint, moe, sparse-training, llm-training, distributed

t: SmoothE: Differentiable E-Graph Extraction
th: differentiable e-graph extraction for scalable compiler optimization
pb: E-graph extraction—selecting the optimal expression from a compact equality-saturation graph—suffers from an unfavorable scalability-quality trade-off: exact methods are slow, and fast heuristics produce suboptimal results. Current methods also only support simple linear cost functions, limiting applicability to realistic optimization objectives (e.g., non-linear, learned cost models).
me: SmoothE formulates e-graph extraction as a continuous, differentiable optimization problem by relaxing the discrete, combinatorial node-selection problem to a smooth objective over real-valued weights. Gradient-based optimization (e.g., gradient descent) is then applied to find the optimal extraction, enabling the use of arbitrary differentiable cost functions including learned neural cost models. The relaxation is designed so that the continuous optimum closely corresponds to a valid discrete extraction.
nv: Reformulating e-graph extraction as a differentiable (smooth) continuous optimization problem, enabling gradient-based search and support for arbitrary differentiable cost functions beyond simple linear models.
mx: other: improved scalability-quality trade-off over existing extractors; specific numbers not in abstract
tg: e-graphs, equality-saturation, compiler-optimization, differentiable, program-synthesis, extraction

t: MoE-Lightning: High-Throughput MoE Inference on Memory-constrained GPUs
th: CPU-GPU-IO pipeline for high-throughput MoE inference on memory-constrained GPUs
pb: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs have very large total parameter counts that exceed the VRAM of commodity GPUs, forcing weight offloading to CPU memory or NVMe, which creates severe I/O bottlenecks and low GPU utilization during batch inference.
me: MoE-Lightning introduces CGOPipe (CPU-GPU-I/O Pipelining) with paged weight management: expert weights are stored in pages that are streamed between CPU memory and GPU memory in a pipeline overlapping expert computation with prefetching of the next expert's weights. A Hierarchical Roofline Model (HRM) performance model guides policy selection by predicting throughput as a function of batch size, GPU memory, CPU memory, and I/O bandwidth. The system supports multi-GPU configurations for even larger models (Mixtral 8x22B, DBRX) on 2-4 T4 GPUs.
nv: CGOPipe: a CPU-GPU-I/O pipeline with paged expert weights, guided by a Hierarchical Roofline Model, that achieves near-peak offloading throughput with significantly less CPU memory than prior work.
mx: speedup: 10.3x throughput over state-of-the-art offloading-enabled LLM inference (Mixtral 8x7B on single T4 16GB GPU) · other: 2-3x less CPU memory at throughput upper bound
tg: moe, llm-inference, offloading, memory-constrained, pipelining, roofline-model

t: Instruction-Aware Cooperative TLB and Cache Replacement Policies
th: cooperative instruction-aware TLB and cache replacement for server workloads
pb: Modern server and data center applications have large instruction footprints that cause frequent instruction-side TLB and cache misses, with instruction TLB (iTLB) misses being particularly harmful because they cause pipeline stalls that block forward progress. Existing TLB and cache replacement policies treat instruction and data streams equivalently and do not account for the criticality of instruction accesses.
me: The paper proposes instruction-aware cooperative replacement policies that distinguish instruction accesses from data accesses in both the TLB and cache. The cooperative approach coordinates eviction decisions between the iTLB and the instruction cache (iCache), so that evicting a page from the iTLB also triggers or informs iCache eviction decisions and vice versa, reducing redundant refills. Replacement decisions are guided by instruction-access frequency and recency, with policy cooperation preventing the two structures from working at cross-purposes during instruction working set thrashing.
nv: Cooperative replacement policies that jointly manage iTLB and iCache evictions using instruction-access awareness, preventing the two structures from independently evicting and refilling the same instruction working set.
mx: other: reduced instruction TLB and cache miss rates in server workloads; specific numbers not in abstract
tg: tlb, cache-replacement, instruction-cache, server-workloads, cooperative, microarchitecture

t: OctoCache: Caching Voxels for Accelerating 3D Occupancy Mapping in Autonomous Systems
th: cache-aware acceleration of octree-based 3D mapping
pb: OctoMap, a widely used octree-based 3D mapping framework for autonomous robots, suffers from slow update performance due to costly and irregular memory accesses into the octree structure. The lack of cache-friendly access patterns and parallelism limits real-time deployment on autonomous platforms such as UAVs.
me: OctoCache is a software-level acceleration system with three techniques: (1) optimized cache memory access patterns that restructure octree node traversal to improve spatial locality, (2) refined voxel ordering that reorders ray-casting updates to maximize cache reuse, and (3) workflow parallelization that concurrently executes independent map-update tasks. No custom hardware is introduced; the system targets general-purpose CPUs.
nv: Cache-aware voxel ordering combined with parallelized workflow scheduling to transform the inherently irregular OctoMap access pattern into a cache-friendly, concurrent workload without modifying the octree data structure.
mx: speedup: 45.63–88.01% on 3D construction; up to 3.02x in UAV navigation · other: mission completion time reduced by up to 28%
tg: 3d-mapping, octree, cache-optimization, autonomous-systems, uav, robotics

t: HyperHammer: Breaking Free from KVM-Enforced Isolation
th: Rowhammer-based hypervisor escape from KVM guest VMs
pb: Existing Rowhammer attacks against virtualized cloud environments can compromise co-resident VMs but have not demonstrated the ability to attack the hypervisor itself, and a key primitive enabling such attacks (double-sided hammering or similar) has been disabled by hypervisor mitigations. This paper develops a new Rowhammer attack capable of breaking KVM-enforced isolation to compromise the hypervisor from a guest VM.
me: HyperHammer constructs a new Rowhammer attack path from within a KVM guest VM that circumvents existing KVM-level mitigations. The attack likely leverages alternative hammering primitives or physical memory addressing techniques (e.g., virtual-to-physical mapping exploitation, huge-page-based addressing) to induce bit flips in hypervisor memory regions, enabling privilege escalation from guest to hypervisor level.
nv: First demonstrated Rowhammer attack that escapes KVM-enforced guest isolation to directly compromise the hypervisor, bypassing the mitigations that rendered prior hypervisor Rowhammer attacks obsolete.
mx: other: successful hypervisor compromise demonstrated; specific success rates not stated in abstract
tg: rowhammer, virtualization, kvm, hypervisor, security, side-channel

t: Concerto: Automatic Communication Optimization and Scheduling for Large-Scale Deep Learning
th: Automatic computation-communication overlap scheduling for distributed DL training
pb: In large-scale distributed DNN training, collective communication (all-reduce, all-gather, etc.) remains a major bottleneck that existing frameworks address only through hand-crafted, framework-specific overlap strategies tightly coupled to particular parallelism schemes. There is no general, automatic mechanism to overlap computation and communication across arbitrary parallelism configurations.
me: Concerto is a compiler framework that decouples communication optimization from the parallelism strategy. It formulates communication scheduling as a resource-constrained project scheduling problem (RCPSP) and applies an off-the-shelf solver to find near-optimal schedules. An auto-decomposition pass splits synchronous (critical-path) communication operations to create overlap opportunities with computation, without requiring manual annotation. The resulting schedule is emitted as a program that any parallelism backend can execute.
nv: Automatic decomposition of synchronous collective communications combined with RCPSP-based scheduling to achieve computation-communication overlap generalized across all parallelism strategies without manual tuning.
mx: speedup: matches or outperforms state-of-the-art frameworks including Megatron-LM, JAX/XLA, DeepSpeed, Alpa (specific numbers not in abstract)
tg: distributed-training, communication-overlap, compiler, scheduling, parallelism, collective-communication

t: HALO: Loop-aware Bootstrapping Management for Fully Homomorphic Encryption
th: Loop-aware automatic bootstrapping placement for FHE programs
pb: FHE programs using repeated multiplications deplete the ciphertext noise budget (level), requiring bootstrapping to reset it; existing compiler-based bootstrapping placement tools cannot handle loops, severely limiting automated support for practical FHE programs that use iterative constructs.
me: HALO is a compiler that extends automatic bootstrapping placement to programs containing loops. It performs loop-aware level analysis to track ciphertext noise levels across loop iterations, determines the minimum set of bootstrapping operations required to prevent level underflow throughout the loop body and across all iterations, and inserts them automatically. The compiler reasons about loop-carried level dependencies to place bootstrapping at loop boundaries or within the loop body only where necessary.
nv: First compiler to support automatic bootstrapping placement inside loops for FHE programs, enabling safe and efficient execution of iterative encrypted computations without programmer intervention.
mx: other: Specific performance numbers not stated in abstract; reduction in programming burden is the primary claim
tg: fhe, homomorphic-encryption, bootstrapping, compiler, cryptography, loop-analysis

t: Reload+Reload: Exploiting Cache and Memory Contention Side Channel on AMD SEV
th: Cache and memory contention side-channel attacks on AMD SEV-SNP
pb: AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) is designed to protect guest VMs in multi-tenant clouds via memory encryption, but two previously unknown side channels—cache flush timing and memory contention—expose information even through the SEV-SNP isolation boundary.
me: The authors discover and formalize two AMD-specific side channels: (1) a cache flush side channel exploitable via flush-set timing (RRFS), and (2) a memory contention side channel (RRMB). They construct two Reload+Reload attack variants that exploit these channels to observe memory access patterns without relying on the disabled Flush+Reload primitive. RRFS is used to build a covert channel for a Spectre attack; RRMB is used for AES-128 key extraction by timing memory block contention across VM boundaries under SEV-SNP.
nv: Discovery of two new AMD SEV side channels (cache flush timing and memory block contention) enabling Reload+Reload attacks that bypass SEV-SNP isolation and outperform Prime+Probe in noise resistance and bandwidth.
mx: other: RRFS covert channel demonstrates superior noise resistance and higher capacity than Prime+Probe; AES-128 key fully extracted
tg: side-channel, amd-sev, cache-attack, rowhammer, tee, security

t: AnA: An Attentive Autonomous Driving System
th: Query-driven attentive perception scheduling for autonomous driving
pb: Current autonomous driving perception modules execute unconditionally and uniformly regardless of driving context, wasting compute on irrelevant scenes and missing safety-critical events that require focused attention—a mismatch from how humans selectively allocate perception resources.
me: AnA refactors the ADS perception-planning interface with three mechanisms: (1) a query interface that lets the planning module express interest in specific perceptual targets using driving knowledge; (2) a query executor that maps these queries to an optimal subset of active perception tasks; and (3) a monitor that uses driving knowledge to detect and handle anomalous task executions. The system distinguishes between ambient awareness (broad, low-cost perception) and focused attention (targeted, high-fidelity perception on safety-critical elements), dynamically switching modes based on planner queries.
nv: A query-driven perception architecture that couples planning knowledge to selective activation of perception tasks, enabling human-like attentive driving that reduces compute by 44% while halving collisions on adversarial benchmarks.
mx: speedup: 44% compute reduction without compromising driving safety · other: 2x reduction in collisions on adversarial events
tg: autonomous-driving, perception, attention, scheduling, safety, system-design

t: Treelet Accelerated Ray Tracing on GPUs
th: Treelet-based BVH traversal with ray virtualization for GPU ray tracing
pb: GPU ray tracing suffers from poor memory access locality because rays traverse a BVH tree in divergent order, causing excessive DRAM traffic; while treelet-based traversal (grouping BVH subtrees and batching rays per treelet) reduces memory traffic on specialized accelerators, applying it to GPUs is non-trivial and naive implementations are ineffective.
me: The paper proposes Virtualized Treelet Queues with two main components. First, ray virtualization terminates raygen shaders after issuing their trace-ray instruction to free CUDA cores, increasing the number of rays concurrently in flight and enabling more cache reuse within treelets. Second, a dynamic treelet queue architecture switches between traversal modes (intra-treelet vs. inter-treelet) at runtime to maximize efficiency. Additionally, warp repacking is applied to the RT unit to improve SIMT efficiency during treelet traversal.
nv: Ray virtualization that reclaims CUDA cores from waiting raygen shaders to multiply in-flight rays, paired with a dynamic treelet queue to exploit the resulting cache reuse—achieving 95% average speedup on a baseline GPU with hardware RT acceleration.
mx: speedup: 95% average speedup vs. baseline GPU with RT acceleration (LumiBench, path tracing, 1 spp, 3 bounces)
tg: ray-tracing, gpu, bvh, treelet, memory-bandwidth, rendering

t: COGENT: Adaptable Compiler Toolchain for Tagging RISC-V Binaries
th: General-purpose LLVM compiler toolchain for RISC-V binary metadata tagging
pb: Adding hardware-enforced metadata tags to RISC-V binaries for security and testing policies currently requires tedious, architecture-specific compiler modifications; there is no flexible, reusable toolchain that can emit variable-width tags at multiple granularities (instruction, basic block, function) from a single compilation pipeline.
me: COGENT is an LLVM-based compiler toolchain for RISC-V that generates instruction-level metadata tags. It supports variable-width tags (1–32 bits per instruction) and arbitrary-width tags per function or basic block, at selectable granularities. The toolchain includes a tag-aware disassembler and a tag integrity checker. A control-flow label emission pass marks branch targets and call sites, enabling CFI enforcement downstream. The pipeline is extensible to new tag policies without modifying the core compiler.
nv: A single, policy-agnostic LLVM-based tagging toolchain for RISC-V that supports variable-width tags across multiple granularities (instruction/block/function) with integrity checking, rather than requiring bespoke compilers per tagging policy.
mx: other: Cycle count overhead 0.94% (best case) to 5.24% (worst case) for tagged code
tg: risc-v, compiler, metadata-tagging, security, cfi, llvm

t: Energy-aware Scheduling and Input Buffer Overflow Prevention for Energy-harvesting Systems
th: Energy-aware scheduling with IBO prevention for energy-harvesting IoT devices
pb: Energy-harvesting IoT devices capture data at a fixed rate but process it at a dynamically varying rate determined by available ambient power; when capture rate exceeds processing rate the fixed-size input buffer overflows and events are permanently lost, and no existing dynamic solution prevents this across varying energy and workload conditions.
me: Quetzal combines a hardware power-measurement circuit with a two-part software runtime. The energy-aware scheduler selects jobs by minimizing end-to-end latency including projected energy recharging time, not just execution time. The runtime uses queueing-theory models to predict whether the selected job will cause an input buffer overflow before it completes; if overflow is imminent, it degrades the scheduled job (e.g., reduces quality or shortens duration) to lower processing latency and prevent buffer saturation. The hardware circuit is simple and system-agnostic, providing real-time power readings to the scheduler.
nv: Integration of queueing-theory-based IBO prediction with energy-recharge-aware scheduling and job degradation, enabled by a lightweight hardware power measurement circuit, to dynamically prevent input buffer overflow on energy-harvesting devices.
mx: other: Up to 4.2x reduction in events missed due to input buffer overflow vs. baselines
tg: energy-harvesting, iot, scheduling, buffer-overflow, intermittent-computing, queueing-theory

t: Optimizing Deep Learning Inference Efficiency through Block Dependency Analysis
th: Block-granularity dependency analysis for inter-operator DNN compiler optimization
pb: ML compilers perform data dependency analysis at element or operator granularity, which creates overly complex inter-operator dependencies that block efficient fusion and overlap, and obscures parallelizable computation opportunities, leaving significant GPU utilization on the table.
me: BlockDepend introduces a block-level dependency analysis framework in the ML compiler pipeline. By operating at the level of tile/block computations (below operator level but above scalar element level), it extracts simplified dependency relationships between operators and identifies previously hidden parallelizable computation pairs. These dependencies drive targeted inter-operator memory access optimizations (e.g., producer-consumer fusion, shared memory reuse) and expose additional kernel-level parallelism that can be scheduled concurrently on GPU compute units.
nv: Block-level (tile-granularity) dependency analysis in an ML compiler that simultaneously simplifies inter-operator dependencies and reveals hidden parallelism opportunities, achieving up to 2.88x speedup over production compilers.
mx: speedup: 1.71x over NVIDIA TensorRT; 2.88x over AMD MIGraphX across various workloads
tg: ml-compiler, dependency-analysis, gpu, inference, operator-fusion, parallelism

t: H-Houdini: Scalable Invariant Learning
th: Scalable invariant learning for large hardware formal verification
pb: Formal hardware verification via invariant learning (e.g., IC3/PDR) does not scale to large hardware designs because the invariant search space grows exponentially with state size, causing state-of-the-art tools to time out on real-world RTL designs.
me: H-Houdini extends the Houdini invariant-learning algorithm with scalability improvements targeting large hardware designs. The likely approach involves decomposing the hardware design into manageable sub-modules or abstract components, learning invariants compositionally (e.g., assume-guarantee or abstraction-refinement), and propagating learned invariants across the design hierarchy to avoid full-state enumeration. Specific algorithmic details are not disclosed in the available abstract.
nv: Scalable extension of Houdini-style invariant learning to large hardware designs that previously exceeded the capacity of existing formal verification tools.
mx: other: Scalability to larger hardware designs than prior tools; specific numbers not in abstract
tg: formal-verification, invariant-learning, hardware-design, rtl, scalability, model-checking

t: Earth+: On-Board Satellite Imagery Compression Leveraging Historical Earth Observations
th: Cross-constellation reference-based on-board satellite imagery compression
pb: Satellite downlink capacity is so limited that over 90% of captured earth-observation images are never downloaded; existing on-board compression techniques treat each image independently and cannot exploit the rich temporal and spatial redundancy available across an entire satellite constellation.
me: Earth+ implements a change-detection-based compression pipeline on the satellite. Ground stations upload recently captured reference images from other satellites in the same constellation to each on-board satellite via the uplink. On-board processing compares each newly captured image against the latest matching reference image and transmits only the changed regions (delta encoding). The system manages reference image currency and on-board storage to ensure that references are temporally close to the captured images, maximizing delta sparsity and thus compression.
nv: First system to use cross-constellation reference images uploaded from ground stations to enable inter-satellite temporal redundancy exploitation for on-board compression, reducing downlink usage 3.3x over state-of-the-art without sacrificing image quality.
mx: speedup: 3.3x reduction in downlink usage vs. state-of-the-art on-board compression without quality loss or extra resource consumption
tg: satellite, edge-computing, image-compression, delta-encoding, constellation, on-board-processing

t: Hopps: Leveraging Sparsity to Accelerate Automata Processing
th: sparsity-driven automata processing acceleration
pb: Automata processing (AP) workloads execute many finite state machines (FSMs) in parallel over streaming symbol data, but existing AP accelerators suffer poor utilization because most FSMs are inactive (in a non-matching state) for any given input symbol. The irregular, state-dependent activation pattern makes it hard to exploit spatial parallelism efficiently.
me: Hopps exploits the observation that only a sparse subset of FSMs transition on each input symbol. It uses a sparsity-aware representation that tracks only active states across all FSMs and a compressed activation bitmap to skip idle FSMs entirely during each symbol step. The architecture couples this with a tiled SRAM storage layout so that state-transition tables for active FSMs are fetched in bursts, reducing off-chip memory traffic proportional to the active-FSM fraction.
nv: Hopps is the first AP accelerator to exploit cross-FSM input-driven sparsity at runtime by compressing the active-state set into a compact bitmap and skipping computation for inactive automata entirely.
mx: speedup: not stated quantitatively in abstract
tg: automata-processing, sparsity, finite-state-machine, pattern-matching, accelerator

t: ARC: Warp-level Adaptive Atomic Reduction in GPUs to Accelerate Differentiable Rendering
th: warp-level atomic reduction for differentiable rendering
pb: During the backward pass of rasterization-based differentiable rendering (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting), gradient computation requires a large volume of atomic add operations to accumulate gradients from many Gaussian primitives into shared parameters, overwhelming the atomic units in the GPU L2 cache and causing long stalls that dominate training time.
me: ARC introduces warp-level adaptive atomic reduction, a GPU microarchitecture extension that intercepts atomic add operations at the warp level before they reach the L2 cache atomic units. Within a warp, threads targeting the same memory address are first reduced together using warp-level shuffle instructions (or a small dedicated reduction buffer), producing a single atomic operation per warp instead of one per thread. The approach adaptively decides whether to apply warp-level reduction based on detected contention levels, avoiding overhead when atomics are already sparse.
nv: Warp-level coalescing of atomic reduction operations before they reach the L2 cache, adaptively gated by contention detection, specifically targeting the gradient accumulation bottleneck in differentiable rendering.
mx: speedup: not stated in abstract
tg: differentiable-rendering, atomic-reduction, GPU, 3D-gaussian-splatting, memory-contention

t: Hardware Sentinel: Protecting Software Applications from Hardware Silent Data Corruptions
th: software-driven silent data corruption detection in production fleets
pb: Silent Data Corruptions (SDCs) caused by silicon defects in CPUs propagate undetected through large-scale data center applications, causing unpredictable failures (segfaults, crashes, log anomalies) that are difficult to attribute to hardware without systematic cross-layer analysis.
me: Hardware Sentinel is a top-down framework that correlates software-layer failure indicators—segmentation faults, core dumps, application crashes, and structured logs—with underlying hardware-layer defect signals across CPUs. It builds statistical models linking application failure patterns to CPU hardware identities, enabling SDC attribution across diverse workload, kernel, and hardware configurations. The framework was validated over 6 years of failure data spanning 13 workloads across 27 data center regions, using fleet-wide telemetry ingestion and cross-referencing with out-of-production (Fleetscanner) and in-production (Ripple) hardware tests.
nv: A production-validated, software-failure-driven SDC detection framework that identifies defective CPUs from application-layer signals without requiring dedicated hardware test circuits, achieving broader coverage than existing hardware testing methods.
mx: other: SDC detection coverage: 1.74x over Fleetscanner, 1.92x over Ripple
tg: silent-data-corruption, reliability, CPU, data-center, fault-detection

t: Orion: A Fully Homomorphic Encryption Framework for Deep Learning
th: automated FHE compilation for deep learning inference
pb: Mapping arbitrary deep neural networks to Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) primitives is intractable with existing tools because FHE requires packing large vectors, managing noise budget through bootstrap placement, and translating general convolutions to the limited FHE instruction set—challenges that have limited FHE neural inference to shallow or small networks.
me: Orion is an automated compiler that accepts PyTorch DNNs and emits FHE programs. It introduces a single-shot multiplexed packing strategy for arbitrary convolution layers that avoids the combinatorial explosion of prior slot-packing schemes. Orion also introduces an automated bootstrap placement algorithm with scale management that tracks noise accumulation across layers and inserts bootstrapping operations at minimum-cost positions. Together these enable end-to-end compilation of deep networks (ResNet-20, ResNet-50, YOLO-v1 with 139M parameters) without manual FHE engineering.
nv: A novel single-shot multiplexed packing strategy for arbitrary convolutions combined with automated bootstrap placement and scale management, enabling fully automated FHE compilation of large, real-world CNNs.
mx: speedup: 2.38x over state-of-the-art on ResNet-20 · other: First FHE YOLO-v1 (139M params) and FHE ResNet-50 on ImageNet reported
tg: homomorphic-encryption, privacy-preserving-inference, CNN, compiler, neural-inference

t: ElasticMiter: Formally Verified Dataflow Circuit Rewrites
th: formally verified dataflow circuit optimization for HLS
pb: Dataflow circuits produced by high-level synthesis (HLS) compilers cannot be optimized via standard sequential equivalence verification because their latency-insensitive handshake semantics are incompatible with traditional notions of sequential equivalence, leaving no sound basis for automated datapath simplification.
me: ElasticMiter develops a generic equivalence verification framework for latency-insensitive dataflow circuits by constructing a miter circuit that detects functional divergence under all possible token arrival patterns. It then defines a graph rewriting system over dataflow circuit DAGs where each rewrite rule is verified by the framework before being applied, guaranteeing the rewritten circuit is equivalent to the original. The approach handles elastic buffering, fork/join nodes, and control tokens that are absent in traditional sequential circuits.
nv: The first formally verified dataflow circuit transformation system that constructs a latency-insensitive miter to prove graph rewrite rules sound for HLS-generated circuits.
mx: area: circuit simplification (area reduction) shown via graph rewrites
tg: HLS, dataflow-circuits, formal-verification, graph-rewriting, equivalence-checking

t: Klotski: Efficient Mixture-of-Expert Inference via Expert-Aware Multi-Batch Pipeline
th: multi-batch expert-aware scheduling for offloaded MoE inference
pb: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs with trillion-scale parameters must be offloaded to CPU/disk memory when GPU VRAM is insufficient, but each expert's compute time per token is shorter than the I/O time to load it, creating large pipeline bubbles that negate the benefit of overlapping I/O and computation.
me: Klotski introduces an expert-aware multi-batch pipeline that maintains multiple batches in flight simultaneously and schedules which experts to prefetch and compute based on expert routing decisions across batches. By batching tokens that activate the same expert across multiple concurrent requests, Klotski increases per-expert compute volume to exceed I/O time, eliminating pipeline bubbles. The system tracks expert access patterns across batches and uses an expert prefetching scheduler that co-optimizes I/O and compute assignment to saturate both the memory bus and compute units.
nv: An expert-aware multi-batch pipeline for MoE offloading that batches tokens across multiple concurrent requests routed to the same expert to amortize I/O cost and eliminate pipeline bubbles.
mx: speedup: not stated in abstract · other: pipeline bubble reduction for offloaded MoE inference
tg: MoE, LLM-inference, offloading, scheduling, pipeline

t: StreamGrid: Streaming Point Cloud Analytics via Compulsory Splitting and Deterministic Termination
th: streaming point cloud analytics via spatial splitting and deterministic termination
pb: Point cloud processing accelerators generate frequent off-chip memory traffic because conventional line-buffer streaming techniques—which eliminate off-chip traffic for image-based workloads—cannot be applied to point clouds due to their irregular, non-grid computation patterns that cause unpredictable data access boundaries and non-deterministic termination conditions.
me: StreamGrid introduces two techniques: compulsory splitting, which partitions the point cloud spatial domain into fixed-size grid cells that guarantee bounded on-chip working sets despite irregular neighborhoods; and deterministic termination, which statically determines when each streaming computation unit finishes processing its spatial partition, enabling on-chip buffering without deadlock or stall. StreamGrid combines these into a framework with an automated on-chip buffer size optimizer that minimizes SRAM under a given accuracy constraint.
nv: Compulsory spatial splitting paired with deterministic termination conditions that together enable fully-streaming point cloud processing with conventional line-buffer discipline despite irregular point cloud access patterns.
mx: speedup: 10.0x over state-of-the-art accelerators · energy_or_tops_w: 3.9x energy efficiency over state-of-the-art accelerators; 40.5% energy reduction vs. baselines · area: 61.3% on-chip memory reduction · accuracy: marginal accuracy loss
tg: point-cloud, streaming, on-chip-memory, accelerator, spatial-computing

t: AMuLeT: Automated Design-Time Testing of Secure Speculation Countermeasures
th: automated design-time security testing for speculative execution countermeasures
pb: Multiple hardware-based Spectre countermeasures have been proposed and then shown to be insecure, yet there is no automated tool to test speculation security guarantees early in the design phase—leaving designers without rapid feedback during hardware prototyping.
me: AMuLeT is an automated design-time testing framework for secure speculation countermeasures. It generates targeted micro-architectural test programs (a.k.a. litmus tests) that systematically exercise speculative execution paths across possible speculation windows and covert-channel observability conditions. The tool evaluates candidate countermeasures against these tests using a hardware RTL or ISA-level simulator, reporting which Spectre attack variants the countermeasure fails to block. AMuLeT integrates with rapid prototyping workflows to provide early-stage security feedback.
nv: Automated generation and evaluation of speculation security litmus tests targeting the design phase, enabling rapid iteration on secure speculation countermeasures without manual security analysis.
mx: other: detection of known insecurities in published Spectre countermeasures
tg: spectre, secure-speculation, microarchitecture, security-testing, CPU

t: TNIC: A Trusted NIC Architecture: A hardware-network substrate for building high-performance trustworthy distributed systems
th: hardware NIC root-of-trust for Byzantine-tolerant distributed systems
pb: Distributed systems deployed in heterogeneous cloud environments face Byzantine failures from untrusted hardware and software, but existing trusted execution environments (TEEs) are CPU-centric and incur high performance overhead when attempting to enforce network-level trust guarantees such as non-equivocation and transferable authentication.
me: TNIC builds a minimal, formally verified silicon root-of-trust at the NIC level using SmartNIC hardware. It provides two core cryptographic primitives—transferable authentication (signed message delivery) and non-equivocation (monotonic counters preventing double-send attacks)—implemented in hardware-accelerated network processing logic. The TCB is minimized by placing trust enforcement at the network interface, making it CPU-agnostic. TNIC exposes programming APIs and a recipe for constructing Byzantine-fault-tolerant distributed protocols, demonstrated via four trustworthy distributed systems built on the substrate.
nv: A formally verified silicon root-of-trust at the NIC level that provides CPU-agnostic network-level trust primitives (transferable authentication and non-equivocation) via SmartNIC hardware acceleration, bypassing the CPU TEE entirely.
mx: speedup: up to 6x over CPU-centric TEE systems
tg: SmartNIC, trusted-execution, Byzantine-fault-tolerance, distributed-systems, security

t: Past-Future Scheduler for LLM Serving under SLA Guarantees
th: history-aware future memory estimation for LLM serving scheduler goodput
pb: LLM serving frameworks using continuous batching suffer from either overestimation of memory consumption (conservative schedulers) or underestimation leading to harmful request evictions (aggressive schedulers), because neither accurately accounts for the dynamic memory release profile of concurrently running requests across future decoding steps.
me: The Past-Future scheduler combines two components: (1) output length distribution prediction that samples predicted output lengths from the empirical distribution of recent historical requests (a sliding window of ~1,000 finished requests), updating each running request's predicted remaining length at every decode step using the conditional distribution P(l > l_current); and (2) future required memory estimation that sorts running requests by estimated remaining length, computes memory occupancy at each future completion event, and determines peak future memory as max(M_t+1, M_t+2, ...) across all future completion times. A queued request is admitted only if adding it keeps peak future memory below hardware capacity. This is implemented in LightLLM with <1% scheduling overhead using GPU-parallel computation.
nv: The observation that LLM output length distributions are stable within adjacent time windows enables a parameter-free, model-agnostic historical-distribution sampling approach to precisely estimate peak future KV-cache memory demand for the entire running batch, eliminating both conservative underutilization and aggressive eviction.
mx: speedup: 2-3x higher goodput over aggressive/conservative schedulers under heavy load · other: Memory utilization approaches theoretical optimum (93-94% vs 98% oracle) while eviction rate drops to ~3-7% vs 93% for aggressive at watermark=99%; 50-60% throughput improvement on multimodal LLaVA and Qwen-VL models
tg: LLM-serving, KV-cache, scheduling, SLA, continuous-batching

t: Snowplow: Effective Kernel Fuzzing with a Learned White-box Test Mutator
th: learned white-box mutation for kernel fuzzing
pb: Kernel fuzzers rely on program mutation to generate test programs that explore new kernel code paths, but existing mutation heuristics are unable to navigate the complex control and data flow of kernel code to produce mutations that trigger target code locations or increase coverage, resulting in low fuzzing effectiveness.
me: Snowplow uses a learned white-box test mutator that employs machine learning to guide mutation decisions based on kernel code analysis (control flow graphs and data flow) rather than purely random or hand-coded heuristics. The model is trained to predict which system call insertions, argument value changes, or structural mutations are most likely to move execution toward uncovered or target code regions. The white-box analysis of kernel source provides the coverage feedback signal used during training and inference.
nv: A machine learning model trained on white-box kernel code analysis to guide test program mutation, replacing manual heuristics with learned policies that target specific kernel code locations.
mx: other: improved kernel code coverage and bug-finding rate vs state-of-the-art kernel fuzzers
tg: fuzzing, kernel, machine-learning, white-box, security-testing

t: PIM Is All You Need: A CXL-Enabled GPU-Free System for Large Language Model Inference
th: CXL-scaled PIM-PNM architecture for GPU-free LLM inference
pb: LLM inference is memory-bound (GEMV-dominated decoding stage with ~21% GPU compute utilization on Llama2-70B), yet modern GPU/TPU systems are optimized for compute throughput; simultaneously, large KV-cache requirements per user limit batch sizes, and CXL- or DRAM-density-reduced PIM architectures individually lack sufficient memory capacity or scalability for trillion-parameter LLMs.
me: CENT (CXL-ENabled GPU-Free sysTem) uses a hierarchical PIM-PNM architecture deployed across 32 CXL devices interconnected via a CXL 3.0 switch. Each CXL device contains 16 GDDR6-PIM memory chips (two PIM channels each) housing near-bank MAC reduction-tree processing units (16 MAC units/PU, BF16, 32 GFLOPS/PIM channel), plus PNM units including 32 accumulators, 32 reduction trees, 32 Taylor-series exponent accelerators, and 8 BOOM-2-wide RISC-V cores for non-MAC operations. MAC operations (>99% of arithmetic) execute near-bank; Softmax, RMSNorm, square root, and RoPE are handled by PNM. A custom CXL ISA (MAC_ABK, WR_GB, SEND_CXL, BCAST_CXL, etc.) orchestrates computation and data movement. LLM parallelism is implemented via pipeline parallel (PP: each transformer block to one CXL device, multiple prompts pipelined) and tensor parallel (TP: transformer block partitioned across all devices using broadcast/gather over CXL) mappings, with hybrid TP-PP for QoS balance. The CXL protocol is extended with a broadcast primitive via a reserved H-slot header code in port-based routing flits.
nv: A GPU-free hierarchical PIM-PNM architecture scaled via CXL 3.0 that exploits GDDR6-PIM internal bandwidth (512 TB/s aggregate) to achieve 2.3x higher LLM inference throughput than 4x A100 GPUs at 2.9x lower energy and 5.2x better TCO, with a novel CXL broadcast primitive enabling scalable collective communication across PIM devices.
mx: speedup: 2.3x end-to-end throughput over 4x A100 80GB GPUs (throughput-critical); 4.6x latency reduction (batch=1); 3.3x decoding throughput at 32K context · energy_or_tops_w: 2.9x energy efficiency (tokens/joule) over 4x A100 · area: CXL controller: 19.0 mm2 at 7nm; custom logic: 7.85 mm2 at 28nm · other: 5.2x tokens per dollar (TCO); CENT owned TCO $0.73/hr vs GPU $1.76/hr; rental TCO $1.05/hr vs $5.45/hr
tg: PIM, CXL, LLM-inference, GPU-free, memory-bandwidth

t: Robustness Verification for Checking Crash Consistency of Non-volatile Memory
th: formal crash-consistency verification for NVM
pb: Programs using non-volatile memory (NVM) must explicitly flush pending stores to guarantee persistence; developers routinely miss or mis-order these flushes. Existing crash-consistency checkers are testing-based and require user guidance, leaving the correctness of NVM programs unverified in the general case.
me: The paper introduces a robustness property for NVM crash consistency and proves that checking whether a post-crash NVM state is reachable from a given pre-crash execution reduces to validity of that execution under additional ordering constraints. A search-based algorithm enumerates all partial pre-crash executions and candidate NVM states, then dispatches each reachability query to an SMT solver via symbolic encoding of the program. The approach is integrated into the DPLL(T) framework to prune the search space, and is implemented in the prototype tool PMVerify.
nv: Reduction of crash-consistency checking to SMT-based reachability under the NVM memory consistency model, enabling the first fully automated robustness verification without user-provided test inputs.
mx: other: Bug detection competitive with PSan on PMDK benchmarks
tg: non-volatile-memory, crash-consistency, formal-verification, smt, pmdk

t: PAPI: Exploiting Dynamic Parallelism in Large Language Model Decoding with a Processing-In-Memory-Enabled Computing System
th: dynamic PIM-GPU scheduling for LLM decoding
pb: LLM decoding kernels dynamically shift between memory-bound and compute-bound behavior as request parameters (batch size, sequence length, sampling strategy) change at runtime, making static assignment of kernels to either PIM units or GPU-like compute accelerators suboptimal. Furthermore, existing PIM units are designed with a one-size-fits-all approach that fails to exploit the heterogeneity within memory-bound LLM kernels.
me: PAPI introduces a heterogeneous computing system combining PIM units embedded in DRAM with compute-centric accelerators (GPU-like), and a runtime that dynamically profiles kernel characteristics and remaps each kernel to the most suitable processing element at runtime. The PIM units are co-designed with awareness of intra-PIM heterogeneity to efficiently handle diverse memory-bound kernel patterns (e.g., matrix-vector products, attention, gating). A dynamic parallelism scheduler dispatches work to PIM or compute units based on real-time parameter changes driven by user or system demands.
nv: Runtime dynamic kernel-to-hardware mapping that responds to changing LLM decoding workload characteristics, combined with heterogeneity-aware PIM unit design to exploit intra-PIM variance in memory-bound kernels.
mx: other: Not stated in abstract
tg: pim, llm-decoding, dynamic-scheduling, heterogeneous-architecture, memory-bound

t: Will We Ever have Truly Secure Operating Systems?
th: formal OS security verification
pb: Operating system kernels remain a dominant attack surface despite decades of security research; formal proofs of OS security have historically been limited to small microkernels and have not scaled to binary-level or general-purpose OS kernels.
me: The paper surveys the seL4 microkernel verification program, which produced a proof chain from C implementation correctness, down to binary-level verification, through to security enforcement proofs (confidentiality, integrity) and sound worst-case execution-time analysis, covering 4 ISAs. The approach uses interactive theorem provers (Isabelle/HOL) to formally connect abstract security policies to compiled binary behavior, then discusses speculative early-stage work on extending this methodology to a provably secure general-purpose OS.
nv: First complete proof chain from OS implementation to binary code to security enforcement properties across multiple ISAs, including sound worst-case execution time, for seL4.
mx: other: Proofs cover 4 ISAs; first binary-level + security enforcement proof chain for an OS kernel
tg: formal-verification, operating-system, security, seL4, microkernel

t: ShadowLoad: Injecting State into Hardware Prefetchers
th: active prefetcher state injection attack
pb: Hardware prefetchers in modern CPUs maintain internal state (e.g., stride tables, stream detectors) that persists across security boundaries, and prior work showed this state leaks information across processes, user/kernel space, and trusted execution environments (TEEs). This paper extends the threat by demonstrating that an attacker can actively inject crafted state into a victim's prefetcher, turning it into a covert communication channel or an amplification primitive.
me: ShadowLoad crafts memory access sequences that train the hardware prefetcher's internal prediction structures (stride tables, stream buffers) to a desired state from an unprivileged attacker context. When the victim process subsequently executes, the pre-injected prefetcher state causes speculative prefetches that alter the victim's cache state or execution timing, enabling state injection across process, user-kernel, and TEE boundaries. The technique exploits the fact that prefetcher state is not flushed or partitioned at privilege transitions on affected CPUs.
nv: Active injection of attacker-controlled state into hardware prefetcher prediction structures to influence victim execution, as opposed to passive observation of prefetcher-induced side channels.
mx: other: Covert channel bandwidth and cross-boundary injection success rates (details in full paper)
tg: hardware-prefetcher, side-channel, microarchitecture, security, tee

t: Simplifying and Accelerating NOR Flash I/O Stack for RAM-Restricted Microcontrollers
th: simplified NOR flash I/O stack for microcontrollers
pb: NOR flash file systems for RAM-restricted microcontrollers migrate block-level data organization and wear leveling logic from RAM into flash, introducing fine-grained block-level management that causes frequent index updates and full-device scans. This results in severe I/O amplification that worsens when the management layers are decoupled across the I/O stack.
me: The paper redesigns the NOR flash I/O stack to eliminate the decoupled block-level management abstraction, instead employing coarse-grained, integrated data organization that reduces index update frequency. Wear leveling is restructured to operate at a coarser granularity aligned with the NOR flash erase unit, avoiding the fine-grained scanning overhead. The resulting simplified stack collapses previously separate software layers to reduce coupling and I/O amplification jointly.
nv: Collapsing decoupled block-level management layers into a unified, coarse-grained I/O stack design that jointly eliminates index-update amplification and wear-leveling scan overhead for NOR flash on microcontrollers.

t: Wave: Offloading Resource Management to SmartNIC Cores
th: SmartNIC offload of userspace system software
pb: Userspace system software tasks (kernel thread scheduling, memory management, RPC stacks) consume scarce host CPU cores in cloud servers, reducing the compute available to paying tenants. Existing SmartNIC offload frameworks require custom APIs and cannot handle microsecond-scale system software latencies without host CPU involvement.
me: Wave is a framework that runs existing Linux userspace system software (unchanged or minimally modified) as processes/agents on mid-tier SmartNIC ARM cores. It introduces a new host-SmartNIC communication API designed to support microsecond-scale decision latencies, enabling offload of preemption-sensitive tasks such as the kernel thread scheduler. The framework uses Linux userspace system interfaces to align host OS functionality with SmartNIC capabilities, and avoids requiring custom kernel modifications on the host side.
nv: A general framework and microsecond-latency host-SmartNIC communication API that enables offloading of latency-sensitive userspace system software (scheduling, memory management, RPCs) to SmartNIC ARM cores with minimal code changes.
mx: speedup: 11.2% VM performance improvement from offload · other: Saves 16 host cores (memory management), 8 host cores (RPC); 1.1%-7.4% perf overhead vs on-host
tg: smartnic, resource-management, offloading, datacenter, system-software

t: Exo 2: Growing a Scheduling Language
th: extensible user-schedulable compiler language
pb: User-schedulable languages (USLs) fix a single design point for what programmers control and what is automated, but no universal control/automation split exists even in narrow domains, causing USLs to be inextensible when new hardware targets or optimization strategies emerge.
me: Exo 2 enables users to define new scheduling operations externally to the compiler by composing a set of trusted fine-grained primitives (actions for modifying code, inspection for querying code structure, and references for pointing to code locations). The key mechanism is Cursors, a new abstraction that unifies code references across actions, inspections, and scheduling library composition, allowing safe user-defined scheduling transformations. Users build scheduling libraries that amortize transformation effort across related kernels without modifying the compiler internals.
nv: The Cursor abstraction that enables users to write fully externalized, composable scheduling libraries safe from compiler internals, allowing the scheduling language to grow without core modifications.
mx: speedup: Performance competitive with state-of-the-art on 3 platforms · other: Scheduling code reduced by ~10x across 80+ kernels

t: Cinnamon: A Framework for Scale-Out Encrypted AI
th: scale-out FHE acceleration for encrypted AI inference
pb: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) imposes orders-of-magnitude performance overhead for ML inference, and prior FHE accelerators use massive monolithic chip designs that do not scale to large models like BERT and provide poor performance-per-dollar.
me: Cinnamon is a scale-out FHE acceleration framework that exploits parallelism at all program levels using novel algorithms, a compiler, and a chiplet-based hardware design. The compiler identifies and schedules FHE operation parallelism (polynomial NTT, RNS decomposition, key-switching) across multiple chips, while architectural extensions reduce per-chip resource requirements to enable economical scaling. Novel algorithms reduce communication volume between chiplets, enabling a distributed multi-chip FHE accelerator rather than a single monolithic die.
nv: Scale-out chiplet architecture for FHE acceleration with a co-designed compiler and algorithms that distribute FHE polynomial arithmetic across multiple chips, enabling the first feasible FHE inference for large LLMs like BERT.
mx: speedup: 36,600x over CPU; 2.3x over prior state-of-the-art FHE accelerator · ppa: 5x perf/$ vs monolithic; 2.68x perf/$ vs chiplet SotA · other: BERT FHE inference: 17 hours (CPU) -> 1.67 seconds
