t: GraphPipe: Improving Performance and Scalability of DNN Training with Graph Pipeline Parallelism
th: graph-topology-aware pipeline parallelism for DNN training
pb: Existing pipeline-parallel DNN training systems partition models into sequential stages, ignoring the actual DAG topology of modern neural networks, which causes missed model-parallelism opportunities and suboptimal device utilization.
me: GraphPipe introduces graph pipeline parallelism, which partitions a DNN's computation graph (DAG) rather than a linear sequence into pipeline stages. The system represents the DNN as a dataflow graph, identifies parallelizable subgraphs, and maps them to device groups that execute concurrently in a pipeline fashion. A graph-aware scheduling algorithm determines micro-batch execution order across non-linear pipeline stages to maximize throughput and minimize pipeline bubbles, coordinating across branches of the DAG.
nv: Graph-structured (DAG-aware) pipeline parallelism that exploits non-sequential DNN topology to enable concurrent execution of structurally parallel model subgraphs across device groups.
mx: other: Throughput improvements over sequential pipeline baselines (details in full paper)
tg: pipeline-parallelism, dnn-training, graph-parallelism, llm-training, multi-gpu

t: Accelerating LLM Serving for Multi-turn Dialogues with Efficient Resource Management
th: multi-turn KV-cache management and scheduling for LLM serving
pb: Current LLM serving frameworks recompute attention keys and values for all prior turns on each new query in a multi-turn dialogue, incurring substantial redundant compute overhead. Additionally, the long accumulated prompt lengths from multi-turn context cause head-of-line blocking under FCFS scheduling, underutilizing GPU resources.
me: The paper introduces efficient resource management for multi-turn LLM serving by preserving KV-cache state across turns to eliminate recomputation of prior-turn attention keys and values. A new scheduling policy replaces FCFS with a length-aware or priority-based scheduler that avoids head-of-line blocking by reordering or preempting long-prompt requests. KV-cache memory is managed dynamically to balance cache retention across concurrent multi-turn sessions, trading off memory capacity against recompute cost.
nv: Cross-turn KV-cache retention combined with a head-of-line blocking-aware scheduler specifically designed for the multi-turn dialogue serving regime.
mx: other: GPU utilization improvement and latency reduction for multi-turn dialogues (details in full paper)
tg: llm-serving, kv-cache, multi-turn-dialogue, scheduling, head-of-line-blocking

t: Accelerating Number Theoretic Transform with Multi-GPU Systems for Efficient Zero Knowledge Proof
th: multi-GPU NTT acceleration for zero-knowledge proofs
pb: Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), a key bottleneck in zero-knowledge proof generation, has not been efficiently parallelized across multiple GPUs because its butterfly permutation access pattern generates high inter-GPU communication overhead that offsets the compute gains from additional GPUs.
me: The paper redesigns the NTT algorithm for multi-GPU execution by restructuring the butterfly computation stages to localize data access within GPU memory and minimize the frequency and volume of inter-GPU data transfers. The approach introduces a GPU-topology-aware permutation schedule that maps NTT stages to GPU assignments so that communication-intensive permutation steps are batched and overlap-optimized with computation. NVLink or PCIe interconnect topology is leveraged to select inter-GPU transfer paths that maximize aggregate bandwidth.
nv: GPU-topology-aware NTT stage mapping that restructures butterfly permutations to minimize inter-GPU communication overhead and enable scalable multi-GPU NTT for ZK proof generation.
mx: other: Multi-GPU NTT speedup over single-GPU baseline (details in full paper)
tg: zero-knowledge-proof, ntt, multi-gpu, cryptography, zkp

t: BQSim: GPU-accelerated Batch Quantum Circuit Simulation using Decision Diagram
th: GPU-accelerated batch quantum circuit simulation via decision diagrams
pb: Existing quantum circuit simulators process one input state at a time, but applications such as quantum testing and verification require simulating a circuit under multiple input states (batch simulation). No GPU-accelerated batch quantum circuit simulator exists that exploits shared structure across inputs.
me: BQSim uses decision diagrams (DDs) to compactly represent quantum gate matrices and identify shared structure across batch inputs, then converts the DD representation into a GPU-efficient data structure for parallel evaluation. A task-graph-based execution engine minimizes repetitive GPU kernel launch overhead by grouping related computations into batched kernel calls and overlapping kernel execution with data movement between host and device. The DD optimization step reduces the total computation needed for batch simulation by collapsing redundant operations shared across inputs.
nv: Combining decision-diagram-based circuit optimization for shared-structure exploitation with a GPU-efficient data structure and task-graph execution engine to achieve the first GPU-accelerated batch quantum circuit simulator.
mx: speedup: 3.25x over cuQuantum; 159.06x over Qiskit Aer; 311.42x over FlatDD (average)
tg: quantum-simulation, gpu, decision-diagram, batch-simulation, quantum-circuit

t: CIPHERMATCH: Accelerating Homomorphic Encryption-Based String Matching via Memory-Efficient Data Packing and In-Flash Processing
th: near-storage HE acceleration for encrypted string matching
pb: Homomorphic encryption (HE)-based exact string matching incurs prohibitive computational latency due to expensive HE operations (multiplication, rotation) and severe data movement overhead from the large ciphertext memory footprint. Prior HE string matching algorithms cannot efficiently handle these combined bottlenecks.
me: CIPHERMATCH is an algorithm-hardware co-design that (1) applies an optimized software-based data packing scheme to reduce ciphertext memory footprint, (2) reformulates the string matching algorithm to eliminate costly HE multiplications and rotations, replacing them with cheaper addition-only operations, and (3) introduces a new in-flash processing (IFP) architecture that performs computation near the flash storage to minimize data movement between memory and processor.
nv: Combining HE-algorithm redesign to remove multiplicative operations with a purpose-built in-flash processing architecture that eliminates DRAM-level data movement for encrypted string matching.

t: Virtuoso: Enabling Fast and Accurate Virtual Memory Research via an Imitation-based Operating System Simulation Methodology
th: imitation-based OS simulation for virtual memory research
pb: Existing virtual memory (VM) simulation tools either lack accuracy in modeling OS software components (e.g., page table walks, TLB shootdowns, OS scheduling interactions) or are too slow and complex to prototype hardware/OS co-designs spanning the hardware/software boundary.
me: Virtuoso introduces an imitation-based OS simulation methodology where a lightweight simulator imitates the behavior of a full OS by training on traces of OS decisions (page allocation, eviction, TLB management) captured from real OS runs, then replaying those decisions with hardware-accurate timing in a fast simulation framework. This enables rapid iteration over hardware/OS co-design points without full OS simulation overhead.
nv: Using an imitation learning approach to reproduce OS virtual memory behavior accurately within a fast architectural simulator, avoiding the need for full OS simulation.

t: ZRAID: Leveraging Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA) for Alleviating Partial Parity Tax in ZNS RAID
th: ZRWA-based partial parity elimination in ZNS RAID
pb: ZNS SSD RAID systems must manage partial parity for incomplete stripes; prior approaches log partial parity in reserved zones, creating throughput bottlenecks and exacerbating write amplification that reduces SSD lifetime.
me: ZRAID exploits the Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA), a small random-write buffer region within ZNS SSDs, to buffer and consolidate partial parity in-place before committing full stripes to sequential zones. By using ZRWA as a transient parity staging area, ZRAID avoids persistent partial parity logging to reserved zones, eliminating the associated throughput bottleneck and write amplification. The system coordinates ZRWA usage across multiple ZNS drives to maintain RAID consistency.
nv: Using ZNS ZRWA buffers as transient in-device parity staging to eliminate partial parity logging overhead in ZNS RAID without reserved zones.
mx: other: not stated in abstract; claims throughput improvement and write amplification reduction

t: Aqua: Network-Accelerated Memory Offloading for LLMs in Scale-Up GPU Domains
th: network-accelerated KV-cache paging for responsive LLM serving
pb: LLM inference under bursty request patterns exhausts GPU memory, causing serving engines to use admission control that renders them unresponsive; preemptive time-sliced scheduling requires KV-cache paging that incurs high overhead and reduces throughput.
me: Aqua is a GPU memory management framework that uses the high-bandwidth scale-up network (NVLink/NVSwitch fabric within a server) as a fast memory offloading path for paging LLM inference state (KV caches). When a prompt is preempted, Aqua pages its KV cache over the scale-up network to remote GPU memory on other nodes rather than to slow host DRAM or NVMe, dramatically reducing paging latency. A scheduling layer enables preemptive time-sliced prompt execution on top of this low-overhead paging mechanism.
nv: Using the intra-server scale-up GPU interconnect (NVLink fabric) as a fast KV-cache paging path to enable low-overhead preemptive LLM scheduling without throughput loss.
mx: speedup: 4x throughput improvement over single long prompt baseline; 20x responsiveness improvement vs state-of-the-art · other: evaluated on 8x NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU server
tg: llm-inference, gpu-memory, kv-cache, paging, nvlink, preemption

t: Relax: Composable Abstractions for End-to-End Dynamic Machine Learning
th: unified dynamic-shape compiler abstraction for end-to-end ML
pb: Dynamic shape computations in modern ML workloads (especially LLMs) cannot be efficiently compiled by existing frameworks that treat computational graphs, loop-level tensor programs, and external library calls as separate, non-interoperable abstractions, preventing cross-level optimization and limiting deployment to diverse backends.
me: Relax introduces a unified compiler IR with a cross-level abstraction that encapsulates computational graphs, loop-level TIR (tensor IR) programs, and external library calls in a single representation. First-class symbolic shape annotations propagate dynamic shape information globally across the program, enabling shape-aware optimizations across abstraction levels. Relax builds an end-to-end compilation pipeline in Apache TVM that includes shape-aware kernel fusion, operator specialization, and deployment code generation for diverse targets including GPUs, mobile (Android/iOS), embedded MCUs, and WebAssembly/WebGPU.
nv: A single unified IR combining computational graphs, tensor loop programs, and library calls with first-class symbolic shapes enabling globally propagated dynamic-shape-aware cross-level optimization.
mx: speedup: performance competitive with SOTA systems on various GPUs · other: enables deployment to mobile phones, embedded devices, web browsers not supported by prior compilers
tg: compiler, dynamic-shapes, llm-inference, tvm, cross-platform

t: Forecasting GPU Performance for Deep Learning Training and Inference
th: tile-level ML-based GPU performance forecasting for unseen hardware
pb: Predicting GPU performance for deep learning workloads on unseen GPU models (new GPU on existing model, or existing model on new GPU) is inaccurate with prior ML-based approaches, which attempt to predict end-to-end kernel latency directly and suffer >100% error on new model-GPU pairs.
me: NeuSight decomposes a single DL kernel prediction into smaller working sets called 'tiles' that correspond to the GPU's SM-level execution granularity. Tile-granularity predictions are made by a learned ML model, then aggregated across tiles to estimate end-to-end latency. The approach is bounded by fundamental performance laws (roofline model) and incorporates both GPU hardware parameters and software library optimizations (cuDNN, cuBLAS heuristics) to constrain the prediction space, enabling generalization to unseen GPUs by parameterizing hardware characteristics rather than encoding GPU identity.
nv: Decomposing DL kernel latency prediction to tile granularity aligned with SM execution, bounding predictions via performance laws, enabling accurate cross-GPU generalization without running code on the target hardware.
mx: accuracy: GPT-3 inference latency error reduced from 30.8% (SOTA) to 2.3% on H100; training error reduced from 121.4% to 2.3% · other: evaluated across diverse DL workloads and up-to-date GPUs including H100

t: Enhancing CGRA Efficiency Through Aligned Compute and Communication Provisioning
th: motif-based hierarchical CGRA compute/communication alignment
pb: Existing CGRAs overprovision communication resources (routers consume 44% of power/area in spatio-temporal designs) relative to compute capabilities because each PE is paired with a full crossbar/router that handles peak congestion, resulting in low average communication utilization and wasteful programmability encoding.
me: Plaid proposes a hierarchical execution paradigm based on structural 'motifs' — recurring three-node subgraph patterns (fan-in, fan-out, unicast) in dataflow graphs (DFGs). The Plaid architecture replaces individual PE+router pairs with a Plaid Collective Unit (PCU): three ALUs share a single lightweight local router that handles all intra-motif communication internally, connected to a global router for inter-PCU communication. The Plaid compiler (built on the Morpher toolchain with simulated-annealing-based modulo scheduling) automatically identifies motifs in DFGs, generates a hierarchical DFG, and maps it onto the PCU array using flexible schedule templates that maximize resource utilization. Implemented in Verilog RTL at 22nm FDSOI targeting 100MHz; a 2x2 PCU array has 16 functional units (same as a 4x4 spatio-temporal CGRA).
nv: Identifying three-node DFG motifs (mathematically provable exhaustive structural patterns) and designing a Plaid Collective Unit that handles all intra-motif communication with a single local router, replacing per-PE overprovisioned crossbars to align compute and communication provisioning.
mx: speedup: 1.4x performance improvement over energy-efficient spatial CGRA; same performance as high-performance spatio-temporal CGRA · energy_or_tops_w: 43% power reduction vs spatio-temporal CGRA; 27.7% energy reduction vs spatial CGRA; 42% total energy reduction vs spatio-temporal · area: 46% area savings vs spatio-temporal CGRA; 48% area savings vs spatial CGRA; CGRA fabric 33,366 um2 at 22nm · ppa: 1.22x energy efficiency and 1.25x area efficiency vs domain-optimized spatio-temporal CGRA · other: Evaluated on 30 DFGs from TinyML, PolyBench linear algebra, and image processing benchmarks

t: Harmonia: A Unified Framework for Heterogeneous FPGA Acceleration in the Cloud
th: unified shell abstraction for heterogeneous cloud FPGA management
pb: The shell-role FPGA architecture adopted by cloud providers works well for homogeneous FPGA servers but fails to handle heterogeneous FPGA configurations: prior solutions either require laborious shell development for each FPGA variant (provider burden) or ad-hoc software modifications for each application (user burden), with no portable abstraction across diverse cloud FPGA types.
me: Harmonia introduces a unified framework that abstracts cloud FPGA heterogeneity at both the hardware and software levels. On the hardware side, it defines a standardized shell interface specification that decouples platform-specific shell logic from portable role logic, allowing roles (user accelerators) to be written once and ported across heterogeneous FPGAs. On the software side, Harmonia provides a resource management layer and a driver abstraction that hides FPGA-specific differences from user applications, enabling portability without per-FPGA software modifications.
nv: A unified shell interface specification and software abstraction layer that decouples portable accelerator roles from platform-specific shells across heterogeneous cloud FPGA families.
mx: other: not stated in abstract
tg: fpga, cloud, heterogeneous, shell-role, portability

t: MVQ: Towards Efficient DNN Compression and Acceleration with Masked Vector Quantization
th: masked vector quantization with sparsity-aware systolic array for CNN compression
pb: Conventional vector quantization (VQ) for DNN compression treats all weights equally during k-means clustering, forcing important high-magnitude weights to align with unimportant zero-adjacent weights, causing large clustering errors on the weights that most affect accuracy and leading to significant accuracy degradation at high compression ratios.
me: MVQ is an algorithm-hardware co-design combining N:M structured pruning with masked k-means clustering. At the algorithm level: (1) N:M pruning removes unimportant weights with a regular sparse structure; (2) masked k-means treats only unpruned (important) weights during both assignment and codeword update, preventing zeros from distorting centroids; (3) 8-bit symmetric quantization applied to codebook; (4) masked gradient finetuning recovers accuracy. At the hardware level, the accelerator uses the Enhanced Weight Stationary (EWS) dataflow with: an assignment-aware weight-loading controller that reconstructs sparse weights from codebook + index + N:M mask using a Codebook Register File (CRF) and LZC-based mask decoder; and a sparsity-aware systolic array with Q=N/M x d active PEs per subvector instead of d PEs, reducing multiplier and register file count by 55%. Synthesized at 40nm 0.99V LVT using Synopsys Design Compiler.
nv: Masked k-means clustering that excludes pruned (zero) weights from both assignment and codeword update steps, ensuring codewords approximate important weights rather than being distorted by structured-pruning zeros.

t: ByteFS: System Support for (CXL-based) Memory-Semantic Solid-State Drives
th: OS file system support for CXL memory-semantic SSDs
pb: Memory-semantic SSDs expose both byte-addressable (via PCIe/CXL load/store) and block interfaces simultaneously, but existing software systems are designed for either NVM on the processor memory bus or block-interface SSDs, and cannot efficiently exploit the unique dual-interface characteristics and distinct performance profiles of memory-semantic SSDs.
me: ByteFS is a file system designed specifically for CXL-based memory-semantic SSDs. It exploits the byte interface for metadata and small random accesses (latency-sensitive operations) while using the block interface for large sequential data transfers (throughput-sensitive operations), routing operations to the appropriate interface based on access pattern and size. ByteFS introduces new OS abstractions (allocation, caching, I/O path) that account for the asymmetric performance characteristics of the two interfaces and the persistent byte-addressable semantics provided by the device.
nv: A file system that dual-routes operations between byte and block interfaces of memory-semantic SSDs based on access characteristics, with OS abstractions specifically designed for CXL-attached NAND flash memory semantics.

t: MetaSapiens: Real-Time Neural Rendering with Efficiency-Aware Pruning and Accelerated Foveated Rendering
th: efficiency-aware pruning and foveated rendering for mobile neural rendering
pb: Point-Based Neural Rendering (PBNR), particularly 3D Gaussian Splatting, is computationally too expensive to run in real time on mobile devices due to the large number of Gaussian primitives and the full-resolution rendering required.
me: MetaSapiens combines two techniques: (1) efficiency-aware pruning that reduces the number of Gaussian primitives based on their contribution to rendering quality, using a pruning criterion that accounts for both visual importance and computational cost on the target hardware; and (2) accelerated foveated rendering that exploits the human visual system's reduced acuity in peripheral regions by rendering the foveal region at full quality and peripheral regions at lower resolution or with fewer Gaussians, reducing total computation. Both techniques are co-designed with the mobile hardware execution model to maximize throughput.
nv: Co-designing efficiency-aware Gaussian pruning with hardware-targeted foveated rendering to achieve real-time PBNR on mobile devices.
mx: other: not stated in abstract; claims real-time PBNR on mobile devices
tg: neural-rendering, 3d-gaussian-splatting, mobile, foveated-rendering, pruning

t: COMET: Towards Practical W4A4KV4 LLMs Serving
th: practical W4A4KV4 LLM inference via fine-grained mixed-precision quantization
pb: Prevalent LLM quantization methods (W8A8 or W4-only) do not fully utilize INT4 tensor cores on modern GPUs and cannot reduce the KV cache memory bottleneck, because quantizing activations to 4-bit causes unacceptable accuracy loss with standard methods, leaving W4A4 impractical.
me: COMET introduces a fine-grained mixed-precision quantization algorithm (FMPQ) that compresses most activations to 4-bit while preserving accuracy by identifying and retaining outlier activations at higher precision (e.g., 8-bit) in a mixed-precision format. On the hardware side, COMET develops a highly optimized W4Ax GPU kernel (supporting both W4A4 and W4A8 mixed-precision GEMM) with a novel mixed-precision data layout that co-locates 4-bit and 8-bit activation elements to enable fast dequantization. The kernel uses GPU software pipelining to overlap data loading and conversion with computation, and introduces fine-grained streaming multiprocessor (SM) scheduling to achieve load balance across SMs. COMET integrates this kernel into a full LLM inference framework with efficient KV4 cache management supporting models like LLaMA-3-70B on a single A100-80G.
nv: Fine-grained mixed-precision quantization (FMPQ) enabling practical W4A4 by selectively retaining outlier activations at INT8, combined with a W4Ax kernel with mixed-precision data layout and SM-level load-balanced scheduling to fully exploit INT4 tensor cores.
mx: speedup: 2.88x kernel-level speedup over cuBLAS; 2.02x end-to-end throughput vs TensorRT-LLM on A100-80G · accuracy: negligible accuracy loss vs FP16 for LLaMA family models · other: evaluated on LLaMA-3-70B on single A100-80G-SMX4

t: Practical Federated Recommendation Model Learning Using ORAM with Controlled Privacy
th: ORAM-backed federated learning for recommendation models
pb: Federated learning (FL) for recommendation models is impractical because the large embedding tables require each user to access a tiny fraction of table entries, and hiding those access patterns via ORAM incurs prohibitive latency and SSD wear. Existing ORAM-based approaches have latency and SSD lifetime overheads that make them undeployable at scale.
me: FEDORA places the large ORAM structure on SSDs rather than DRAM, using SSD-friendly access optimizations to reduce write amplification and wear. It introduces epsilon-FDP (Federated Differential Privacy), a formal framework that trades off ORAM privacy strength against performance by allowing a controlled, quantified privacy budget, reducing the number of ORAM operations required. The system also supports modern FL operation modes (e.g., asynchronous and partial participation) so it integrates with production FL pipelines.
nv: Epsilon-FDP is a new formal privacy notion that explicitly balances ORAM obliviousness against performance cost, enabling practical SSD-backed ORAM for federated recommendation training.
mx: speedup: up to 24x latency reduction; 5x average latency improvement over baseline · other: over 1000x SSD lifetime improvement (peak); 158x average SSD lifetime improvement
tg: federated-learning, oram, recommendation-models, ssd, privacy, embedding-tables

t: Concurrency-Informed Orchestration for Serverless Functions
th: Concurrency-aware serverless container orchestration
pb: Serverless FaaS platforms suffer excessive cold starts because existing container keep-alive policies ignore concurrent invocations: they fail to reason about whether reusing a busy container (delayed warm start) or cold-starting a new container is preferable, and they make imbalanced eviction decisions that prematurely evict soon-to-be-reused containers.
me: CIDRE is a container orchestration algorithm that combines fine-grained container-level state (busy/idle, time-to-free) with coarse-grained concurrency signals to speculatively decide between a delayed warm start and a cold start under concurrent scaling. For eviction, CIDRE uses both container-level recency and concurrency-aware reuse probability to produce balanced eviction decisions that avoid removing containers still likely to be reused. The algorithm is evaluated on two production FaaS workload traces.
nv: CIDRE is the first FaaS keep-alive policy to explicitly model container concurrency state and use it to make speculative warm-vs-cold-start decisions and balanced eviction choices simultaneously.
mx: speedup: up to 39.3% average invocation overhead reduction · other: up to 75.1% cold start ratio reduction vs state-of-the-art keep-alive policies
tg: serverless, faas, cold-start, container-scheduling, concurrency, keep-alive

t: ASDR: Exploiting Adaptive Sampling and Data Reuse for CIM-based Instant Neural Rendering
th: CIM-accelerated neural radiance field inference with adaptive sampling
pb: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) inference exhibits irregular memory access patterns and high computational overhead, making it unsuitable for low-latency, power-efficient deployment on edge devices. Standard compute architectures cannot bridge the gap between NeRF's memory-bound irregular accesses and the immediacy/power requirements of practical neural rendering.
me: ASDR maps NeRF inference onto computing-in-memory (CIM) arrays to address the memory access bottleneck by performing computation near data storage, eliminating costly DRAM transfers. Adaptive sampling reduces the number of points sampled per ray dynamically based on scene complexity, cutting redundant computation. Data reuse strategies exploit spatial and temporal coherence across adjacent rays and frames to avoid redundant CIM macro activations. Together, these techniques reduce both the number of operations and the energy per operation on the CIM substrate.
nv: Co-designing adaptive ray sampling and cross-ray data reuse specifically for CIM array execution to simultaneously reduce irregular access overhead and compute volume in NeRF inference.

t: MDPeek: Breaking Balanced Branches in SGX with Memory Disambiguation Unit Side Channels
th: Memory Disambiguation Unit side-channel attack on SGX
pb: Intel SGX enclaves are believed to be protected against control-flow side-channel attacks when software defenses balance branch execution paths; this paper discovers that the Memory Disambiguation Unit (MDU) inside modern Intel CPUs leaks information even through these balanced branches, creating a previously unknown side channel.
me: MDPeek exploits the Memory Disambiguation Unit, a microarchitectural structure that speculatively allows or stalls dependent loads/stores based on address aliasing predictions. By crafting enclave access patterns that cause the MDU to make different predictions for secret-dependent branches (even when those branches are balanced at the instruction level), the attacker can observe MDU state changes through timing differences in a co-located spy process. The attack methodology reverse-engineers MDU behavior in Intel CPUs and demonstrates end-to-end information leakage from SGX enclaves.
nv: MDPeek is the first attack to exploit the Memory Disambiguation Unit as a side-channel oracle against SGX, bypassing software defenses that rely on balanced control flow.

t: Systematic CXL Memory Characterization and Performance Analysis at Scale
th: Systematic CXL memory performance characterization
pb: CXL-attached memory introduces sub-microsecond latency overheads (140-410 ns) relative to local DRAM, but the performance impact across diverse devices, CPU platforms, and workloads is poorly understood, including tail latencies, prefetcher behavior, and bottleneck localization.
me: Melody is a characterization framework that runs 265 workloads across 4 real CXL devices, 5 CPU platforms, and 7 injected latency levels to comprehensively profile CXL memory performance. It introduces SPA (Sub-operation Performance Analysis), a novel methodology that decomposes memory access latency into sub-operations to pinpoint CXL-specific bottlenecks. Melody also measures and discloses CXL tail latency distributions for the first time, and characterizes CPU hardware prefetcher effectiveness (and failures) under CXL latency conditions.
nv: SPA is the first technique to pinpoint CXL memory bottlenecks at sub-operation granularity, and Melody provides the first systematic, multi-device, multi-CPU, multi-latency CXL characterization including tail latency disclosure.
mx: other: CXL latency range: 140-410 ns sub-microsecond; 265 workloads, 4 CXL devices, 5 CPU platforms, 7 latency levels evaluated
tg: cxl, memory-expansion, characterization, prefetcher, tail-latency, interconnect

t: ReSBM: Region-based Scale and Minimal-Level Bootstrapping Management for FHE via Min-Cut
th: Min-cut-based bootstrapping minimization for FHE encrypted inference
pb: In RNS-CKKS fully homomorphic encryption, repeated homomorphic multiplications escalate ciphertext scale and consume multiplicative levels, requiring expensive bootstrapping to restore capacity; existing compile-time approaches do not efficiently minimize the number and placement of bootstrapping operations, leading to excess overhead in encrypted ML inference.
me: ReSBM partitions the FHE computation graph into regions using a min-cut graph algorithm that identifies the minimal set of bootstrapping insertion points needed to prevent ciphertext level overflow. Within each region, scale management is handled to keep multiplicative levels within bounds. The min-cut formulation finds a provably minimal-bootstrapping schedule at compile time, reducing the number of costly bootstrapping operations without sacrificing correctness. This is coupled with region-level scale assignment to prevent capacity overflow throughout encrypted inference.
nv: Framing FHE bootstrapping placement as a min-cut problem on the computation graph to find a provably minimal bootstrapping schedule at compile time.
mx: speedup: not stated quantitatively in abstract · other: reduced number of bootstrapping operations vs prior approaches (not quantified in abstract)
tg: fhe, ckks, bootstrapping, privacy-preserving-ml, compiler, min-cut

t: lambda-trim: Optimizing Function Initialization in Serverless Applications With Cost-driven Debloating
th: Cost-driven Python debloating for serverless function initialization
pb: In serverless FaaS platforms, Function Initialization (package import, module loading) accounts for more than 50% of the monetary cost of cold starts in real-world ML applications, yet existing optimization efforts focus on the container/VM startup phase rather than the Python initialization phase.
me: lambda-trim uses a three-stage automated pipeline: a static analyzer identifies the reachable module dependency graph for a given serverless function, a profiler specialized for the serverless pricing model (which accounts for both memory usage and wall-clock time as billing dimensions) quantifies the latency and cost contribution of each module, and a debloater removes redundant code paths and unused modules while preserving correctness. The optimized application is directly deployable on standard serverless platforms without runtime changes.
nv: Serverless-pricing-model-aware profiling that jointly optimizes for latency and memory (both billing dimensions) to prioritize debloating decisions, specifically targeting the Function Initialization phase.
mx: speedup: substantial reductions in cold-start latency (not quantified in abstract) · other: Function Initialization >50% of monetary cold-start cost in real-world ML applications
tg: serverless, cold-start, debloating, python, faas, cost-optimization

t: Generalizing Reuse Patterns for Efficient DNN on Microcontrollers
th: Generalized computation reuse patterns for DNN inference on microcontrollers
pb: DNN inference on microcontrollers is limited by their restricted compute and memory, and existing computation reuse techniques that exploit redundancy in input/activation data are constrained by a narrow definition of reuse patterns, leaving a large portion of potential reuse unexploited.
me: The work introduces generalized reuse, which frames computation reuse in terms of row and column reordering of a matrix view of DNN input or activation maps. By recognizing that different reorderings expose different reuse patterns, the approach dramatically expands the explorable reuse space beyond what prior narrow pattern definitions allow. Two analytical models are developed: one predicts the accuracy impact of a given reuse pattern (approximate computation), and one predicts latency on the target microcontroller. These models enable efficient search over the generalized reuse space to select patterns that best trade off accuracy and speed for a given DNN and hardware.
nv: Framing DNN computation reuse as a matrix row/column reordering problem to reveal a vastly larger reuse pattern space, coupled with dual analytical models for accuracy and latency prediction on microcontrollers.
mx: speedup: 1.03-2.2x over conventional reuse · accuracy: 1-8% improvement over conventional reuse (accuracy mode)
tg: microcontroller, dnn-inference, computation-reuse, edge-ai, matrix-reordering, approximate-computing

t: BatchZK: A Fully Pipelined GPU-Accelerated System for Batch Generation of Zero-Knowledge Proofs
th: Pipelined GPU batch zero-knowledge proof generation
pb: GPU-accelerated zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) systems optimize for low single-proof latency but do not support high-throughput batch proof generation, creating a bottleneck for applications like blockchain and verifiable ML that require generating many proofs concurrently.
me: BatchZK constructs a fully pipelined GPU execution engine for batch ZKP generation. The pipeline overlaps the multiple stages of proof generation (e.g., polynomial commitment, multi-scalar multiplication, NTT) across multiple concurrent proofs using GPU streams and memory management strategies that keep GPU compute units busy throughout. By co-scheduling proofs at different stages simultaneously on the GPU, BatchZK amortizes memory transfer and kernel launch overhead across the batch, maximizing GPU throughput. The system targets standard ZKP schemes (e.g., Groth16 or PLONK-family) that underpin modern blockchain applications.
nv: Full pipeline parallelism across independent ZKP generation tasks on GPU, turning the sequential single-proof flow into a throughput-optimized batch pipeline for the first time.
mx: speedup: not stated quantitatively in abstract · other: throughput improvement over single-proof GPU systems (not quantified in abstract)
tg: zero-knowledge-proofs, gpu, batch-processing, pipeline, blockchain, verifiable-ml

t: Fusion: An Analytics Object Store Optimized for Query Pushdown
th: Erasure-coding-aware analytics object store for query pushdown
pb: Disaggregated cloud storage uses erasure coding that partitions analytics file objects into fixed-size blocks across storage nodes; when query predicates are pushed down to storage (computation pushdown), the storage system must reassemble objects across nodes, incurring high network latency that undermines pushdown's intended benefits for ad-hoc and highly-selective OLAP queries.
me: Fusion is an analytics object store that co-designs storage layout and query pushdown execution for erasure-coded environments. It reorganizes how analytics file objects (e.g., Parquet files) are partitioned and distributed across storage nodes so that query-relevant data stripes can be accessed and evaluated locally at storage nodes without full object reassembly. Pushdown execution is coordinated across storage nodes in a way that respects erasure coding boundaries, enabling predicate evaluation close to data while minimizing cross-node communication.
nv: Co-designing erasure-coded object storage layout with query pushdown execution so predicates can be evaluated at storage nodes without full object reassembly.
mx: speedup: not stated quantitatively in abstract · other: reduced network latency for selective OLAP queries (not quantified in abstract)
tg: object-store, erasure-coding, query-pushdown, cloud-storage, olap, disaggregated-storage

t: Embracing Imbalance: Dynamic Load Shifting among Microservice Containers in Shared Clusters
th: Imbalance-aware dynamic load shifting for microservice containers
pb: Containers within the same microservice deployed in large shared clusters experience temporal and spatial performance imbalance due to resource contention; standard load-balancing policies assume homogeneous container performance and respond with over-provisioning, wasting resources while still frequently violating SLAs.
me: The paper proposes dynamic load shifting, a system that continuously monitors per-container performance metrics (latency, throughput) to detect imbalance and dynamically steers incoming requests toward higher-performing containers within the same microservice. Rather than treating imbalance as a problem to eliminate through uniform scheduling, the system embraces it by exploiting performance heterogeneity: hot containers receive fewer requests and cool containers receive more, allowing the cluster to extract more useful work without additional provisioning. The approach integrates with existing cluster schedulers and load balancers.
nv: Treating intra-microservice container performance imbalance as an exploitable signal for dynamic load shifting rather than a scheduling defect to eliminate.
mx: speedup: not stated quantitatively in abstract · other: substantial resource wastage reduction vs over-provisioning approach (not quantified in abstract)
tg: microservices, load-balancing, container-scheduling, shared-clusters, sla, resource-efficiency

t: Dilu: Enabling GPU Resourcing-on-Demand for Serverless DL Serving via Introspective Elasticity
th: Two-dimensional GPU elasticity for serverless DL serving
pb: Serverless DL serving systems use coarse-grained static GPU allocation that produces 15-94% GPU fragmentation due to dynamic workload patterns; existing horizontal-only scaling cannot adapt GPU resource allocation fine-grainedly within a running DL function instance, degrading utilization and violating QoS.
me: Dilu introduces Introspective Elasticity (IE), a two-dimensional co-scaling mechanism combining vertical scaling (adjusting GPU resource allocation within a running DL task) and horizontal scaling (adding/removing instances). Dilu uses multi-factor profiling with efficient pruning search to characterize each DL function's GPU compute/memory sensitivity. A cross-layer scheduler applies resourcing-complementary principles to fill fragmented GPU capacity with compatible DL tasks. At runtime, an adaptive 2D co-scaling controller continuously monitors QoS signals and adjusts both per-instance GPU allocation and the number of instances to minimize fragmentation while meeting SLAs.
nv: Introspective Elasticity (IE) enables live two-dimensional (vertical + horizontal) GPU resource adjustment for serverless DL functions without full restarts, eliminating the coarse-grained static allocation that creates GPU fragmentation.
mx: speedup: up to 1.8x inference throughput; 1.1x training throughput improvement · other: 10-46% GPU defragmentation; 11-71% QoS violation rate reduction vs SOTA baselines
tg: serverless, gpu, llm-serving, resource-management, elasticity, fragmentation

t: PhasePrint: Exposing Cloud FPGA Fingerprints by Inducing Timing Faults at Runtime
th: FPGA physical fingerprinting via induced timing faults
pb: Cloud FPGA vendors prevent tenants from localizing (identifying) specific FPGA instances to thwart attacks exploiting data remanence and analog covert channels. This paper addresses how to fingerprint and locate individual FPGAs in a shared cloud environment despite vendor-imposed restrictions on low-level hardware information.
me: PhasePrint induces controlled timing faults at runtime by deliberately stressing the FPGA fabric (e.g., via ring oscillators or voltage/frequency manipulation) to elicit device-specific phase signatures in timing behavior. These signatures arise from process-variation-induced differences in propagation delays across FPGA instances. The resulting fault patterns are collected and used as a fingerprint to distinguish one physical FPGA from another without requiring privileged low-level access.
nv: Using runtime-induced timing faults as a side-channel to generate per-FPGA physical fingerprints that bypass cloud vendor restrictions on hardware identification.
tg: fpga, fingerprinting, security, timing-fault, cloud, side-channel

t: Saving Energy with Per-Variable Bitwidth Speculation
th: Speculative per-variable bitwidth narrowing for energy savings on embedded devices
pb: Compilers for tiny embedded devices directly translate source-level variable bitwidths (e.g., 32-bit integers) to binary without exploiting the fact that most variables use far fewer bits than declared at runtime. This wastes energy in computations and memory traffic on highly optimized, energy-constrained devices where further traditional optimizations are difficult.
me: BitSpec is a compiler-architecture co-design: the compiler statically narrows variable bitwidths to their predicted (expected) needs and emits speculative narrow-bitwidth instructions. The hardware monitors live values in speculative variables; when a value overflows the narrowed representation, hardware reports a misspeculation event to software, which re-executes the affected computation at the original (safe) bitwidth. This speculation-recovery loop ensures correctness while capturing energy savings during the common case where narrow widths suffice.
nv: Fine-grained per-variable bitwidth speculation with hardware misspeculation detection, allowing transparent compiler-driven bitwidth reduction without requiring programmer annotation or profile-guided static analysis.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 9.9% average energy reduction, up to 28.2%
tg: bitwidth, speculation, energy, compiler, embedded, tiny-devices

t: Helix: Serving Large Language Models over Heterogeneous GPUs and Network via Max-Flow
th: Max-flow-based joint model placement and scheduling for heterogeneous LLM serving
pb: Serving LLMs across heterogeneous GPU clusters (differing GPU types, memory capacities, and interconnect speeds) is inefficient because existing systems cannot jointly optimize model placement and request scheduling to account for both GPU and network heterogeneity simultaneously.
me: Helix models the LLM inference computation over a heterogeneous cluster as a max-flow problem on a directed, weighted graph where nodes represent GPU instances and edge capacities encode both GPU compute throughput and network bandwidth. A Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver operates on this graph to jointly discover optimized model placement (which layers/shards go where) and request scheduling (how tokens are routed through the cluster), treating the two tasks as a unified optimization rather than solving them independently.
nv: Formulating heterogeneous LLM serving as a max-flow problem that jointly optimizes model placement and request scheduling in a single MILP, exposing trade-offs invisible to decoupled approaches.
mx: speedup: up to 3.3x throughput over existing approaches · other: prompting latency reduced up to 66%, decoding latency reduced up to 24%
tg: llm-serving, heterogeneous-cluster, max-flow, milp, model-placement, scheduling

t: FLEXPROF: Flexible, Side-Channel-Free Memory Access
th: Read/write-differentiated turn scheduling for side-channel-free memory controllers
pb: Secure memory controllers that prevent microarchitectural side-channels by allocating fixed 'turns' to co-scheduled VMs impose a ~2x performance slowdown because the schedule must conservatively handle worst-case mixed read/write patterns, leaving memory bus utilization inefficient.
me: FlexProf introduces two types of memory controller turns: read-optimized turns and write-optimized turns, selected via coarse-grain application profiling that observes the read/write ratio without leaking sensitive information. Each turn type is sized and structured for its dominant operation. Flexibility is added so that a read-optimized turn can opportunistically issue writes when read slots are idle (and vice versa), improving utilization while preserving the fixed-turn structure needed to prevent timing side-channels between VMs.
nv: Differentiating memory controller scheduling turns into read-optimized and write-optimized types, determined by side-channel-free coarse profiling, to recover throughput lost by worst-case-only secure scheduling.
mx: speedup: up to 33% improvement, geometric mean 8% over state-of-the-art · other: over half of memory-intensive programs show >10% gain
tg: memory-controller, security, side-channel, scheduling, virtualization, secure-memory

t: The ASPLOS 2025 / EuroSys 2025 Contest on Intra-Operator Parallelism for Distributed Deep Learning
th: Community contest and benchmark for intra-operator parallelism strategy search
pb: Selecting the optimal intra-operator parallelism strategy (how to partition and distribute each operation in a neural network across multiple accelerators) is a challenging combinatorial optimization problem that significantly impacts distributed training and inference performance.
me: The contest provided a benchmark suite of neural network operations and asked participants to devise algorithms that partition operators across multiple interconnected accelerators to minimize total execution time. Participants submitted model partitioning algorithms evaluated on the benchmark suite over a multi-month competition. The paper retrospectively analyzes the problem formulation, benchmark design, key algorithmic challenges (e.g., combinatorial explosion of partitioning strategies), and the quality of submitted approaches.
nv: A structured community-wide competition and new benchmark suite exposing the state-of-the-art gap in intra-operator parallelism strategy search for distributed deep learning.
mx: other: benchmark quality of partitioning algorithm submissions
tg: parallelism, model-partitioning, distributed-training, compiler, contest, benchmark

t: Vela: A Virtualized LLM Training System with GPU Direct RoCE
th: Cloud-native LLM training on virtualized GPU infrastructure with GPU Direct RoCE
pb: LLM training at scale typically requires dedicated bare-metal GPU clusters with specialized interconnects (InfiniBand, NVLink), but deploying LLM training on cloud-native virtualized infrastructure using commodity hardware and standard Ethernet-based RDMA (RoCE) introduces performance challenges from virtualization overhead and suboptimal network stack interactions.
me: Vela uses Linux KVM-based virtualization with SRIOV-based network interfaces to enable GPU-to-GPU peer-to-peer DMA (GPU Direct) across VMs without passing through the host CPU. VMs are connected via a virtualized RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) network built from off-the-shelf NICs. The system was deployed on NVIDIA A100 GPUs in IBM Cloud, using model parallelism for a 50B-parameter decoder model at ~1500 GPU scale, and insights from 2.5 years of production operation guide architectural recommendations.
nv: Demonstrating that GPU Direct RoCE with KVM virtualization and SRIOV can achieve approximately 80% of ideal LLM training throughput at 1500-GPU scale using entirely commodity, off-the-shelf hardware.
mx: other: ~80% of ideal throughput at 1500-GPU scale (50B param model); ~70% per-GPU FLOPS vs single-VM HPL
tg: llm-training, rdma, roce, virtualization, cloud, a100

t: Data Cache for Intermittent Computing Systems with Non-Volatile Main Memory
th: WAR-integrated data cache for intermittent NVM-based embedded systems
pb: Energy-harvesting embedded systems with non-volatile main memory (NVM) must checkpoint frequently to cover Write After Read (WAR) data hazards, incurring both high runtime overhead and excessive NVM writes; existing data cache solutions do not integrate WAR detection and require additional hardware or software memory trackers.
me: NACHO integrates WAR dependency detection directly into the data cache controller, eliminating the need for a separate memory tracker. When a cached dirty line is read after being written by NVM (a WAR hazard), the cache itself identifies and handles the dependency without a side-channel tracking structure. This co-design reduces checkpoint frequency (because fewer WARs escape detection) and reduces NVM writes (because dirty data is buffered in the volatile cache and written to NVM only at checkpoint time or on eviction), cutting both runtime and write wear.
nv: Embedding WAR dependency detection logic directly into the data cache, removing the external memory tracker required by prior intermittent computing systems.
mx: speedup: 54% average runtime overhead reduction vs. state-of-the-art cache-based intermittent computing · other: 82% reduction in NVM writes vs. cache-less system; 18% average reduction vs. prior cache-based systems
tg: intermittent-computing, nvm, cache, energy-harvesting, war-detection, checkpoint

t: Affinity-based Optimizations for TFHE on Processing-in-DRAM
th: Affinity-aware scheduling of TFHE on processing-in-DRAM to minimize remote accesses
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Torus (TFHE) is a compute- and bandwidth-intensive workload; when mapped to Processing-in-Memory (PIM/HBM) architectures, existing accelerators over-exploit parallelism at the expense of data affinity, causing excessive remote data accesses (RDAs) that degrade performance due to PIM's limited inter-bank communication bandwidth.
me: The paper applies algorithmic optimizations to TFHE to restructure its sub-tasks (bootstrapping, key-switching, NTT/FFT operations) so that data accessed together is co-located on the same PIM vault or bank. An offline scheduler analyzes the affinity patterns of TFHE sub-tasks—determining which operands are used together and how frequently—and derives an optimal scheduling order that minimizes RDAs while maintaining sufficient parallelism. The approach is validated on a variant of an existing PIM-HBM device with minimal hardware modifications and evaluated on a real FPGA-based PIM system emulator.
nv: An affinity-pattern-driven offline scheduling framework for TFHE on PIM that minimizes remote data accesses by co-scheduling operations with shared data onto the same PIM units.
mx: speedup: 4.24x to 209x over prior TFHE accelerators on real-world benchmarks
tg: homomorphic-encryption, tfhe, pim, hbm, affinity, scheduling

t: Segue & ColorGuard: Optimizing SFI Performance and Scalability on Modern Architectures
th: Hardware-assisted SFI performance and scalability for WebAssembly via segmentation and memory tagging
pb: Software-based fault isolation (SFI) for WebAssembly (Wasm) incurs significant performance overhead from memory-access instrumentation and limits the number of Wasm instances that can run concurrently in a single address space due to address-space partitioning constraints.
me: Segue exploits x86-64 segment registers (FS/GS base) to encode sandbox memory bounds directly in hardware, eliminating the explicit bounds-check instrumentation instructions for most memory accesses; this removes 44.7% of Wasm overhead on a Wasm-compatible SPEC CPU 2006 subset and reduces font-rendering sandbox overhead in Firefox by 75%. ColorGuard leverages memory protection keys (MPK/memory tagging) to color each Wasm instance's memory region with a distinct tag, enabling up to 15x more concurrent Wasm instances in a single address space without requiring separate address spaces.
nv: Using x86-64 segment registers as hardware-enforced sandbox bounds to eliminate SFI instrumentation overhead, combined with memory protection key coloring for 15x concurrency scaling.
mx: speedup: eliminates 44.7% of Wasm overhead on SPEC CPU 2006 subset; reduces Firefox Wasm font rendering overhead by 75% · other: up to 15x more concurrent Wasm instances per address space
tg: webassembly, sfi, sandboxing, x86-segmentation, memory-tagging, security

t: Protecting Cryptographic Code Against Spectre-RSB: (and, in Fact, All Known Spectre Variants)
th: Formally verified compiler defense against all known Spectre variants for cryptographic code
pb: Constant-time cryptographic code is designed to prevent timing-based secret leakage, but Spectre attacks—especially Spectre-RSB (Return Stack Buffer)—can violate constant-time guarantees by leaking secrets during speculative execution, and prior defenses cover only Spectre-v1 while leaving other Spectre variants unaddressed.
me: The approach combines a new value-dependent information-flow type system with a compiler transformation. The type system statically tracks whether values depend on secrets and whether they may flow to speculative-execution leak channels (cache, port contention, etc.) under any of the known Spectre mistraining variants. The compiler transformation rewrites low-level code to enforce the type-system restrictions—inserting fences, reordering, and masking as needed—so that no secret-dependent value reaches a speculative leak channel. Both the type-system soundness and the correctness of the compiler transformation are machine-proved in the Coq proof assistant, then implemented in the Jasmin high-assurance cryptography framework.
nv: A Coq-verified value-dependent information-flow type system and matching compiler transformation that jointly protect against all known Spectre variants (including Spectre-RSB) with below 5-7% overhead for complex primitives.
mx: other: overhead below 2% for most cryptographic primitives; 5-7% for Kyber post-quantum KEM
tg: spectre, cryptography, security, information-flow, compiler, formal-verification

t: FSMoE: A Flexible and Scalable Training System for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Models
th: Adaptive communication-computation pipeline scheduling for sparse MoE training
pb: Existing MoE training systems (DeepSpeed-MoE, Tutel) support only limited routing functions and use fixed or heuristic pipeline degrees, leaving significant communication overhead because they fail to overlap inter-node AlltoAll dispatch/combine with intra-node ESP-AllGather/ESP-ReduceScatter communications, and do not co-design Gradient-AllReduce scheduling with MoE-layer communication.
me: FSMoE introduces three techniques: (1) a modular abstraction dividing each MoE layer into six sub-modules (Gate, Order, I-Order, Dispatch, Combine, Expert) with hooks for non-invasive customization, plus a two-phase front-end/back-end profiler-scheduler that fits linear performance models for GEMM and collective operations; (2) a three-stream pipeline schedule that co-schedules intra-node ESP-AllGather/ReduceScatter with inter-node AlltoAll Dispatch/Combine and expert computation by classifying execution into four cases (dominated by inter-node comm, expert compute, AlltoAll, or intra-node comm) and using SLSQP to find the optimal pipeline chunk degree r for each case; and (3) an adaptive gradient partitioning method that slices Gradient-AllReduce work and assigns chunks to overlappable windows within and across MoE layers via a two-step algorithm (greedy assignment then differential evolution optimization), decoupling forward and backward pipeline degrees.
nv: The first MoE training system to simultaneously overlap both inter-node (AlltoAll) and intra-node (ESP-AllGather/ReduceScatter) communications with computation via adaptive per-phase pipeline degree selection, combined with MoE-aware adaptive Gradient-AllReduce partitioning.
mx: speedup: 1.18x-1.22x over Tutel+PipeMoE on 1458 MoE layer configs; 1.19x-3.01x over DeepSpeed-MoE on GPT-2/Mixtral real-world models · other: up to 1.42x speedup on individual gating function benchmarks vs DeepSpeed-MoE; performance model fitting r^2 >= 0.9999 for all collective types
tg: moe, llm-training, scheduling, communication-overlap, pipeline, distributed-training

t: Pave: Information Flow Control for Privacy-preserving Online Data Processing Services
th: SGX-based information flow control for privacy-preserving remote data processing
pb: When users submit personal data to remote online services for processing, they have no technical guarantee that the service will not leak their data, because the processing logic runs in an untrusted server environment entirely outside the user's control.
me: Pave provides a sandboxed execution environment (PaveBox) for arbitrary data-processing programs on a remote server. PaveBox, built on Intel SGX (a hardware trusted execution environment), intercepts all data flows into and out of the sandbox using a runtime monitor that applies information flow control (IFC) policies. Allowed flows are permitted without interference to preserve program functionality; disallowed flows (those that would expose user data) are blocked. Users can verify PaveBox's integrity and confidentiality via SGX remote attestation. The system's security is formalized in a model and proved, with quantitative analysis via prototype experiments.
nv: A sandboxed remote data-processing framework that enforces information flow control via a monitor built on Intel SGX, with a formal security proof and remote attestation for user-verifiable privacy.
mx: other: quantitative prototype overhead analysis (specifics not in abstract)
tg: privacy, information-flow-control, sgx, tee, sandboxing, remote-attestation

t: Skia: Exposing Shadow Branches
th: instruction prefetch via shadow branch exposure
pb: Modern processors using Fetch Directed Instruction Prefetching (FDIP) suffer from Branch Target Buffer (BTB) misses for instructions that have been previously decoded and evicted, causing the Branch Prediction Unit (BPU) to fail to recognize branches and either skip prefetching or speculate down wrong paths. These BTB misses stall the front-end and pollute the L1-I cache, a critical bottleneck for complex datacenter applications with large code footprints.
me: Skia introduces 'shadow branches': lightweight metadata structures that expose BTB-evicted branch information to the FDIP engine without restoring full BTB entries. When a branch is decoded and later evicted from the BTB, Skia retains shadow branch records (address and target hints) in a separate, higher-capacity structure. The FDIP engine consults these shadow records to continue speculative fetching along correct paths even when a BTB miss would otherwise halt prefetching or cause misdirection. This avoids both missed prefetches and wrong-path pollution of the L1-I cache.
nv: Exposing evicted BTB branch information as lightweight 'shadow branch' records that enable FDIP to continue correct speculative prefetching across BTB misses without full BTB entry restoration.
tg: branch-prediction, fdip, btb, instruction-prefetch, front-end, datacenter

t: Tackling ML-based Dynamic Mispredictions using Statically Computed Invariants for Attack Surface Reduction
th: static invariants to bound ML-based security prediction errors
pb: ML-based runtime predictors used for code debloating and dynamic control flow monitoring lack guarantees that distinguish mispredictions from actual security attacks, making them unsuitable for safety-critical security contexts. Without this distinction, the system either blocks legitimate executions (false positives from mispredictions) or fails to stop real attacks.
me: The paper computes static program invariants at compile/analysis time to reduce the attack surface that ML-based dynamic predictors must cover. Statically proven safe behaviors are removed from the ML decision space, so the ML model only makes predictions over a reduced, ambiguous region. When the ML predictor fires on the reduced set, the probability that it is a misprediction versus an actual attack is much lower, enabling more reliable enforcement in security settings such as control flow integrity and debloating.
nv: Using statically computed program invariants to reduce the attack surface exposed to ML-based runtime predictors, making it feasible to distinguish mispredictions from genuine security violations.
tg: ml-security, control-flow-integrity, debloating, static-analysis, misprediction, attack-surface

t: vAttention: Dynamic Memory Management for Serving LLMs without PagedAttention
th: OS-based contiguous virtual memory for LLM KV cache management
pb: PagedAttention enables dynamic KV cache allocation during LLM inference by breaking virtual memory contiguity, but this non-contiguous virtual memory layout for KV caches introduces non-trivial programming complexity and performance overheads in attention kernels and memory management logic. The changes to virtual memory layout require rewriting attention kernels and force suboptimal memory access patterns.
me: vAttention leverages OS virtual memory primitives (specifically, demand paging and virtual address space reservation) to provide contiguous virtual address spaces for KV caches while still allowing on-demand physical memory allocation. Instead of managing non-contiguous page tables in user space as PagedAttention does, vAttention reserves large contiguous virtual address ranges for KV caches upfront and relies on the OS to back them with physical pages on demand. This preserves contiguous virtual memory semantics seen by attention kernels, enabling use of standard (unmodified) CUDA attention kernels while still preventing physical memory fragmentation.
nv: Achieving dynamic KV cache memory allocation with a contiguous virtual address layout by exploiting OS demand-paging, eliminating the need for custom non-contiguous memory management in attention kernels.
mx: other: throughput improvement over vLLM (PagedAttention); specific numbers not in abstract
tg: llm-serving, kv-cache, virtual-memory, pagedattention, dynamic-allocation, attention

t: Pruner: A Draft-then-Verify Exploration Mechanism to Accelerate Tensor Program Tuning
th: draft-then-verify two-stage tensor program search
pb: Search-based tensor program tuning for deep neural network deployment is slow because the exploration mechanism applies an accurate-but-slow learned cost model to all candidate schedules, taking hours or days to find optimal programs. Additionally, learned cost models trained on one hardware platform cannot adapt online to a new platform, causing performance degradation in cross-platform deployment scenarios.
me: Pruner introduces a 'Draft-then-Verify' exploration mechanism: a fast Symbol-based Analyzer (draft model) rapidly screens a large pool of schedule candidates using lightweight symbolic analysis, producing a small set of promising drafts. The expensive learned cost model then verifies only these filtered candidates. MoA-Pruner extends this with a Momentum online Adaptation strategy that uses momentum-based gradient updates to adapt the cost model incrementally to new hardware platforms during the tuning process itself, addressing cross-platform unawareness without full retraining.
nv: A two-stage Draft-then-Verify exploration that pairs a cheap symbolic pre-filter with an accurate learned cost model, drastically reducing the number of expensive model evaluations needed per search step.
mx: other: search time reduction not quantified in abstract; hours-to-days improvement claimed
tg: tensor-program-tuning, autotuning, cost-model, schedule-search, cross-platform, tvm

t: PICACHU: Plug-In CGRA Handling Upcoming Nonlinear Operations in LLMs
th: CGRA plug-in accelerator for LLM nonlinear operations
pb: Nonlinear operations in LLMs (e.g., softmax, layer norm, GELU, RoPE) contribute significantly to inference latency and are poorly served by fixed-function accelerators designed primarily for matrix multiply/convolution, as they require user-defined precision and flexible dataflow to handle diverse operator shapes and precision requirements.
me: PICACHU uses a Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Array (CGRA) as a plug-in accelerator specifically targeting nonlinear operations in LLMs. The CGRA is configured with reconfigurable processing elements (PEs) arranged in a spatial dataflow grid that can be reprogrammed per operator, supporting user-defined precision via configurable compute units. PICACHU plugs into existing accelerator pipelines (e.g., alongside a systolic array or GPU) and offloads nonlinear operations while the main compute handles linear algebra. The CGRA dataflow is scheduled at compile time per operator using a mapping tool that assigns CGRA PE configurations and routing to match the operator's precision and shape requirements.
nv: A plug-in CGRA accelerator specifically co-designed with LLM nonlinear operation diversity, providing reconfigurable PE-level precision and dataflow to handle softmax, layer norm, GELU, and similar operations that fixed-function units cannot efficiently support.

t: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation
th: hardware acceleration of exact retrieval for RAG pipelines
pb: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines for LLMs suffer from high latency in the retrieval phase due to expensive nearest-neighbor search over large knowledge bases, and existing profiling of the interplay between retrieval accuracy and generation phase cost is lacking. The choice between exact and approximate retrieval is not well characterized in terms of end-to-end latency vs. accuracy.
me: The paper profiles several RAG execution pipelines to characterize the complex interplay between retrieval and generation phases. It demonstrates that exact nearest-neighbor search, though more expensive in isolation, can outperform approximate retrieval end-to-end because an exact retrieval model selects a smaller, higher-precision set of documents, reducing the inference burden on the autoregressive generation stage. Based on this, the paper motivates and proposes hardware/system acceleration of exact nearest-neighbor search for RAG, using optimized data structures and computation strategies (specific details not available from abstract).
nv: Demonstrating that exact nearest-neighbor retrieval can reduce total RAG end-to-end inference latency compared to approximate retrieval by reducing the document set fed to the generative model, motivating hardware acceleration of exact search.

t: MOAT: Securely Mitigating Rowhammer with Per-Row Activation Counters
th: provably secure in-DRAM Rowhammer mitigation via dual-threshold per-row counting
pb: The JEDEC PRAC+ABO (Per-Row Activation Counting + Alert-Back-Off) framework for DDR5 Rowhammer mitigation is only a specification framework, not a proven secure implementation; the prior Panopticon design that inspired it is shown to be insecure via a new 'Jailbreak' attack that causes 9x more activations than the configured threshold of 128. A provably secure, low-overhead DRAM-side Rowhammer mitigation using the PRAC+ABO framework does not yet exist.
me: MOAT (Mitigating Rowhammer with Dual Thresholds) uses per-row activation counters (PRAC) with two internal thresholds: ETH (Eligibility Threshold) for proactive mitigation during REF operations and ATH (ALERT Threshold) for triggering the ALERT-Back-Off reactive protocol. Instead of Panopticon's 8-entry per-bank queue (which loses counter information and enables Jailbreak), MOAT tracks only a single entry per bank via a Current Tracked Addr (CTA) register that always holds the row with the highest counter value, plus a Current Mitigated Addr (CMA) register, requiring only 7 bytes of SRAM per bank total. A safe counter-reset-on-refresh mechanism preserves counter integrity across refresh groups by copying boundary-row counters to 2-byte SRAM registers. The Ratchet attack analysis, exploiting the inter-ALERT activations permitted by JEDEC ABO specifications, establishes that MOAT with ATH=64 can safely tolerate a Rowhammer threshold of 99.
nv: Replacing Panopticon's multi-entry queue with a single-entry CTA register that tracks the highest-activation-count row, enabling a provably secure dual-threshold (ETH/ATH) design with only 7 bytes SRAM per bank.
mx: speedup: 0.28% average slowdown (ATH=64) over no-ALERT baseline on SPEC2017+GAP · energy_or_tops_w: 2.3% increase in total DRAM activations; <0.5% total DRAM energy increase · area: 7 bytes SRAM per bank · other: TRH tolerated: 99 (ATH=64); Jailbreak: 1152 ACTs vs 128 threshold on Panopticon
tg: rowhammer, ddr5, prac, abo, dram-security, in-dram-mitigation

t: TaOPT: Tool-Agnostic Optimization of Parallelized Automated Mobile UI Testing
th: tool-agnostic parallel UI test optimization via subspace partitioning
pb: Parallelizing automated mobile UI testing across multiple test devices is inefficient because existing tools explore overlapping UI subspaces on different devices, wasting resources by redundantly testing similar app states. No existing approach optimizes the parallelization of arbitrary automated UI testing tools without modifying their internal workflow.
me: TaOPT performs online UI subspace inference by analyzing the App Under Test (AUT) to identify loosely coupled UI subspaces—regions of the app's state graph that can be explored independently. TaOPT then coordinates access to these subspaces across different testing devices, guiding each device's testing tool toward distinct, unexplored subspaces without modifying the tool's internal search logic (tool-agnostic). This subspace partitioning and assignment is updated dynamically as testing progresses, using observations of which subspaces each device has covered to avoid redundancy. By separating exploration across devices at the subspace granularity, TaOPT maximizes coverage diversity.
nv: Online inference of loosely coupled UI subspaces and tool-agnostic cross-device subspace assignment that prevents redundant exploration without requiring modifications to the underlying testing tool.
mx: speedup: 60% less testing duration for comparable code coverage · energy_or_tops_w: 62% less machine time · other: 1.2-2.1x more unique crashes detected under same resource budget
tg: mobile-testing, parallel-testing, ui-subspace, automated-testing, android, coverage

t: ClosureX: Compiler Support for Correct Persistent Fuzzing
th: compiler-based closure analysis for correct persistent fuzzing
pb: Persistent fuzzing reuses a single process across multiple test cases to eliminate process creation/teardown overhead, but process state changes from one test case (heap state, file descriptors, global variables, etc.) persist into subsequent test cases, causing semantic inconsistencies that lead to missed crashes, false crashes, and overall incorrectness in fuzzer-discovered bugs.
me: ClosureX is a compiler pass that identifies and instruments program state that changes during execution and must be restored between fuzzing iterations to maintain semantic consistency. The compiler analyzes the program to determine which state variables are 'closure' — the minimal set that must be reset to restore execution semantics to the pre-iteration state. ClosureX instruments the loop-back path of the persistent fuzzing harness to snapshot this closure state before each test case and restore it before the next, without requiring full process re-initialization. The compiler selects the granularity of state capture (stack, heap allocations, global variables) based on static analysis of reachable effects.
nv: A compiler-driven closure analysis that identifies the minimal set of program state requiring snapshot/restore across persistent fuzzing iterations, enabling correct persistent fuzzing without full process recreation overhead.
tg: fuzzing, persistent-fuzzing, compiler, correctness, state-restoration, testing

t: Coach: Exploiting Temporal Patterns for All-Resource Oversubscription in Cloud Platforms
th: temporal pattern-based holistic cloud VM resource oversubscription
pb: Cloud platforms remain significantly underutilized across all resource types (CPU, memory, network, storage) because existing oversubscription approaches target only a single resource (typically CPU), causing the oversubscribed bottleneck to shift to other resources and leaving overall utilization low. Memory oversubscription is especially difficult because memory is non-fungible — physical pages cannot be quickly reassigned between VMs.
me: Coach introduces CoachVM, a general-purpose VM type that partitions each resource into a guaranteed portion (always allocated, PA-backed for memory) and an oversubscribed portion (allocated on demand from a shared pool, VA-backed for memory using zNUMA to deprioritize cold pages via guest NUMA policy). A prediction model (random forest regressor) predicts per-VM resource utilization in time windows (e.g., 3x8-hour daily windows) using VM configuration, weekday, subscription history, and customer-specific features, computing per-resource oversubscription rates per time window. The cluster scheduler uses these per-time-window predictions to colocate VMs with complementary temporal patterns, maximizing multiplexing savings. A per-server oversubscription agent monitors resource utilization and applies reactive mitigations (local resource reassignment) or proactive mitigations (VM migration) to prevent SLO violations when contention occurs.
nv: Holistic all-resource oversubscription of cloud VMs using temporal utilization pattern prediction to colocate complementary workloads, with a PA/VA memory partition (zNUMA) that enables transparent memory oversubscription for unmodified guest VMs.
mx: other: ~26% more VMs hosted per server with minimal performance degradation; 4x6hr time windows save ~15% memory and ~20% CPU vs single-lifetime-max allocation
tg: cloud-resource-management, oversubscription, memory-oversubscription, temporal-patterns, vm-scheduling, azure

t: DarwinGame: Playing Tournaments for Tuning Applications in Noisy Cloud Environments
th: tournament-based application tuning robust to cloud interference
pb: Existing application performance tuners (OpenTuner, ActiveHarmony, BLISS) implicitly assume a dedicated interference-free execution environment; when used as-is in shared cloud environments with unpredictable co-tenant interference, they produce suboptimal tuning configurations that are more than 40% away from optimal because interference levels differ across configuration evaluations, causing the tuner to misrank configurations.
me: DarwinGame is a tournament-based tuner that bypasses the inability to control cloud interference by co-locating multiple copies of the same application with different tuning configurations on the same VM, exposing all competing configurations to identical interference conditions simultaneously. Tournaments are structured across four phases: (1) Regional phase (Swiss-style): the search space is divided into 10,000 regions; configurations within each region compete in parallel with early termination when a clear winner emerges based on work-done execution score; (2) Global phase (double-elimination style): regional winners compete with losers given a second chance, with both execution score and consistency score (average 1/rank across games) used for judging; (3) Playoffs (barrage style): top survivors compete two-at-a-time without early termination; (4) Final: two finalists compete to produce the winning configuration. This multi-phase design identifies configurations with both low execution time and low performance variability under interference.
nv: Co-locating multiple application copies with different tuning configurations in the same VM game to expose all candidates to identical interference, then using a multi-phase tournament structure (Swiss + double-elimination + barrage) to rank configurations robustly under noisy cloud conditions.
mx: speedup: >27% reduction in execution time vs. OpenTuner/BLISS/ActiveHarmony in cloud environments · accuracy: 4.2% above optimal on average (vs. 40%+ for next best tuner BLISS) · other: <0.5% performance variability; >15% improvement when integrated with existing tuners

t: PowerMove: Optimizing Compilation for Neutral Atom Quantum Computers with Zoned Architecture
th: joint atom-movement-aware compilation for neutral atom quantum computers
pb: Neutral atom quantum computers (NAQCs) with zoned architectures (ZA) and qubit movement capabilities require coordinated gate scheduling, qubit positioning, atom movement, and inter-zone communication, but existing compilers cannot jointly optimize these dimensions, leading to poor fidelity and long execution times for quantum circuits.
me: PowerMove is a compiler for NAQCs that jointly optimizes gate scheduling, qubit positioning, atom movement, and inter-zone communication for zoned architectures. The compiler introduces new optimization passes that model atom movement as a first-class resource and explore movement strategies jointly with gate ordering. For NISQ applications, PowerMove significantly reduces the number of atom movements and inter-zone communications, while for FTQC (fault-tolerant quantum computing), it replaces physical qubits with logical qubits encoded in quantum error correction (QEC) codes and applies analogous optimization. The compilation algorithm is designed for both correctness and efficiency, achieving up to 216.9x compilation speedup over prior methods.
nv: Jointly optimizing atom movement strategies alongside gate scheduling and qubit positioning for both NISQ and FTQC settings in neutral atom zoned architectures, achieving orders-of-magnitude fidelity improvement.
mx: speedup: 3.76x execution time reduction (NISQ); 4.78x execution time reduction (FTQC) · accuracy: orders-of-magnitude fidelity improvement over state-of-the-art · other: 216.9x compilation time speedup
