t: Composing Distributed Computations Through Task and Kernel Fusion
th: Cross-library task and kernel fusion for distributed GPU applications
pb: Distributed task-based programs composed from multiple libraries incur significant overhead from redundant data movement and kernel launch costs when tasks from different libraries are executed separately, yet existing compilers and runtimes cannot see across library boundaries to fuse these tasks.
me: Diffuse introduces an intermediate representation (IR) for distributed computation that captures task graphs from multiple libraries in a unified form, enabling cross-boundary analysis. A JIT compiler then fuses compatible distributed tasks into single merged tasks, and further fuses the GPU kernels within those tasks using kernel fusion. The IR is general enough to represent computations from cuPyNumeric and Legate Sparse without modification to application code, and the JIT compilation is performed at runtime as task graphs become available.
nv: A unified distributed-computation IR that enables cross-library task and kernel fusion at runtime, allowing high-level Python programs to match or exceed MPI performance.
mx: speedup: 1.86x average (geo-mean), 0.93x–10.7x range on up to 128 GPUs
tg: kernel-fusion, task-fusion, distributed, jit-compiler, hpc, gpu

t: Debugger Toolchain Validation via Cross-Level Debugging
th: Cross-level oracle-based debugger toolchain validation
pb: Existing debugger toolchain validation techniques detect bugs in debug information by comparing execution traces between optimized and unoptimized executables, but compiler optimizations make such traces incomparable and leave bugs in debugger toolchains undetected when the unoptimized executable itself contains toolchain errors.
me: The paper introduces Cross-Level Debugging (CLD), which compares execution traces obtained from debugging the same executable using source-level and instruction-level debugging strategies within the same debugger. CLD formalizes three invariant relations—reachability preservation of program locations, order preservation for reachable locations, and value consistency at program locations—that must hold between the two trace levels regardless of optimization level. The Devil framework implements these relations as test oracles, generates diverse test programs, runs them under both debugging levels, and flags violations as toolchain bugs.
nv: Using source-level versus instruction-level debugging of the same executable as a built-in oracle, eliminating the need to compare across different executables and enabling detection of toolchain bugs even in unoptimized binaries.
mx: other: 27 new bug reports found; 18 confirmed, 12 fixed by developers in GDB and LLDB
tg: debugger, testing, toolchain-validation, gdb, lldb, oracle

t: KernelGPT: Enhanced Kernel Fuzzing via Large Language Models
th: LLM-assisted syscall specification generation for kernel fuzzing
pb: Kernel fuzzing effectiveness depends critically on syscall specifications that define the syntax and semantics of system calls, but generating these specifications is largely manual work, leaving large numbers of important syscalls uncovered and limiting automated kernel vulnerability discovery.
me: KernelGPT uses large language models to automatically generate and repair syscall specifications for kernel fuzzing. The system prompts an LLM with kernel source code and documentation to synthesize syscall specifications in the format expected by the Syzkaller fuzzer, then uses an iterative refinement loop where fuzzing feedback is fed back to the LLM to repair invalid or incomplete specifications. This LLM-guided specification generation covers previously uncovered syscalls and improves the semantic validity of generated syscall sequences.
nv: Using LLMs to automatically synthesize and iteratively repair syscall specifications from kernel source code, dramatically expanding coverage of syscalls available to a kernel fuzzer.
mx: other: increased syscall specification coverage; new kernel bugs discovered (exact numbers not available from abstract)
tg: kernel-fuzzing, llm, syscall, security, specification-generation

t: QECC-Synth: A Layout Synthesizer for Quantum Error Correction Codes on Sparse Architectures
th: Automated MaxSAT-based layout synthesis for quantum error correction codes
pb: Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes require dense qubit connectivity that does not match the sparse qubit coupling graphs of current hardware architectures, and existing QEC circuit compilation approaches either underutilize QEC circuit structure or rely on manual, architecture-specific designs that do not generalize.
me: QECC-Synth is an automated compiler that uses the ancilla bridge technique—inserting ancilla qubits to implement long-range interactions over sparse coupling graphs—and systematically classifies the design space flexibilities of this technique. It then formulates the layout synthesis problem as a MaxSAT optimization problem over these flexibility dimensions, finding globally near-optimal ancilla placement and routing for a given QEC code and hardware architecture. This approach is architecture-agnostic and handles diverse QEC codes (e.g., surface code, color code) without manual redesign.
nv: Formulating QEC layout synthesis as a MaxSAT problem over a systematically classified ancilla bridge design space, enabling automated, architecture-agnostic compilation of diverse QEC codes onto sparse hardware.
mx: other: significantly outperforms existing methods on QEC circuit quality across diverse QEC codes and hardware architectures (exact numbers not available from abstract)
tg: quantum, qec, fault-tolerant, layout-synthesis, maxsat, compiler

t: Medusa: Accelerating Serverless LLM Inference with Materialization
th: Materialization of LLM inference state to eliminate serverless cold-start latency
pb: Serverless LLM inference suffers from excessive cold-start latency caused by three distinct loading stages: model weight loading to device memory, KV cache initialization (profiling and reserving memory), and CUDA graph capturing for different batch sizes—all of which must repeat on every cold start and negate serverless scalability benefits.
me: Medusa uses materialization: it pre-computes and persists the KV cache initialization state and the CUDA graphs for all relevant batch sizes as serialized artifacts on fast storage (materialized snapshots), so that cold starts bypass both stages entirely and load the pre-built state directly to the GPU. The system manages a catalog of materialized snapshots per model and batching configuration, and restores them during cold start with minimal deserialization overhead. The materialization is done offline or lazily on first warm start.
nv: Materializing both the KV cache initialization state and pre-built CUDA graphs as persistent snapshots to eliminate the two dominant LLM-specific cold-start overheads in serverless inference.
mx: other: significant cold-start latency reduction for LLM serverless inference (exact numbers not available from abstract)
tg: serverless, llm-inference, cold-start, cuda-graphs, kv-cache, materialization

t: Fault Escaping: Improving Robustness of DPU Enhanced Platform with Mutual Assisted VM Recovery
th: VM fault tolerance via peer redundancy in DPU-split hypervisor architectures
pb: Modern cloud servers that use DPUs to offload virtualization split VM state across the DPU SoC and the host, so a failure in either component crashes the entire machine and all hosted VMs, with no fault-tolerant mechanism designed for this split-hypervisor architecture.
me: The paper proposes fault escaping: a scheme that treats the split hypervisors on the DPU SoC and the host as redundant peers. Using hybrid synchronization, the full VM state (in a verified, consistent snapshot) is kept accessible on either the DPU or the host with minimal synchronization overhead (kilobytes of data). When one side fails, VMs migrate their state to the surviving peer and resume execution there, bypassing the failed component rather than attempting to recover it. The hybrid synchronization protocol differentiates hot and cold VM state to minimize cross-component bandwidth.
nv: Treating DPU and host hypervisors as redundant peers that can each host the full VM state, enabling VMs to escape from a failing component rather than waiting for in-place recovery.
mx: other: kilobytes of synchronization overhead (vs. full VM state transfer); VM recovery latency improvement (exact numbers not available from abstract)
tg: dpu, vm-fault-tolerance, cloud, hypervisor, reliability, migration

t: Hierarchical Prefetching: A Software-Hardware Instruction Prefetcher for Server Applications
th: Coarse-grained hierarchical instruction prefetching for server front-end bottlenecks
pb: Server-side applications have large instruction working sets that cause severe front-end bottlenecks even with state-of-the-art fetch-directed instruction prefetching (FDIP), because record-and-replay prefetchers lose coverage and timeliness when actual control flow diverges from predicted control flow.
me: Hierarchical Prefetching identifies coarse-grained functionality blocks called Bundles—spanning tens to hundreds of kilobytes of code—through lightweight static software analysis of the server binary. Hardware then uses a compact record-and-replay mechanism (under 2KB of on-chip SRAM) that prefetches entire Bundles when a bundle entry point is detected, rather than individual cache lines. Most Bundle metadata is stored in main memory, keeping on-chip storage minimal. The bundle formation analysis groups functionally related code regions that tend to execute together, tolerating control flow variability by prefetching the entire functional region rather than a precise sequence.
nv: Defining coarse-grained code Bundles (10s–100s KB) through software analysis and prefetching them wholesale in hardware, achieving high coverage and timeliness despite control flow variability with under 2KB of on-chip storage.
mx: speedup: 6.6% average performance gain over FDIP across 11 server workloads
tg: instruction-prefetching, server, front-end, cache, software-hardware-codesign

t: Pirate: No Compromise Low-Bandwidth VR Streaming for Edge Devices
th: Low-bandwidth real-time VR stereo streaming via stereo similarity exploitation
pb: High-quality VR streaming for edge devices requires simultaneously satisfying two competing demands: extremely low bandwidth (the edge uplink is constrained) and real-time rendering at high frame rates (90 FPS), while previous approaches sacrifice one for the other.
me: Pirate exploits stereo similarity—the high structural redundancy between left-eye and right-eye VR video frames—to avoid transmitting both views. Only one eye's view is transmitted at any time, alternating left and right, together with precomputed disparity maps and optical flow information. The target eye view is iteratively synthesized on-device from the single transmitted view using only this lightweight geometric information (no large ML model), at extremely low bitrates down to 0.1 bits per pixel. The alternating transmission schedule further amortizes bandwidth by recycling synthesized frames across time.
nv: Iterative stereo view synthesis using only disparity and optical flow—without large ML models—enabling real-time VR streaming at 90 FPS under bandwidths as low as 0.1 bpp on edge devices.
mx: speedup: 90 FPS real-time operation at 0.1 bpp · other: 20%–40% bandwidth reduction vs. prior approaches; similar quality maintained
tg: vr-streaming, edge, stereo-synthesis, bandwidth, real-time, vision

t: PUSHtap: PIM-based In-Memory HTAP with Unified Data Storage Format
th: PIM two-dimensional access for unified HTAP without data format duplication
pb: Hybrid transaction/analytical processing (HTAP) systems cannot simultaneously achieve workload-specific optimization, performance isolation, and data freshness because OLTP demands row-store format while OLAP demands column-store format, and existing solutions (single format, multi-instance with rebuilding, or mixed delta-store) compromise at least one goal.
me: PUSHtap maps HTAP rows to the CPU's interleaved access dimension (ADE) and columns to the PIM's localized access dimension (IDE) in a single-instance DRAM store. A compact aligned format uses a bin-packing algorithm with a tunable threshold to group columns of similar width into parts, minimizing zero-padding while preserving alignment for both CPU and PIM bandwidth efficiency. Block-circulant placement rotates column-to-PIM-device mapping every 1024-row block, ensuring uniform PIM parallelism load balance across all columns. MVCC is implemented with a data region and delta region; snapshotting encodes row visibility as compact bitmaps that are written to each device in parallel, and defragmentation is offloaded to PIM units when row width exceeds a computed threshold. A modified memory controller adds a scheduler and polling module to support fine-grained interleaved CPU/PIM concurrent access, with a two-phase load/compute OLAP execution model that limits CPU access blocking to 300 microseconds per load phase.
nv: Exploiting the orthogonality of CPU interleaved access (ADE, row-dimension) and PIM localized access (IDE, column-dimension) to implement a single unified data format that simultaneously serves both OLTP and OLAP without format duplication or rebuilding.
mx: speedup: 3.4x OLAP and 4.4x OLTP throughput vs. multi-instance PIM-based HTAP; PUSHtap (HBM) achieves 1.4x additional OLAP speedup vs. DIMM at 8M transactions · other: PIM effective bandwidth 97.4% at th=0.6; snapshot bitmap overhead 2.3% of storage; zero-padding overhead 0.8% of storage; memory controller derived at TSMC 90nm 2.4GHz
tg: pim, htap, database, dram, mvcc, unified-format

t: Tally: Non-Intrusive Performance Isolation for Concurrent Deep Learning Workloads
th: GPU multi-tenant scheduling with performance isolation
pb: GPU sharing for concurrent deep learning workloads suffers from high interference between co-running jobs, causing up to 188.9% latency overhead on high-priority inference tasks. Existing GPU sharing mechanisms impose high integration costs, offer inadequate performance isolation, and have limited application compatibility.
me: Tally implements a non-intrusive GPU sharing mechanism based on fine-grained thread-block-level kernel scheduling. It intercepts GPU kernel launches and dynamically schedules thread blocks across co-running workloads without requiring application modification, allowing the system to control interference between high-priority inference and best-effort training tasks at the thread-block granularity rather than at the kernel or process level.
nv: Thread-block-level GPU kernel scheduling that enforces performance isolation between concurrent workloads without any application-side code changes or framework integration.
mx: other: P99 latency overhead: 7.2% (Tally) vs. 188.9% (TGS); throughput: >80% of TGS
tg: gpu-sharing, performance-isolation, thread-block-scheduling, multi-tenancy, inference-training-colocation

t: Be CIM or Be Memory: A Dual-mode-aware DNN Compiler for CIM Accelerators
th: CIM compiler with adaptive compute-memory mode switching
pb: CIM accelerators can dynamically switch between compute mode and memory mode, but existing DNN compilers ignore this capability and statically assign resources, leaving performance on the table especially for LLMs with diverse memory and compute demands. No existing compilation framework models or optimizes the compute-memory mode switch in CIM hardware.
me: CMSwitch introduces a new hardware abstraction attribute that exposes the compute-memory mode switch to the compiler optimization space. A compilation optimization pass uses dynamic programming and mixed-integer programming (MIP) to identify the optimal network segment boundaries and mode-resource allocations. A tailored meta-operator expresses the compiled result in a generalized manner that maps across different CIM hardware targets.
nv: First CIM compiler that co-optimizes compute-mode and memory-mode resource allocation using dynamic programming and MIP to adapt to each DNN layer's resource demands.
mx: speedup: 1.31x average over SOTA CIM compilers
tg: cim, compiler, mode-switching, dnn-acceleration, mixed-integer-programming

t: Selectively Uniform Concurrency Testing
th: Uniform randomized concurrency testing for rare bug discovery
pb: Randomized concurrency testing algorithms fail to uniformly sample thread interleavings, causing them to miss bugs that manifest only in rare, infrequent interleavings. Prior algorithms are biased in their sampling, leading to poor coverage of the exponentially large interleaving space.
me: SURW (Selectively Uniform Random Walk) is an online randomized concurrency testing algorithm that achieves interleaving-uniformity by carefully selecting a subset of program events and applying a uniform sampling strategy over their interleaving space. The algorithm operates as a black-box randomized technique that requires only minimal additional information about the program to achieve uniformity over broad classes of programs and arbitrary event subsets.
nv: First black-box randomized concurrency testing algorithm to provably achieve interleaving-uniformity for a wide class of programs, enabling systematic exploration of rare buggy interleavings.
mx: other: More bugs exposed and faster than comparable randomized algorithms on leading concurrency benchmarks
tg: concurrency-testing, randomized-algorithms, thread-interleaving, bug-detection, program-analysis

t: DeepContext: A Context-aware, Cross-platform, and Cross-framework Tool for Performance Profiling and Analysis of Deep Learning Workloads
th: Cross-stack DL performance profiling with context correlation
pb: Existing DL profiling tools fail to bridge the semantic gap between high-level Python/framework operations and low-level GPU execution, making it difficult to identify the root cause of performance bottlenecks across the full software stack. No existing tool provides correlated, context-aware profiling spanning Python, DL frameworks, C/C++ libraries, and GPU kernels simultaneously.
me: DeepContext uses a framework-agnostic shim layer that intercepts calls between the DL framework and underlying C/C++ libraries, correlating them with GPU hardware performance metrics and Python-level program context. This shim layer enables causal linking of high-level operator invocations to their low-level GPU execution without modifying framework source code. An automated performance analyzer then processes the correlated trace to generate actionable optimization guidance.
nv: Framework-agnostic shim layer that automatically correlates program context across all layers of the DL software stack (Python, framework, C/C++, GPU) to expose cross-layer performance bottlenecks.
mx: speedup: 1.06x to 1.66x on real-world DL applications after guided optimization · other: Low profiling overhead (not quantified in abstract)
tg: profiling, cross-stack, performance-analysis, deep-learning, bottleneck-detection

t: Squeezing Operator Performance Potential for the Ascend Architecture
th: Component-based roofline analysis and operator optimization for Ascend DSA
pb: Huawei's Ascend domain-specific architecture requires manual management of memory operations and operator execution, creating complex performance bottlenecks that are difficult to diagnose with existing roofline models. Existing roofline models suffer from visualization complexity and inaccurate performance assessment when applied to Ascend's component-level architecture.
me: The paper introduces a component-based roofline model that abstracts individual hardware components (compute units, memory subsystems, data pipelines) to capture per-component performance ceilings and identify bottleneck components. This model is combined with a structured optimization process derived from practical operator optimization case studies on Ascend, identifying common performance issues (e.g., memory bandwidth saturation, pipeline bubbles) and their targeted optimization strategies.
nv: Component-based roofline model that abstracts Ascend hardware into distinct components to enable precise bottleneck identification and operator-level performance optimization on DSAs requiring manual memory management.
mx: speedup: 1.07x to 2.15x end-to-end model speed improvement
tg: ascend, dsa, roofline-model, operator-optimization, performance-analysis

t: Controlled Preemption: Amplifying Side-Channel Attacks from Userspace
th: Controlled preemption to amplify microarchitectural side-channel attacks
pb: Many microarchitectural side-channel attacks are hampered by low temporal resolution measurements, which can preclude or significantly complicate extraction of sensitive information. Userspace attackers lack a mechanism to synchronize their observations with victim activity at fine-grained time resolution.
me: The paper introduces controlled preemption, a technique that allows a userspace attacker to precisely manipulate OS preemption timing in order to achieve fine-grained, synchronized measurement of victim microarchitectural state. By forcing preemption at attacker-chosen moments, the technique amplifies the signal quality of side-channel observations without requiring privileged access or hardware modifications.
nv: Userspace-accessible controlled preemption mechanism that amplifies microarchitectural side-channel attacks by enabling precise attacker-controlled timing of OS preemption events.
mx: other: Amplified side-channel attack success rates (specific numbers not in abstract)
tg: side-channel, microarchitecture, security, os-scheduling, preemption

t: Syno: Structured Synthesis for Neural Operators
th: Automated neural operator synthesis via structured stochastic search
pb: Neural architecture search (NAS) and tensor compilers both optimize over existing manually designed operators and cannot discover fundamentally new operator designs with better accuracy-performance tradeoffs. There is no systematic method to automatically synthesize novel neural operators that satisfy structural constraints required for trainability and hardware efficiency.
me: Syno defines a set of fine-grained primitives operating on tensor dimensions that enforce properties needed for stable model training (e.g., dimension matching, associativity). Expression canonicalization techniques prune redundant candidates during search. A guided synthesis flow constrains valid operators to specified input/output dimension sizes, and stochastic tree search (Monte Carlo-style) efficiently explores the large design space. The resulting operators are compiled and evaluated on real hardware.
nv: End-to-end neural operator synthesis framework using fine-grained tensor-dimension primitives and stochastic tree search to automatically discover novel operators that outperform manually designed and NAS-optimized baselines.
mx: speedup: 1.37x to 2.06x average on various hardware and compiler choices · accuracy: <1% accuracy loss vs. NAS-optimized models
tg: operator-synthesis, neural-architecture-search, tensor-primitives, stochastic-search, compiler

t: Gigaflow: Pipeline-Aware Sub-Traversal Caching for Modern SmartNICs
th: Pipeline-aware caching for scalable vSwitch offload on SmartNICs
pb: Virtual switch (vSwitch) offloading to SmartNICs suffers from high cache miss rates and poor scalability as the flow rule space grows, because existing solutions cannot efficiently store or traverse the large and complex flow rule tables that modern cloud tenants require. This leads to bottlenecks in packet processing throughput at the NIC level.
me: Gigaflow introduces pipeline-aware sub-traversal caching, which decomposes multi-stage vSwitch packet processing pipelines into sub-traversals and caches intermediate traversal results rather than only caching complete flow lookups. By being aware of the pipeline structure, Gigaflow identifies which sub-traversal results can be safely reused across multiple packets, reducing redundant flow rule table traversals and improving NIC cache hit rates even for large flow rule spaces.
nv: Pipeline-aware sub-traversal caching that caches intermediate pipeline stages rather than only full flow lookups, enabling scalable flow rule matching on SmartNICs with large flow tables.
mx: other: Improved packet processing throughput and reduced cache miss rates (specific numbers not in abstract)
tg: smartnic, vswitch, flow-caching, packet-processing, cloud-networking

t: BitMoD: Bit-serial Mixture-of-Datatype LLM Acceleration
th: mixed-datatype bit-serial LLM weight quantization accelerator
pb: LLM deployment is constrained by large weight memory footprints; existing low-precision quantization schemes either sacrifice too much accuracy or lack hardware support for multiple heterogeneous data types simultaneously. Current accelerators cannot efficiently process mixed numerical formats (e.g., INT4, FP4, NF4) within a single design.
me: BitMoD is an algorithm-hardware co-design that introduces fine-grained per-group (128-weight) data-type adaptation, selecting from a set of carefully designed numerical types to minimize quantization error per group. On the hardware side, a bit-serial processing element natively handles multiple precisions by decomposing weights into bit-planes; a unified representation maps all data types to a common internal format, and a dedicated bit-serial dequantization unit rescales per-group partial sums with minimal overhead.
nv: Fine-grained per-group mixture-of-datatype assignment with a matched bit-serial hardware that processes all types through a unified representation, eliminating the need for separate datapaths per format.
mx: speedup: 1.69x over ANT, 1.48x over OliVe · accuracy: <0.5% accuracy loss at 4-bit (discriminative); better perplexity than prior at 3-bit (generative)
tg: llm-inference, quantization, bit-serial, mixed-precision, asic, co-design

t: Push Multicast: A Speculative and Coherent Interconnect for Mitigating Manycore CPU Communication Bottleneck
th: proactive LLC-to-sharer multicast for NoC bandwidth reduction
pb: In manycore processors running parallel workloads, multiple cores repeatedly fetch the same shared cacheline at different times, consuming redundant LLC and NoC bandwidth through independent demand requests. The reactive cache hierarchy does not exploit temporal redundancy in same-data accesses across cores.
me: Push Multicast transforms the LLC into a proactive agent: when it services a demand request, it simultaneously pushes the data to other predicted sharers via multicast, amortizing the bandwidth cost of same-data deliveries. A coherent in-network filter is installed in routers to prune outstanding demand requests that match an in-flight push, preventing redundant traffic. A dynamic pause/resume mechanism adaptively disables pushing when contention is detected, avoiding interference between push-traffic and normal demand traffic.
nv: Converting the LLC from a reactive responder to a proactive multicast pusher, coupled with a coherent in-network filter that prunes redundant in-flight requests along the push delivery path.
mx: speedup: geomean 1.02x (max 1.56x) in 16-core; geomean 1.11x (max 2.08x) in 64-core · other: 33% avg NoC BW saving (16-core), 43% avg NoC BW saving (64-core)
tg: noc, multicast, cache-coherence, manycore, bandwidth, prefetching

t: LEGO: Spatial Accelerator Generation and Optimization for Tensor Applications
th: automatic spatial accelerator RTL generation via affine dataflow representation
pb: Existing spatial accelerator design frameworks either rely on a small set of hand-written RTL/HLS templates (limiting design space coverage) or cannot automatically generate synthesizable RTL, forcing designers to hand-craft hardware for each new tensor operation and dataflow combination. Existing polyhedral and STT representations entangle control flow with dataflow, causing 2x-2.6x area/power overhead in control logic.
me: LEGO uses a relation-centric, affine-transformation-based hardware representation that maps temporal/spatial iteration indices to computation indices via linear matrices, fully decoupling computation logic, data paths, and memory from one another. The LEGO frontend solves integer linear equations to find FU interconnections exploiting data reuse, runs a Minimum Spanning Tree (Chu-Liu/Edmonds algorithm) to prune redundant connections, and applies a BFS-based heuristic to plan direct interconnections across multiple fused dataflows with conflict-free banked memory. The backend translates the FU-level Architecture Description Graph (ADG) into a primitive-level Detailed Architecture Graph (DAG) and applies linear-programming-based delay matching and pin rewiring passes to minimize pipeline register count and eliminate unused logic, yielding synthesizable RTL.
nv: A unified affine-transformation-based representation that decouples control flow from dataflow, enabling automatic generation of synthesizable RTL for any combination of spatial dataflows without hand-written templates, while reducing control logic overhead by 2x-6.5x versus prior polyhedral/STT approaches.
mx: speedup: 3.2x over Gemmini · energy_or_tops_w: 2.4x energy efficiency over Gemmini · area: 35% area savings from backend optimization over naive RTL generation · other: 6.5x flip-flop savings and 5.0x LUT savings vs AutoSA; 2.0x area, 2.6x power savings vs TensorLib
tg: spatial-accelerator, rtl-generation, dataflow, affine-transform, compiler, foundation-models

t: VQ-LLM: High-performance Code Generation for Vector Quantization Augmented LLM Inference
th: codebook-cache-centric GPU kernel generation for vector-quantized LLM inference
pb: Vector quantization (VQ) achieves higher compression ratios than element-wise quantization for LLM weights and KV cache (down to 1-2 bits), but existing VQ kernel implementations are slower than FP16 baselines due to two root causes: inefficient codebook access (excessive shared memory usage, bank conflicts, poor L1 hit rate at 12.45%) and uncoordinated dataflow between codebook loading and subsequent GEMM/attention computation (duplicated off-chip loads and shared-memory-to-register layout mismatches).
me: VQ-LLM introduces a codebook cache abstraction that hierarchically places codebook entries across GPU memory levels based on offline-profiled access frequency: hot entries in thread-local registers (eliminating bank conflicts), medium-frequency entries in shared memory, and cold entries in global memory, with two configurable boundaries. Centered on this cache, the codebook-centric dataflow partitions and parallelizes computation along codebook-switch axes (rather than reduction axes) so each thread block loads exactly one codebook, eliminating duplicate global-to-shared traffic; an adaptive split factor balances the resulting global reduction overhead. Codebook-centric hierarchical fusion extends shared-memory-level fusion with register-level fusion using GPU intra-warp shuffle (shfl.xor) instructions to rearrange dequantized data layouts without shared memory round-trips, with the fusion level chosen adaptively based on the number of shuffle operations required versus shared-memory latency. Adaptive heuristics tune nreg, nshared, and the split factor per VQ configuration and GPU.
nv: A codebook cache abstraction with frequency-based hierarchical placement (register/shared/global) combined with codebook-centric dataflow partitioning and register-level intra-warp shuffle fusion, converting VQ from a latency liability into a practical speedup over element-wise quantization.
mx: speedup: 64.36% to 99.1% latency reduction vs open-source VQ implementations · other: Competitive with AWQ and QoQ at equivalent bit-widths on RTX 4090 and A40
tg: vector-quantization, llm-inference, gpu-kernel, codebook, kernel-fusion, kv-cache

t: Efficient Memory Side-Channel Protection for Embedding Generation in Machine Learning
th: compute-based DHE as memory side-channel protection for embedding table lookups
pb: Embedding table lookups in ML models (DLRMs, LLMs) leak sensitive input features (user IDs, token indices) through memory access patterns, making them vulnerable to side-channel attacks; protecting these accesses with conventional ORAM incurs prohibitive overhead due to the massive size of embedding tables.
me: The paper evaluates three protection strategies: (1) linear scan of the embedding table (accesses all rows, hiding which row is used); (2) ORAM protection with optimized implementation; and (3) Deep Hash Embedding (DHE), which replaces the table lookup entirely with a hash-based neural network computation that takes the embedding index as input and produces an embedding vector through compute rather than memory access, eliminating the memory access pattern. A hybrid scheme combines DHE for large embedding tables (where its compute cost is amortized) with linear scan for small tables, selected per table based on profiled break-even points.
nv: Replacing embedding table lookups with compute-based DHE (Deep Hash Embedding) as a side-channel protection mechanism, which eliminates the memory access pattern rather than obfuscating it, yielding 4x performance improvement over optimized ORAM with up to 1116x memory footprint reduction.
mx: speedup: 4x for large DLRM embedding tables vs ORAM; up to 3.08x end-to-end vs optimized ORAM; 1.32x prefill and 1.07x decoding for GPT-2 vs ORAM · other: Up to 1116x memory footprint reduction
tg: side-channel, privacy, embedding, dlrm, llm, oram

t: Ariadne: A Hotness-Aware and Size-Adaptive Compressed Swap Technique for Fast Application Relaunch and Reduced CPU Usage on Mobile Devices
th: hotness-aware adaptive compressed swap for mobile application relaunch optimization
pb: Mobile devices under memory pressure use ZRAM (RAM-based compressed swap) to defer app eviction, but ZRAM prolongs relaunch latency and wastes CPU time because it applies uniform compression settings regardless of data hotness, does not differentiate compression chunk size, and lacks prefetching of soon-to-be-needed decompressed data.
me: Ariadne introduces three coordinated techniques: (1) a low-overhead hotness-aware data organization scheme that classifies anonymous memory pages as hot, warm, or cold based on observed relaunch access patterns, allowing reuse of hotness labels across consecutive relaunches; (2) a size-adaptive compression scheme that uses small chunk sizes for hot/warm data (enabling fast decompression on the critical relaunch path) and large chunk sizes for cold data (improving compression ratio); and (3) a proactive decompression scheme that predicts the next set of pages needed during relaunch and decompresses them in advance to overlap decompression with computation.
nv: Hotness-aware adaptive compression chunk sizing that applies small fast-decompressing chunks to relaunch-critical data and large high-ratio chunks to cold data, combined with proactive decompression based on observed relaunch locality.
mx: speedup: 50% reduction in application relaunch latency vs ZRAM · other: 15% reduction in CPU usage for compression/decompression vs ZRAM
tg: mobile, compressed-swap, memory-management, relaunch-latency, hotness, zram

t: Anaheim: Architecture and Algorithms for Processing Fully Homomorphic Encryption in Memory
th: PIM architecture for FHE element-wise modular arithmetic bottleneck relief
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) workloads on GPUs are bottlenecked not by NTT (number-theoretic transform) computation but by simple element-wise modular arithmetic operations that saturate off-chip DRAM bandwidth, preventing GPUs from being practical FHE accelerators despite their computational resources.
me: Anaheim is a PIM (processing-in-memory) architecture for FHE that augments DRAM with versatile PIM units supporting modular integer arithmetic instructions (addition, multiplication, NTT butterfly, etc.) to execute element-wise operations in-memory, eliminating the off-chip bandwidth bottleneck. The design includes optimized FHE execution flows that partition computation between GPU (NTT-heavy phases) and PIM units (element-wise phases), efficient data mapping algorithms that exploit DRAM's internal structure (bank/row organization) to minimize data movement overhead within DRAM, and an end-to-end software framework for GPU-PIM co-execution.
nv: Identifying that FHE's GPU bottleneck is element-wise operations (not NTT) and designing a PIM architecture specifically targeting these operations in DRAM, with data mapping that exploits DRAM internal bank structure to minimize in-DRAM data access overhead.
mx: other: Substantial performance and energy efficiency improvement over GPU-only FHE (specific numbers not stated in abstract)
tg: fhe, pim, cryptography, near-memory, dram, privacy

t: QuCLEAR: Clifford Extraction and Absorption for Quantum Circuit Optimization
th: Clifford extraction and classical absorption for quantum circuit gate count reduction
pb: Near-term quantum devices have high gate error rates, and the dominant approach of reducing two-qubit gate count via peephole optimization or routing-aware compilation leaves substantial overhead from Clifford subcircuits that could be eliminated rather than merely rearranged.
me: QuCLEAR is a compilation framework with two sequential optimization steps. First, Clifford Extraction identifies and extracts Clifford subcircuits from the original circuit, commuting them to the end of the circuit via a series of gate commutation rules while simultaneously optimizing (reducing) the remaining non-Clifford gates; this process changes the structure of the remaining circuit to expose further simplifications. Second, Clifford Absorption leverages the classical simulatability of Clifford circuits to compute their effect analytically and absorb (classically post-process) the extracted Clifford subcircuit rather than executing it on quantum hardware, eliminating those gates entirely from the quantum circuit.
nv: Clifford Absorption that classically post-processes extracted Clifford subcircuits at the end of quantum circuits rather than executing them on noisy hardware, enabling up to 84.1% reduction in entangling depth beyond what gate-level optimization alone achieves.
mx: other: Up to 77.7% CNOT gate count reduction; up to 84.1% entangling depth reduction vs state-of-the-art
tg: quantum-computing, circuit-optimization, clifford, nisq, compiler, cnot

t: DPUaudit: DPU-assisted Pull-based Architecture for Near-Zero Cost System Auditing
th: DPU pull-based system auditing for near-zero overhead intrusion detection
pb: Existing hardware-based system auditing frameworks offload log processing to isolated hardware but still suffer high runtime overhead (>10% slowdown) because they use a push-based architecture requiring a log sender to run on the monitored host, which necessitates heavy software protection mechanisms that consume significant CPU resources.
me: DPUaudit replaces the push-based log sender on the monitored host with a pull-based architecture using a DPU (Data Processing Unit/SmartNIC) to actively pull system events directly from the monitored host's memory over the network interconnect. By removing the log sender from the monitored host entirely, DPUaudit eliminates the need for complex software protection mechanisms guarding it, achieving near-zero overhead. The DPU handles log collection, processing, and integrity verification in an isolated SmartNIC environment, physically separated from the monitored host.
nv: Inverting the auditing data flow from host-pushed to DPU-pulled, which eliminates the log sender on the monitored host and its associated protection overhead, achieving at most 2.1% runtime overhead versus one order-of-magnitude higher overhead in prior work.
mx: other: Average 2.1% runtime overhead (vs at least 10x higher in existing approaches) for 6 data center application workloads
tg: security, auditing, dpu, smartnic, data-center, pull-based

t: SpecMPK: Efficient In-Process Isolation with Speculative and Secure Permission Update Instruction
th: speculative MPK permission update for low-overhead in-process isolation
pb: Memory Protection Keys (MPK) enable user-space access control for in-process isolation, but the permission update instruction (WRPKRU) is serialized, imposing significant performance overhead when applications require frequent domain switches to enforce isolation of critical data and pointers.
me: SpecMPK speculatively executes the MPK permission update instruction (WRPKRU) out-of-order rather than serializing it. A lightweight microarchitecture enhancement monitors all subsequent memory instructions that follow a speculative permission update: any instruction that would access a memory region whose permission was transiently upgraded (i.e., a potential speculative access to protected data) is blocked from committing until the permission update instruction itself becomes non-squashable (i.e., past the point of no return in the ROB). This prevents transient permission upgrades from being exploited by speculative execution attacks while allowing the processor to overlap permission update latency with useful computation.
nv: Allowing speculative out-of-order execution of WRPKRU while preventing speculative access to transiently upgraded memory regions through a blocking mechanism tied to the instruction's non-squashable commit point.
mx: speedup: Average 12.21% performance improvement for frequent-domain-switch SPEC workloads vs serialized WRPKRU
tg: memory-protection, mpk, speculative-execution, in-process-isolation, security, microarchitecture

t: No Rush in Executing Atomic Instructions
th: contention-aware dynamic eager/lazy scheduling of atomic RMW instructions
pb: Modern x86 processors implement unfenced atomic RMW instructions (no implicit serializing fences), enabling eager execution as soon as operands are ready, but eager execution locks cachelines early which prolongs the lock duration and harms other threads attempting to acquire the same contended cacheline. Conversely, lazy execution (waiting until the atomic is oldest in the load queue and the store buffer is empty) minimizes cacheline lock time but exposes full memory access latency on non-contended accesses.
me: Rush or Wait (RoW) is a hardware mechanism that dynamically selects between eager and lazy atomic execution via a 64-entry, 4-bit saturating-counter contention predictor indexed by the XOR of the 12 least-significant PC bits. At issue, the predictor determines the execution mode; at completion, it updates using three progressively refined contention detection mechanisms: (1) Execution Window (EW) — marks an atomic contended if an external coherence invalidation/downgrade arrives while the cacheline is locked; (2) Ready Window (RW) — extends tracking to the window from when the atomic's operands are ready by computing the address eagerly and snooping the Atomic Queue (AQ) for address matches on external requests; (3) Directory detection (RW+Dir) — additionally marks an atomic contended when the cacheline arrives from another core's private cache with latency exceeding a 400-cycle threshold, catching cases where contention is resolved before an external request reaches the core. Store-to-load forwarding from older regular stores overrides a lazy prediction to improve atomic locality. Total storage: 64 bytes (256-bit predictor + 256-bit AQ augmentation).
nv: The first analysis of the eager-vs-lazy execution trade-off for unfenced atomic RMWs, and a hardware contention predictor (RoW) that dynamically switches between eager and lazy atomic execution based on predicted cacheline contention with only 64 bytes of state.
mx: speedup: 9.2% average execution time reduction (up to 43%) vs eager atomic baseline across Splash-4, PARSEC 3.0, and fine-grain synchronization benchmarks · area: 64 bytes total storage overhead · other: RW+Dir Sat achieves 7.3% reduction vs eager; 5.5% vs lazy; modeled on 32-core Intel Alder Lake parameters
tg: atomic-instructions, cache-coherence, contention-prediction, x86, out-of-order, synchronization

t: Efficient Caching with A Tag-enhanced DRAM
th: in-DRAM tag comparison for efficient DRAM-based cache with conditional data response
pb: DRAM-based caches (e.g., HBM3-as-cache) suffer from high miss penalties due to two-step tag-then-data access, wasted data movement on cache misses where data is fetched then discarded, and interference between demand requests and miss-fetched data on the data bus. Existing DRAM cache designs cannot perform in-DRAM tag comparison or conditional data response, so they always transfer data regardless of hit/miss status.
me: TDRAM adds small, low-latency metadata/tag mats to an HBM3 die alongside the existing data mats, enabling lockstep tag-and-data access, in-DRAM tag comparison, and conditional data response (data is only transferred to the CPU if the comparison indicates a hit), eliminating wasted data bus transfers on misses. Opportunistic early tag probing allows tag lookups to start before the full row is available, reducing both hit and miss latencies. A flush buffer stores conflicting dirty data on write misses within the DRAM, eliminating data bus turnaround delays caused by writing back dirty evictees before fetching new data.
nv: Adding low-latency tag mats directly to the HBM3 die enabling in-DRAM tag comparison and conditional data response, mirroring SRAM cache semantics (no wasted data transfer on miss) in a DRAM-based cache.
mx: speedup: 1.23x speedup vs state-of-the-art commercial and research DRAM caches · energy_or_tops_w: 21% less energy consumption vs state-of-the-art · other: 2.65x faster tag checks
tg: dram-cache, hbm, tag-comparison, cache-design, memory-system, hpc

t: Architecting Space Microdatacenters: A System-level Approach
th: TCO-driven heterogeneous architecture for space-based computing
pb: There is no principled cost-aware methodology for architecting server-based computing systems deployed on low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites (Space Microdatacenters, SuDC). Prior work proposes the concept but does not model Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) to guide hardware design decisions.
me: The authors build a TCO model for SuDC that decomposes costs into compute power, mass, monetary hardware cost, and communication. They perform a design space exploration over heterogeneous accelerator configurations (high FLOPs/W devices), collaborative compute constellations (EO satellites with onboard accelerators), monolithic vs. distributed architectures, and compute overprovisioning strategies. TCO sensitivity analysis reveals power dominates sublinearly; monetary cost and mass are secondary.
nv: First TCO-driven architecture framework for space microdatacenters, showing that extreme heterogeneity (high FLOPs/W ASICs/NPUs) reduces TCO by 116x despite poor FLOPs/$ characteristics.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 116x TCO reduction with extreme heterogeneity (high FLOPs/W) vs. homogeneous baseline · other: 1.31-1.74x additional TCO improvement with collaborative constellations; 10% TCO reduction distributed vs. monolithic
tg: space-computing, tco, heterogeneous-architecture, edge-inference, leo-satellite, system-design

t: ChameleonEC: Exploiting Tunability of Erasure Coding for Low-Interference Repair
th: Adaptive erasure code repair scheduling to minimize foreground traffic interference
pb: Erasure coding repair traffic in distributed storage systems contends with foreground I/O traffic over shared network bandwidth, slowing repair progress and degrading service quality. Existing repair mechanisms lack dynamic adaptability to varying foreground traffic patterns and unexpected slow nodes (stragglers).
me: ChameleonEC decomposes repair plans into fine-grained repair tasks and uses three mechanisms: (1) repair task assignment that saturates unoccupied bandwidth while avoiding contention with foreground traffic; (2) repair path establishment that orchestrates elastic transmission routings across dispatched tasks; (3) straggler-aware re-scheduling that dynamically retunes task transmissions and repair plans to bypass slow nodes. The system is implemented and evaluated on Amazon EC2.
nv: Dynamic decomposition and elastic routing of erasure code repair tasks that co-adapts in real time to foreground traffic occupancy and straggler nodes, without modifying the underlying erasure code.
mx: speedup: 4.9-498.2% repair acceleration for various erasure codes; 25.4-73.5% speedup in storage-bottlenecked scenarios
tg: erasure-coding, repair-bandwidth, distributed-storage, straggler-mitigation, network-scheduling, fault-tolerance

t: SoMa: Identifying, Exploring, and Understanding the DRAM Communication Scheduling Space for DNN Accelerators
th: Compiler-driven DRAM communication scheduling across fused DNN layers
pb: As on-chip buffers on DNN accelerators grow large enough to hold most single-layer weights, single-layer dataflow optimization no longer meaningfully reduces DRAM bandwidth pressure. Multi-layer fusion and DRAM communication scheduling (timing of prefetches and stores across fused layers) remain an open, poorly-characterized optimization problem.
me: SoMa introduces a Tensor-centric Notation (TCN) to formally represent and enumerate DRAM communication scheduling schemes across fused layer groups. An end-to-end scheduling compiler framework explores this space jointly optimizing prefetch timing, data store scheduling, and layer fusion decisions for diverse accelerators and workloads. SoMa has been deployed as a compiler for a commercial accelerator product.
nv: Tensor-centric Notation that formally defines and spans the DRAM communication scheduling space for multi-layer fused DNN execution, enabling systematic compiler-driven exploration beyond single-layer dataflow.
mx: speedup: 2.11x average performance improvement vs. Cocco · energy_or_tops_w: 37.3% energy reduction vs. Cocco
tg: dram-scheduling, layer-fusion, compiler, dnn-accelerator, dataflow, multi-layer-optimization

t: Chronus: Understanding and Securing the Cutting-Edge Industry Solutions to DRAM Read Disturbance
th: On-DRAM-die RowHammer mitigation with concurrent counter updates and adaptive refresh
pb: The DDR5 Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC) RowHammer mitigation introduces non-trivial DRAM access latency overhead (counter increment in critical path) and is vulnerable to the 'wave attack' adversarial pattern, forcing overly conservative refresh thresholds that degrade performance.
me: Chronus is an on-DRAM-die RowHammer mitigation that separates activation counters from data arrays, allowing counter updates to proceed concurrently with data accesses (eliminating the latency penalty). It also dynamically controls the number of preventive refreshes issued per back-off signal to neutralize the wave attack — which forces repeated activation bursts to exhaust a fixed-refresh budget. The mechanism requires only in-DRAM modifications and is open-sourced.
nv: Decoupling activation counters from data storage arrays enables concurrent counter updates during memory accesses, eliminating PRAC's critical-path latency penalty while dynamic refresh count control defeats wave attacks.
mx: speedup: Near-zero performance overhead for modern DRAM chips; very low overhead for future chips · other: Outperforms 3 PRAC variants and 3 other state-of-the-art read disturbance solutions
tg: rowhammer, dram-security, prac, ddr5, read-disturbance, memory-reliability

t: Veritas - Demystifying Silent Data Corruptions: uArch-Level Modeling and Fleet Data of Modern x86 CPUs
th: Microarchitecture-level modeling of silent data corruptions in x86 arithmetic units
pb: Silent Data Corruptions (SDCs) caused by silicon defects in arithmetic units (integer and FP units) of modern x86 CPUs are poorly characterized at the microarchitecture level; no public data exists on SDC incident rates across CPU microarchitectures or workloads at fleet scale.
me: A full-system gem5-based fault injector models hardware faults in arithmetic units (integer and floating-point) of five modern x86 microarchitectures. Fault injection experiments measure SDC probability and rates across arithmetic unit types and instruction classes. Real-world defect rate data from large-scale datacenter experiments is integrated with the simulation model to estimate SDC incident rates in deployed fleets.
nv: First microarchitecture-level SDC characterization of arithmetic units (not just array structures) across five x86 microarchitectures, combined with real fleet defect data to estimate actual SDC incident rates.
mx: other: SDC probability and incident rates quantified across 5 x86 microarchitectures; integrated with 1-in-1000 fleet defect rate
tg: silent-data-corruption, fault-injection, x86, reliability, datacenter, arithmetic-units

t: Mithril: A Scalable System for Deep GNN Training
th: Layer-level model parallelism for scalable deep GNN distributed training
pb: Distributed full-graph deep GNN training does not scale to many layers because inter-GPU communication volume grows with graph size and number of layers, overwhelming existing graph parallelism approaches which partition the graph across GPUs and require massive cross-partition neighbor data exchange.
me: Mithril applies layer-level model parallelism to full-graph GNN training: each GPU owns a disjoint subset of consecutive GNN layers and processes all graph nodes for those layers. This reduces per-epoch communication by a factor equal to the number of GNN layers compared to graph parallelism. Pipeline parallelism across layer-partitioned GPUs is realized by partitioning the graph into dependent chunks; inter-chunk embedding dependencies are broken using embedding speculation (speculative forward pass). A hybrid scheme combines Mithril's layer parallelism with graph parallelism for large graphs to improve GPU utilization and ensure convergence.
nv: First application of layer-level model parallelism to full-graph GNN training, combined with embedding speculation to resolve cross-layer data dependencies in a pipelined execution.
mx: speedup: Up to 2.34x (avg 1.49x) on InfiniBand; up to 10.21x (avg 7.16x) on commodity Ethernet vs. graph parallelism baseline · other: Communication volume reduction: up to 22.89x (avg 6.78x) per epoch
tg: gnn, distributed-training, model-parallelism, communication-reduction, embedding-speculation, layer-parallelism

t: NVMePass: A Lightweight, High-performance and Scalable NVMe Virtualization Architecture with I/O Queues Passthrough
th: Hardware-assisted NVMe I/O queue passthrough virtualization with in-device VM isolation
pb: Existing NVMe virtualization approaches either suffer severe performance degradation (Virtio software path) or require dedicated hardware with limited VM scalability (VFIO/SR-IOV hardware passthrough). No solution simultaneously achieves near-native I/O performance, zero CPU overhead, and high VM count scalability.
me: NVMePass is a software-hardware co-design that passes NVMe I/O queues directly to VMs, enabling VMs to submit commands and receive completions without hypervisor involvement. DMA and interrupt remapping are handled without hypervisor interposition. A new hardware primitive, the NVMe Resource Domain (NRD), is implemented in the NVMe controller to enforce VM-level isolation by intercepting illegal I/O requests. Logical block address ranges and I/O queues are exclusively allocated per VM for isolation without per-operation hypervisor overhead.
nv: NVMe Resource Domain (NRD) implemented in the NVMe controller hardware enforces VM isolation at the storage device level, enabling full I/O queue passthrough without any hypervisor involvement in the data path.
mx: speedup: 40% lower latency vs. SPDK-Vhost at 150 VMs; 68% IOPS improvement vs. SPDK-Vhost in real-world app at 100 VMs · other: 100.1-100.5% IOPS of VFIO (near-native)
tg: nvme, storage-virtualization, i/o-passthrough, cloud-storage, vm-isolation, hardware-co-design

t: AsyncDIMM: Achieving Asynchronous Execution in DIMM-Based Near-Memory Processing
th: Asynchronous host-NMA co-execution in DIMM-based near-memory processing
pb: DIMM-based near-memory processing (NMP) architectures cannot efficiently support asynchronous execution between host CPUs and near-memory accelerators (NMAs) because independent memory controllers on both sides cause memory bus contention and potential DRAM errors when issuing concurrent accesses. Existing designs resort to synchronous execution, wasting either host or NMA compute.
me: AsyncDIMM introduces three operational modes on existing memory buses: single access (host or NMA only), concurrent access, and seamless mode switching. An offload-schedule-return mechanism with explicit and implicit synchronization ensures correct memory access semantics across modes. Optimized timing constraints reduce offload latency; a locality-aware switch-recovery method minimizes mode-switch overhead; adaptive batching with timing-division multiplexing notifications improves return bandwidth. Hardware modifications are limited to conventional host and NMA memory controllers and validated on FPGA.
nv: Offload-schedule-return mechanism with dual synchronization modes (explicit and implicit) enabling correct concurrent host+NMA DRAM access on existing unmodified memory buses without protocol changes.
mx: speedup: 1.19x-1.92x over four NMP baselines · other: Up to 2.25x bandwidth utilization uplift; 47% access latency reduction
tg: near-memory-processing, dimm, asynchronous-execution, memory-controller, bandwidth, fpga-validation

t: Grad: Intelligent Microservice Scaling by Harnessing Resource Fungibility
th: Gradient-based joint microservice scaling exploiting resource fungibility
pb: Microservice applications deployed alongside co-located services suffer resource contention that degrades end-to-end latency; existing auto-scaling solutions focus only on scaling critical (bottleneck) microservices and ignore non-critical microservices, missing resource efficiency opportunities through inter-service resource fungibility.
me: Grad uses three components: (1) a modular learning approach that profiles individual microservice latency as a function of environmental conditions (resource allocation, interference); (2) gradient-based extraction from these profiles to design a scalable optimization module that dynamically selects the optimal set of microservices to scale (both critical and non-critical); (3) an end-to-end latency predictor serving as a real-time simulator to provide rapid feedback during SLA violation response. Evaluated on real microservice benchmarks and production traces.
nv: Gradient-based resource fungibility framework that jointly optimizes scaling of both critical and non-critical microservices by modeling their latency-resource trade-offs and inter-service resource substitutability.
mx: other: 49.1% resource usage reduction; 3.7x lower SLA violation probability vs. state-of-the-art
tg: microservices, auto-scaling, resource-fungibility, sla, cloud-scheduling, latency-optimization

t: Gaze into the Pattern: Characterizing Spatial Patterns with Internal Temporal Correlations for Hardware Prefetching
th: Spatial hardware prefetching using intra-footprint temporal correlations
pb: Existing spatial-region hardware prefetchers predict memory access footprints using system-level context features (trigger PC, data address) that fail to capture the intrinsic characteristics of spatial access patterns, resulting in poor flexibility and suboptimal prefetch accuracy across diverse workloads.
me: Gaze extracts footprint-internal temporal correlations — the ordering and timing relationships among cache line accesses within a spatial region — as the primary feature for characterizing and predicting spatial access patterns. This avoids dependence on trigger PC or address-based context lookup. For spatial streaming patterns (very high access density within a region), Gaze applies a dedicated two-stage prefetch approach to suppress over-prefetching: a first stage filters high-density streaming footprints and a second stage applies targeted prefetch decisions to avoid redundant prefetches.
nv: Using footprint-internal temporal correlation (access ordering within spatial regions) rather than external context (trigger PC/address) as the core feature for spatial pattern characterization in a hardware prefetcher.
mx: speedup: 5.7% and 5.4% single-core; 11.4% and 8.8% eight-core IPC improvement vs. PMP and vBerti respectively
tg: hardware-prefetching, spatial-locality, temporal-correlation, cache, memory-hierarchy, over-prefetching

t: eDKM: An Efficient and Accurate Train-Time Weight Clustering for Large Language Models
th: Memory-efficient train-time weight clustering for LLM compression
pb: Differentiable KMeans (DKM) weight clustering achieves state-of-the-art compression accuracy for LLMs but its memory complexity makes train-time application to billion-parameter LLMs nearly impossible, requiring far more GPU memory than available on any single device.
me: eDKM reduces DKM memory footprint during the backward pass by: (1) uniquification — detecting and deduplicating identical tensors before CPU offload to avoid redundant copies; (2) sharding — splitting large tensors across memory partitions for further compression. Both techniques apply to the intermediate tensors that must be retained on CPU during DKM's backward pass. This reduces the train-time memory footprint of a decoder layer by 130x, enabling fine-tuning and compression of a 7B LLaMA model to 3b/weight on standard GPU hardware.
nv: Uniquification-plus-sharding of DKM backward-pass tensors offloaded to CPU, reducing per-decoder-layer memory by 130x and making train-time weight clustering tractable for 7B-parameter LLMs.
mx: accuracy: PIQA: 77.7%; Winogrande: 66.1% at 3b/weight for LLaMA 7B · other: 130x reduction in train-time memory per decoder layer; model size: 12.6 GB to 2.5 GB
tg: weight-clustering, non-linear-quantization, llm-compression, mobile-inference, memory-efficient-training, dkm

t: Bit-slice Architecture for DNN Acceleration with Slice-level Sparsity Enhancement and Exploitation
th: Joint input-weight bit-slice sparsity exploitation for DNN acceleration
pb: Existing bit-slice DNN accelerator architectures exploit sparsity only at coarse granularity — either input or weight sparsity independently — failing to simultaneously leverage both input and weight sparsity at fine (bit-slice chunk) granularity, leaving substantial computational savings unrealized.
me: BADA (Bit-slice Architecture for DNN Acceleration) introduces a front-end unit that generates bit-slices from operands and selectively gathers only non-zero slices using a packed-nonzero selection mechanism, forwarding them to a back-end signed MAC unit. The architecture skips computation for (a) bit-slice chunks containing all zeros (coarse-grained) and (b) any operand pair where either input or weight bit-slice is zero (fine-grained joint sparsity). Two algorithmic optimizations complement the hardware: (1) a novel 8-bit data bit-slice representation with no additional hardware overhead (vs. 6-7 bit limits in prior work); (2) a training-time weight distribution narrowing technique that increases the proportion of zero-valued higher-order bit-slices, enhancing slice-level weight sparsity.
nv: Joint exploitation of both input and weight sparsity at the bit-slice chunk granularity using a front-end non-zero selection unit, combined with a training-aware weight distribution narrowing to amplify higher-order slice sparsity.
mx: speedup: 2.67x throughput vs. LUTein (state-of-the-art bit-slice architecture) · energy_or_tops_w: 2.15x energy efficiency vs. LUTein · area: 1.52x area efficiency vs. LUTein
tg: bit-slice, sparsity, dnn-accelerator, mixed-precision, weight-sparsity, asic

t: Enhancing Large-Scale AI Training Efficiency: The C4 Solution for Real-Time Anomaly Detection and Communication Optimization
th: Collective-communication-driven fault detection and traffic optimization for distributed LLM training
pb: Large-scale distributed LLM training across thousands of GPUs suffers from efficiency loss due to (1) hardware failures that are slow to detect and isolate, and (2) network traffic collisions that cause prolonged GPU idle time during collective communication synchronization steps.
me: C4 exploits two properties of distributed training workloads: (1) homogeneous, iteration-structured load means hardware anomalies produce detectable syndromes in collective communication patterns, enabling rapid faulty-component identification, isolation, and task restart without waiting for software-level timeouts; (2) collective communication involves a small number of long-lived, predictable flows, allowing C4 to perform proactive traffic planning that eliminates bandwidth contention among these flows and reduces collision-induced queuing.
nv: Using collective-communication traffic patterns as a real-time anomaly detection signal, treating the periodic synchronization structure of training iterations as a diagnostic oracle for hardware faults.
mx: other: System efficiency improved 30-45%; error-induced overhead reduced 30%; communication cost reduced 15%
tg: distributed-training, anomaly-detection, collective-communication, network-congestion, llm-training

t: R.I.P. Geomean Speedup Use Equal-Work (Or Equal-Time) Harmonic Mean Speedup Instead
th: Correct statistical methodology for reporting aggregate speedup in computer architecture
pb: Geometric mean speedup, the dominant metric for summarizing multi-workload performance in computer architecture research, is mathematically ill-defined for speedup ratios and produces incorrect average speedup values that can lead to wrong architectural conclusions.
me: The paper derives the harmonic mean speedup from first principles under two explicit assumptions: equal-work (same total work executed on target and baseline, measuring how much faster the target finishes) and equal-time (same elapsed time, measuring how much more work is done). It demonstrates algebraically that equal-work harmonic mean correctly captures the aggregate speedup for a fixed workload mix, while the geometric mean does not. The paper further shows via concrete examples that geometric mean and harmonic mean can give opposite orderings of competing architectures.
nv: Formally establishing that equal-work harmonic mean speedup is the correct aggregate performance metric for computer architecture evaluation and providing a drop-in replacement methodology with clear semantics.
mx: other: Methodology paper; no hardware numbers
tg: methodology, benchmarking, performance-metrics, harmonic-mean, evaluation

t: CORDOBA: Carbon-Efficient Optimization Framework for Computing Systems
th: Carbon-aware hardware design-space optimization with lifecycle carbon metrics
pb: Optimizing the carbon footprint of computing systems across large hardware design spaces is intractable with existing methods because it requires simultaneously trading off operational carbon, embodied carbon, performance, power, and area (PPA) under uncertainty in carbon intensity parameters.
me: CORDOBA introduces the total Carbon Delay Product (tCDP) metric — product of total lifecycle carbon (operational + embodied) and application execution time — as a single scalar objective for carbon-efficient hardware optimization. The framework performs design-space exploration by sweeping hardware configurations (e.g., core count, memory hierarchy, 2D vs. 3D integration via chiplet stacking) and evaluating tCDP under parametric uncertainty in carbon intensity, eliminating up to 98% of the design space as Pareto-dominated. Two case studies apply CORDOBA to real CPU systems: halving cores from 8 to 4 and adopting 3D-stacked logic+memory integration.
nv: The tCDP metric that jointly captures operational carbon, embodied carbon, and performance in one optimization target, enabling principled design-space pruning for carbon-efficient specialized hardware.
mx: other: tCDP improved 1.25x (8→4 cores); tCDP improved 6.9x (3D stacking vs. 2D); 98% design-space elimination
tg: carbon-efficiency, embodied-carbon, design-space-exploration, 3d-stacking, sustainability

t: WarpDrive: GPU-Based Fully Homomorphic Encryption Acceleration Leveraging Tensor and CUDA Cores
th: GPU kernel optimization for Fully Homomorphic Encryption via concurrent CUDA and Tensor Core execution
pb: GPU-based acceleration of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is bottlenecked by frequent pipeline stalls from memory-latency-bound Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) operations and by suboptimal utilization of GPU hardware units, leaving both CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores underused for FHE workloads.
me: WarpDrive applies three key optimizations: (1) computation decomposition of NTT that reduces total instruction count by 73% through arithmetic restructuring; (2) fine-grained memory access design that pipelines loads to eliminate 86% of pipeline stalls; (3) a concurrent-execution framework that runs CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores simultaneously within a single NTT kernel — the first such combined use — exploiting both unit types' complementary throughput characteristics. Additionally, intra-ciphertext parallelism is maximally extracted without requiring ciphertext batching.
nv: First framework to concurrently utilize CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores within the same NTT kernel for FHE, exceeding the throughput of either unit type alone.
mx: speedup: 13.4x NTT throughput, 3.5x homomorphic multiplication, 2.8x FHE workload vs TensorFHE on A100 · other: 1218 KOPS NTT, 305 KOPS homomorphic multiplication on A100; 73% instruction reduction; 86% pipeline stall reduction
tg: fhe, homomorphic-encryption, ntt, tensor-cores, gpu-acceleration

t: Rethinking Dead Block Prediction for Intermittent Computing
th: Power-failure-aware cache dead block prediction for intermittent energy-harvesting systems
pb: Existing dead block predictors, designed for conventional always-on systems, are ineffective in energy-harvesting intermittent computing systems because they do not account for power failures that invalidate cache blocks before they can be reused, causing unnecessary leakage energy waste on blocks that are nominally 'live' but will be lost.
me: EDBP (Enhanced Dead Block Predictor) augments existing dead block predictors with a power-failure-aware prediction layer. It identifies cache blocks that, though predicted live by a conventional predictor, are unlikely to be accessed before the next anticipated power failure. These blocks are deactivated (gated off) to eliminate leakage energy, freeing energy budget for forward execution. EDBP is combined with the Cache Decay predictor to achieve near-theoretical-minimum cache leakage across 20 Mediabench and MiBench applications.
nv: Incorporating power failure prediction into dead block identification, enabling leakage reduction for blocks that are live under a conventional model but unreachable due to imminent energy exhaustion.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 9.8% total energy reduction (EDBP + Cache Decay) · other: 11.9% performance improvement; 6.5% energy reduction standalone; 20 Mediabench/MiBench applications
tg: intermittent-computing, dead-block-prediction, cache-leakage, energy-harvesting, iot

t: Anda: Unlocking Efficient LLM Inference with a Variable-Length Grouped Activation Data Format
th: Adaptive variable-precision activation data format and accelerator for efficient FP-INT LLM GEMM
pb: Weight-only quantized LLMs retain floating-point (FP) activations for accuracy, which shifts the energy and latency bottleneck to costly FP memory accesses and FP-INT GEMM computation; existing LLM accelerators optimize computation alone without jointly addressing data representation and movement for FP activations.
me: Anda proposes a new adaptive activation data type with a group-shared exponent and dynamically allocated mantissa bits per group, enabling variable precision per LLM module. An iterative post-training precision search algorithm determines per-module bit-widths to balance accuracy and efficiency without retraining. On the hardware side, Anda uses a bit-plane-based data organization, bit-serial computation processing elements, and a runtime bit-plane compressor to simultaneously shrink storage, computation, and memory footprint. The result is a hardware-software co-designed accelerator targeting FP-INT GEMM in LLMs.
nv: The Anda data type: a variable-length grouped format with shared exponent and dynamic mantissa allocation that adapts precision per LLM module, jointly optimizing FP data movement and computation for FP-INT GEMM.
mx: speedup: 2.4x over GPU-like FP-FP baseline (FP-INT GEMM) · energy_or_tops_w: 3.1x energy efficiency improvement · area: 4.0x area efficiency improvement
tg: llm-inference, activation-quantization, adaptive-precision, bit-serial, fp-int-gemm

t: NOVA: A Novel Vertex Management Architecture for Scalable Graph Processing
th: Decoupled reduction-propagation vertex management for scalable large-graph hardware processing
pb: Existing graph processing hardware accelerators require temporal graph partitioning to fit the working set into on-chip memory, limiting scalability to large graphs and causing bandwidth inefficiency from repeated DRAM accesses across partition sweeps.
me: NOVA decouples reduction and propagation operations in the vertex-centric graph processing paradigm, allowing the entire working set to reside in off-chip DRAM rather than being partitioned across on-chip memory. On-chip memory is repurposed as a prefetch/access buffer to hide DRAM latency rather than as a traditional cache holding graph state. The design enables spatial tiling across multiple NOVA nodes for scale-out, achieving near-perfect weak and strong scaling. A cycle-accurate gem5-based model validates the architecture.
nv: Decoupling reduction and propagation in the vertex-centric paradigm to eliminate the requirement for temporal graph partitioning, enabling direct DRAM-resident large-graph processing with latency-hiding on-chip buffers.
mx: speedup: 2.35x over PolyGraph on 134M-vertex 2.14B-edge synthetic graph
