t: PROCA: Programmable Probabilistic Processing Unit Architecture with Accept/Reject Prediction & Multicore Pipelining for Causal Inference
th: Programmable PIM-based MCMC accelerator with accept/reject prediction for causal inference
pb: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms for probabilistic programming and causal inference are extremely compute-intensive and inherently sequential, preventing effective parallelization on CPUs and GPUs; existing MCMC accelerators are not programmable across arbitrary posterior distribution forms.
me: PROCA is a programmable MCMC processing unit using processing-in-memory (PIM) function units to generate Markov chain samples. A novel accept/reject prediction methodology predicts whether a proposed sample will be accepted before completing full posterior evaluation, enabling multi-core pipelining: compute for the next sample begins before the current accept/reject decision finalizes. The architecture is programmable to support arbitrary posterior distribution forms compatible with software probabilistic programming frameworks (e.g., PyMC). Implemented using commercial process development kits and validated on 9 benchmarks spanning PyMC tutorials, single-variable problems, and real-world causal inference tasks.
nv: Accept/reject prediction that breaks the sequential dependency of MCMC sampling chains, enabling multi-core pipelined execution of arbitrary posterior distributions with PIM-based sample generation.
mx: speedup: 172-4871x over Intel Xeon Gold CPU; 42-1058x over NVIDIA A100 GPU; 1.765x over SOTA MCMC accelerator · energy_or_tops_w: 9.47x energy efficiency over SOTA MCMC accelerators
tg: mcmc, probabilistic-programming, causal-inference, processing-in-memory, bayesian-inference

t: The Importance of Generalizability in Machine Learning for Systems
th: OOD generalization and Bayesian uncertainty estimation for ML-driven cloud resource management
pb: ML models deployed in cloud system management tasks frequently encounter out-of-distribution (OOD) data — workloads or resource demand patterns not represented in training data — causing silent mispredictions that degrade server resource balance without any indication of model unreliability.
me: The paper analyzes several ML models used for resource balance in Google's production fleet, empirically demonstrating OOD failure modes. It evaluates multiple OOD detection techniques (distance-based, confidence-based, ensemble methods) and quantifies their trade-offs in precision, recall, and inference overhead. It then demonstrates that Bayesian models — which produce calibrated uncertainty estimates over their outputs — can effectively flag low-confidence predictions to a human operator or fallback policy, improving reliability of ML-driven resource balancing.
nv: Using Bayesian models with native uncertainty quantification as a practical OOD detection mechanism for production ML-for-systems deployments, demonstrated at Google fleet scale.
mx: other: Qualitative and empirical demonstration of OOD detection efficacy on Google fleet; specific numbers not stated in abstract
tg: ml-for-systems, out-of-distribution, bayesian-inference, cloud-resource-management, generalization

t: ER-DCIM: Error-Resilient Digital CIM Architecture with Run-Time MAC-Cell Error Correction
th: Run-time MAC-level error correction for reliable low-voltage digital compute-in-memory
pb: Digital compute-in-memory (DCIM) macros are susceptible to SRAM cell errors under low-voltage operation (needed for high energy efficiency), but traditional SRAM error correcting codes (ECC) that correct errors in a single read-out row are incompatible with DCIM's simultaneous multi-row readout for MAC computation, leaving MAC-cell errors uncorrected.
me: ER-DCIM introduces three mechanisms: (1) a residue code-based MAC error correction scheme that detects and corrects additive errors in the MAC accumulation result in real time during DCIM computation — the first such mechanism for DCIM; (2) a progressive cell error correction mechanism that identifies and corrects underlying SRAM cell errors incrementally without stalling computation; (3) a mode switcher that repurposes redundant error-resilient logic (reserved for low-voltage protection) to boost performance in high-voltage mode, avoiding area waste.
nv: Residue code-based real-time MAC error correction for digital CIM, the first mechanism to correct additive errors in DCIM MAC results during live computation rather than at the SRAM cell or row level.
mx: other: Maintains accuracy without loss in both low-voltage and high-voltage modes; no accuracy degradation stated vs. baseline
tg: compute-in-memory, error-correction, sram, low-voltage, reliability

t: GSArch: Breaking Memory Barriers in 3D Gaussian Splatting Training via Architectural Support
th: Architectural support for memory-efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting training via hot/cold Gaussian buffering
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training is bottlenecked by three memory system inefficiencies: redundant off-chip DRAM loads for large 'hot' Gaussians accessed repeatedly across pixels, expensive atomic write operations during gradient accumulation, and severe bank conflicts during on-chip buffer reads during backward propagation.
me: GSArch introduces three architectural mechanisms targeting the three bottlenecks: (1) Hybrid memory management that classifies Gaussians as 'hot' (large, high pixel overlap, repeatedly loaded) or 'cold' and caches hot Gaussians in a fast on-chip buffer to eliminate redundant DRAM fetches; (2) Gradient informativeness filtering that identifies low-contribution gradients and skips their atomic write operations during backward propagation; (3) A rearrangement unit that packs conflicting on-chip memory read requests into non-conflicting bundles to eliminate bank conflicts. These techniques combine to accelerate the backward pass of 3DGS training.
nv: Gaussian 'hotness' classification for hybrid on-chip/off-chip memory management that eliminates the dominant redundant DRAM load pattern in 3DGS training backward propagation.
mx: speedup: Up to 6.49x over A100 GPU; up to 15.42x over Jetson AGX Xavier · energy_or_tops_w: Substantially lower energy consumption (not quantified in abstract)
tg: 3d-gaussian-splatting, neural-scene-representation, memory-management, gradient-sparsity, training-accelerator

t: EXION: Exploiting Inter-and Intra-Iteration Output Sparsity for Diffusion Models
th: Inter- and intra-iteration output sparsity exploitation for diffusion model acceleration via FFN-Reuse and ConMerge
pb: Diffusion model inference requires up to 1000 denoising iterations through transformer blocks (dominant 38-100% of operations), resulting in excessive energy consumption and latency; existing transformer accelerators target only QKV projection and attention computation within a single iteration and do not exploit the iterative structure or the dominant FFN layer overhead.
me: EXION is a SW-HW co-designed diffusion accelerator exploiting two types of output sparsity. First, the FFN-Reuse algorithm identifies temporal data redundancy across iterations in FFN GELU outputs: one dense iteration is computed fully, then N sparse iterations reuse the GELU output for low-magnitude elements (achieving 70-97% sparsity in the 1st FFN layer, reducing FFN ops by 52-85%). Second, an improved eager prediction algorithm using two-step leading-one detection (TS-LOD) predicts attention scores via log-domain approximation to identify and skip negligible attention computation within each iteration (20-95% intra-iteration sparsity, skipping avg. 26% Q and 22% KV projections). The ConMerge data compaction mechanism converts resulting unstructured sparse output matrices into compact dense forms via column condensing (removing all-zero columns) and block merging (merging sparse and dense tiled blocks using conflict-vector tracking). The dedicated hardware Diffusion-Sparsity Aware Core (DSC) contains: a Sparse-Dense Unified Engine (SDUE) with a 16x16 DPU array with per-DPU input/weight/conflict-vector switches enabling flexible ConMerge-aware dataflow; a ConMerge Assistant Unit (CAU) with sparsity-level sorting and ConMerge vector generation; an Eager Prediction Engine (EPRE) with TS-LOD-enhanced log-domain DPU array; and a Configurable SIMD Engine (CFSE) for special functions. Synthesized at 14nm, 800MHz, 0.8V.
nv: FFN-Reuse: the first algorithm exploiting temporal data redundancy in FFN GELU outputs across diffusion iteration steps to create inter-iteration output sparsity, combined with a ConMerge hardware mechanism that converts unstructured output sparsity into compact matrices executable at high utilization.
mx: speedup: 3.2-379.3x over RTX 6000 Ada (server GPU); 42.6-1090.9x over Jetson Orin Nano (edge GPU); 5.2x vs Cambricon-D on DiT · energy_or_tops_w: 45.1-3067.6x energy efficiency over server GPU; 196.9-4668.2x over edge GPU · area: EXION24 (24 DSCs + 64MB GSC): 152.28mm2 vs. RTX 6000 Ada 609mm2 · ppa: Single DSC: 4.37mm2, 1511.43mW at 14nm 800MHz 0.8V · accuracy: Negligible accuracy loss across 7 models (FFN-Reuse: zero accuracy impact; EP+TS-LOD: minimal PSNR/FID degradation) · other: FFN-Reuse: 52-85% FFN op reduction; ConMerge: 77.4%->8.4% remaining cols (Stable Diffusion); CAU area: 0.94% of DSC
tg: diffusion-model, output-sparsity, ffn-reuse, sw-hw-codesign, asic-accelerator, attention-sparsity

t: M-ANT: Efficient Low-bit Group Quantization for LLMs via Mathematically Adaptive Numerical Type
th: per-group adaptive quantization for LLM accelerators
pb: Existing adaptive data types for LLM group quantization provide adaptivity at the tensor level, but small quantization groups within the same tensor exhibit markedly different distributions that tensor-level formats cannot accommodate. Additionally, dynamically generated KV caches require efficient real-time quantization that existing approaches do not support well.
me: MANT defines a mathematically adaptive numeric type with a flexible encoding paradigm covering a wider range of data distributions than prior adaptive types. A hardware framework assigns the appropriate MANT variant to each quantization group dynamically. A dedicated processing element (PE) fuses decoding and computation, and a real-time quantization unit handles dynamic KV cache quantization. These PEs are integrated into a systolic array, unifying weight and KV cache quantization in a single datapath.
nv: A per-group adaptive numeric type with a decoding-computation fusion mechanism that simultaneously handles both weight quantization and real-time KV cache quantization in a systolic array accelerator.
mx: speedup: 2.99x average (up to 4.46x) over state-of-the-art LLM accelerator · energy_or_tops_w: 2.81x average (up to 4.10x) energy reduction
tg: group-quantization, adaptive-numeric-type, kv-cache, systolic-array, llm-inference

t: EFFACT: A Highly Efficient Full-Stack FHE Acceleration Platform
th: full-stack FHE hardware acceleration
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) suffers from massive ciphertext expansion (thousands of times over plaintext) and enormous off-chip memory bandwidth demands during bootstrapping and privacy-preserving ML inference, making it impractically slow on existing hardware.
me: EFFACT combines a compiler with comprehensive optimizations and vector-friendly hardware targeting both FPGA and ASIC. Key mechanisms include: (1) a streaming memory access scheme that achieves high throughput with limited on-chip SRAM by overlapping data movement with computation; (2) a circuit-level function unit reuse scheme that reduces computing resources without performance loss; (3) novel NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) and automorphism hardware units designed for cost-sensitive architectures. An ISA and compiler backend support multiple FHE schemes (CKKS, BGV, BFV), and design space exploration determines optimal SRAM sizing.
nv: A streaming memory access optimization that enables high NTT throughput with limited on-chip SRAM by exploiting the sequential access pattern of FHE kernels, combined with a circuit-level function unit reuse scheme.
mx: speedup: FPGA version 1.22x geomean over SOTA FPGA FHE accelerators; ASIC shows improved performance per chip area and performance per Watt vs SOTA ASIC works
tg: fhe, homomorphic-encryption, ntt, fpga, asic, privacy-preserving-ml

t: Efficient Optimization with Encoded Ising Models
th: encoded constraint enforcement for Ising-based combinatorial optimization
pb: Ising solvers (quantum, oscillator-based, and probabilistic computers) must include penalty terms to enforce constraints for combinatorial optimization problems, causing solvers to spend the majority of compute time exploring infeasible states and often failing to find any feasible solution.
me: The Encoded Ising Model (E-I model) extends the standard Ising model by inserting a digital encoding circuit between the solver and the energy landscape, restricting the search space to only feasible states without penalty terms. The Fuse software framework provides a high-level API to describe such constrained functions and automatically lowers them to a p-computer target. The encoding circuit uses a combinational logic layer that maps solver spin states to legal variable assignments, reducing the fraction of iterations spent on infeasible solutions by orders of magnitude.
nv: Inserting a digital encoding circuit into the Ising solver loop to structurally eliminate infeasible states from the search space, replacing penalty-term energy barriers with hard logical constraints.
mx: speedup: 7.2x to 52000x reduction in iterations to solution · accuracy: Up to 100% higher estimated success probability over baseline Ising formulations
tg: ising-model, probabilistic-computing, combinatorial-optimization, quantum-computing, constraint-encoding

t: SparseWeaver: Converting Sparse Operations as Dense Operations on GPUs for Graph Workloads
th: sparse-to-dense graph operation conversion via GPU hardware extension
pb: Real-world graph workloads have sparse and skewed adjacency structures that cause severe warp-level load imbalance on GPUs, where existing software or hardware balancing schemes incur memory overhead or excessive inter- and intra-warp synchronization cost.
me: SparseWeaver is a hardware-software co-design that converts sparse graph operations into balanced dense operations by exploiting graph topology. A lightweight GPU functional unit microarchitecture called Weaver is added to GPU cores; it analyzes common sparse-to-dense conversion patterns identified via static/dynamic analysis and implements the conversion directly in the execution pipeline, leveraging memory access locality without additional synchronization. The design is prototyped on the open-source RISC-V Vortex GPU.
nv: Converting sparse graph operations to dense ones at the hardware level using a dedicated Weaver functional unit that exploits topology-driven patterns, eliminating the memory and synchronization overhead of prior software balancing schemes.
mx: speedup: 2.36x faster execution time vs SOTA schemes · area: 0.045% area overhead from added dedicated logic registers
tg: graph-processing, sparse-to-dense, gpu-microarchitecture, warp-balancing, risc-v-gpu

t: EIGEN: Enabling Efficient 3DIC Interconnect with Heterogeneous Dual-Layer Network-on-Active-Interposer
th: dual-layer RL-guided network-on-active-interposer for chiplet systems
pb: Chiplet-based 3DIC systems using active interposers struggle with heterogeneous and high-load inter-chiplet network traffic patterns because their interconnects are tightly coupled to top-die designs, preventing flexible topology adaptation and causing high latency and traffic congestion.
me: EIGEN implements a heterogeneous dual-layer interconnect on the active interposer: an application-aware switch-programmable layer (AspLayer) for static topology optimization and a dynamic packet-routing layer (DynLayer) for adaptive traffic management. A reinforcement learning (RL)-based path routing framework is trained with a state space covering topology, network, and memory metrics, with reward defined as the product of average packet latency and link utilization. The two layers cooperate to route inter-chiplet traffic with reduced hops and congestion.
nv: A dual-layer active-interposer NoC that separates static topology programmability from dynamic adaptive routing, coordinated by an RL-based framework trained on combined latency-utilization reward.
mx: speedup: Up to 11.21% runtime reduction vs SOTA · other: Up to 67.16% latency reduction, 53.89% hop reduction; scalable from 4x4 to 32x32 chiplets
tg: chiplet, active-interposer, noc, reinforcement-learning, 3dic, interconnect

t: Zebra: Efficient Redundant Array of Zoned Namespace SSDs Enabled by Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA)
th: ZNS RAID partial parity management via ZRWA exploitation
pb: Integrating ZNS SSDs into RAID configurations requires handling partial parity updates (PPUs) that arise from ZNS's append-only write semantics; existing metadata-zone-based solutions become performance bottlenecks under high PPU workloads.
me: Zebra exploits the Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA), the SSD's internal write buffer in front of each zone, to handle PPUs in-place. By ensuring that parity chunks fit within the ZRWA window, Zebra performs partial parity overrides within the buffer rather than writing to separate metadata zones. A set of complementary techniques maintain high performance and reliability across both large-zone and small-zone ZNS SSD models.
nv: Using the ZRWA (the SSD's native write buffer window) as the target storage for parity partial updates in ZNS RAID, matching the repeated sequential overwrite I/O pattern of PPUs to the ZRWA's random-write capability.
mx: speedup: 1.1x to 4.2x throughput improvement vs RAIZN ZNS RAID system
tg: zns-ssd, raid, storage, parity, zrwa, io-system

t: throttLL'eM: Predictive GPU Throttling for Energy Efficient LLM Inference Serving
th: predictive GPU frequency scaling for energy-efficient LLM inference serving
pb: LLM inference serving on GPUs consumes excessive energy while providers must simultaneously satisfy Service-Level Objectives (SLOs); static GPU frequency settings over-provision compute resources when request load is low or KV cache pressure is manageable.
me: throttLL'eM uses instance sizing and GPU frequency scaling guided by an ML model that predicts future KV cache usage and batch size. The ML model receives projections of these metrics as inputs and outputs per-iteration performance estimates, enabling iteration-level frequency decisions. The R^2 score exceeds 0.97 and misprediction is under 1 iteration/second on average. Frequency scaling and instance count adjustments are applied jointly to reduce energy while keeping within SLO bounds.
nv: Iteration-granularity GPU frequency scaling for LLM inference driven by a predictive ML model of KV cache usage and batch size, enabling proactive throttling rather than reactive power capping.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: Up to 43.8% lower energy; at least 1.71x energy efficiency improvement under SLOs vs NVIDIA Triton server
tg: llm-inference, gpu-throttling, energy-efficiency, slo, kv-cache, frequency-scaling

t: Panacea: Novel DNN Accelerator using Accuracy-Preserving Asymmetric Quantization and Energy-Saving Bit-Slice Sparsity
th: asymmetric-quantization-aware bit-slice sparsity acceleration
pb: Symmetric quantization introduces unacceptable accuracy loss for large-scale DNNs due to asymmetric activation distributions, but existing asymmetric quantization schemes produce many nonzero bit-slices that cannot be exploited by bit-slice GEMM accelerators designed for symmetric (zero-heavy) representations.
me: Panacea introduces Asymmetrically-Quantized bit-Slice GEMM (AQS-GEMM), which compresses frequent nonzero slices generated by asymmetric quantization and skips their computation. Two algorithm-hardware co-optimization techniques increase slice-level sparsity: zero-point manipulation (adjusting quantization zero points to shift frequent values toward zero) and distribution-based bit-slicing (selecting bit-slices that maximize sparsity based on activation distribution). Panacea's dataflow is specialized for sparse/dense mixed workloads on tiled AQS-GEMM, with run-length encoding to maximize data reuse and minimize off-chip memory traffic.
nv: AQS-GEMM: the first bit-slice GEMM formulation that compresses and skips nonzero slices produced by asymmetric quantization rather than only exploiting symmetric zero slices.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 1.97x energy efficiency over Sibia, 3.26x over SIMD on OPT-2.7B · speedup: 1.88x throughput over Sibia, 2.41x over SIMD on OPT-2.7B
tg: asymmetric-quantization, bit-slice-sparsity, gemm, dnn-accelerator, llm-inference

t: Multi-Dimensional Vector ISA Extension for Mobile In-Cache Computing
th: multi-dimensional vector ISA for mobile in-SRAM computing
pb: Existing long-vector ISA extensions (RISC-V RVV, Arm SVE) provide only 1D strided and random memory accesses, which cannot efficiently utilize the 8192-lane SIMD width of in-SRAM vector engines built from mobile L2 caches because mobile data-parallel kernels expose limited 1D parallelism (average 635 elements) across multiple multi-dimensional data structures.
me: MVE (Multi-dimensional Vector ISA Extension) introduces up to 4D strided and random vector memory accesses, where each dimension can use stride modes: replicate (stride=0), sequential (stride=1), row-stride (stride=previous_dim x length), or arbitrary CR-configured stride. A dimension-level masked execution mechanism masks entire outer-dimension iterations using a compact mask control register, avoiding expensive per-lane scalar mask computation. The ISA operates on physical registers spanning all in-SRAM compute arrays (8192 lanes of 32-bit data), with a cache-geometry-hiding register abstraction. The MVE controller in the L2 cache flattens multi-dimensional logical register accesses to physical SRAM bitline coordinates, uses a Transpose Memory Unit (TMU) with 8T transpose bit-cells and a crossbar to route data into vertical bit-serial layout, and manages cache coherency by checking L1 presence bits and evicting L1 lines before in-cache writes. Compiler support includes liveness analysis for register width, list-hybrid instruction scheduling, and greedy register allocation to minimize in-cache register spills.
nv: A multi-dimensional vector ISA (up to 4D strided + random memory accesses with dimension-level masked execution) that hides cache geometry from programmers while raising in-cache SIMD lane utilization from 23% to 60% for mobile workloads.
mx: speedup: 2.9x vs Arm Neon; 9.3x vs Adreno 640 GPU; 2.0x vs RISC-V RVV on same in-cache engine; 1.5x vs Duality Cache (SIMT model) · energy_or_tops_w: 8.8x energy reduction vs Arm Neon; 5.2x energy reduction vs Adreno 640 GPU · area: 3.6% area overhead to mobile core (at 7nm)
tg: in-cache-computing, isa-extension, mobile-processor, sram-compute, multi-dimensional-vector, in-sram

t: BrokenSleep: Remote Power Timing Attack Exploiting Processor Idle States
th: remote C-state-based timing side-channel attack
pb: Modern processors support multiple C-state (idle) levels with different wake-up latencies; an attacker can remotely detect which C-state a victim processor core is in by measuring network response timing, enabling covert and side-channel communication across nodes without requiring co-location on the same machine.
me: BrokenSleep exploits the deterministic wake-up latency differences between processor C-states (C0 active, C1/C1E/C6 sleep) to encode information in the timing of network responses from a victim server. The attacker sends network requests and measures response latency; the victim's current C-state (determined by its workload idle pattern) is deduced from the latency profile. Both covert channel (data exfiltration across security boundaries without direct network access) and side-channel (keystroke timing inference) variants are demonstrated. The attack affects both Intel and ARM processors, exploiting standard ACPI power management without any microarchitectural vulnerability.
nv: The first remote timing attack based purely on processor idle-state (C-state) wake-up latency differences, eliminating the co-location requirement of all prior power-based side-channel attacks.
mx: other: Demonstrated covert channel and keystroke timing inference over external network on Intel and ARM CPUs
tg: side-channel, covert-channel, c-state, power-attack, remote-timing, security

t: Ditto: Accelerating Diffusion Model via Temporal Value Similarity
th: temporal difference sparsity exploitation for diffusion model acceleration
pb: Diffusion models require many iterative denoising steps, each a full forward pass of a large network, causing prohibitive computation and memory overhead; adjacent time steps produce outputs with high value similarity and narrow differences that are not exploited by existing accelerators.
me: Ditto exploits temporal value similarity: adjacent time-step outputs differ narrowly, and these differences are quantized to reduced bit-widths (often zero). The Ditto algorithm performs a full-precision pass on the first time step, then computes subsequent steps using quantized temporal differences and the distributive property of layer operations, avoiding redundant computation for near-zero or zero differences. Ditto execution flow optimization reorganizes memory access patterns to reduce the memory overhead of storing and retrieving temporal difference data. The Ditto hardware accelerator is co-designed with the algorithm, with specialized units for dynamic difference sparsity exploitation.
nv: Algorithm-hardware co-design that quantizes inter-timestep activation differences to exploit temporal sparsity in diffusion model denoising, performing near-zero or zero-difference skipping without accuracy loss.
mx: speedup: Up to 1.5x speedup vs other accelerators · energy_or_tops_w: 17.74% energy saving vs other accelerators
tg: diffusion-model, temporal-similarity, quantization, sparsity, hardware-accelerator

t: LSQCA: Resource-Efficient Load/Store Architecture for Limited-Scale Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
th: load/store memory architecture for resource-efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing
pb: Current fault-tolerant quantum computer (FTQC) floorplan strategies devote 50% of qubit memory space to routing/overhead required for unit-time random access to all logical qubits, leaving only half the qubit count available for data storage when qubits are scarce.
me: LSQCA (Load/Store Quantum Computer Architecture) separates logical qubit memory into Computational Registers (CR), a small fast-access region, and Scan-Access Memory (SAM), a dense storage region accessed with variable latency. An instruction set is defined over these abstractions, with concrete implementations as point-SAM and line-SAM architectures. Access latency in SAM is hidden by overlapping it with other computational bottlenecks, exploiting access locality patterns identified through static analysis of quantum program memory reference timestamps. Optimization techniques leverage locality in memory reference ordering to further reduce effective latency penalties.
nv: Separating quantum memory into fast Computational Registers and dense Scan-Access Memory, achieving nearly 100% memory density (vs 50% state-of-the-art) by tolerating variable-latency qubit access and hiding latency via static analysis-guided scheduling.
mx: other: ~90% memory density vs ~50% for conventional FTQC floorplans; only 5% execution time increase
tg: quantum-computing, fault-tolerant, floorplan, qubit-memory, resource-efficiency

t: Revisiting Reliability in Large-Scale Machine Learning Research Clusters
th: ML cluster reliability and failure characterization
pb: Large-scale ML training clusters suffer from frequent job failures whose impact on training efficiency is not well characterized across different job sizes and cluster configurations. Existing failure models do not adequately capture workload diversity or provide actionable metrics like Effective Training Time Ratio (ETTR).
me: The authors conducted an 11-month observational study across two large multi-tenant A100 GPU clusters totaling 4 million jobs and over 150 million GPU-hours. They developed a failure taxonomy, computed Mean Time to Failure (MTTF) as a function of GPU count by fitting a failure model to operational data, and derived an analytical estimator for Effective Training Time Ratio (ETTR) as a function of job parameters (checkpoint interval, restart overhead, failure rate). The ETTR model is used to project the efficacy of software mitigations such as more frequent checkpointing.
nv: Introducing the Effective Training Time Ratio (ETTR) metric and its analytical model, enabling quantitative projection of software mitigation strategies across different GPU scales.
mx: other: MTTF projected for various GPU scales; ETTR derived analytically; 4M jobs, 150M+ A100 GPU-hours analyzed
