t: PAISE: PIM-Accelerated Inference Scheduling Engine for Transformer-based LLM
th: PIM-accelerated LLM attention offloading
pb: LLM inference on GPUs is memory-bound due to the attention layer's low arithmetic intensity and high memory traffic from frequent KV-cache updates, leading to elevated latency under autoregressive token generation. GPU-only execution under-utilizes available bandwidth for attention operations.
me: PAISE offloads memory-intensive attention operations from an AMD MI100 GPU to HBM-PIM devices via a GPU-PIM heterogeneous scheduling framework. A scheduling algorithm determines per-operation offload decisions based on model configuration (layer type, head count) and PIM hardware specifications (bandwidth, FLOPS). An enhanced PIM kernel implements transaction-wise interleave-batched GEMM, restructuring data layout so multiple attention heads' KV reads are interleaved across PIM banks, maximizing memory-level parallelism within the HBM-PIM device.
nv: Transaction-wise interleave-batched GEMM on HBM-PIM that reorders KV-cache data layout to exploit bank-level parallelism, combined with a model-aware scheduling algorithm that decides which transformer layers to offload.
mx: speedup: up to 48.3% execution time reduction vs GPU-only for attention layer
tg: pim, llm-inference, attention, hbm-pim, heterogeneous-computing, kv-cache

t: Let-Me-In: (Still) Employing In-pointer Bounds Metadata for Fine-grained GPU Memory Safety
th: fine-grained GPU memory safety via in-pointer metadata
pb: GPU programs written in C/C++ inherit memory safety vulnerabilities such as out-of-bounds accesses. The heterogeneous GPU memory hierarchy (heap, local memory, thousands of concurrent threads) makes it difficult to enforce fine-grained bounds checking with low overhead.
me: LMI aligns GPU memory allocations to powers-of-two boundaries and performs static analysis at compile time to identify and mark pointer arithmetic instructions. Bounds metadata (base and size) is encoded into the unused upper bits of 64-bit GPU virtual address pointers, eliminating separate metadata memory structures. Hardware bounds-checking logic validates each memory access against the in-pointer metadata before issuing the request, adding minimal per-access latency even under thousands of concurrent threads.
nv: Storing per-object bounds metadata entirely within the unused upper bits of GPU pointers, made feasible by power-of-two allocation alignment and static pointer-arithmetic tagging, eliminating separate metadata tables and their associated overhead.
mx: area: negligible hardware overhead (claimed) · other: negligible performance overhead vs baseline GPU execution
tg: gpu-security, memory-safety, bounds-checking, pointer-tagging, static-analysis

t: VR-Pipe: Streamlining Hardware Graphics Pipeline for Volume Rendering
th: hardware graphics pipeline optimization for volume/radiance-field rendering
pb: Radiance field rendering methods (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting) are evaluated only on software-based shader pipelines, leaving performance on fixed-function GPU hardware graphics units unexplored and suboptimal for volume rendering workloads.
me: VR-Pipe integrates two hardware innovations into the fixed-function GPU graphics pipeline: (1) native early termination support by repurposing existing special-purpose hardware (e.g., depth test units) to terminate ray marching when accumulated opacity saturates; (2) multi-granular tile binning with quad merging, which opportunistically blends fragments in programmable shader cores before passing them to fixed-function blending units, reducing blending bottlenecks. The design targets the 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline as a concrete instantiation.
nv: Repurposing existing GPU fixed-function hardware for early termination in volume rendering and introducing multi-granular tile binning with quad merging to pre-blend fragments in shader cores before fixed-function blending.
mx: speedup: up to 2.78x over conventional GPU graphics pipeline · area: negligible hardware overhead
tg: gpu-graphics, volume-rendering, 3d-gaussian-splatting, early-termination, tile-binning, neural-rendering

t: Marching Page Walks: Batching and Concurrent Page Table Walks for Enhancing GPU Throughput
th: batched concurrent GPU page table walking to reduce queuing latency
pb: GPU page table walkers handle only a single walk request at a time, creating severe queuing latency when thousands of concurrent threads simultaneously demand address translation across wide virtual address ranges.
me: Marching Page Walks (MPW) scans the pool of pending walk requests to identify groups that can share memory accesses (e.g., walks to nearby pages sharing a page table entry lookup). It batches these requests and concurrently issues multiple memory instructions per walker to service several walks simultaneously, exploiting the observation that GPU workloads access pages in wide but often co-located address ranges.
nv: Enabling a single GPU page table walker to issue multiple memory instructions concurrently by batching pending walk requests that share page table structure accesses, directly attacking queuing latency rather than walker count.
mx: speedup: 55.6% average GPU performance improvement over baseline · other: 86.7% reduction in page walk queuing latency
tg: gpu-mmu, page-table-walk, address-translation, virtual-memory, throughput

t: Uni-Render: A Unified Accelerator for Real-Time Rendering Across Diverse Neural Renderers
th: unified reconfigurable ASIC accelerator for diverse neural rendering pipelines
pb: Existing neural rendering accelerators are designed for a single specific rendering pipeline, making them unable to efficiently support the diverse and evolving landscape of neural rendering algorithms (NeRF, 3DGS, hybrid methods) required for different application scenarios.
me: Uni-Render is a reconfigurable hardware ASIC accelerator that identifies common operators shared across diverse neural rendering pipelines (ray marching, Gaussian rasterization, MLP inference, volume compositing) and implements a configurable dataflow engine that dynamically adjusts dataflow and operator mapping to match the computational profile of each specific rendering algorithm. The hardware architecture supports both typical and hybrid rendering pipelines through runtime reconfiguration of its processing elements and memory hierarchy.
nv: A single reconfigurable accelerator architecture that covers the full breadth of representative neural rendering pipelines by exploiting their shared computational operators while dynamically adapting dataflow for each pipeline's specific requirements.
mx: speedup: up to 119x over state-of-the-art neural rendering hardware · energy_or_tops_w: ~5W power budget (edge device constraint) · other: >30 FPS real-time rendering achieved
tg: neural-rendering, unified-accelerator, reconfigurable-hardware, edge-inference, 3d-gaussian-splatting, nerf

t: LUT-DLA: Lookup Table as Efficient Extreme Low-Bit Deep Learning Accelerator
th: vector-quantization LUT accelerator for extreme low-bit DNN inference
pb: Scalar quantization cannot reduce DNN bit-width below 1-bit, capping compression gains; existing accelerators lack hardware support for vector-quantization-based LUT approaches that could push beyond this limit.
me: LUT-DLA converts DNN weight tensors into lookup tables via vector quantization, replacing multiply-accumulate operations with LUT index lookups and accumulations. The LUTBoost algorithm trains DNNs through a multistage process to learn LUT-compatible vector codebooks. A co-design space exploration framework evaluates the trade-off between LUT table size, codebook dimensionality, model accuracy, and hardware cost to select optimal hardware configurations. The ASIC accelerator implements LUT fetch-and-accumulate dataflow units that directly consume quantized indices to perform inference.
nv: Replacing conventional scalar MAC units with vector-quantization LUT fetch-and-accumulate hardware, achieving extreme sub-1-bit-equivalent compression through a hardware-algorithm co-design framework including the LUTBoost multistage training algorithm.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 1.4-7.0x power efficiency improvement · area: 1.5-146.1x area efficiency improvement · accuracy: 0.1-3.8% accuracy drop on CNNs; 1.4-3.0% on transformers
tg: lookup-table, vector-quantization, extreme-low-bit, dnn-accelerator, hardware-algorithm-codesign

t: Adyna: Accelerating Dynamic Neural Networks with Adaptive Scheduling
th: hardware-software co-design for dynamic neural network inference acceleration
pb: Dynamic neural networks (DynNNs) conditionally skip computation based on input difficulty, but current GPUs and specialized accelerators lack dataflow and architecture support to realize the theoretical efficiency gains, because the dynamic execution patterns defeat static resource allocation.
me: Adyna uses a unified representation to model diverse DynNN variants and introduces a dynamism-aware multi-kernel selection paradigm. At runtime, a dataflow scheduler observes the distribution of dynamic size values (e.g., number of active tokens or blocks) and selects among multiple precompiled kernels, each optimized for a specific dynamic-size bucket. An effective kernel sampling algorithm chooses the minimal set of kernels to precompile and cache on the accelerator, balancing coverage against on-chip memory cost. The hardware architecture supports multi-tile and multi-tenant execution to handle concurrent dynamic workloads.
nv: A dynamism-aware multi-kernel selection paradigm that precompiles and caches a small set of specialized kernels covering the distribution of dynamic computation sizes, enabling optimal hardware utilization across varying input-dependent workload sizes.
mx: speedup: 1.70x over multi-tile accelerator (avg), up to 2.32x; 1.57x over multi-tenant accelerator (avg), up to 2.01x
tg: dynamic-neural-networks, adaptive-scheduling, multi-kernel, early-exit, conditional-computation

t: Integrating Prefetcher Selection with Dynamic Request Allocation Improves Prefetching Efficiency
th: fine-grained per-request prefetcher selection to reduce hybrid prefetcher conflicts
pb: Hybrid hardware prefetchers sharing the same MSHRs and bandwidth resources create conflicts where competing prefetch requests from different algorithms negate each other's coverage, and existing prefetcher selection algorithms use inaccurate demand request allocation and coarse-grained selection criteria.
me: Alecto is a prefetcher selection algorithm that intercepts each demand request before routing it to prefetchers. For each demand request, Alecto determines the most suitable prefetcher(s) by evaluating fine-grained per-request suitability metrics (accuracy, coverage, timeliness). It then dynamically routes each demand request only to the prefetcher(s) best suited for that specific access, rather than broadcasting to all prefetchers. This per-request allocation prevents table pollution in temporal prefetchers and reduces resource contention.
nv: Per-demand-request prefetcher selection that routes each request only to the most suitable prefetcher, simultaneously improving accuracy, coverage, and timeliness while drastically reducing prefetcher table energy by avoiding unnecessary training.
mx: speedup: 2.76% IPC improvement (single-core) and 7.56% (eight-core) over Bandit; 5.25% on memory-intensive · energy_or_tops_w: 48% prefetcher table energy reduction; 7% full memory hierarchy energy reduction · area: <1 KB storage overhead
tg: hardware-prefetching, prefetcher-selection, memory-hierarchy, hybrid-prefetcher, energy-efficiency

t: TidalMesh: Topology-Driven AllReduce Collective Communication for Mesh Topology
th: topology-native AllReduce algorithm for 2D mesh scale-out interconnects
pb: Existing AllReduce algorithms are topology-aware adaptations of generic algorithms (ring, tree) to physical 2D mesh networks, resulting in a mismatch between logical and physical communication patterns that wastes bandwidth and increases latency.
me: TidalMesh is a topology-driven AllReduce algorithm designed natively for 2D mesh networks. It pushes data flows between endpoint nodes in a wave-like (tidal) pattern that aligns with the mesh grid structure, fully utilizing bidirectional links and minimizing congestion. Sparse TidalMesh minimizes the bandwidth overhead of the base algorithm. Collective communication unrolling enables software pipelining by superimposing different AllReduce phases (ReduceScatter, AllGather) so that compute and communication overlap across multiple concurrent AllReduce operations, effectively hiding collective communication latency.
nv: A topology-driven AllReduce algorithm designed natively for 2D mesh interconnects that pushes tidal flows between endpoint nodes to achieve near-optimal bandwidth utilization, rather than adapting topology-agnostic ring/tree algorithms.
mx: speedup: up to 24% AllReduce performance improvement on 64-node 8x8 2D mesh
tg: collective-communication, allreduce, 2d-mesh, interconnect, distributed-training, software-pipelining

t: Reuse-Aware Compilation for Zoned Quantum Architectures Based on Neutral Atoms
th: reuse-aware compilation for zoned neutral-atom quantum architectures
pb: Neutral-atom quantum computers use heterogeneous zoned architectures (storage, entangling, readout zones), and compiling quantum circuits for them requires efficiently managing qubit movement between zones to minimize fidelity-degrading data movement overhead.
me: ZAC (Zoned Architecture Compiler) introduces qubit reuse as a core optimization: qubits already in the entanglement zone are kept there if an immediate entangling gate is pending, avoiding round-trip movement to storage. ZAC additionally introduces novel data placement strategies that anticipate future gate scheduling needs, a new instruction scheduling algorithm for zoned operations, a flexible specification language for diverse zoned architectures, and ZAIR, an intermediate representation capturing zoned-architecture-specific constraints. The compiler is evaluated on circuits showing 22x fidelity improvement over monolithic architectures.
nv: Reuse-aware compilation that keeps qubits in the entanglement zone when subsequent entangling operations are imminent, dramatically reducing inter-zone data movement which is the dominant fidelity-degrading cost in zoned neutral-atom architectures.
mx: accuracy: 22x fidelity improvement over monolithic architectures; 10% fidelity gap from ideal on average
tg: quantum-computing, neutral-atom, compiler, zoned-architecture, qubit-reuse, circuit-compilation

t: CROSS: Compiler-Driven Optimization of Sparse DNNs Using Sparse/Dense Computation Kernels
th: compiler-driven sparse-dense kernel co-optimization for sparse DNN GPU inference
pb: Exploiting DNN weight sparsity on GPUs is hindered by the overhead of index-based encoding/decoding required by sparse formats, making sparse computation kernels slower than dense kernels even at high sparsity ratios.
me: CROSS is an end-to-end compilation framework that analyzes parameter distribution locality to identify regions where dense computation remains efficient. It decomposes sparse DNN workloads into multiple components across different sparsity levels and maps each component to either a specialized sparse kernel or a high-performance dense kernel. A novel sparse graph translation technique transforms the sparse computation graph into a form compatible with dense computation kernels, reconciling the sparse DNN computation with optimized BLAS-level dense routines on GPU. The framework accommodates various sparsity patterns (unstructured, structured, N:M) and optimization techniques.
nv: Exploiting parameter distribution locality to reconcile sparse DNN computation with high-performance dense GPU computation kernels via sparse graph translation, avoiding expensive index-based sparse format overhead while still skipping zero computations.
mx: speedup: average 2.03x speedup over 7 state-of-the-art solutions · other: smaller memory footprints vs baselines
tg: sparsity, compiler, gpu-kernel, sparse-dense-codesign, dnn-inference

t: HATT: Hamiltonian Adaptive Ternary Tree for Optimizing Fermion-to-Qubit Mapping
th: quantum circuit compilation
pb: Mapping Fermionic quantum systems to qubit systems produces Hamiltonians with high Pauli weight, inflating quantum circuit gate count and depth. Existing Fermion-to-qubit mappings are not tailored to specific Hamiltonian structures, leading to unnecessary overhead.
me: HATT constructs ternary tree-based Fermion-to-qubit mappings using a bottom-up procedure that is adaptive to the specific Fermionic Hamiltonian being compiled. The algorithm analyzes Hamiltonian term structure to guide tree construction, reducing Pauli weight compared to generic mappings such as Jordan-Wigner or Bravyi-Kitaev. The complexity is reduced from O(N^4) to O(N^3) while preserving vacuum state properties required for correctness of simulation.
nv: A Hamiltonian-aware bottom-up ternary tree construction that jointly optimizes the Fermion-to-qubit mapping for a specific target Hamiltonian, reducing algorithmic complexity from O(N^4) to O(N^3).
mx: other: 5-25% reduction in Pauli weight, gate count, and circuit depth over baseline mappings
tg: quantum-computing, fermion-qubit-mapping, circuit-compilation, ternary-tree, hamiltonian-simulation

t: TB-STC: Transposable Block-wise N:M Structured Sparse Tensor Core
th: transposable structured sparsity for tensor cores
pb: Existing N:M structured sparsity for DNN accelerators causes significant accuracy degradation (e.g., >6% on OPT-6.7B and Llama2-7B at 50% sparsity) because one-dimensional structured sparsity patterns diverge far from the unstructured optimal. Hardware support for sparsity must simultaneously deliver high bandwidth utilization and computational efficiency.
me: The paper introduces Transposable Block-wise Structured (TBS) sparsity, which exploits the transpose relationship between forward and backward pass weight matrices during training to find a 2D block sparsity pattern that more closely approximates unstructured sparsity. At the micro-architecture level, TB-STC implements a Transposable Block-wise N:M Sparse Tensor Core with an adaptive codec for on-the-fly storage format conversion supporting both row-wise and column-wise sparse access, and an I/O-aware configurable scheduler for sparsity-aware compute scheduling. This enables 1.47x bandwidth utilization and 1.57x computational utilization improvements.
nv: Exploiting the transpose symmetry of forward/backward weight matrices to derive a 2D block-wise sparsity pattern that simultaneously maintains structured hardware efficiency and near-unstructured accuracy.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 3.82x average EDP improvement over existing work · accuracy: up to 2.58% accuracy improvement over other structured sparsity methods at same sparsity degree · other: 1.47x bandwidth utilization, 1.57x computational utilization
tg: structured-sparsity, tensor-core, n:m-sparsity, llm, training-inference

t: Make LLM Inference Affordable to Everyone: Augmenting GPU Memory with NDP-DIMM
th: near-DRAM processing for affordable LLM inference
pb: Deploying large LLMs (e.g., LLaMA2-70B) on consumer-grade GPUs with limited VRAM is impractical; offloading model weights to host DRAM or NVMe storage creates severe bandwidth bottlenecks on the PCIe interconnect, resulting in very low inference throughput.
me: Hermes partitions LLM weights into 'hot' neurons (~20% of parameters, ~80% of compute) and 'cold' neurons (~80% of parameters, ~20% of compute) based on activation sparsity. Hot neurons are mapped to the consumer GPU for compute-efficient execution, while cold neurons are offloaded to near-data processing (NDP) units embedded in commodity DRAM DIMMs. A lightweight runtime predictor dynamically classifies neurons as hot or cold based on input activations. A window-based online scheduler maintains load balance across multiple NDP-DIMM modules, enabling pipelined heterogeneous execution between GPU and NDP-DIMMs.
nv: Exploiting LLM activation sparsity to drive a hot/cold neuron partition that maps cold weights to NDP-DIMMs, bypassing the PCIe bandwidth bottleneck by keeping computation near DRAM.
mx: speedup: 75.24x average over state-of-the-art offloading-based inference on consumer hardware · other: LLaMA2-70B: 13.75 tokens/s on consumer GPU
tg: llm-inference, ndp-dimm, activation-sparsity, consumer-gpu, memory-offloading

t: Mascot: Predicting Memory Dependencies and Opportunities for Speculative Memory Bypassing
th: unified memory dependence and speculative bypass prediction
pb: Memory dependence prediction (MDP) and speculative memory bypassing (SMB) require conflicting predictor properties: MDP tolerates false positives but not false negatives, while SMB tolerates false negatives but not false positives. Prior TAGE-based predictors for either mechanism fail to learn patterns of non-dependence, causing inaccuracy.
me: Mascot is a TAGE-inspired predictor that learns both dependence and non-dependence contexts. Unlike prior designs that only learn dependence patterns, Mascot tracks the history of non-aliasing outcomes in the TAGE table entries, enabling low false negative rates required for MDP and low false positive rates required for SMB from a single shared structure. The predictor is used in two modes: MDP-only (for load issue gating) and combined MDP+SMB (for value forwarding from store to load bypassing address resolution).
nv: A unified TAGE-based predictor that explicitly learns non-dependence patterns, enabling both memory dependence prediction and speculative memory bypassing with a single compact hardware structure.
mx: speedup: 1.9% average IPC improvement (peak 26%) for MDP+SMB over baseline; 0.4% IPC gain vs prior MDP predictor · area: 10.1 KiB (Mascot-opt compact variant) · other: Evaluated on SPEC CPU 2017
tg: memory-dependence, speculative-execution, tage-predictor, ilp, out-of-order

t: Cooperative Warp Execution in Tensor Core for RISC-V GPGPU
th: cooperative warp tensor core for open-source RISC-V GPGPU
pb: Tensor cores integrated into RISC-V GPGPU architectures (e.g., Vortex) are severely under-utilized in many configurations, and simply increasing compute capacity does not yield proportional performance gains due to memory bandwidth limitations and warp divergence.
me: The paper integrates a tensor core into the open-source Vortex RISC-V GPGPU with a suite of GEMM intrinsics. Analysis of utilization identifies that memory bandwidth and warp-level resource contention bottleneck performance. The proposed cooperative warp execution mechanism allows multiple warps to share a single tensor core invocation, reducing per-warp memory requirements for GEMM operands and enabling better pipelining of data movement and computation. Hardware warp cooperation support is added to the tensor core datapath to manage the cooperative scheduling.
nv: Cooperative warp execution in tensor core that allows multiple warps to collaboratively share a tensor core operation, reducing memory pressure and improving utilization by up to 3x over the baseline tensor core.
mx: speedup: up to 3x over baseline tensor core implementation
tg: risc-v, gpgpu, tensor-core, warp-cooperation, gemm

t: Variable Read Disturbance: An Experimental Analysis of Temporal Variation in DRAM Read Disturbance
th: temporal variability of DRAM read disturbance thresholds
pb: DRAM read disturbance (RowHammer/RowPress) mitigation techniques rely on accurate per-row read disturbance threshold (RDT) characterization, but the RDT of individual DRAM rows is not static: it varies significantly and unpredictably over time, making accurate characterization with a limited number of measurements infeasible.
me: Experimental characterization of 160 DDR4 chips and 4 HBM2 chips from three major manufacturers using repeated RDT measurements on the same rows over time. The study observes that the minimum RDT of a row only appears after up to 94,467 repeated measurements, with the minimum being 3.5x smaller than the observed maximum. Analysis covers the effects of chip density, technology node, data pattern, aggressor row open time, and temperature on RDT variability. Guardbanding and ECC (SECDED/Chipkill) approaches are evaluated as mitigations.
nv: First experimental demonstration that DRAM row RDT varies substantially and unpredictably over time (Variable Read Disturbance), fundamentally challenging the correctness of existing RowHammer characterization and mitigation strategies.
mx: other: Minimum RDT is 3.5x smaller than maximum observed; appears only after up to 94,467 measurements; 50% guardband causes ~45% performance loss
tg: rowhammer, rowpress, dram-reliability, read-disturbance, security

t: ARTEMIS: Agile Discovery of Efficient Real-Time Systems-on-Chips in the Heterogeneous Era
th: scheduler-integrated SoC design space exploration
pb: Design space exploration (DSE) for heterogeneous real-time SoCs (targeting applications like autonomous driving and AR/VR) must jointly optimize microarchitectural parameters and dynamic task-to-hardware mappings under deadline, power, and area constraints, resulting in an intractably large combined design space.
me: ARTEMIS integrates a dynamic SoC-level scheduler into the DSE loop to eliminate the mapping dimension from the search space, dramatically pruning the effective design space. The scheduler incorporates policies such as task procrastination and memory-traffic/energy-aware task assignment. DSE heuristics use real-time deadline-aware and power/area-aware ranking mechanisms to guide the remaining architecture search. The method is validated on FPGA hardware and evaluated on autonomous vehicle and AR/VR application suites.
nv: Integrating a dynamic SoC scheduler directly into the DSE loop to collapse the task-mapping dimension, enabling 5.1-12.8x faster convergence while discovering SoCs that meet 100% real-time deadlines.
mx: speedup: DSE converges 5.1-12.8x faster than state-of-the-art · area: up to 2.4x lower area at iso-input-rate · other: 1.2-3x better throughput at iso-area; 100% real-time deadline satisfaction
tg: soc-design, design-space-exploration, real-time, heterogeneous, autonomous-driving

t: InstAttention: In-Storage Attention Offloading for Cost-Effective Long-Context LLM Inference
th: in-storage attention computation for long-context LLM inference
pb: Long-context LLM inference at large batch sizes generates KV caches that exceed GPU VRAM capacity; offloading KV caches to SSDs via PCIe creates a critical bandwidth bottleneck that severely limits throughput.
me: InstAttention offloads both the attention computation and KV cache storage to Computational Storage Drives (CSDs), which have high internal NAND bandwidth not limited by PCIe. A flash-aware in-storage attention engine executes the attention decode phase directly inside the CSD, with KV cache management mechanisms tailored to flash access patterns (e.g., large sequential reads). Optimized P2P transmission between GPU and CSDs eliminates unnecessary data migration back across PCIe. The system targets offline inference of a 13B model on an NVIDIA A6000 GPU.
nv: Offloading attention computation itself (not just storage) to in-storage CSD compute units, leveraging internal flash bandwidth to bypass the PCIe bottleneck for long-sequence KV cache access.
mx: speedup: up to 11.1x throughput improvement over FlexGen for long-sequence inference (13B model, A6000 GPU)
tg: llm-inference, kv-cache, in-storage-compute, csd, long-context

t: EDA: Energy-Efficient Inter-Layer Model Compilation for Edge DNN Inference Acceleration
th: adaptive inter-layer operator scheduling for edge NPU energy efficiency
pb: Inter-layer operator scheduling on edge NPUs can reduce DRAM traffic by reusing layer outputs in on-chip SRAM, but naive deep traversal of DNN operator graphs greatly increases off-chip memory transactions when on-chip SRAM is small, negating energy savings.
me: EDA is a DNN compilation framework that first transforms the DNN model into a tensor-splitting model and decomposes the model graph into subgraphs. An inter-layer cost model rapidly determines the optimal operator traversal depth for each subgraph given the available on-chip SRAM. EDA then manages the on-chip shared memory space to prevent overflow, and applies operator grouping to improve MAC unit and SRAM space utilization. The resulting compilation avoids both excessive DRAM traffic (from too-deep traversal) and under-utilization (from too-shallow traversal).
nv: An inter-layer cost model that adaptively determines the optimal DNN operator traversal depth per subgraph, balancing on-chip reuse against DRAM traffic for small-SRAM edge NPUs.
mx: speedup: 2.39x geomean performance improvement over NPU with designated memory buffers · energy_or_tops_w: 2.08x geomean energy efficiency improvement
tg: npu, edge-inference, inter-layer-scheduling, dnn-compilation, energy-efficiency

t: FHENDI: A Near-DRAM Accelerator for Compiler-Generated Fully Homomorphic Encryption Applications
th: near-DRAM acceleration for fully homomorphic encryption
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) workloads are both compute- and memory-intensive, and even dedicated FHE ASICs are bottlenecked by expensive memory transfers due to large ciphertext operands and limited bank-to-bank communication, die-to-die bandwidth, and memory access latency within near-DRAM processing.
me: FHENDI is a hierarchical near-DRAM processing (NDP) architecture that exploits four levels of FHE parallelism (element-wise, limb-wise, coefficient-wise, ciphertext-wise) mapped to different hierarchy levels. Bank-to-bank communication is addressed via a conflict-free mapping algorithm using localized permutation networks that enable element-wise and butterfly operations within DRAM subarrays. Die-to-die bandwidth constraints are addressed by pipelining parallel bootstrapping operations identified by the HElayers compiler. Memory access latency is hidden using a dual-banking scheme combined with subarray-level parallelism (SLP). The system is evaluated with compiled FHE programs for CNN/Transformer ML inference, database range query, and sorting.
nv: A conflict-free localized permutation network enabling efficient bank-local element-wise and butterfly NTT operations in near-DRAM, eliminating the need for inter-bank communication in FHE.
mx: speedup: 2145.8x vs server CPU, 118.29x vs GPU, 2.45x vs FHE ASIC (mean across workloads)
tg: fhe, near-dram, ndp, cryptography, privacy-preserving-ml

t: FIGLUT: An Energy-Efficient Accelerator Design for FP-INT GEMM Using Look-Up Tables
th: LUT-based FP-INT GEMM for weight-only quantized LLM inference
pb: Weight-only quantization for LLM deployment produces FP-INT mixed-precision GEMM operations where one operand is floating-point (activations) and the other is low-bit integer (weights); this FP-INT compute is difficult to implement efficiently on conventional GPU multiply-accumulate hardware.
me: FIGLUT implements GEMM using a look-up table (LUT) approach: rather than performing FP-INT multiplications directly, the hardware precomputes all possible products of the floating-point activation values with each possible weight pattern and stores them in LUTs. At inference time, the LUT is indexed by weight bits to retrieve the precomputed partial product. A half-size LUT variant is introduced along with a dedicated decoding and multiplexing unit to reduce LUT storage overhead. The design supports multiple bit precisions and quantization methods in a single fixed hardware configuration.
nv: A half-size LUT with dedicated decode/mux that replaces FP-INT multipliers with table lookups, enabling configurable multi-precision weight-only quantized GEMM with 59% higher TOPS/W than prior LUT-based accelerators.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 59% higher TOPS/W than state-of-the-art at same 3-bit precision; 98% higher TOPS/W at matched perplexity using 2.4-bit · accuracy: 20% lower perplexity than state-of-the-art at 3-bit weight precision
tg: weight-only-quantization, lut, fp-int-gemm, llm-inference, energy-efficiency

t: AutoRFM: Scaling Low-Cost in-DRAM Trackers to Ultra-Low Rowhammer Thresholds
th: subarray-granularity RFM for scalable in-DRAM Rowhammer mitigation
pb: In-DRAM Rowhammer mitigation using the DDR5 Refresh Management (RFM) command stalls the entire DRAM bank for 200-400ns per invocation; at ultra-low Rowhammer thresholds (sub-100), the required RFM frequency causes up to 33% performance slowdown with existing low-cost trackers such as MINT.
me: AutoRFM performs transparent RFM at the subarray granularity rather than the full bank level: it targets only one subarray at a time for mitigation while all other subarrays continue to service requests uninterrupted. If an activation request arrives for the subarray currently under mitigation, the DRAM chip issues an ALERT signal to the Memory Controller to retry after a bounded 200ns wait. Randomized Memory Mapping breaks spatial correlation between consecutive bank accesses to prevent repeated targeting of the same subarray. A Fractal Mitigation Algorithm handles transitive Rowhammer attacks (e.g., Half-Double) without recursive same-subarray mitigations. The design is evaluated with SPEC, GAP, and stream workloads.
nv: Subarray-granularity transparent RFM that allows parallel servicing of non-targeted subarrays during mitigation, breaking the bank-level stall bottleneck of standard RFM.
mx: other: 3.1% average slowdown at Rowhammer threshold 74; vs 33% slowdown with bank-level RFM at threshold 100
tg: rowhammer, dram-mitigation, rfm, subarray, memory-security

t: SPARK: Sparsity Aware, Low Area, Energy-Efficient, Near-memory Architecture for Accelerating Linear Programming Problems
th: near-cache ILP/LP acceleration with sparsity awareness
pb: Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and Linear Programming (LP) solvers run for tens of hours on large parallel computers because their sparse, branch-intensive algorithms are poorly matched to CPUs and GPUs. GPUs suffer from thread divergence on ILP branching and require frequent host interactions, while CPU solvers like Gurobi cannot meet real-time decision thresholds (seconds to minutes).
me: SPARK reconfigures the existing L1 cache in a CPU to act as a near-cache compute accelerator with ~1.4% area overhead. It integrates sparsity detection and sparsity-aware compute units near the cache to skip insignificant multiplications in sparse matrix operations, and exploits reuse patterns inherent to ILP algorithms (e.g., simplex pivots, branch-and-bound traversal) through a reuse-aware datapath. The architecture is reconfigurable to handle both sparse and dense ILPs and LPs without separate hardware.
nv: Near-L1-cache reconfiguration that enables sparsity-aware, reuse-aware computation for ILP/LP directly within the CPU pipeline at minimal area cost (~1.4% of a CPU).
mx: speedup: 15x over Zen3 CPU, 20x over V100 GPU (sparse ILP); 7-17x over CPU, 103-250x over GPU (sparse LP) · energy_or_tops_w: 152x energy improvement over Zen3 CPU, 740x over V100 GPU (sparse ILP) · area: ~1.4% of a CPU die area overhead
tg: near-cache-compute, ilp-acceleration, sparsity, cpu-augmentation, linear-programming

t: Architecting Value Prediction around In-Order Execution
th: value prediction for in-order processor performance
pb: In-order processors suffer from stalls when long-latency instructions block younger independent instructions from issuing, and the compiler cannot always find sufficient independent work to fill the pipeline. Conventional branch prediction techniques fail to resolve hard-to-predict (delinquent) branches quickly enough to prevent pipeline bubbles.
me: The paper integrates both address-based value prediction and direct value prediction into an in-order pipeline (based on a scaled-up CVA6 RISC-V core), exploiting the property that in-order execution allows aggressive value speculation without recovery penalties (a mispredicted value simply overwrites its slot when the real result arrives). A reworked cache hierarchy adds a fast first-level cache that can be written speculatively. A 32-entry scoreboard 4-issue in-order pipeline is augmented without full register renaming or out-of-order memory hazard handling.
nv: Demonstrating that in-order execution's deterministic instruction ordering enables penalty-free aggressive value speculation, achieving near-OOO performance without register renaming or out-of-order memory hazard resolution.
mx: speedup: 38.4% geomean IPC improvement over baseline in-order CVA6; 86.7% of OOO (32/16 ROB) gains; 46.3% of OOO (64/32 ROB) gains
tg: value-prediction, in-order-execution, risc-v, speculation, cva6

t: Machine Learning-Guided Memory Optimization for DLRM Inference on Tiered Memory
th: ML-guided embedding placement for DLRM on tiered memory
pb: Deep learning recommendation models (DLRMs) have embedding tables at terabyte scale that cannot fit in DRAM alone; tiered memory (DRAM + cheaper capacity tiers) is cost-effective but embedding access patterns have long and irregular reuse distances that defeat classical caching and prefetching heuristics.
me: RecMG uses separate ML models for caching and prefetching of embedding vectors. The caching model predicts which vectors have long reuse distances or few future reuses and should stay in fast memory. The prefetching model uses a novel differentiable loss function to narrow the search space for candidate vectors to prefetch, minimizing on-demand fetches. Data labeling is tailored to DLRM inference characteristics (sparse accesses, variable reuse distances). Both models operate at inference time to guide real-time placement decisions on tiered memory systems.
nv: A differentiable loss function for the prefetching ML model that narrows the prefetching candidate space and directly minimizes on-demand fetches for DLRM embedding vectors on tiered memory.
mx: speedup: Up to 43% reduction in end-to-end DLRM inference time · other: On-demand fetch reduction: 2.2x vs temporal, 2.8x vs spatial, 1.5x vs ML-based prefetchers
tg: dlrm, tiered-memory, embedding-caching, ml-prefetching, recommendation-inference

t: HILP: Accounting for Workload-Level Parallelism in System-on-Chip Design Space Exploration
th: workload-level parallelism modeling for heterogeneous SoC design space exploration
pb: Early-stage heterogeneous SoC design space exploration tools (MultiAmdahl, Gables) only model minimum and maximum workload-level parallelism (WLP) extremes; they cannot model realistic mixed-application workloads where multiple independent multi-phase applications share an SoC's heterogeneous cores and accelerators.
me: HILP formulates SoC workload scheduling as a job-shop scheduling problem: a set of independent multi-phase applications with phase-level dependencies is to be scheduled across heterogeneous cores and accelerators. This is solved using an integer linear programming (ILP) solver to find a near-optimal schedule that minimizes total workload execution time subject to power and memory bandwidth constraints. The ILP captures the full continuum of WLP (not just extremes) and can be used to sweep large design spaces efficiently during early exploration.
nv: Modeling heterogeneous SoC workload scheduling as a job-shop scheduling ILP, enabling early-stage design space exploration that captures the full spectrum of workload-level parallelism rather than just min/max extremes.
mx: other: Validated against Amdahl's law, memory wall, and dark silicon; large design space sweep showing impact of WLP on optimal SoC configuration
tg: soc-design-space, workload-parallelism, job-shop-scheduling, ilp, heterogeneous-soc

t: FACIL: Flexible DRAM Address Mapping for SoC-PIM Cooperative On-device LLM Inference
th: flexible DRAM address mapping for cooperative SoC-PIM LLM inference
pb: On-device LLM inference requires the same model weights to be accessed by both DRAM-based PIM units (for GEMV in the memory-bound decode phase) and SoC processors (for GEMM in the compute-bound prefill phase), but PIM-operable tensor layouts require different DRAM bank mappings from those preferred by SoC processors, creating costly re-layout overheads when switching between the two.
me: FACIL introduces a flexible DRAM address mapping scheme in the memory controller that assigns different DRAM address mappings to the page offset bits of each huge page. A user-level library determines the appropriate mapping for each tensor, allowing LLM weights to be placed in DRAM banks that are simultaneously PIM-operable and contiguously addressable by the SoC processor. This dual-mapping eliminates the need to copy or re-layout tensor data when switching between PIM-executed GEMV and SoC-executed GEMM operations.
nv: Per-huge-page configurable DRAM address mapping in the memory controller that allows the same physical tensor to be accessed coherently by both PIM hardware and SoC processors without data re-layout.
mx: speedup: 2.37x TTFT reduction (short conversation), 2.63x TTFT reduction (code autocompletion) over SoC-PIM baseline
tg: pim, dram-address-mapping, on-device-llm, edge-inference, gemv-gemm

t: Delinquent Loop Pre-execution Using Predicated Helper Threads
th: predicated helper threads for delinquent branch pre-execution
pb: Helper-thread branch pre-execution fails when delinquent branches are control-dependent on other delinquent branches: prior work must branch-predict the first delinquent branch (b1) in the helper thread to decide whether to pre-execute the second (b2), merely shifting the misprediction bottleneck to the helper thread. Additionally, stores that both influence a delinquent branch and are control-dependent on it create a disambiguation problem in helper threads.
me: Phelps (Predicated Helper Threads) constructs a helper thread for each inner loop containing delinquent branches and unconditionally pre-executes all delinquent branches (including control-dependent ones) in every loop iteration. Per-branch queues are managed in lockstep with loop iterations, so the main thread can correctly consume or ignore b2 outcomes based on b1 results. Influential stores that are control-dependent on delinquent branches are predicated on those branch outcomes in the helper thread. A dual decoupled helper thread scheme handles outer-inner loop pairs with short/unpredictable inner-loop trip counts.
nv: Unconditional pre-execution of all delinquent branches (including control-dependent ones) via loop-iteration-lockstep per-branch queues, eliminating the need to predict delinquent branches within the helper thread itself.
mx: other: Not stated in abstract
tg: helper-threads, branch-prediction, pre-execution, speculation, loop-optimization

t: Piccolo: Large-Scale Graph Processing with Fine-Grained in-Memory Scatter-Gather
th: non-arithmetic in-memory scatter-gather for graph processing
pb: Graph processing requires irregular fine-grained random memory accesses incompatible with DDR memory access granularity, leading to massive bandwidth waste and cache capacity waste; existing approaches using graph tiling (maximizing on-chip reuse) or PIM (placing arithmetic near memory) each have limitations when implemented with DDR standards, and combining them is difficult.
me: Piccolo implements non-arithmetic function-in-memory focused specifically on fine-grained random scatter-gather operations in off-chip memory, avoiding expensive arithmetic units inside DRAM. The accelerator's cache and miss-handling architecture (MHA) are redesigned to work compatibly with in-memory scatter-gather, enabling both graph tiling (on-chip data reuse) and in-memory operations simultaneously. The scatter-gather function-in-memory reduces off-chip traffic without requiring the expensive multi-operation support that makes traditional PIM impractical.
nv: Placing only non-arithmetic scatter-gather function-in-memory rather than full arithmetic units, enabling cost-effective fine-grained random access reduction while preserving compatibility with graph tiling through a redesigned cache and MHA.
mx: speedup: Up to 3.28x (1.62x geomean) over prior graph processing accelerators · energy_or_tops_w: Up to 59.7% energy reduction
tg: graph-processing, in-memory-computing, scatter-gather, ddr, accelerator

t: PIMnet: A Domain-Specific Network for Efficient Collective Communication in Scalable PIM
th: domain-specific PIM interconnect for scalable collective communication
pb: PIM compute units can only access their local memory; inter-bank communication in PIM systems must route through the host CPU, which becomes a bottleneck for collective communication operations (e.g., all-reduce, broadcast) that are common in many workloads, limiting PIM's scalability.
me: PIMnet is a PIM-controlled interconnection network providing direct connectivity between PIM compute units across banks and chips, bypassing the host CPU. It exploits bandwidth parallelism by allowing concurrent inter-bank and inter-chip communication. The network topology matches the DRAM packaging hierarchy with a multi-tier architecture (intra-chip and inter-chip tiers). Unlike traditional network-on-chip designs, PIMnet is managed by the PIM logic itself, not the host, to minimize hardware overhead and optimize collective communication patterns.
nv: A PIM-controlled multi-tier interconnect that matches DRAM packaging hierarchy and enables direct bank-to-bank collective communication, removing the host CPU from the inter-PIM communication path.
mx: speedup: Up to 85x on collective communications; 11.8x on real applications vs. baseline PIM
tg: pim, collective-communication, noc, upmem, scalability

t: Concord: Rethinking Distributed Coherence for Software Caches in Serverless Environments
th: hardware-inspired software cache coherence for serverless computing
pb: Serverless functions incur high latency from frequent global storage accesses; existing node-local caching schemes either restrict each data item to a single cache node (causing frequent remote reads) or allow multi-node replication but impose heavy coherence overhead, neither being optimal for serverless access patterns characterized by frequent reads, strong temporal locality, and few concurrent writers.
me: Concord implements a directory-based distributed software cache coherence protocol inspired by hardware cache coherence, adapted for serverless environments. It allows multiple replicas of the same data item across nodes and satisfies reads locally from any replica. To maintain coherence, a directory tracks replica locations and manages invalidation/update messages on writes. The protocol minimizes coherence traffic by exploiting serverless access patterns, reduces contention points in the directory, and handles node failures and frequent coherence domain changes (as serverless function instances spin up/down). Two additional capabilities are unlocked: transactional storage accesses and transparent data-aware function placement.
nv: A directory-based hardware-cache-coherence-inspired software coherence protocol tailored to serverless access patterns, enabling multi-node read replication with efficient invalidation while supporting transactional storage and data-aware placement.
mx: speedup: 2.4x execution speedup, 1.7x throughput improvement vs. state-of-the-art serverless caching on 16-node cluster · other: Only 6.2MB (4.8% of application memory) overhead
tg: serverless, cache-coherence, distributed-caching, software-cache, directory-protocol

t: DynamoLLM: Designing LLM Inference Clusters for Performance and Energy Efficiency
th: dynamic energy management for LLM inference GPU clusters
pb: LLM inference clusters running on GPU-dense infrastructure consume excessive energy and incur high operational carbon emissions because existing systems provision resources for peak load at maximum GPU frequency and tensor parallelism, ignoring the strong heterogeneity in request types (input/output length variation) and diurnal load fluctuations that create large energy-saving opportunities.
me: DynamoLLM is a hierarchical three-level energy management framework (Cluster Manager, Pool Manager, Instance Manager) that dynamically reconfigures a GPU cluster across three knobs: number of inference server instances (scale in/out), tensor parallelism (shard up/down), and GPU frequency (scale up/down). The cluster is partitioned into per-request-type instance pools (classified by input/output token length into SS/SM/.../LL buckets); a BERT-based output-length predictor routes requests to the appropriate pool. Configuration selection is formulated as a MILP optimization using offline energy-performance profiles, with a hierarchical approximation heuristic for real-time operation. Reconfiguration overheads are minimized by: pre-warming VMs from snapshots, direct NVLink weight re-sharding via a bipartite graph matching algorithm (minimizing weight transfers), and keeping nvidia-smi loaded in-memory for rapid GPU frequency changes.
nv: A hierarchical multi-knob (instance count + tensor parallelism + GPU frequency) dynamic reconfiguration framework for LLM inference clusters that maintains per-request-type resource pools and minimizes reconfiguration overheads via weight-stationary NVLink re-sharding and proactive VM pre-warming.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 53% energy saving, 38% carbon reduction vs. static SinglePool baseline · other: 61% cost reduction to customer; DynamoLLM vs. single-knob baselines: ScaleInst 4.1%, ScaleShard 7%, ScaleFreq 19%, DynamoLLM 35% energy reduction in cluster experiment
tg: llm-inference, energy-management, gpu-cluster, tensor-parallelism, gpu-frequency-scaling, slo

t: Lincoln: Real-Time 50~100B LLM Inference on Consumer Devices with LPDDR-Interfaced, Compute-Enabled Flash Memory
th: LPDDR-interfaced compute-enabled Flash for on-device LLM inference
pb: Consumer devices cannot run large 50-100B LLM models in real time because: (1) Flash storage has insufficient internal read bandwidth for per-iteration weight loading, and (2) the conventional Flash interface (NVMe/UFS) offers far lower transmission bandwidth to the NPU than DRAM interfaces, making both the prefill and decode phases severely bandwidth-limited.
me: Lincoln is a device-architecture co-design with two complementary solutions for the two LLM phases. For the compute-intensive prefill phase, Flash devices use the existing high-speed LPDDR interface (normally used for DRAM) to transmit weights to the NPU at much higher bandwidth than conventional Flash interfaces, while maintaining cost/area efficiency. For the memory-intensive decode phase, hybrid-bonding-based near-Flash computing performs matrix-vector operations directly on Flash dies to exploit the full internal Flash bandwidth without transmission bottlenecks, coupled with speculative decoding to further reduce latency. On the device level, Flash internal bandwidth is increased by improving array shrinking methods (lower read latency, more parallel Flash planes per die), leveraging 3D hybrid bonding already in consumer Flash products.
nv: Phase-specific dual strategy: using the LPDDR high-speed interface for prefill-phase weight streaming from Flash, and hybrid-bonding near-Flash compute for decode-phase GEMV execution directly on Flash dies.
mx: speedup: Up to 13.23x prefill speedup, 254.1x generation speedup over conventional SSD-based systems
tg: on-device-llm, flash-memory, near-flash-computing, lpddr-interface, speculative-decoding, edge-inference

t: IRIS: Unleashing ISP-Software Cooperation to Optimize the Machine Vision Pipeline
th: ISP-software cooperative adaptive resolution for mobile CV pipelines
pb: Continuous Vision (CV) SoC pipelines capture entire scenes at uniform high resolution (e.g., 4K), wasting memory bandwidth and backend compute on low-information regions (sky, road) that do not require full-resolution processing, while the ISP discards intermediate computations (edge masks, motion vectors) that could guide resolution reduction.
me: IRIS augments the frontend ISP with three lightweight hardware units: (1) an IRIS Saliency Scorer that reuses ISP byproducts (the edge mask from Edge Enhancement and motion vectors from Temporal Denoising's Block Matching Algorithm) to compute a per-region saliency score (ISS = EDM + alpha * EDM * MM) without any new image analysis; (2) a Quad Unit that applies a hierarchical quadtree-like grouping (16x16, 32x32, 64x64 pixel regions) and compares maximum quadblock ISS to a backend-provided threshold to decide resolution; and (3) a Downsampling Unit that reduces selected quadblocks from 32x32 or 64x64 to 16x16 in-pipeline. The resulting mixed-resolution frame with a Region Resolution Map metadata is stored in the framebuffer. On the backend, for Vision Transformers IRIS feeds a mixed-resolution tokenizer (Quadformer-style), and for visual localization (ORB-SLAM3) IRIS enables an iterative feature extraction algorithm that processes regions in descending ISS order and stops on diminishing marginal feature increase. The ISP extension is validated as cycle-accurate RTL that never stalls the ISP pipeline.
nv: Repurposing already-computed ISP internal byproducts (edge mask from Edge Enhancement and motion vectors from Temporal Denoising) as a zero-additional-compute saliency scorer to drive per-region adaptive spatial resolution downsampling in the ISP pipeline before framebuffer write.
mx: speedup: Localization: 22.8% avg latency reduction, 10.5% tail latency reduction; Classification: 37.5% avg latency reduction, 9% tail latency reduction · energy_or_tops_w: Localization: 22.5% energy reduction; Classification: 41.5% energy reduction · area: Synthesized at 14nm with Synopsys; area overhead not quoted in headline but reported as negligible vs. ISP · accuracy: ViT top-1 accuracy within 1% of baseline at ISS threshold 0.3; ORB-SLAM APE below 5mm at ISS=0.2, MFI=3% · other: ~70% average image size reduction at threshold 0.5; 55% image size reduction at threshold 0.3
tg: isp, computer-vision, mixed-resolution, adaptive-sampling, saliency, edge-inference

t: MLPerf Power: Benchmarking the Energy Efficiency of Machine Learning Systems from μWatts to MWatts for Sustainable AI
th: ML system energy-efficiency benchmarking
pb: There is no standardized, cross-platform methodology for benchmarking the energy efficiency of ML systems spanning the full deployment range from sub-milliwatt IoT devices to megawatt-scale datacenter clusters. Existing benchmarks focus on throughput/latency without capturing power consumption in a reproducible, comparable way across heterogeneous hardware.
me: MLPerf Power extends the MLPerf benchmark suite with standardized power measurement rules and best practices developed by a consortium of 20+ industry organizations. The methodology defines measurement protocols for power metering at different granularities (device, rack, facility) and applies them to representative ML workloads (inference and training) across edge, mobile, and datacenter deployment scales. 1,841 reproducible measurements were collected from 60 systems, enabling cross-architecture energy-efficiency comparisons.
nv: The first industry-wide, consortium-developed benchmarking framework that unifies ML energy-efficiency measurement across the full deployment spectrum from microwatts to megawatts.
mx: other: 1,841 measurements across 60 systems; power range from μW to MW
tg: benchmarking, energy-efficiency, mlperf, sustainable-ai, power-measurement

t: Understanding RowHammer Under Reduced Refresh Latency: Experimental Analysis of Real DRAM Chips and Implications on Future Solutions
th: RowHammer mitigation via reduced refresh latency
pb: RowHammer mitigations based on preventive refresh incur growing performance and energy overheads as DRAM technology scaling reduces the activation threshold for bit-flip induction. The interaction between refresh latency and RowHammer vulnerability in real DRAM chips has not been rigorously characterized.
me: The authors perform the first experimental characterization of refresh-latency vs. RowHammer interactions on 388 real DDR4 chips from three manufacturers, varying preventive refresh (tRFM) latency below nominal values. They find that refresh latency can be reduced by 64% with only a 0.54% increase in required refresh count. Building on these findings, they design PaCRAM (Partial Charge Restoration for Aggressive Mitigation), a mechanism that reduces tRFM for preventive refreshes and compensates by slightly increasing refresh frequency, thus lowering the performance tax of five state-of-the-art RowHammer defenses.
nv: First silicon-validated demonstration that preventive DRAM refresh latency can be substantially reduced (by 64%) with minimal extra refresh count, enabling a new low-cost operating point for RowHammer mitigation.
mx: other: Refresh latency reduced by 64%; preventive refresh count increase of only 0.54%; performance and energy improvements over 5 state-of-the-art mitigations
tg: rowhammer, dram, preventive-refresh, memory-security, reliability

t: To Cross, or Not to Cross Pages for Prefetching?
th: Selective page-cross prefetch filtering for L1D caches
pb: L1D cache prefetchers operating with virtual addresses can issue prefetch requests across page boundaries, but whether page-cross prefetching is beneficial or harmful is workload- and phase-dependent, and existing prefetchers lack the intelligence to selectively enable or suppress these cross-page requests.
me: MOKA is a holistic framework for designing Page-Cross Filters that attach to existing L1D prefetchers. It combines three components: (i) hashed perceptron predictors using prefetcher-independent program features (PC, stride, memory access history) to estimate page-cross benefit, (ii) system-state-adaptive predictors that account for TLB pressure and MSHR occupancy, and (iii) a dynamic phase-switching scheme that periodically recalibrates filter decisions across changing execution phases. The resulting prototype filter, DRIPPER, is instantiated for Berti, IPCP, and BOP prefetchers without modifying their core logic.
nv: A systematic, predictor-agnostic framework (MOKA) for selectively gating page-cross prefetch requests using phase-adaptive hashed perceptron predictors that account for both program features and live system state.
mx: speedup: 1.7% over always-cross Berti (single-core); 2.5% over never-cross Berti; 2.0%/3.3% geomean on 8-core mixes vs always/never-cross
tg: prefetching, cache, l1d, page-boundary, perceptron-predictor

t: Interleaved Logical Qubits in Atom Arrays
th: Movement-free fault-tolerant quantum architecture for neutral atom arrays
pb: Neutral atom quantum computers require physical qubit movement to perform two-qubit gates, which introduces an unavoidable latency bottleneck and may eliminate quantum advantage in fault-tolerant computations. Existing surface code architectures in atom arrays are movement-dependent and do not scale efficiently.
me: The paper proposes a movement-free QEC architecture based on interleaved surface code groups using dual-species neutral atom arrays. Within a group, transversal CNOTs are executed at high fidelity by leveraging asymmetric interaction strengths: interspecies interactions decay as 1/r^3 (long-range) while intraspecies decay as 1/r^6 (short-range). Between groups, interleaved lattice surgery creates high-capacity routing channels for logical qubit communication. The architecture is validated through numerical circuit simulations and benchmarked via compilation of key quantum algorithms.
nv: A movement-free fault-tolerant quantum architecture for neutral atom arrays that exploits dual-species asymmetric interaction scaling to enable transversal CNOTs within interleaved surface code groups.
mx: speedup: ~3x reduction in compute time vs. movement-based architectures in high-parallelism regimes
tg: quantum-computing, neutral-atoms, surface-code, fault-tolerance, qec

t: Enterprise Class Modular Cache Hierarchy
th: Modular enterprise cache hierarchy for mission-critical and AI workloads
pb: Enterprise mission-critical workloads demand cache hierarchies that deliver consistent low-latency performance at sustained processor utilization above 90% across diverse and highly virtualized workloads, while remaining extensible across processor generations and new technology insertions.
me: The IBM Telum and Telum II processors introduce a modular, horizontally federated cache hierarchy in which last-level cache slices are distributed across chiplets and interconnected through high-bandwidth on-chip links. An adaptive horizontal cache persistence algorithm dynamically adjusts which cache levels retain hot data across different access patterns and workload phases. The paper details how fetch events flow through this hierarchy and how cache size changes affect system-level performance, culminating in the Telum II design that simultaneously supports traditional enterprise workloads and generative AI inference.
nv: An industry-deployed modular and horizontally federated cache hierarchy with adaptive persistence algorithms designed for 90%+ sustained utilization in mission-critical enterprise and generative AI workloads.
mx: other: Sustained processor utilization >90%; specific speedup numbers not disclosed in abstract
tg: cache-hierarchy, enterprise, ibm-z, modular-design, ai-inference

t: CogSys: Efficient and Scalable Neurosymbolic Cognition System via Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design
th: Neurosymbolic AI accelerator with reconfigurable compute and adaptive scheduling
pb: Neurosymbolic AI workloads—combining neural network inference with symbolic reasoning (e.g., probabilistic logic, abduction)—exhibit high memory intensity, compute heterogeneity, and irregular access patterns that cause severe underutilization on commodity CPU/GPU/TPU hardware.
me: CogSys is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework with three layers: (1) Algorithm: an efficient tensor factorization technique to reduce the compute and memory footprint of symbolic reasoning operations; (2) Hardware: a scalable ASIC architecture with reconfigurable neuro/symbolic processing elements (nsPEs) and a bubble streaming (BS) dataflow with spatial-temporal (ST) mapping that enables highly parallel, pipelined execution of heterogeneous neural and symbolic kernels; (3) System: an adaptive workload-aware scheduler (adSCH) that orchestrates the assignment of neural vs. symbolic kernels to nsPEs for high resource utilization, evaluated under TSMC 28nm.
nv: Reconfigurable nsPE tiles with bubble streaming dataflow that unify neural and symbolic computation in a single spatial architecture with adaptive kernel scheduling, enabling real-time abductive reasoning for the first time.
mx: speedup: >75x over TPU-like systolic array; 4x-96x over desktop/edge GPUs · area: 4mm^2 at TSMC 28nm · energy_or_tops_w: 1.48W power; <5% area overhead vs systolic array baseline
tg: neurosymbolic, asic, co-design, symbolic-reasoning, edge-ai

t: Reviving In-Storage Hardware Compression on ZNS SSDs through Host-SSD Collaboration
th: Host-SSD collaborative hardware compression for ZNS SSDs
pb: Zoned Namespace (ZNS) SSDs cannot benefit from traditional host-transparent in-storage hardware compression because the ZNS interface's sequential write constraint makes it impossible to locate variable-length compressed chunks and reclaim the space freed by compression without exposing this information to the host.
me: CCZNS (Collaborative Compression for ZNS) decouples compression execution from indexing by introducing a new ZNS interface extension where the SSD hardware performs compression but exposes chunk boundaries and offset metadata to the host rather than hiding them. The host (e.g., RocksDB with ZenFS) uses this metadata to manage address mapping and space reclamation, while the SSD accelerates the compression compute. A case study on RocksDB/ZenFS demonstrates how the host software is adapted to consume CCZNS metadata.
nv: Decoupling in-storage compression execution from index management via a host-SSD collaborative interface, which is the first solution to revive hardware compression on ZNS SSDs.
mx: other: Significantly outperforms existing system solutions (specific numbers not given in abstract)
tg: zns-ssd, compression, storage, host-ssd-collaboration, rocksdb

t: LAD: Efficient Accelerator for Generative Inference of LLM with Locality Aware Decoding
th: KV cache access reduction via attention score locality for LLM inference acceleration
pb: In LLM autoregressive decoding, the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length, and at lengths beyond 2048 tokens the attention mechanism's repeated read of the full KV cache becomes the dominant bottleneck, consuming over 50% of total inference time on GPU-based systems.
me: LAD (Locality Aware Decoding) is a dedicated ASIC accelerator that exploits numerical locality in attention scores across consecutive decoding steps. The key insight is that when an attention score at a specific sequence position remains approximately constant across several consecutive decoding steps, the corresponding key and value vectors need not be re-fetched at every step. LAD implements a locality detection engine that identifies stable-score positions and caches their contribution, dramatically reducing KV cache access frequency while maintaining decoding accuracy. The hardware includes specialized attention decoding units paired with on-chip score history buffers to track and exploit inter-step score locality.
nv: Exploiting inter-step attention score numerical locality to suppress redundant KV cache reads across consecutive decoding steps, implemented as a dedicated hardware accelerator.
mx: speedup: 10.7x attention speedup vs A100 GPU (KV cache >2048); 2.3x end-to-end speedup · energy_or_tops_w: 52.4x energy efficiency for attention vs A100; 13.4x end-to-end energy efficiency · accuracy: Average ROUGE-1 similarity 97% vs original model
tg: llm-inference, kv-cache, attention, asic, locality

t: OASIS: Object-Aware Page Management for Multi-GPU Systems
th: Object-aware adaptive page management for multi-GPU unified virtual memory
pb: Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) in multi-GPU systems applies a single, application-object-agnostic page placement and migration policy to all data, failing to account for the fact that different data objects and different execution phases of the same object benefit from different page management strategies.
me: OASIS dynamically identifies application object access patterns at runtime by monitoring page-access counters and tracking object-level access behaviors across execution phases. Based on the detected patterns, it proactively assigns one of several page management policies—on-touch migration, access-counter-based migration, or duplication—to each object on a per-phase basis. The policy decision logic runs in software/hardware coordination and uses lightweight profiling to adapt to phase changes without manual programmer annotation.
nv: Runtime object-aware, phase-adaptive page management that automatically selects among migration and duplication policies per data object in multi-GPU UVM systems.
mx: speedup: 64% over on-touch migration; 35% over access-counter migration; 42% over duplication; 12% over GRIT
tg: multi-gpu, uvm, page-management, memory-system, data-placement

t: Prosperity: Accelerating Spiking Neural Networks via Product Sparsity
th: Product sparsity for SNN acceleration via combinatorial inner product reuse
pb: Existing SNN accelerators exploit bit sparsity (zero-valued spikes) to skip zero multiplications, but this approach leaves substantial redundancy unexploited: non-zero spike patterns that produce structurally identical inner products across matrix rows are recomputed independently, wasting significant compute.
me: Product Sparsity is a new sparsity paradigm that identifies combinatorially similar binary spike patterns across matrix rows: if two rows share identical non-zero positions, their dot products with the same weight vector are identical and only one needs to be computed, with the result reused for the other. Prosperity implements this via a real-time pattern matching engine that groups rows by their spike pattern hash, computes the inner product once per unique pattern, and distributes results to all matching rows. This is applied to both fully-connected and convolutional layers of SNNs with binary activations.
nv: Product Sparsity: a novel combinatorial sparsity paradigm that reuses inner product results across matrix rows with matching binary spike patterns, achieving far higher effective sparsity than bit-level zero-skipping alone.
mx: speedup: 7.4x over PTB SNN accelerator; 1.8x over A100 GPU · energy_or_tops_w: 8.0x energy efficiency over PTB; 193x energy efficiency over A100
tg: snn, sparsity, binary-activation, asic, computation-reuse

t: QPRAC: Towards Secure and Practical PRAC-based Rowhammer Mitigation using Priority Queues
th: Priority-queue-based secure RowHammer mitigation for PRAC/ABO DDR5
pb: The JEDEC PRAC (Per Row Activation Counting) framework for DDR5 enables RowHammer mitigation via Alert Back-Off (ABO) signaling, but existing PRAC implementations (e.g., Panopticon) are either insecure when instantiated per JEDEC specification, or impractical (e.g., UPRAC) due to requiring oracle knowledge of the top-N most-activated rows.
me: QPRAC designs a Priority-based Service Queue (PSQ) in the memory controller that maintains pending mitigation requests sorted by row activation count, using PRAC's per-row counters to prioritize mitigations. High activation-count rows are served first, preventing adversarial bypass. The PSQ is co-designed with two complementary mechanisms: opportunistic mitigation during Refresh Management (RFM) operations (piggybacking extra mitigations at low cost), and proactive mitigation during standard DRAM refresh (REF) operations to drain the queue before ABO events fire, minimizing performance impact.
nv: A priority-based service queue (PSQ) that orders RowHammer mitigations by activation count within the PRAC/ABO framework, providing principled security while opportunistic and proactive refresh co-design reduces ABO-induced slowdowns to near zero.
mx: speedup: 0.8% slowdown for benign workloads (0% with proactive mitigations) at threshold=71
tg: rowhammer, ddr5, prac, memory-security, dram

t: DAPPER: A Performance-Attack-Resilient Tracker for RowHammer Defense
th: Perf-Attack-resilient RowHammer tracking via secure hashing and double-hash reset strategies
pb: Host-side RowHammer mitigation mechanisms rely on shared counter or tracking structures that are vulnerable to Performance Attacks (Perf-Attacks), where adversaries reverse-engineer the shared structure's mapping to artificially inflate DRAM access counters or trigger early resets, degrading performance of co-running benign applications.
me: DAPPER introduces secure hashing to randomize the mapping of DRAM rows to shared tracking structures, preventing adversaries from predicting counter locations. DAPPER-S provides a base secure hashing template using a single hash function. DAPPER-H extends this with double-hashing, novel reset strategies that avoid predictable early resets, and mitigative refresh techniques that piggyback RowHammer mitigations onto scheduled refresh operations to amortize overhead. The combined design uses only 96KB of SRAM per 32GB of DRAM, validated against 57 workloads from SPEC2006, SPEC2017, TPC, Hadoop, MediaBench, and YCSB.
nv: Secure double-hashing with adaptive reset strategies that simultaneously thwart RowHammer bit-flip attacks and Perf-Attacks on shared tracking structures, using under 100KB SRAM per 32GB DRAM.
mx: speedup: 0.9% slowdown under Perf-Attacks at threshold=500 · area: 96KB SRAM per 32GB DRAM
tg: rowhammer, memory-security, performance-attack, hashing, dram

t: A Hardware-Software Design Framework for SpMV Acceleration with Flexible Access Pattern Portfolio
th: reconfigurable SpMV acceleration with access pattern portfolio
pb: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is difficult to accelerate due to highly irregular data access patterns that vary by input matrix structure. Static accelerators optimized at compile time cannot handle the dynamic matrix structures encountered in large practical SpMV workloads.
me: SPASM is a hardware-software co-design framework that extracts local data access patterns from input matrices and derives a portfolio of template patterns to encode matrix tiles. A reconfigurable hardware computing structure supports vectorized computation and flexible run-time switching between different template patterns per tile. Global composition analysis of input matrices drives hardware configuration and workload scheduling to improve load balancing across parallel processing units. The template portfolio can be optimized for expected input sets while retaining flexibility for unseen patterns.
nv: A customizable portfolio of data access pattern templates combined with reconfigurable hardware enables both specialization for known matrices and graceful degradation for novel input patterns at run time.
mx: speedup: 2.81x average over state-of-the-art SpMV accelerator
tg: spmv, sparse-linear-algebra, reconfigurable, dataflow, access-pattern, load-balancing

t: Exploring the Performance Improvement of Tensor Processing Engines through Transformation in the Bit-weight Dimension of MACs
th: MAC bit-weight dimension optimization for tensor processing engines
pb: Existing tensor processing engine (TPE) designs for GEMM focus on dataflow and operand reuse at the matrix level but neglect optimization opportunities within the multiply-accumulator (MAC) microarchitecture itself. There is no systematic framework for reasoning about and transforming the bit-level structure of MACs to improve TPE PPA.
me: The paper introduces a novel bit-weight dimension perspective on matrix multiplication and a finer-grained TPE notation based on matrix triple loops that exposes the internal MAC structure. Four optimization techniques are derived from transformations in this bit-weight space: they target timing, area, and power at the PE microarchitecture level. The design is implemented in RTL using SMIC-28nm and applied to four canonical TPE architectures (systolic array, 3D-Cube, multiplier-adder tree, 2D-Matrix) and a bit-slice architecture.
nv: A new algebraic notation capturing the bit-weight dimension of MACs enables four distinct PE microarchitecture optimizations that are orthogonal to existing dataflow or operand-reuse strategies.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 1.04-1.56x energy efficiency vs. four classic TPEs; 12.10x vs. Laconic (bit-slice) · area: 1.27-1.56x area efficiency vs. four classic TPEs; 2.85x vs. Laconic (bit-slice) · ppa: SMIC-28nm synthesis results provided

t: HSMU-SpGEMM: Achieving High Shared Memory Utilization for Parallel Sparse General Matrix-Matrix Multiplication on Modern GPUs
th: high shared memory utilization for GPU SpGEMM
pb: Hash-based SpGEMM algorithms on GPUs fail to simultaneously minimize hash collisions and efficiently utilize fast shared memory, causing significant performance degradation when executing sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication.
me: HSMU-SpGEMM introduces a novel accumulator design that maximizes shared memory utilization on modern GPUs by rethinking the hash-based accumulation strategy to reduce collision overhead while packing more active data into shared memory. The approach also optimizes the symbolic stages of SpGEMM (row count, product computation) to complement the new accumulator. Evaluation is performed on three GPU microarchitectures (Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Turing).
nv: A new GPU accumulator design that achieves high shared memory utilization for SpGEMM by decoupling collision reduction from memory packing efficiency.
mx: speedup: significant improvement over Nsparse, spECK, OpSparse, cuSPARSE (exact numbers not stated in abstract)

t: BOSS: Blocking algorithm for optimizing shuttling scheduling in Ion Trap
th: shuttling scheduling optimization for ion trap quantum computers
pb: Shuttling operations in ion trap quantum computers cause significant fidelity loss and elongated execution times, particularly as circuit sizes grow to 4000+ two-qubit gates across 64-78 qubits.
me: BOSS is a blocking algorithm that groups quantum operations into blocks to reduce the total number of shuttle operations required during circuit execution. The algorithm is evaluated on realistic experimental parameters incorporating sympathetic cooling for higher fidelity and more accurate execution time estimation. Experiments cover circuits with up to 4000+ two-qubit gates and 64-78 qubits.
nv: A blocking strategy specifically tailored to ion trap shuttling that reduces shuttle count by up to 96.1% by exploiting operation locality across the trap.
mx: accuracy: fidelity loss reduction via sympathetic cooling simulation · other: shuttle count reduction: up to 96.1%
