t: Choco-Q: Commute Hamiltonian-based QAOA for Constrained Binary Optimization
th: commute Hamiltonian QAOA for constrained binary optimization
pb: Existing QAOA approaches for constrained binary optimization based on penalty terms or cyclic Hamiltonian simulation fail to encode arbitrary linear constraints, yielding near-zero success rates (as low as 0.02%) and long end-to-end latency. Decomposing the resulting Hamiltonians into deployable quantum circuits has exponential time and memory complexity.
me: Choco-Q encodes constraints by selecting a driver Hamiltonian that commutes with the constraint operator (the commute Hamiltonian), exploiting the Heisenberg picture to guarantee that constraint expectation values remain invariant during quantum evolution, achieving 100% in-constraints rate. Three optimization passes reduce circuit complexity for NISQ deployment: (1) Hamiltonian serialization decomposes the global commute Hamiltonian into independent local sub-Hamiltonians (proven via Lemma 1 to preserve constraint satisfaction), reducing circuit depth from ~4000 to ~24; (2) equivalent decomposition converts each local commute Hamiltonian into control-phase gates and CX gates with linear O(n) time complexity and O(n) circuit depth (Lemma 2), replacing exponential Trotter-Suzuki decomposition; (3) variable elimination reduces the constraint matrix dimension by removing variables with the most non-zero solution entries, shrinking qubit count and circuit depth at the cost of additional classical measurements. Evaluation is conducted on IBMQ Fez (159-qubit Heron r2), Sherbrooke, and Osaka (127-qubit Eagle r3) platforms, plus a classical GPU simulator (A100).
nv: Using the commute Hamiltonian as the QAOA driver Hamiltonian provides a universal hard-constraint encoding for arbitrary linear constraints, paired with a linear-complexity exact decomposition that makes it deployable on current NISQ hardware.
mx: speedup: 4.69x end-to-end over cyclic Hamiltonian-based QAOA on real IBMQ hardware · accuracy: 235x improvement in success rate; 100% in-constraints rate; 658x improvement in approximation ratio gap vs. cyclic Hamiltonian · other: 10^6x decomposition time reduction; circuit depth reduction from ~10^4 to ~100; 2.65x in-constraints rate improvement on IBMQ
tg: quantum-computing, qaoa, constrained-optimization, hamiltonian, nisq, circuit-compilation

t: UniNDP: A Unified Compilation and Simulation Tool for Near DRAM Processing Architectures
th: unified compilation and simulation for near-DRAM processing architectures
pb: Existing simulators and compilers for Near DRAM Processing (NDP) architectures are designed for specific DRAM technologies and NDP configurations, preventing cross-architecture evaluation and optimal data placement and workload scheduling for machine learning workloads.
me: UniNDP proposes a unified tree-based NDP hardware abstraction and corresponding instruction set that spans multiple DRAM technologies and NDP configurations. A cycle-accurate, instruction-driven simulator tracks working status of memory elements and processing units at fine granularity to accurately evaluate hardware performance. An NDP compiler optimizes data partition, mapping, and workload scheduling across DRAM hierarchies, using a hardware status-guided search space pruning strategy and a fast performance predictor parameterized by DRAM timing parameters to improve compilation efficiency.
nv: A unified tree-based hardware abstraction with a matching instruction set that enables a single compilation and simulation framework to target diverse NDP architectures built on different DRAM technologies.
mx: speedup: 1.05-3.43x over existing mapping and compilation methods across multiple NDP architectures
tg: near-dram-processing, pim, compiler, simulation, memory-wall, ml-inference

t: I-DGNN: A Graph Dissimilarity-based Framework for Designing Scalable and Efficient DGNN Accelerators
th: one-pass chained matrix multiplication for dynamic GNN acceleration
pb: Dynamic Graph Neural Network (DGNN) execution requires passing each graph snapshot through the entire DGNN pipeline from layer to layer, generating excessive intermediate data and off-chip memory access, even when consecutive snapshots differ only slightly.
me: I-DGNN proposes a one-pass DGNN computing model that extracts graph update as a chained matrix multiplication between evolving graphs through rigorous mathematical derivation, decoupling inter-snapshot computation from the full DGNN pipeline and expressing it as an independent kernel. A unified accelerator architecture is dynamically configured to support the computation characteristics of this model, providing improved data and pipeline parallelism. A new dataflow and mapping tailored to I-DGNN improves data locality for inter-kernel data across the DGNN pipeline. The framework reduces intermediate data movement across layers.
nv: Reformulating inter-snapshot DGNN computation as a standalone chained matrix multiplication kernel eliminates the need to route evolving graph data through the entire DGNN pipeline, cutting both compute redundancy and off-chip data movement.
mx: speedup: 65.9%, 71.1%, 58.8% execution time reduction vs. three state-of-the-art DGNN accelerators · energy_or_tops_w: 88.4%, 87.0%, 85.9% energy efficiency improvement vs. three state-of-the-art DGNN accelerators

t: GoPIM: GCN-Oriented Pipeline Optimization for PIM Accelerators
th: pipeline-aware ReRAM PIM optimization for GCN training
pb: ReRAM-based PIM accelerators for GCN training suffer from severe pipeline underutilization due to skewed execution times across GCN stages (aggregation, combination) and skewed degree distributions of graph vertices, causing crossbar resource imbalance.
me: GoPIM employs an ML-based scheme that dynamically allocates ReRAM crossbar resources to the most needed pipeline stages to streamline overall execution and eliminate stage bottlenecks. A selective vertex updating technique interleaves vertex mapping across crossbars to evenly distribute vertices despite skewed degree distributions. These two mechanisms reduce overall execution time while maintaining accuracy. A practical architecture design for GoPIM is also provided.
nv: An ML-based crossbar resource allocation policy for GCN pipeline stages that adapts to runtime stage imbalance, combined with interleaved vertex mapping to handle skewed graph degree distributions in ReRAM PIM.
mx: speedup: up to 191x vs. state-of-the-art · energy_or_tops_w: 16.1x energy saving vs. state-of-the-art · accuracy: maintained (minor loss noted)

t: Hydra: Scale-out FHE Accelerator Architecture for Secure Deep Learning on FPGA
th: scale-out multi-FPGA FHE acceleration for secure deep learning
pb: Existing FHE accelerators for deep learning focus on single-node throughput by stacking parallelized compute clusters, which cannot leverage application-level parallelism across model layers and are not scalable beyond a single card for increasingly large models.
me: Hydra partitions the deep learning model (CNN and LLM layers) across multiple FPGA-based server nodes, each handling a portion of the model governed by a central scheduling mechanism on the host server. The architecture supports multi-server scaling with theoretically arbitrary numbers of compute nodes, enabling pipeline parallelism at the model level in addition to intra-node parallelism. Hydra achieves scale-out by distributing ciphertext operations across nodes with the host managing data routing and synchronization.
nv: A scale-out multi-FPGA architecture for FHE-based deep learning inference that exploits application-level model parallelism rather than simply stacking parallelized single-card designs.
mx: speedup: 74x and 160x over Poseidon and FAB (single-card); 12-21x over 8-card FAB-2; 8.1x and 2.5x over CraterLake and SHARP for LLM OPT-6.7B · energy_or_tops_w: comparable or superior to ASIC accelerators under same chip technology

t: Buffalo: Enabling Large-Scale GNN Training via Memory-Efficient Bucketization
th: memory-efficient node bucketization for large-scale GNN training
pb: Training GNNs on large graphs using partitioning strategies causes a memory explosion problem driven by the long-tail degree distribution of graph nodes, and suffers from expensive graph partitioning, difficult memory estimation per partition, and slow data preparation (block generation).
me: Buffalo introduces node bucketization: a flexible mapping between nodes and partitions that addresses memory explosion by allowing nodes to be distributed to non-contiguous buckets based on degree, preventing any single partition from holding too many high-degree nodes. Fast graph partitioning is implemented based on node bucketing without requiring expensive global partitioning algorithms. A lightweight analytical model estimates memory consumption per partition before allocation, and graph sampling reduces block generation time during data preparation. Evaluation covers real-world billion-scale GNN datasets.
nv: Node bucketization that flexibly maps high-degree nodes across partitions to eliminate the memory explosion caused by long-tail degree distributions, enabling scalable large-scale GNN training within strict memory budgets.
mx: speedup: 70.9% end-to-end training time reduction on average vs. DGL, PyG, Betty · other: enables training on billion-scale graphs that exceed GPU memory capacity

t: LegoZK: A Dynamically Reconfigurable Accelerator for Zero-Knowledge Proof
th: dynamically reconfigurable ASIC for zero-knowledge proof generation
pb: Existing ZKP accelerators are designed at the granularity of core operators and exhibit low hardware resource utilization and limited adaptability across the different computation stages of proof generation (e.g., NTT, MSM, polynomial operations).
me: LegoZK uses finite field arithmetic units (FAUs) as fundamental building blocks integrated via a hierarchical on-chip NoC. By dynamically configuring the FAUs and the NoC interconnect at runtime, LegoZK can target each computation stage of proof generation without hardware specialization per stage. For the most time-consuming stage (Multi-Scalar Multiplication, MSM), LegoZK proposes a fast, fully pipelined bucket reduction algorithm based on lookup tables, significantly reducing MSM latency. The NoC topology and FAU configuration are switched between proof stages.
nv: Using finite field arithmetic units as universal reconfigurable primitives connected by a hierarchical NoC allows a single hardware design to efficiently accelerate all stages of ZKP proof generation, rather than requiring per-operator specialization.
mx: speedup: 31.96x over PipeZK (ASIC); 11.30x over GZKP (GPU) in proof generation · energy_or_tops_w: 37.7% power reduction vs. PipeZK · area: 50.1% area reduction vs. PipeZK

t: Gaussian Blending Unit: An Edge GPU Plug-in for Real-Time Gaussian-Based Rendering in AR/VR
th: edge GPU plug-in for real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting on edge GPUs (e.g., Jetson Orin NX) achieves only 7-17 FPS for AR/VR rendering, far below the 60+ FPS threshold for immersive experiences, because the Gaussian Blending Stage—computing each Gaussian's contribution at every pixel—dominates compute time and is poorly suited to conventional GPU pipelines.
me: GBU is an edge GPU plug-in hardware module for the Gaussian Blending Stage. It introduces an intra-row sequential shading (IRSS) dataflow that processes pixels left-to-right within each row, using a two-step coordinate transformation that: (1) shares intermediate coordinate values between adjacent pixels, reducing per-pixel computation by up to 5.5x, and (2) enables early termination of Gaussians contributing minimally to pixels, reducing per-pixel computation by up to 93%. GBU adds a dedicated rendering engine that aggregates computations from multiple Gaussians across rows to balance workload. A Gaussian Reuse Cache reduces off-chip memory accesses by 44.9%. GBU integrates with conventional edge GPUs to support a wide range of AR/VR applications.
nv: The IRSS dataflow exploits spatial coherence between horizontally adjacent pixels during Gaussian blending via a two-step coordinate transformation, enabling both intermediate value sharing and early Gaussian culling in a single unified streaming pass.
mx: speedup: 1.72x on GPU with IRSS dataflow alone; real-time (60+ FPS) achieved with full GBU plug-in on Jetson Orin NX (vs. 7-17 FPS baseline) · accuracy: SOTA rendering quality maintained · other: off-chip memory access reduced by 44.9%; per-pixel computation reduced by up to 93%
tg: 3d-gaussian-splatting, ar-vr, edge-gpu, rendering, dataflow, plug-in-accelerator

t: Palermo: Improving the Performance of Oblivious Memory using Protocol-Hardware Co-Design
th: ORAM protocol-hardware co-design for bandwidth-efficient secure memory
pb: Oblivious RAM (ORAM) protocols impose severe performance penalties because classical ORAM enforces strict sequential dependencies between memory operations, leaving memory bandwidth severely underutilized. Prior prefetching and request-elimination approaches are fragile under low-locality workloads and create additional ORAM stash pressure overhead.
me: Palermo redesigns the RingORAM protocol to allow overlapping of memory operations both within a single ORAM request and across multiple concurrent requests, without violating correctness or security invariants. A dedicated ORAM controller hardware implements this relaxed protocol by concurrently issuing memory requests while tracking and enforcing only the necessary inter-request dependencies to maintain a consistent ORAM tree view. The architecture manages stash and position-map structures in hardware to prevent stash overflow while enabling pipelined DRAM accesses.
nv: A protocol-hardware co-design that removes artificial sequential constraints in classical ORAM, enabling concurrent multi-request memory access without breaking security or correctness guarantees.
mx: speedup: 2.9x over RingORAM baseline · area: 5.78mm^2 ORAM controller (<2% overhead in 12th-gen Intel CPU after technology scaling) · other: 2.14W power; outperforms PageORAM, PrORAM, IR-ORAM
tg: oram, secure-memory, protocol-design, memory-bandwidth, hardware-security, co-design

t: Predicting DRAM-Caused Risky VMs in Large-Scale Clouds
th: VM-granularity DRAM failure prediction for cloud reliability
pb: DRAM failures in large-scale clouds are currently mitigated at node granularity, requiring migration of all VMs on a node even when errors affect only a small fraction of the memory address space. This coarse-grained approach consumes excessive resources and causes unnecessary VM disruptions.
me: Pegasus introduces an Error-VM mapping framework that correlates DRAM ECC error addresses to specific VM memory regions using address space management metadata. A predictor combines ECC correction event features with spatio-temporal clustering features to identify VMs whose working sets overlap with DRAM regions exhibiting uncorrectable error risk. The system operates at VM granularity rather than DIMM/node granularity, enabling selective migration of only at-risk VMs.
nv: First VM-level DRAM failure prediction system that maps DRAM error addresses to specific virtual machines, enabling fine-grained proactive migration rather than whole-node migration.
mx: other: >70% lower migration cost vs. node-level; >10% fewer VM crashes; deployed on 300,000+ production nodes

t: NeuVSA: A Unified and Efficient Accelerator for Neural Vector Search
th: Unified neural vector search accelerator via PQ-based algorithm-architecture co-design
pb: Neural Vector Search (NVS) systems require both a neural embedding stage and a vector search stage, but existing accelerators treat these as separate compute kernels with incompatible memory access patterns, causing insufficient parallelization, frequent data access conflicts, and poor scheduling.
me: NeuVSA uses Product Quantization (PQ) as a unifying computational primitive, reformulating both the embedding and search stages into the same computing and memory access paradigm via a learned PQ-based algorithm with end-to-end joint training of the codebook and index. The hardware is a homogeneous ASIC with multiple sub-accelerators, each exploiting all exposed parallelism through a structured index assignment strategy and an elastic on-chip buffer that prevents data access conflicts. A hardware-aware scheduling strategy coordinates sub-accelerators to maximize throughput. The joint training strategy improves recall by 4.6% and accuracy by 43.5% over LUT-NN.
nv: Algorithm-architecture co-design that unifies neural embedding and vector search into a single PQ-centric compute paradigm, eliminating inter-stage separation for the first time.
mx: speedup: 2.82x-416.17x lower latency over CPU, GPU, DFX+ANNA, PQA+ANNA · other: 49.60x higher throughput over CPU; 10.57x over GPU; 65.2% area reduction vs. PQA+ANNA; 4.6% recall improvement over separated strategy

t: AccelES: Accelerating Top-K SpMV for Embedding Similarity via Low-bit Pruning
th: Low-bit two-stage pruning for accelerated Top-K sparse embedding similarity
pb: Top-K sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) for recommendation system embedding similarity suffers from high latency due to inefficient memory access patterns when scanning full-precision sparse matrices to identify the most relevant embeddings.
me: AccelES employs a two-stage computation scheme: Stage 1 uses a compact low-bit (pruned) representation of the sparse matrix to rapidly identify the top-K candidate entries with minimal data movement, and Stage 2 performs full-precision SpMV only on this pruned candidate subset. Two novel sparse matrix storage formats, Ultra-CSR and Random-CSR, are introduced to optimize memory bandwidth utilization for irregular access patterns inherent in SpMV. The low-bit approximation in Stage 1 filters out irrelevant entries early, reducing the volume of full-precision computation dramatically.
nv: Two-stage low-bit pruning that decouples candidate identification (low-bit/low-cost) from precise scoring (full-precision/selective), enabling asymmetric computation allocation for Top-K SpMV.
mx: speedup: 3.4x over FPGA, 2.5x over GPU, 153.3x over CPU
tg: spmv, embedding-similarity, recommendation-systems, low-bit, sparsity, fpga

t: RpcNIC: Enabling Efficient Datacenter RPC Offloading on PCIe-attached SmartNICs
th: PCIe-aware SmartNIC hardware-software co-design for datacenter RPC offload
pb: RPC processing has become a dominant datacenter tax in microservice/serverless environments, but existing RPC accelerators either integrate logic into the CPU or use specialized low-latency interconnects unavailable in commodity servers, preventing broad deployment.
me: RpcNIC is a software-hardware co-designed SmartNIC on Xilinx U280 FPGA using three techniques to mitigate PCIe overhead: (1) a target-aware deserializer that batches cross-PCIe writes on SmartNIC SRAM using compacted hardware data structures to reduce PCIe transaction count; (2) a memory-affinity CPU-SmartNIC collaborative serializer that trades host memory copies for slow PCIe transfers, keeping data on the host side for NUMA-affine access; and (3) an automatic field update mechanism that dynamically reconfigures RPC kernel schema encoding to minimize redundant PCIe traversals when application schemas change.
nv: A three-pronged PCIe-aware co-design that makes commodity PCIe-attached SmartNICs competitive with specialized low-latency interconnect RPC accelerators for datacenter workloads.
mx: speedup: 2.3x lower RPC layer processing time vs. comparable RPC accelerator; 2.6x achievable throughput in end-to-end cloud workload
tg: smartnic, rpc-offload, pcie, microservices, serialization, fpga

t: Gemina: A Coordinated and High-Performance Memory Deduplication Engine
th: Coordinated huge-page-aware memory deduplication to recover TLB performance
pb: Memory deduplication (via KSM) eliminates duplicate pages but forces huge pages to split into 4KB base pages, degrading TLB hit rates and memory access performance by up to 43%; asynchronous huge page promotion cannot recover this loss because deduplication breaks the uniformity of page attributes required for promotion.
me: Gemina coordinates huge page management with memory deduplication through three components: (1) a fine-grained detector that separately classifies pages by both redundancy and access hotness to decouple deduplication decisions from page-size decisions; (2) a distributor that conservatively processes pages to avoid frequent hot/cold and size-class switches; and (3) an adapter that reorganizes memory layout to enable fast base-to-huge-page conversion. Together, these components preserve huge page availability by selectively deferring or avoiding deduplication of hot pages while still capturing most memory savings.
nv: Jointly optimizing memory deduplication and huge page management through a coordinated three-component system that preserves huge page promotability while retaining near-full deduplication savings.
mx: other: 96.1% of KSM memory savings retained; 43.1% memory access performance improvement vs. naive KSM-based deduplication
tg: memory-deduplication, huge-pages, tlb, ksm, os-memory-management, cloud-systems

t: SkyByte: Architecting an Efficient Memory-Semantic CXL-based SSD with OS and Hardware Co-design
th: OS-hardware co-design for byte-granular CXL-SSD memory expansion efficiency
pb: CXL-based SSDs enable byte-granular memory expansion at low cost, but suffer from long flash access latency, unpredictable garbage collection stalls, and a fundamental mismatch between byte-granular CXL access and page-granular flash I/O that wastes significant bandwidth.
me: SkyByte co-designs the host OS and SSD controller with three mechanisms: (1) opportunistic OS context switches triggered when the processor detects long CXL-SSD access delays, hiding latency via thread-level parallelism; (2) a cacheline-level write log and page-level data cache within SSD controller DRAM that coalesces byte-granular writes and performs data merging at log cleaning time to reduce flash I/O traffic; and (3) adaptive page migration that promotes hot CXL-SSD pages to fast host DRAM based on access frequency. The combination reduces both stall cycles and unnecessary flash I/O amplification.
nv: OS-level opportunistic context switching combined with a two-tier SSD controller DRAM structure (cacheline write log + page cache) that bridges the byte-granular CXL access and page-granular flash I/O mismatch.
mx: speedup: 6.11x over current CXL-based SSD · other: 23.08x reduction in flash chip I/O traffic; achieves 75% of ideal unlimited-DRAM performance
tg: cxl, ssd, memory-expansion, flash, os-co-design, byte-addressable

t: MeHyper: Accelerating Hypergraph Neural Networks by Exploring Implicit Dataflows
th: Microedge-centric dataflow accelerator for redundancy-free HGNN computation
pb: Hypergraph Neural Networks (HGNNs) based on hyperedge-centric dataflow independently process vertex and hyperedge aggregation tasks, causing significant computational redundancy from recalculating shared information (intermediate feature values) across these tasks.
me: MeHyper introduces a microedge concept that captures fine-grained shared information between aggregation tasks, replacing the hyperedge-centric model with a microedge-centric dataflow that processes shared information once and distributes it to all dependent tasks. The execution follows a Read-Process-Activate-Generate model optimized for parallel microedge task processing. The hardware accelerator features a decoupled pipeline for improved computational parallelism and a hierarchical feature management strategy that partitions on-chip memory across feature granularities to reduce off-chip DRAM accesses for the large intermediate feature vectors generated during microedge aggregation.
nv: First identification and exploitation of implicit dataflow dependencies within HGNNs via the microedge abstraction, eliminating inter-task computational redundancy across vertex and hyperedge aggregation.
mx: speedup: 1032.23x over PyG-CPU; 10.51x over HyperGef (GPU) · energy_or_tops_w: 1169.03x energy efficiency over PyG-CPU; 9.96x over HyperGef
tg: hypergraph-neural-network, gnn-accelerator, dataflow, redundancy-elimination, asic, graph-analytics

t: NearFetch: Saving Inter-Module Bandwidth in Many-Chip-Module GPUs
th: Routing-path data forwarding to reduce inter-module bandwidth waste in MCM GPUs
pb: In many-chip-module (MCM) GPUs, inter-module bandwidth is physically constrained by organic substrate or silicon interposer manufacturing limits, and fetching data from remote modules causes bandwidth contention that reduces effective achieved bandwidth, degrading GPU performance on high-sharing workloads.
me: NearFetch is a routing-based solution that exploits data locality across GPU modules on the routing path between a requesting module and remote memory. When a memory request traverses intermediate GPU modules, NearFetch checks if those intermediate modules already hold the requested data locally; if so, data is forwarded from the nearer intermediate module rather than from the distant memory partition. A topology-aware Miss Status Handling Register (MSHR) coalescing scheme records memory address information to support future forwarding decisions on cache misses. NearFetch introduces a new Inter-Module Bandwidth per Access (IBPA) metric to quantify bandwidth waste from multi-hop fetches.
nv: Routing-path data forwarding that exploits data sharing among modules along the inter-module network path, reducing effective hop count for memory fetches without modifying the MCM topology.
mx: speedup: 52.2% average performance improvement (up to 98.1%) for high-sharing workloads · other: 42.6% reduction in Inter-Module Bandwidth per Access (IBPA)
tg: mcm-gpu, chiplet, inter-module-bandwidth, data-forwarding, noc, bandwidth-efficiency

t: Criticality-Aware Instruction-Centric Bandwidth Partitioning for Data Center Applications
th: Criticality-aware instruction-level memory bandwidth partitioning for LC/BE co-location
pb: Co-locating latency-critical (LC) and best-effort (BE) tasks on shared datacenter nodes causes memory bandwidth contention that results in priority inversion, where BE tasks monopolize bandwidth and cause LC tasks to violate quality-of-service (QoS) requirements.
me: Pivot is a bandwidth partitioning system that prioritizes LC memory accesses at every component along the full memory path (L1/L2/L3 caches, DRAM controller) rather than at a single bottleneck point. Critically, Pivot selectively prioritizes only performance-critical loads—those causing long stalls on the re-order buffer (ROB)—rather than all LC accesses. A two-phase profiling technique identifies these critical loads offline with minimal runtime overhead: Phase 1 profiles whole-execution hit/miss behavior per load PC, and Phase 2 uses those profiles to tag critical loads for hardware prioritization during production runs.
nv: Instruction-centric identification of ROB-stalling critical loads combined with full-memory-path prioritization, avoiding bandwidth waste from protecting non-critical LC accesses.
mx: other: Up to 34.5% effective machine utilization improvement; up to 2.76x BE throughput improvement vs. state-of-the-art
tg: bandwidth-partitioning, co-location, qos, critical-loads, rob, datacenter

t: From Optimal to Practical: Efficient Micro-op Cache Replacement Policies for Data Center Applications
th: Near-optimal uop cache replacement policy design from theoretical bound to practical profile-guided implementation
pb: Data center applications suffer frequent micro-op (uop) cache misses because no effective uop-cache-specific replacement policy exists; the uop cache has fundamentally different cost characteristics from conventional caches (variable and disproportional miss costs, partial hits), making standard policies like LRU and even Belady's algorithm suboptimal.
me: FLACK is introduced as a near-optimal offline replacement policy that accounts for uop cache-specific properties: variable miss costs (due to disproportional re-fetch penalties) and partial hits (when only some micro-ops of an instruction group are cached). FLACK substantially outperforms Belady's algorithm, establishing a new uop-cache-specific optimality bound. FURBYS is then designed as a practical online policy that mimics FLACK via profile-guided methods, using three components: (1) whole-execution hit/miss profiles per static instruction, (2) detection of locally/transiently hot data, and (3) selective ignorance of entries with profiled low hit rates during replacement decisions.
nv: FLACK—a near-optimal offline uop cache replacement algorithm that accounts for variable miss costs and partial hits, surpassing Belady's algorithm and providing a new theoretical bound for practical policy design.
mx: speedup: 3.10% performance-per-watt improvement for CPU core · other: 14.34% average miss reduction over LRU (1.84x over state-of-the-art); FLACK: 30.21% average miss reduction bound, 4.46% greater than Belady
tg: micro-op-cache, replacement-policy, cpu-frontend, profile-guided, datacenter, cache-optimization

t: ANVIL: An In-Storage Accelerator for Name-Value Data Stores
th: In-storage near-data processing for key-value workloads
pb: Large-scale name-value pair (NVP) lookups saturate both external and internal SSD bandwidth because every NVP must be sent to the host CPU to check for a name match. Existing NVP optimizations are limited to a single data store format, leaving the broad heterogeneity of NVP encodings unaddressed.
me: ANVIL implements in-storage processing by pushing name-match logic directly into the NAND flash chips of a conventional SSD. Rather than streaming all key-value data to the host, ANVIL performs name-match filtering inside the storage device, discarding non-matching NVPs before they traverse the SSD-host interface. The system is designed as an end-to-end in-storage accelerator that supports multiple NVP formats (arrays, dictionaries, key-value stores, data mining structures) through a unified near-storage computation model.
nv: ANVIL is the first end-to-end in-storage system that accelerates a broad range of NVP data store formats by filtering non-matching names inside NAND flash chips, eliminating unnecessary host-bound I/O.
mx: speedup: 4.0x (database), 25x (analytics), 14.6% (graph processing) over conventional SSD · other: Reduced disk I/O and metadata overhead
tg: in-storage processing, name-value pairs, NAND flash, near-data computing, key-value store, SSD accelerator

t: Leveraging control-flow similarity to reduce branch predictor cold effects in microservices
th: Cold-start branch prediction using inter-request control-flow similarity for microservices
pb: Microservices suffer from severe branch mispredictions due to cold branch predictor state when cores are shared across interleaved service invocations or power-gated between requests. This cold-start effect degrades tail latency under strict SLA constraints.
me: The authors propose Similarity-based Branch Prediction (SBP), a hybrid predictor that augments conventional history-based and static-hint predictors with a similarity component (CHESS). CHESS encodes the control flow of prior request executions into a compact reference execution trace, then identifies branches that are hard to predict via conventional means and redirects them to the similarity predictor. The similarity predictor leverages dynamic control-flow reconvergence analysis to replay past execution paths for matching current requests, requiring only 18.1 KB of additional storage.
nv: CHESS exploits inter-request control-flow similarity in microservices—encoding prior execution traces as reference paths—to warm-start branch prediction for cold-predictor scenarios without requiring actual predictor state persistence.
mx: speedup: Within 95% of warm baseline performance · accuracy: 94% branch MPKI reduction vs. cold predictor; 78% vs. state-of-the-art warm predictor · other: 18.1 KB additional storage overhead
tg: branch prediction, microservices, cold-start, control-flow similarity, datacenter, hybrid predictor

t: Reconfigurable Stream Network Architecture
th: Circuit-switched streaming ISA for heterogeneous FPGA DNN overlays
pb: FPGA-based DNN overlay accelerators suffer from layer-granularity serialization: von Neumann-style coarse-grained ISAs treat each layer instruction atomically, preventing dynamic layer fusion, inter-layer pipelining, and fine-grained bandwidth orchestration across heterogeneous resources (FPGA fabric + AI Engines).
me: RSN (Reconfigurable Stream Network) abstracts the datapath as a circuit-switched network of stateful functional units (FUs) connected by latency-insensitive data streams. Programming a computation means triggering a path through the FU network; multiple non-conflicting paths enable spatial and pipeline parallelism. A three-level instruction decoder fuses multiple FU uOP streams into a single RSN instruction stream with packet-level reuse to minimize instruction overhead (1 byte drives up to 1.6 GFLOPs). RSN-XNN, the prototype on Versal VCK190, virtualizes both FPGA BRAMs/DSPs and AI Engine tiles as heterogeneous FUs through a common stream interface, enabling dynamic sequential layer pipelining and fine-grained DDR/LPDDR bandwidth interleaving during phase transitions.
nv: RSN introduces a circuit-switched streaming network ISA abstraction that enables dynamic multi-layer pipelining and fine-grained bandwidth orchestration on FPGA overlays without per-layer bitstream reconfiguration—the first FPGA design to achieve this.
mx: speedup: 6.1x latency reduction for BERT vs. SOTA on VCK190; 2.4x–3.2x throughput for BERT/ViT/NCF/MLP · energy_or_tops_w: 2.1x higher energy efficiency in FP32 vs. A100 at same 7nm node · other: Matches T4 GPU latency with only 18% of its memory bandwidth
tg: FPGA overlay, streaming ISA, dataflow, heterogeneous accelerator, DNN inference, layer fusion

t: FATE: Boosting the Performance of Hyper-Dimensional Computing Intelligence with Flexible Numerical DAta TypE
th: Per-dimension mixed-precision quantization for hyperdimensional computing on edge FPGA
pb: Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) requires high-precision representations for cosine similarity calculations, making multiplication-heavy computation expensive on resource-constrained edge FPGAs. Binary HDC reduces cost but degrades accuracy significantly.
me: FATE introduces a per-dimension mixed numerical data type scheme for HDC, applying different quantization bitwidths to different dimensions of the hypervector based on their importance. This is combined with sparsity to further reduce computation. The co-design targets embedded FPGA deployment and leverages the observation that not all HDC dimensions contribute equally, enabling high-accuracy inference at lower average precision than uniform quantization.
nv: FATE applies different numerical data types to different dimensions of HDC hypervectors, breaking from the uniform-quantization paradigm to jointly exploit dimension-level importance heterogeneity and sparsity for FPGA acceleration.
mx: accuracy: Maintains competitive accuracy vs. full-precision HDC while reducing compute cost vs. binary HDC
tg: hyperdimensional computing, mixed precision, quantization, FPGA, edge inference, sparsity

t: Unified Memory Protection with Multi-granular MAC and Integrity Tree for Heterogeneous Processors
th: Adaptive multi-granular memory integrity protection for heterogeneous SoC processors
pb: Hardware memory protection in heterogeneous SoCs (CPU + GPU + NPU) causes significant performance degradation because conventional fixed-granularity MACs and integrity trees are optimized for CPU access patterns but perform poorly under the diverse, irregular memory access patterns of GPUs and NPUs.
me: The authors propose a unified multi-granular MAC and integrity tree mechanism that supports four granularity levels for both MACs and counters. A multi-granular tree stores coarse-grained and fine-grained counters at different tree levels, and a dynamic detection mechanism selects the most appropriate granularity per memory region based on the observed access pattern from each processing unit. The design is further combined with prior sub-tree techniques to reduce tree traversal overhead.
nv: The unified multi-granular MAC and tree mechanism is the first device-independent approach supporting adaptive granularity selection for both MACs and integrity tree counters simultaneously, enabling efficient memory protection across heterogeneous CPU/GPU/NPU access patterns.
mx: speedup: 14.2% execution time reduction over fixed-granular MAC and tree; 21.1% with sub-tree techniques
tg: memory protection, integrity tree, MAC, heterogeneous SoC, security, NPU

t: Transitive Array: An Efficient GEMM Accelerator with Result Reuse
th: Multiplication-free GEMM via transitive result reuse
pb: General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) in DNNs and LLMs incurs high computational cost and memory bandwidth demand, especially in resource-constrained deployments. Existing quantization and sparsity methods reduce precision but do not exploit reusable intermediate partial results within GEMM computation.
me: The paper introduces transitive sparsity, a novel paradigm where previously computed GEMM results are reused transitively via directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) that encode reuse relationships between partial products. An optimal DAG execution order is determined to resolve dependency and parallelism constraints. The Transitive Array accelerator exploits this sparsity through a multiplication-free design that distributes work across multiple parallel lanes for balanced throughput.
nv: Transitive sparsity reuses previously computed intermediate GEMM results via DAG-ordered execution, enabling a multiplication-free accelerator architecture for LLM inference.
mx: speedup: 7.46x over Olive, 3.97x over BitVert · energy_or_tops_w: 2.31x energy reduction over Olive, 1.65x over BitVert · accuracy: comparable model accuracy on LLaMA
tg: gemm, transitive-sparsity, multiplication-free, llm-inference, result-reuse

t: Oaken: Fast and Efficient LLM Serving with Online-Offline Hybrid KV Cache Quantization
th: Online-offline hybrid KV cache quantization for LLM serving
pb: LLM serving with large batch sizes is bottlenecked by KV cache memory bandwidth and capacity: HBM provides high bandwidth but limited capacity, while high-capacity LPDDR memory lacks bandwidth. Existing KV cache quantization approaches either incur excessive online outlier detection overhead (e.g., topK sorting at O(n log n)) or sacrifice accuracy through coarse-grained grouping.
me: Oaken uses an online-offline hybrid KV cache quantization scheme: offline profiling (~100 inferences) determines per-layer, data-agnostic outlier thresholds, which are applied online to partition per-token KV vectors into three groups (outer/large outliers, inner/small outliers, middle/inliers). Group-shift quantization subtracts offline thresholds to narrow each group's value range before applying 4/5-bit uniform quantization. Outliers are stored in COO sparse format fused into zeroed elements of the dense 4-bit inlier matrix (8 bits per sparse entry total), and a custom DMA-integrated quantization/dequantization engine with a page-based MMU handles bandwidth-maximizing burst memory access. The accelerator is built on an LPU architecture synthesized in TSMC 28nm with HBM or LPDDR memory.
nv: Offline profiling of per-layer KV distribution thresholds eliminates expensive online sorting while enabling fine-grained mixed-precision grouping, and fused dense-and-sparse encoding reduces outlier storage from 23 to 8 bits per entry.
mx: speedup: 1.79x over vLLM, 1.58x over QServe at batch size 256 · accuracy: 0.54% average accuracy loss vs. state-of-the-art KV quantization baselines · area: 8.21% area overhead for Oaken modules · other: KV bitwidth reduction up to 70%; synthesized at TSMC 28nm
tg: kv-cache, quantization, llm-serving, mixed-precision, memory-bandwidth

t: Lumina: Real-Time Neural Rendering by Exploiting Computational Redundancy
th: Hardware-algorithm co-design for real-time 3DGS neural rendering on mobile SoCs
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) neural rendering is computationally demanding for mobile SoCs, with high rasterization costs and redundant computation across temporally-coherent frames preventing real-time performance.
me: Lumina integrates two algorithmic optimizations: S2 (Spatial-temporal Skipping) exploits temporal coherence to skip recomputation of unchanged Gaussian contributions across frames, and RC (Radiance Caching) caches intermediate color integration values to reduce rasterization frequency. The LuminCore hardware accelerator is co-designed with these algorithms to efficiently support cache lookups and address rasterization inefficiencies inherent in the standard 3DGS pipeline on mobile hardware.
nv: The combination of temporal-coherence-based Gaussian skipping (S2) and radiance caching (RC) reduces both compute and rasterization frequency, enabled by a purpose-built mobile accelerator (LuminCore).
mx: speedup: 4.5x over mobile Volta GPU · energy_or_tops_w: 5.3x energy reduction over mobile Volta GPU · accuracy: less than 0.2 dB PSNR reduction
tg: neural-rendering, 3d-gaussian-splatting, mobile-soc, temporal-coherence, radiance-caching

t: Accelerating Simulation of Quantum Circuits under Noise via Computational Reuse
th: Tree-based intermediate result reuse for noisy quantum circuit simulation
pb: Noisy quantum circuit simulation on HPC systems is prohibitively slow because simulators must iteratively re-execute nearly identical circuits thousands of times across different noise model trials, recomputing the same intermediate quantum states from scratch each time.
me: TQSim (Tree-Based Quantum Circuit Simulation) dynamically partitions a quantum circuit into subcircuits and constructs a tree of intermediate results that can be reused across different noisy simulation trials. The system identifies which subcircuit branches diverge due to noise injection and reuses cached intermediate density matrix or statevector results for the converging branches, avoiding redundant re-simulation. The approach is designed for multi-node distributed HPC setups with tight fidelity bounds on the approximation.
nv: Tree-based dynamic partitioning of quantum circuits enables reuse of intermediate quantum state results across noisy simulation trials, reducing total computation proportionally to reuse opportunities.
mx: speedup: up to 3.89x over Qulacs-based noisy simulator baseline
tg: quantum-simulation, noisy-circuits, computational-reuse, hpc, tree-based

t: Folded Banks: 3D-Stacked HBM Design for Fine-Grained Random-Access Bandwidth
th: 3D-stacked HBM bank folding for fine-grained random-access bandwidth
pb: HBM has seen substantial improvements in sequential (peak) bandwidth across generations but irregular/random-access bandwidth has stagnated, limiting performance for applications with non-sequential memory access patterns such as graph analytics, recommendation, and sparse workloads.
me: Folded Banks (FB-HBM) redistributes DRAM bank subarrays by folding them across multiple dies in a 3D stack and relocating command/control logic and global sense amplifiers to a new dedicated base layer implemented in a logic process. Intra-bank column select lines (CSLs) and master data lines (MDLs) are routed vertically through thin-pitch through-silicon vias (TSVs) and hybrid bonds, dramatically reducing RC power losses from long horizontal routing. Self-timed sense amplifiers eliminate the need for costly dummy subarrays, further reducing power and area on the DRAM dies.
nv: Redistributing bank subarrays across stacked dies with vertical TSV/hybrid-bond routing and a dedicated logic base layer eliminates the power and area penalties of conventional horizontal global wiring in DRAM, enabling fine-grained random-access activation at lower energy.
mx: other: 6.4x increase in sequential bandwidth over two HBM generations cited as baseline gap; random-access improvement metric not quantified in abstract
tg: hbm, 3d-stacking, random-access-bandwidth, dram-architecture, tsv

t: HPVM-HDC: A Heterogeneous Programming System for Accelerating Hyperdimensional Computing
th: Retargetable HDC programming system with DSL and heterogeneous compiler
pb: Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) programs are manually written in target-specific languages (CUDA, C++, Python) that cannot be retargeted to HDC-specific accelerators (digital ASICs, ReRAM devices), and no programming system enables productive development with efficient code generation across CPUs, GPUs, and multiple HDC accelerators.
me: The system provides two components: HDC++, a C++-based DSL built on Hetero-C++ that exposes 24 HDC-specific primitives (hypervector/hypermatrix ops, Hamming distance, cosine similarity, encoding/training/inference loop constructs) in a target-agnostic unified programming model; and HPVM-HDC, a heterogeneous compiler that extends LLVM/HPVM IR with HDC-specific intrinsics and compiles HDC++ to CPUs (via HPVM CPU backend), GPUs (via CUDA/cuBLAS/Thrust), a 40nm digital HDC ASIC (Hamming-distance pipelined, 0.78 TOPS/W), and a ReRAM HDC accelerator simulator. Two approximation optimizations exploit HDC error resilience: automatic binarization propagation (taint analysis reducing element bitwidth to 1 bit) and reduction perforation (strided or segmented loop iteration over hypervector dimensions for Hamming/cosine similarity and matmul operations).
nv: HDC++'s high-level stage primitives (encoding_loop, training_loop, inference_loop) allow the same source to be lowered to coarse-grained accelerator instructions on ASICs/ReRAM and to fine-grained CUDA/HPVM IR on CPUs/GPUs, enabling the first execution of complete HDC applications on both a taped-out digital ASIC and a ReRAM accelerator.
mx: speedup: 1.17x geomean over optimized CUDA on GPU; up to 3.4x with approximation optimizations · other: 1.6x reduction in total LOC across CPU+GPU baselines; first HDC application execution on digital ASIC and ReRAM accelerator
tg: hyperdimensional-computing, heterogeneous-compiler, dsl, reram, asic

t: Caravan: A Hardware/Software Co-Design for Efficient SIMD Neighbor Search on Point Clouds
th: SIMD-aware hardware/software co-design for k-d tree neighbor search
pb: Neighbor search in 3D point cloud processing via k-d trees is compute-intensive and exhibits SIMD underutilization: consecutive queries follow similar tree paths but diverge at deeper levels, causing sparse VPU lane usage that standard SIMD instructions cannot efficiently handle.
me: Caravan-SW batches consecutive neighbor search queries that visit similar k-d tree nodes and processes them in parallel using SIMD (AVX512) instructions. At deeper tree levels where query navigation diverges, Caravan-HW adds two new ISA instructions that enable re-indexing of valid (non-empty) SIMD lanes and fast operand shuffling, allowing dense SIMD operations on the remaining active lanes. The hardware modification is lightweight, requiring only 0.032 mm2 of additional silicon area.
nv: Two new ISA instructions that re-index and shuffle valid SIMD elements at divergent k-d tree leaf levels, eliminating the runtime sparsity penalty of batched neighbor search without a full custom accelerator.
mx: speedup: 5.19x neighbor search speedup (1.97x end-to-end) with Caravan-HW; 4.05x (1.85x end-to-end) with SW only · area: 0.032 mm2 additional area for HW extension
tg: point-cloud, kd-tree, simd, neighbor-search, isa-extension

t: Avalanche: Optimizing Cache Utilization via Matrix Reordering for Sparse Matrix Multiplication Accelerator
th: on-chip cache optimization for sparse matrix multiplication
pb: Sparse Matrix Multiplication (SpMM) accelerators suffer from poor on-chip memory utilization due to irregular memory access patterns; existing designs fail to cache both input matrices efficiently, leading to redundant DRAM accesses and low throughput.
me: Avalanche applies three complementary techniques: (1) Mat-Reorder reorders columns of matrix B to maximize data locality and enable early completion of row computations in matrix A; (2) DP-Evict (Dead-Product Early Eviction) immediately evicts fully-computed intermediate products from on-chip SRAM to reclaim capacity; (3) RM-Caching (Reuse Distance-Aware Matrix Caching) prioritizes retention of matrix B elements with short reuse distances in the on-chip cache. Together these techniques keep both operand matrices resident in a 6.15 mm2 chip with minimal spill-to-DRAM.
nv: Column reordering of the sparse input matrix (Mat-Reorder) to align non-zero access patterns with on-chip cache capacity, enabling simultaneous caching of both operand matrices.
mx: speedup: 1.97x average over state-of-the-art SpMM accelerator · area: 6.15 mm2 chip area
tg: spmm, sparse, on-chip-cache, matrix-reordering, data-locality

t: Enabling Ahead Prediction with Practical Energy Constraints
th: energy-efficient ahead branch prediction
pb: Branch predictors require multiple pipeline cycles to produce a prediction, causing a latency penalty; ahead prediction solves this by starting early but must consider all 2^N possible histories for the N intermediate branches, increasing energy by 14.6x and making the approach impractical.
me: The authors observe that most of the 2^N possible intermediate branch-direction combinations never actually occur at runtime; only one or two patterns are observed in practice. They modify the TAGE predictor to track and eliminate non-materializing history patterns, reducing the number of parallel prediction paths that must be evaluated. This allows the ahead predictor to operate with only 1.5x energy overhead instead of the previously assumed 14.6x, while delivering 4.4% IPC improvement.
nv: Observation that intermediate branch history patterns rarely materialize reduces the effective branching factor of ahead prediction from exponential to near-constant, making practical ahead prediction feasible.
mx: speedup: 4.4% performance improvement · energy_or_tops_w: 1.5x energy increase (vs 14.6x baseline assumption)
tg: branch-prediction, ahead-prediction, TAGE, energy-efficiency, front-end

t: AMALI: An Analytical Model for Accurately Modeling LLM Inference on Modern GPUs
th: analytical GPU performance modeling for LLM inference
pb: Existing GPU analytical models cannot accurately predict LLM inference performance because they mismodel tensor core throughput, ignore constant and instruction cache effects, and abstract away warp-level execution details critical to LLM kernels.
me: AMALI introduces three modeling innovations: (1) an instruction-modifier and throughput-based tensor core model that captures math-pipe throttle stalls by accurately modeling the pipeline fill/drain behavior of tensor cores; (2) micro-benchmark-derived analytical models for constant cache and instruction cache that measure CUDA kernel launching latencies; (3) a multi-warp model using warp instruction number distributions to reflect the heterogeneous occupancy and scheduling behavior of LLM inference kernels. All three components are validated against real A100 hardware measurements.
nv: The explicit modeling of instruction-cache and constant-cache latencies via micro-benchmarks, combined with a throttle-stall-aware tensor core model, reduces LLM inference MAPE from 127.56% to 23% on A100.
mx: accuracy: MAPE reduced from 127.56% to 23% on A100
tg: analytical-model, LLM-inference, GPU, tensor-core, performance-modeling

t: GCStack+GCScaler: Fast and Accurate GPU Performance Analyses Using Fine-Grained Stall Cycle Accounting and Interval Analysis
th: fast and accurate GPU performance analysis and design-space exploration
pb: Existing GPU performance analysis tools use coarse-grained, issue-stage-centric, priority-based cycle stacks that exaggerate memory-side stalls, hide concurrent stall events, and require expensive cycle-level simulation repetition for each design variant.
me: GCStack captures all concurrently occurring stall events within each cycle and represents performance as a fine-grained cycle stack by attributing each stall cycle to all simultaneously active stall types rather than the single highest-priority one. GCScaler then uses interval analysis to analytically scale the fine-grained cycle stack from a baseline GPU to an alternative design point without re-simulation, applying separate analytical scaling models for idle and synchronization stalls. The combined method allows exploration of 1,000 GPU designs from a single simulation trace.
nv: Fine-grained concurrent stall accounting (GCStack) combined with interval-analysis-based analytical stall scaling (GCScaler) enables simultaneous accurate bottleneck attribution and fast design-space exploration from a single baseline simulation.
mx: speedup: 32.7x faster design exploration over repetitive timing simulation · accuracy: 6.37% mean absolute performance estimation error across 47 benchmarks
tg: GPU, performance-analysis, stall-accounting, interval-analysis, design-space-exploration

t: REIS: A High-Performance and Energy-Efficient Retrieval System with In-Storage Processing
th: in-storage processing for RAG retrieval acceleration
pb: The retrieval stage of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a throughput bottleneck because Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) on large embedding databases incurs massive data movement between host and storage; existing In-Storage Processing (ISP) approaches use storage-agnostic ANNS algorithms, do not accelerate the subsequent data-fetch step, and require heavy SSD hardware modifications.
me: REIS co-designs the ANNS algorithm with ISP hardware inside the storage system to avoid host-storage data movement. It adopts an ISP-tailored ANNS algorithm that exploits the internal bandwidth and parallelism of NAND flash controllers without large hardware modifications. REIS additionally accelerates the data-retrieval step for items selected by ANNS, overlapping fetch and search computations. The system is designed to minimize changes to storage hardware while maximizing throughput.
nv: ISP-tailored ANNS algorithm that co-designs the search procedure with the flash storage controller's internal architecture, simultaneously accelerating both vector search and subsequent data retrieval without significant hardware modification.
mx: other: High performance and energy efficiency claimed; specific numbers not reported in abstract
tg: RAG, in-storage-processing, ANNS, LLM-inference, near-data-processing

t: Ecco: Improving Memory Bandwidth and Capacity for LLMs via Entropy-Aware Cache Compression
th: entropy-aware cache compression for LLM inference on GPU
pb: LLM inference is severely memory-bandwidth-bound and memory-capacity-constrained due to large KV caches and weight tensors; the KV cache alone can consume 72.7% of GPU memory. Existing quantization schemes (AWQ, SmoothQuant, Quarot) reduce storage but introduce high runtime decompression overheads that negate bandwidth savings or compromise accuracy.
me: Ecco integrates a parallel compressor/decompressor pair between the GPU L2 cache and HBM. Weights and KV cache are compressed 4x using group-wise (group size 128) non-uniform k-means quantization with 64 shared k-means patterns per tensor, plus clipped/padded Huffman coding with 4 per-pattern codebooks; activations use a simpler 2x uniform INT8 scheme. The 4x decompressor deploys 64 parallel Huffman sub-decoders operating on overlapping 15-bit windows of the 512-bit compressed block, fused with a 6-stage tree-based concatenator and 128 parallel mappers. The compressor uses a bitonic sorter for scale factor / outlier extraction and a min/max fitness score to select among 16 shared k-means patterns online. Both components are replicated 20x to match the 5120 B/cycle L2 throughput, implemented in 28nm (scaled to 7nm).
nv: A parallel multi-stage Huffman decoder that breaks the sequential decoding barrier using 64 overlapping sub-decoders fused with a tree concatenation stage, achieving two-orders-of-magnitude latency reduction and GPU L2-comparable throughput for a lossy, entropy-aware compression scheme.
mx: speedup: 2.9x over TensorRT FP16 (avg), 2.9x over AWQ, 2.4x over Olive, 1.9x over SmoothQuant on LLaMA-13B decode · area: 5.11 mm2 total hardware addition on A100 (826 mm2 die), <1% area overhead; 7.36 W power (<10% of A100 idle power) · accuracy: LLaMA2-7B perplexity 5.65 (W4A8KV4) vs AWQ 5.83; outperforms all baselines on LLaMA/LLaMA2 7B-70B · other: 4x memory capacity enlargement for weights and KV cache; 2x for activations
tg: cache-compression, huffman-coding, llm-inference, kv-cache, quantization, gpu-memory

t: Adaptive CHERI Compartmentalization for Heterogeneous Accelerators
th: CHERI capability extension to heterogeneous accelerators for fine-grained memory protection
pb: Hardware accelerators in heterogeneous systems lack fine-grained memory protection: IOMMU-based isolation operates at page granularity, leaving intra-page accesses unprotected, while per-accelerator memory safety modifications require significant engineering effort and do not scale across diverse accelerator types.
me: CapChecker is an adaptive hardware interface inserted between CHERI-unaware accelerators and the system memory bus. It imports capability metadata from the CPU's CHERI register file and enforces pointer-level bounds and permission checks on every memory access issued by the accelerator, without modifying the accelerator architecture itself. The interface interposes on the accelerator's memory request channel, decodes the capability tag and bounds from the CPU-managed capability table, and raises a fault on any out-of-bounds or permission-violating access. Capability grants from the CPU are communicated through a lightweight descriptor mechanism that maps accelerator DMA addresses to CHERI capabilities.
nv: A general-purpose, accelerator-architecture-agnostic capability enforcement shim (CapChecker) that extends CHERI pointer-level memory protection to CHERI-unaware accelerators by importing CPU capabilities at the hardware interface, requiring zero accelerator modification.
mx: other: 1.4% average performance overhead vs. CHERI-unaware accelerators across benchmark set
tg: cheri, memory-safety, heterogeneous-systems, security, capability-hardware, accelerator

t: Need for zkSpeed: Accelerating HyperPlonk for Zero-Knowledge Proofs
th: ASIC acceleration of zero-knowledge proof generation
pb: Generating zero-knowledge proofs using the HyperPlonk zkSNARK protocol is prohibitively slow on CPUs, requiring minutes to hours, due to its four heterogeneous proof phases that demand large-bitwidth (255-381 bit) modular arithmetic over polynomials of degree up to 2^24. Existing ZKP accelerators target simpler protocols (Groth16, Orion, Spartan) that either require per-application trusted setups or produce large proofs, leaving HyperPlonk—which avoids both pitfalls—unaccelerated.
me: zkSpeed is a modular ASIC comprising eight dedicated hardware units: a unified SumCheck unit (handling ZeroCheck, PermCheck, and OpenCheck variants with shared modular multipliers across terms), an MSM unit based on Pippenger's algorithm with improved bucket aggregation reducing aggregation latency by 92%, a Multifunction Tree Unit (MTU) using hybrid DFS/BFS tree traversal for Build MLE, MLE Evaluate, and Product MLE, a FracMLE unit using constant-time Binary Extended Euclidean Algorithm (BEEA) with Montgomery batching (batch size 64) to amortize modular inversion costs, and an MLE Combine unit with resource sharing between sequential OpenCheck phases. Units communicate via a 4-channel shared bus; global SRAM stores compressed on-chip MLE tables (10-11x compression via binary packing), while streaming SumCheck computations flow through HBM (2 TB/s target). A full-chip simulator sweeps thousands of design configurations for Pareto-optimal area-performance tradeoffs.
nv: A unified SumCheck PE architecture that handles all three HyperPlonk SumCheck variants (ZeroCheck, PermCheck, OpenCheck) with shared modular multipliers—saving 48.9% area—combined with a novel hybrid DFS/BFS Multifunction Tree Unit and Montgomery-batched modular inversion pipeline that together cover the complete HyperPlonk proving protocol in a single ASIC.
mx: speedup: 801x geomean over AMD EPYC 7502 CPU at iso-compute area (366mm2, 2 TB/s HBM) · area: 366mm2 at 7nm (full chip, excluding HBM PHY) · other: 48.9% area saved on SumCheck PE via multiplier sharing; 92% reduction in MSM bucket aggregation latency; 41.6% area saved via Multifunction Tree unit reuse; 10-11x on-chip MLE compression
tg: zkp, zero-knowledge-proofs, hyperplonk, sumcheck, msm, asic-accelerator

t: Variational Quantum Algorithms in the era of Early Fault Tolerance
th: Partial quantum error correction for variational algorithms in early fault tolerance
pb: Emerging 10,000-qubit devices with ~0.1% two-qubit error rates enable lightweight quantum error correction (QEC) but cannot afford the full qubit overhead of surface codes near threshold, leaving a regime—Early Fault Tolerance (EFT)—where error correction is partial and resource allocation strategy is unclear. Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) must be adapted to exploit EFT resources efficiently without the hardware or qubit budget of full fault tolerance.
me: The work introduces partial QEC (pQEC) for VQAs in the EFT regime, which error-corrects Clifford operations using lightweight codes while performing non-Clifford (Rz) rotations via magic state injection rather than the more expensive T-state distillation. Architectural optimizations reduce circuit latency by 2x, and a qubit packing strategy achieves 66% qubit efficiency in the EFT regime. The approach is evaluated by comparing fidelity gains of pQEC-VQA against standard (uncorrected) VQA approaches across multiple EFT device parameter settings.
nv: Adapting partial quantum error correction—Clifford-corrected with magic-state-injected non-Clifford rotations—to Variational Quantum Algorithms in the Early Fault Tolerance regime, achieving 9.27x fidelity improvement without requiring full surface-code QEC overhead.
mx: accuracy: 9.27x fidelity improvement over standard VQA · other: 2x circuit latency reduction; 66% qubit packing efficiency
tg: quantum-computing, variational-quantum-algorithms, error-correction, early-fault-tolerance, magic-state-injection

t: Zettafly: A Network Topology with Flexible Non-blocking Regions for Large-scale AI and HPC Systems
th: Flexible non-blocking network topology for large-scale AI/HPC interconnects
pb: Post-exascale and zettascale AI/HPC systems require interconnection networks that support both scalability and non-blocking communication for concurrent jobs, but existing topologies (e.g., fat-tree, dragonfly) lack mechanisms to flexibly partition non-blocking sub-networks to match the small-to-medium job sizes that dominate compute-core-hour consumption in production systems.
me: Zettafly is a two-layer topology family: non-blocking groups (NB groups) at the bottom layer connected by global routers at the top, structured so that any minimally-routed packet between groups traverses at most one global router (low-diameter property). NB groups are sized and configured to match common job sizes, providing non-blocking communication within each group. The paper introduces simple adaptive routing algorithms tailored to Zettafly's structure and evaluates performance, cost, and scalability via extensive simulation against state-of-the-art topologies (fat-tree, dragonfly variants) under HPC workload traffic patterns including multi-task mixed traffic.
nv: A two-layer network topology that decouples non-blocking group size from global scale, enabling flexible partitioning of large networks into non-blocking sub-networks matched to typical HPC/AI job sizes while maintaining low diameter and cost-effectiveness at zettascale.
mx: other: Performance and cost improvements vs. fat-tree and dragonfly under multi-task mixed traffic (specific numbers not in abstract)
tg: interconnect, network-topology, hpc, non-blocking, zettascale, dragonfly

t: MagiCache: A Virtual In-Cache Computing Engine
th: Cacheline-granularity virtual in-cache computing with dynamic row allocation
pb: Array-level in-cache computing architectures dedicate entire cache arrays as compute arrays, leaving most computing lines idle at runtime while the non-computing arrays absorb large bursty memory accesses—both causing severe on-chip capacity loss and high data movement latency for data-parallel applications.
me: MagiCache introduces cacheline-level in-cache computing: each cache array can dynamically configure individual rows as either computing lines or cachelines with negligible hardware overhead. A virtual engine monitors runtime computation and storage requirements and dynamically reallocates rows within each array between compute and cache roles via cacheline-level space management. An instruction chaining technique enables asynchronous execution of computing arrays, overlapping bursty HBM/DRAM access latency with ongoing computation through pipelined, out-of-order scheduling of memory requests and compute operations.
nv: A virtual in-cache computing engine that performs cacheline-granularity dynamic allocation of SRAM rows between compute and cache roles, eliminating the fixed capacity loss of array-level in-cache architectures while hiding bursty memory access latency via instruction chaining.
mx: speedup: 1.19–1.61x over state-of-the-art in-cache computing architectures · area: 6.5 KB additional storage overhead
tg: in-cache-computing, compute-in-memory, cache-management, data-parallel, virtual-engine

t: FAST: An FHE Accelerator for Scalable-parallelism with Tunable-bit
th: FHE accelerator with hoisting and dual key-switching method support
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) imposes enormous computational overhead compared to plaintext computation, and existing FHE accelerators do not exploit recent cryptographic optimizations—specifically hoisting technology and the gadget decomposition key-switching (KLSS) method—leaving significant performance on the table. Additionally, ciphertext level consumption varies significantly during application execution, causing workload imbalance that accelerators with fixed precision do not address.
me: FAST is an FHE accelerator that integrates hoisting technology (reducing redundant NTT operations in key-switching) and the KLSS gadget decomposition key-switching method. A versatile framework supports both hybrid and KLSS key-switching within a single application execution, dynamically adapting to varying ciphertext levels. The accelerator implements tunable-bit arithmetic to match the differing computational precision requirements of hybrid vs. KLSS key-switching at different ciphertext levels. Scalable parallelism is achieved through a configurable array of processing elements that can be provisioned to match the current workload's level and method requirements.
nv: A single FHE accelerator framework that simultaneously supports hoisting technology and both hybrid and KLSS gadget-decomposition key-switching methods with tunable-bit arithmetic, dynamically adapting to varying ciphertext level requirements within one application execution.
mx: speedup: Not stated in abstract (improved performance over prior FHE accelerators) · other: Specific headline numbers not disclosed in abstract

t: Rethinking Prefetching for Intermittent Computing
th: energy-aware prefetch suppression for intermittent computing
pb: Conventional hardware prefetchers are energy-wasteful on batteryless energy harvesting systems (EHSs) because they aggressively fetch cache lines that are lost on power failure before any hit, wasting harvested energy. Frequent outages on EHSs mean that prefetched data that is never accessed before the next power loss represents pure energy overhead.
me: IPEX (Intermittence-aware Prefetching EXtension) is an add-on layer that wraps existing prefetchers on EHSs without replacing them. It tracks which prefetched cache blocks receive a hit before a power failure and suppresses future prefetches of lines that historically go unused ('useless prefetches'). Additionally, IPEX monitors harvested energy levels to predict imminent outages and dynamically throttles the prefetch degree at that moment, targeting only blocks likely to be accessed before power loss. The result is that harvested energy is redirected from futile prefetches toward productive forward execution progress.
nv: IPEX is the first prefetch extension that actively suppresses prefetches based on predicted power-failure timing and historical usefulness tracking, converting energy that would be wasted on lost cache lines into forward progress.
mx: speedup: 1.09x average (up to 1.23x) vs conventional prefetcher · energy_or_tops_w: 7.86% avg energy reduction (up to 21.64%) vs conventional prefetcher
tg: intermittent-computing, energy-harvesting, prefetching, power-failure, iot, cache

t: NetCrafter: Tailoring Network Traffic for Non-Uniform Bandwidth Multi-GPU Systems
th: traffic shaping for non-uniform bandwidth multi-GPU interconnects
pb: Hierarchical multi-GPU systems connect GPU groups with high-bandwidth intra-group links but lower-bandwidth inter-group links, creating severe performance bottlenecks on the inter-group network when traffic is not carefully managed. Conventional GPU communication treats all network flits uniformly, leaving bandwidth partially unutilized while also generating unnecessary traffic.
me: NetCrafter applies three complementary techniques to the inter-group network: (1) flit stitching, which coalesces partially-filled flits traveling to the same destination to maximize bandwidth utilization; (2) flit trimming, which drops speculative prefetch flits that are not yet needed, eliminating unnecessary traffic; and (3) flit sequencing, which reorders flits in the network so latency-sensitive critical flits reach their destinations ahead of bulk traffic, reducing effective latency for the most time-critical requests. The techniques are applied at the network boundary without modifying GPU compute pipelines.
nv: NetCrafter combines flit-level stitching, demand-driven trimming of speculative flits, and priority-aware sequencing into a unified traffic-shaping layer that exploits the non-uniform bandwidth structure of hierarchical multi-GPU systems.
mx: speedup: significant multi-GPU performance improvement (specific numbers not stated in abstract)
tg: multi-gpu, interconnect, network-traffic, bandwidth, flit, hierarchical

t: Topology-Aware Virtualization over Inter-Core Connected Neural Processing Units
th: topology-aware virtualization for inter-core connected NPUs
pb: Inter-core connected NPUs (e.g., Graphcore IPU, Tenstorrent) require large hardware resources, leading to poor utilization when tasks have imbalanced resource requirements, yet no prior virtualization work accounts for their hardware topology (NoC routing, SRAM-centric cores). Existing MIG-style monolithic virtualization ignores inter-core communication structure and therefore delivers suboptimal performance when multiple workloads share the device.
me: vNPU introduces three integrated techniques: (1) NPU route virtualization redirects instruction and data flow from virtual NPU core IDs to physical cores, constructing a virtual topology over the physical NoC fabric; (2) NPU memory virtualization uses SRAM-centric and NoC-aware address translation to minimize translation stalls and maximize effective memory bandwidth; (3) best-effort topology mapping enumerates candidate virtual topologies and selects the mapping that best balances resource utilization against end-to-end performance for the collocated workload mix. A prototype is validated on FPGA (Chipyard+FireSim) and on a simulator (DCRA).
nv: vNPU is the first virtualization design for inter-core connected NPUs that simultaneously virtualizes routing, SRAM-centric memory translation, and topology mapping to preserve the spatial communication structure of the physical device within each virtual partition.
mx: speedup: up to 1.92x (Transformer) and 1.28x (ResNet) vs MIG-based virtualization
tg: npu, virtualization, inter-core, topology, noc, multi-tenancy

t: WindServe: Efficient Phase-Disaggregated LLM Serving with Stream-based Dynamic Scheduling
th: dynamic scheduling for phase-disaggregated LLM inference serving
pb: Phase-disaggregated LLM serving systems that separate compute-bound prefill from memory-bandwidth-bound decoding still suffer from coarse-grained static scheduling that leaves prefill compute overloaded while decoding resources sit idle, creating queuing delays and underutilization. KV cache transfers between disaggregated phases introduce additional scheduling overhead that further degrades latency SLOs.
me: WindServe implements a global scheduler that continuously monitors compute and memory resource usage across prefill and decoding pools and dynamically orchestrates cross-phase job assignments to reduce queuing delay and KV-cache swapping overhead. A stall-free rescheduling strategy saturates memory resources while minimizing overhead from KV cache transfers between phases. A stream-based pipeline mitigates interference between prefill and decoding jobs running concurrently by separating their execution streams and managing dependencies asynchronously.
nv: WindServe's stall-free rescheduling strategy enables continuous saturation of memory resources during KV cache migration between disaggregated phases without introducing scheduling stalls, enabling fine-grained dynamic load balancing that static schedules cannot achieve.
mx: speedup: 4.28x TTFT median improvement; 1.5x TPOT P99 reduction vs SOTA phase-disaggregated systems · other: improved SLO attainment under high load
tg: llm-serving, phase-disaggregation, scheduling, kv-cache, prefill-decoding, latency-slo

t: Heliostat: Harnessing Ray Tracing Accelerators for Page Table Walks
th: repurposing ray tracing accelerators for GPU page table walks
pb: GPU virtual memory page table walks are a critical performance bottleneck as workloads with large address spaces saturate the GPU Memory Management Unit (GMMU), which cannot be straightforwardly scaled without significant area and power overhead. Existing approaches focus on better utilizing fixed translation bandwidth rather than fundamentally increasing it.
me: Heliostat repurposes the underutilized ray tracing accelerators (RTAs) already present in modern GPUs to perform page table walks, exploiting the structural similarity between ray-box/triangle intersection traversal and radix-tree page table traversal. The design maps page-table-walk state machines onto RTA traversal units to increase total translation bandwidth without adding dedicated GMMU hardware. Heliostat+ extends this by proactively performing predicted future address translations (prefetch-style speculation on the translation path) to further reduce effective TLB-miss latency. This approach democratizes RTA use across all workloads, not just ray-traced rendering.
nv: Heliostat is the first design to repurpose ray tracing accelerators as page table walk engines, leveraging the structural isomorphism between BVH tree traversal and radix page table walks to increase GPU address translation bandwidth at 1.53% the area and 5.8% the power of an equivalently overprovisioned GMMU.
mx: speedup: 1.93x over baseline GPU; 1.92x over SoTA 1; 1.66x over SoTA 2; Heliostat+ further 1.23x over Heliostat · energy_or_tops_w: 5.8% power vs overprovisioned comparable solution · area: 1.53% area vs overprovisioned comparable solution
tg: gpu, virtual-memory, page-table-walk, ray-tracing, tlb, memory-management

t: Magellan: A High-Performance Loop-Guided Prefetcher for Indirect Memory Access
th: compiler-guided software prefetching for irregular memory access
pb: Graph analytics and sparse linear algebra applications rely heavily on indirect memory access (IMA), where pointer-chasing through irregular data structures causes frequent high-latency DRAM accesses due to poor temporal and spatial locality. Existing hardware and software prefetchers for IMA target narrow access patterns and struggle with complex nested-loop IMA patterns in sparse workloads.
me: Magellan is a compiler-based software prefetcher that constructs dependence graphs across loop levels to detect complex multi-level IMA patterns. It captures inner-outer loop semantics to schedule prefetches for both current and future loop iterations, inserting prefetch instructions ahead of the load chain. The compiler analysis extracts the indirection chains (e.g., A[B[i]]) across nested loop boundaries and emits prefetch instructions with appropriate software distances derived from loop trip counts and memory latency estimates.
nv: Magellan is the first software prefetcher to model cross-loop-level dependence graphs and leverage inner-outer loop semantics to prefetch across nested IMA patterns, enabling coverage of access patterns that prior single-level approaches miss.
mx: speedup: 1.14x average, up to 1.41x over best existing IMA software prefetcher · other: 25% cache miss reduction, 14% dynamic instruction count reduction
tg: indirect-memory-access, software-prefetching, graph-analytics, compiler, sparse

t: SpecASan: Mitigating Transient Execution Attacks Using Speculative Address Sanitization
th: hardware-enforced transient execution attack mitigation via memory tagging
pb: Transient execution attacks (Spectre, Meltdown, MDS) exploit speculative execution to leak sensitive data through residual microarchitectural state, and existing defenses either delay speculative execution or require costly shadow structures and dynamic information flow tracking. Providing strong security against transient execution attacks without significant performance overhead remains an open problem.
me: SpecASan extends ARM's Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) from the committed path to the speculative path. When a speculative memory access fails the MTE tag comparison (i.e., the tag on the pointer does not match the tag in memory), that access is stalled until speculation resolves, preventing it from affecting microarchitectural state (caches, TLBs). This is combined with existing Control-Flow Integrity (CFI) enforcement to block gadget construction. The approach models transient execution attacks as software-defined security contract violations and enforces the contracts in hardware using existing MTE tag-check hardware, requiring minimal new hardware.
nv: SpecASan is the first design to repurpose ARM MTE tag checks on the speculative execution path to selectively delay potentially leaking memory accesses, enforcing security contracts without disabling speculation or adding shadow structures.
mx: other: Low performance overhead (exact number not given in abstract); coverage of Spectre + MDS
tg: spectre, transient-execution, memory-tagging, arm-mte, side-channel

t: NUPEA: Optimizing Critical Loads on Spatial Dataflow Architectures via Non-Uniform Processing-Element Access
th: instruction placement near memory on spatial dataflow architectures
pb: On large spatial dataflow architectures (SDAs) where program instructions are distributed across a fabric of processing elements (PEs), some PEs are physically closer to memory than others, creating non-uniform data access latencies (NUPEA).
