Existing approaches focused on NUMA-style data placement, which is complex and often ineffective when critical data is hard to identify statically.
me: NUPEA observes that on large SDAs, placing critical load instructions on PEs physically close to memory reduces data movement costs. The authors implement architecture extensions and compiler optimizations for NUPEA on the Monaco SDA (by Efficient Computer) and its effcc compiler. The compiler identifies critical loads via dependence analysis and maps them to near-memory PEs, while the architecture exposes PE-to-memory proximity information to the compiler. This contrasts with NUMA where data is moved closer to fixed PEs.
nv: NUPEA inverts the data-centric NUMA paradigm: rather than moving data near compute, it places compute (load instructions) near memory on spatial dataflow architectures, which is more tractable for compiler analysis.
mx: speedup: 28% avg over uniform-PE-access SDA; 20% avg over UPEA+NUMA SDA
tg: spatial-dataflow, non-uniform-memory-access, data-movement, compiler, processing-element-placement

t: Single Spike Artificial Neural Networks
th: temporal-signal ANN execution for energy-efficient inference
pb: Standard ANNs require large-scale arithmetic with high energy consumption, while spiking neural networks (SNNs) circumvent this via biologically inspired computation but use fundamentally different algorithms from ANNs, preventing reuse of the mature ANN software stack and optimization techniques. The paper seeks an intermediate approach that achieves the energy efficiency of SNNs while remaining compatible with ANN algorithms and toolchains.
me: The design represents each ANN weight as a delay element and each activation magnitude as the arrival time of a digital signal. Complete ANNs are built on top of these temporal primitives through: (1) spatial and temporal reuse strategies enabling classical dataflows (e.g., weight-stationary) in a systolic array; (2) a noise-tolerant temporal summation operation for accumulation; (3) novel hybrid digital/temporal memory circuits for storing inter-layer activations; and (4) a temporal memory integration that manages activations between layers while preserving ANN algorithmic compatibility.
nv: Encoding ANN weights as delay elements and activation magnitudes as digital signal arrival times, enabling ANN-compatible systolic array dataflows on biologically inspired temporal circuits with 11x better energy than SNNs.
mx: speedup: 4x latency improvement over SNNs · energy_or_tops_w: 11x better energy vs SNNs; 3.5x better energy vs 8-bit digital systolic arrays · accuracy: Inference accuracy evaluated across multiple MLPerf Tiny architectural parameter configurations
tg: temporal-computing, spiking-neural-networks, energy-efficiency, systolic-array, biologically-inspired, mlperf-tiny

t: Cassandra: Efficient Enforcement of Sequential Execution for Cryptographic Programs
th: secure sequential execution enforcement for constant-time cryptographic code
pb: Modern out-of-order processors violate constant-time programming assumptions by transiently executing unintended control-flow paths, enabling Spectre-class transient execution attacks against cryptographic code. Existing mitigations that address control-flow misspeculations impose high performance overhead by broadly restricting speculative execution.
me: Cassandra disables branch prediction for constant-time cryptographic code regions and instead records and replays the deterministic sequential control flow using a Branch Trace Unit (BTU) added to the processor. Exploiting the observation that constant-time programs have mostly static control flow across runs and that cryptographic programs are loop-intensive with highly compressible control-flow patterns, Cassandra performs upfront branch analysis to compress control-flow traces stored in the BTU. The BTU then supplies fetch redirections from compressed trace storage, bypassing speculative branch prediction entirely for protected code regions.
nv: Replacing the branch predictor with a record-and-replay mechanism using compressed control-flow traces for constant-time cryptographic code, achieving security without speculation overhead and even a net average speedup over an unsafe baseline.
mx: speedup: average 1.85% speedup over unsafe baseline processor · other: strong security guarantee against Spectre-class transient execution attacks on constant-time code
tg: transient-execution, spectre, constant-time, branch-prediction, cryptography, security

t: LightNobel: Improving Sequence Length Limitation in Protein Structure Prediction Model via Adaptive Activation Quantization
th: hardware-software co-design for protein structure prediction via adaptive activation quantization
pb: Protein Structure Prediction Models (PPMs) such as AlphaFold2 and ESMFold use a Pair Representation tensor with dimension (Ns, Ns, Hz) that grows quadratically in memory and cubically in attention score computation with sequence length Ns, causing GPU out-of-memory failures beyond ~2000 amino acids and latency dominated (>91%) by Triangular Attention at long sequences. Existing chunking and low-memory attention workarounds do not reduce the fundamental activation size and degrade performance.
me: LightNobel applies Token-wise Adaptive Activation Quantization (AAQ) that exploits a distogram pattern unique to PPM: activations in the Pair Representation have large inter-token variance but small inter-channel variance, making token-wise quantization preferable to channel-wise. AAQ classifies Pair Representation activations into three groups based on value range and outlier density, applying INT8 inliers + INT16 outliers (Group A, high-magnitude pre-LayerNorm), INT4 inliers + INT16 outliers (Group B, post-LayerNorm with some outliers), and INT4 inliers without outlier handling (Group C, low-magnitude). Outliers are identified at runtime using a dynamic top-k algorithm on the VVPU via bitonic sorting. The hardware implements a Reconfigurable Matrix Processing Unit (RMPU) with bit-level reconfigurable adder trees and Reconfigurable Data Aligners (RDAs) that partition tokens into 4-bit chunks and dynamically configure PE Lanes (4 or 5 PE Lanes) to handle multi-precision token streams without per-element dequantization. A Versatile Vector Processing Unit (VVPU) with 128 SIMD Lanes and a Local Crossbar Network handles LayerNorm, Softmax, residual connections, and runtime quantization. A token-wise MHA dataflow similar to FlashAttention avoids materializing the full (Ns, Ns, Ns) score matrix. The design is synthesized at 28nm targeting 1 GHz with 5 HBM2E stacks (80 GB).
nv: Token-wise adaptive activation quantization exploiting PPM-specific distogram patterns in Pair Representation, combined with a bit-level reconfigurable matrix unit (RMPU) that dynamically allocates PE Lane groups (4 or 5) to handle mixed INT4/INT8/INT16 precision streams without full dequantization.
mx: speedup: 8.44x over A100, 8.41x over H100 (Protein Folding Block); 1.74x end-to-end over ESMFold baseline · energy_or_tops_w: 37.29x power efficiency over A100, 43.35x over H100 · area: 28nm synthesis at 1 GHz · accuracy: TM-Score loss <0.001 vs. FP16 baseline across CAMEO, CASP14, CASP15 datasets · other: Peak memory reduced by 120.05x vs. FP16 baseline; activation footprint reduced to 7.90 GB vs. 113.49 GB for sequence length 3364
tg: protein-structure-prediction, activation-quantization, hardware-accelerator, alphafold, token-wise-quantization, reconfigurable-compute

t: Fair-CO2: Fair Attribution for Cloud Carbon Emissions
th: fair game-theoretic carbon footprint attribution for cloud workloads
pb: Existing cloud carbon attribution methods unfairly allocate operational and embodied carbon footprints to tenant workloads by ignoring dynamic demand effects on embodied carbon amortization and interference effects in colocated scenarios. This leads to mispriced carbon signals that fail to incentivize workload-level carbon optimization.
me: Fair-CO2 adopts the Shapley value from cooperative game theory as a theoretically fair ground truth for shared-cost attribution, capturing both dynamic demand effects on embodied carbon (hardware amortized proportionally to actual utilization, not flat time allocation) and interference effects from workload colocation. Because exact Shapley computation scales exponentially with the number of workloads, Fair-CO2 approximates it via two tractable components: demand-aware embodied carbon attribution (adjusting hardware depreciation by real-time utilization) and interference-aware resource cost attribution (accounting for performance degradation from co-tenancy). Monte Carlo simulations over workload schedules and colocation scenarios are used to validate the approximation's fidelity to the exact Shapley solution.
nv: Applying the Shapley value as a principled fairness criterion for cloud carbon attribution and introducing scalable approximations that decompose it into demand-aware embodied and interference-aware operational components.
mx: accuracy: Monte Carlo simulations show Fair-CO2 approximates Shapley ground truth attribution at scale · other: Fair attribution of operational and embodied carbon in colocated cloud scenarios
tg: carbon-attribution, cloud-sustainability, shapley-value, embodied-carbon, colocation, game-theory

t: Telos: A Dataflow Accelerator for Sparse Triangular Solver of Partial Differential Equations
th: Dataflow acceleration of sparse triangular solve for PDE workloads
pb: Sparse triangular solve (SpTRSV) dominates runtime in preconditioned iterative solvers for PDE-derived linear systems due to loop-carried dependencies that severely limit parallelism. Prior accelerators cannot simultaneously achieve high parallelism and good data locality for structured sparsity from stencil-based PDE discretizations.
me: Telos is a dataflow accelerator that exploits structured (stencil-pattern) sparsity in SpTRSV. A plane-parallel pipelining technique maps dependent computations across processing elements (PEs) while preserving data locality within each plane. A cross-plane communication aggregation technique reorganizes inter-plane data transfers into systolic flows, enabling pipelined resolution of loop-carried dependencies with minimal stall overhead. Computation is overlapped with memory accesses to hide latency.
nv: Plane-parallel pipelining that resolves SpTRSV loop-carried dependencies in a systolic, locality-preserving manner by exploiting the regular stencil structure of PDE-derived sparsity.
mx: speedup: 61x over CPU, 8x over GPU, 11x over state-of-the-art accelerator
tg: sparse-linear-algebra, spTRSV, dataflow, stencil, PDE, systolic

t: WarmCache: Exploiting STT-RAM Cache for Low-Power Intermittent Systems
th: Relaxed-retention STT-RAM cache for intermittent energy-harvesting systems
pb: Energy harvesting systems (EHS) suffer from compulsory cache misses after power failures because volatile SRAM caches lose all data across power outages, forcing cold-start cache rebuilding on each power restoration. Existing non-volatile cache designs impose high write energy and latency overhead.
me: WarmCache uses an STT-RAM cache with relaxed thermal stability (reduced retention time) tuned so cache contents survive typical power outage durations without requiring full non-volatile persistence. The compiler partitions the program into regions and performs region-level error correction: at each region boundary, updated cache lines are scrubbed and any multi-bit retention errors trigger re-execution of that region. A region formation technique via stitching (combining short regions) and splitting (dividing long regions) aligns region boundaries with the STT-RAM scrubbing interval.
nv: Using relaxed-retention STT-RAM (not fully non-volatile) to preserve cache warmth across power outages, combined with compiler-driven region-level error correction to handle retention failures without write-back overhead.
mx: speedup: 1.3-1.4x over state-of-the-art EHS cache design
tg: STT-RAM, intermittent-computing, energy-harvesting, non-volatile-cache, error-correction, compiler

t: SEAL: A Single-Event Architecture for In-Sensor Visual Localization
th: In-sensor visual localization via delay-based race logic encoding
pb: Traditional binary-encoded image sensors generate large data volumes that create energy and latency bottlenecks during transfer, storage, and processing for visual localization tasks such as keypoint detection and tracking. Moving these operations off-sensor to a host processor adds significant latency and energy cost.
me: SEAL introduces delay-based (temporal) codes at the pixel array level, replacing binary encoding with analog-to-time converters (ATCs) that represent pixel values as pulse delays (race logic). A temporal processor co-designed with the ATCs implements keypoint detection and tracking using race logic's single-wire-per-variable, single-event-per-wire policy, maximizing energy and area efficiency. A heavily quantized frontend processor then processes temporal outputs before the sensor-processor interface, enabling in-sensor VIO pipeline stages.
nv: End-to-end in-sensor localization pipeline built on delay-based (race logic) encoding instead of binary encoding, enabling keypoint detection and tracking within the pixel sensor itself using fully digital CMOS circuits.
mx: speedup: 16-61x latency reduction for keypoint detection and tracking vs. software baseline on host processor · energy_or_tops_w: 7x energy reduction vs. standard digital pixel sensor · accuracy: ATE RMSE changes: -1.0 cm (HybVIO), +0.3 cm (VINS-Mono) on EuRoC
tg: in-sensor-computing, race-logic, visual-localization, temporal-coding, VIO, keypoint-detection

t: Dadu-Corki: Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Embodied AI-powered Robotic Manipulation
th: Algorithm-architecture co-design for real-time LLM-controlled robotic manipulation
pb: Embodied AI robotic manipulation systems run LLM inference on a frame-by-frame basis, creating cumulative sequential latencies (LLM inference, robot control, data communication) that reach 249 ms per frame and prevent real-time operation at >=30 Hz. LLM inference alone consumes 72.7% of latency and 95.8% of energy per frame.
me: Corki decouples LLM inference from robot control by replacing per-frame discrete action prediction with cubic polynomial trajectory prediction over multiple future steps, reducing LLM inference frequency by up to 5.1x. A custom dataflow ASIC accelerator implements task-space computed torque control (TS-CTC) with pipelined link-level computations (pose, velocity, acceleration, force units connected via FIFOs and line buffers) and an application-specific approximate computing unit that skips matrix recomputation when joint angular movement is below a threshold (saving >51% of matrix updates). Communication latency is hidden by pipelining image capture and transmission concurrent with trajectory execution.
nv: Replacing frame-by-frame discrete action prediction with cubic trajectory prediction decouples the LLM inference rate from the control rate, enabling a purpose-built TS-CTC hardware accelerator with approximate computing that achieves 29x control speedup on FPGA.
mx: speedup: 5.9x end-to-end; 29x control acceleration on FPGA; LLM inference frequency reduced 5.1x · energy_or_tops_w: 9.2x energy reduction (Corki-9 variant) · area: 13.6% DSP, 7.8% FF, 16.9% LUT, 6.6% BRAM on Xilinx Zynq-7000 ZC706 · accuracy: Success rate improvement up to 13.9% (up to 17.3% average job length improvement on seen tasks)
tg: embodied-AI, robot-manipulation, LLM-inference, trajectory-prediction, algorithm-architecture-codesign, approximate-computing

t: TRACI: Network Acceleration of Input-Dynamic Communication for Large-Scale Deep Learning Recommendation Model
th: In-network acceleration of input-dynamic DLRM embedding aggregation
pb: Multi-GPU DLRM training is bottlenecked by embedding layer communication: the Aggregation collective (sparse, input-dependent gather/reduce across GPUs) cannot be accelerated by existing in-network compute solutions designed for All-Reduce because its data transfer patterns are dynamic and depend on input batch content, not topology.
me: TRACI introduces an in-network acceleration architecture with a novel network transaction design that augments messages with input reuse and output reuse identifications, allowing the network switch hardware to proactively identify and exploit message connections on-the-fly. New switch hardware dynamically discovers reuse relationships between embedding lookup requests arriving from different GPUs and performs in-network aggregation or deduplication rather than routing all data to a host.
nv: Network transactions with embedded input-reuse and output-reuse identifiers that enable smart switch hardware to perform on-the-fly aggregation of input-dynamic, sparse DLRM embedding communication.
mx: other: Communication bandwidth reduction for DLRM Aggregation (specific numbers truncated in abstract)
tg: DLRM, in-network-compute, recommendation-model, embedding-aggregation, multi-GPU, smart-switch

t: AQB8: Energy-Efficient Ray Tracing Accelerator through Multi-Level Quantization
th: Integer-native quantized BVH traversal for energy-efficient ray tracing
pb: Ray tracing BVH traversal is bottlenecked by DRAM bandwidth consumed by 32-bit floating-point bounding boxes, and prior 8-bit compression schemes still require decompression back to FP32 for intersection tests, retaining the arithmetic cost of complex FP32 operations.
me: AQB8 constructs a quantized BVH tree using a multi-level quantization scheme where bounding boxes are encoded as 8-bit integers at multiple hierarchy levels, enabling intersection tests to operate directly on low-bit integers without decompression. The hardware replaces FP32 arithmetic units with area-efficient integer units for BVH traversal, eliminating both DRAM bandwidth waste and expensive FP32 arithmetic. A hierarchical error-compensation mechanism propagates quantization bounds across BVH levels to prevent false-negative ray-box misses.
nv: Multi-level quantization of BVH bounding boxes enabling end-to-end integer arithmetic during BVH traversal without any FP32 decompression step.
mx: speedup: 1.82x over modern GPU RT accelerators · energy_or_tops_w: 49% reduction in energy consumption · area: 27% hardware area reduction · accuracy: correctness preserved (no false-negative ray-box misses) · other: 70% reduction in DRAM accesses
tg: ray-tracing, BVH, quantization, integer-arithmetic, graphics, energy-efficiency

t: InfiniMind: A Learning-Optimized Large-Scale Brain-Computer Interface
th: NVM write optimization for continual learning in implanted BCI systems
pb: Deploying continual learning on NVM-assisted implanted BCI systems incurs excessive write overhead on non-volatile memory, drastically reducing NVM endurance (lifetime) and causing performance bottlenecks that make continual adaptation to non-stationary neural signals impractical.
me: InfiniMind proposes four NVM-write optimization schemes implemented in a memory controller: (1) update filtering exploits sparse and recurring nature of BCI signals to skip unnecessary writes; (2) delta buffering uses temporal locality in neural signals to accumulate deltas and batch NVM writes; (3) out-of-place flushing packs multiple sub-page updates into single page writes to reduce write amplification; and (4) waveform compression exploits structural characteristics of neural waveforms to reduce data volume. These are integrated as a memory controller layer on top of an NVM-assisted BCI system running continual learning algorithms.
nv: A memory controller combining four complementary NVM-write optimizations tailored to the sparse, temporally-local, and structurally-regular characteristics of BCI neural signals.
mx: speedup: 5.39x performance improvement · other: 23.52x NVM lifetime extension over state-of-the-art NVM-assisted BCI system
tg: brain-computer-interface, NVM, continual-learning, write-endurance, implantable, memory-controller

t: UPP: Universal Predicate Pushdown to Smart Storage
th: flexible ISA for in-storage predicate evaluation
pb: Existing in-storage processing (ISP) solutions only support simple operators (equality, range comparisons) on fixed-length columns, leaving modern analytical queries that use complex operators and diverse data formats unaccelerated. There is no flexible ISP mechanism that can handle arbitrary filter predicates used in production databases.
me: UPP defines a compact, purpose-built ISA for predicate pushdown that is separate from individual operator implementations. The database software layer recognizes filter predicates, compiles them to UPP-compliant instructions, and ships them to an FPGA (SmartSSD) where bitwise comparison execution leverages lightweight metadata to evaluate predicates directly in storage without reformatting data. The hardware/software co-design avoids changing input data formats on disk while enabling flexible predicate evaluation through this instruction-level abstraction.
nv: A compact ISA tailored explicitly for predicate pushdown allows the database to compile arbitrary, complex filter predicates into storage-executable instructions, achieving generality that prior ISP designs relying on hardwired operator logic cannot.
mx: speedup: 1.2–7.9x end-to-end Spark query speedup on TPC-H 100 GB
tg: in-storage processing, predicate pushdown, fpga, analytics, isa, smart-storage

t: RAGO: Systematic Performance Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Serving
th: schema-driven optimization for RAG serving systems
pb: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) serving is emerging as a critical LLM deployment pattern, but diverse RAG algorithm variants exhibit wildly different workload characteristics (retrieval latency, reranking compute, generation length), making a single optimization strategy inadequate. There is no systematic framework for characterizing and optimizing across the space of RAG pipelines.
me: RAGO introduces RAGSchema, a structured abstraction encoding the components and dataflow of any RAG algorithm, used to characterize and compare workload behaviors. The paper analyzes representative RAG variants with distinct schemas, exposing performance bottlenecks. RAGO then applies algorithm-specific system optimizations—scheduling policies, resource partitioning, and batching strategies—tuned to each RAGSchema's profile, rather than treating all RAG variants uniformly as extended LLM inference workloads.
nv: RAGSchema is the first structured abstraction that captures the full diversity of RAG algorithm variants, enabling principled, schema-driven performance optimization rather than ad-hoc per-system tuning.
mx: speedup: 2x QPS per chip vs. RAG-extended LLM serving systems · other: 55% reduction in time-to-first-token latency
tg: rag, llm-serving, scheduling, retrieval-augmented-generation, system-optimization, transformer

t: Neo: Towards Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption Acceleration using Tensor Core
th: tensor-core acceleration of FHE polynomial arithmetic
pb: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) imposes massive computational overhead—orders of magnitude over plaintext computation—that prevents practical deployment, while existing ASIC accelerators lack generality as FHE algorithms rapidly evolve. GPU-based solutions exist but fail to exploit tensor core (TCU) hardware for the dominant FHE primitives.
me: Neo maps the CKKS FHE scheme's core operations—Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) and polynomial multiplication—onto GPU Tensor Cores (TCUs) by reformulating them as matrix operations compatible with the TCU's INT8/FP16 matrix-multiply-accumulate pipeline. The design includes careful decomposition of NTT butterfly stages and residue number system (RNS) arithmetic to fit TCU matrix dimensions, with custom CUDA kernels orchestrating data layout, twiddle factor injection, and modular reduction to avoid overflow in low-precision arithmetic.
nv: Reformulating FHE polynomial arithmetic (NTT and RNS multiplication for CKKS) as tensor-core matrix operations, enabling use of specialized high-throughput TCU hardware for cryptographic workloads rather than general CUDA cores.
mx: other: Abstract truncated; headline numbers not available
tg: fhe, homomorphic-encryption, tensor-core, gpu, ntt, ckks

t: Evaluating Ruche Networks: Physically Scalable, Cost-Effective, Bandwidth-Flexible NoCs
th: RTL evaluation of Ruche Networks as scalable NoC topology
pb: The standard 2-D mesh NoC topology suffers poor latency and throughput scaling for data-intensive manycore workloads, while prior solutions (concentrated routers, widened channels) rely on outdated assumptions that break under modern streaming-bandwidth requirements and impose significant additional cost. A rigorous, RTL-level evaluation of Ruche Networks as a superior alternative has not been performed.
me: Ruche Networks augment the 2-D mesh topology with uniform long-range bypass links (Ruche channels) that allow non-neighboring routers to communicate in fewer hops, preserving the physical scalability and regular structure of the mesh. The authors implement Ruche Networks at RTL level and compare against 2-D mesh and torus topologies under identical conditions, evaluating network throughput, latency, power consumption, area efficiency, and cycle time across manycore workloads with streaming bandwidth demands.
nv: Ruche Networks retain all physical-scalability properties of 2-D mesh while providing architecturally flexible, cost-effective performance scaling through uniform long-range links that require no structural changes to router or core design.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: Superior power and area efficiency over 2-D mesh and torus (RTL-verified) · area: Better area efficiency than mesh/torus per unit throughput · ppa: Favorable PPA vs. 2-D mesh and torus at RTL level
tg: noc, interconnect, ruche-network, mesh, manycore, rtl

t: DX100: Programmable Data Access Accelerator for Indirection
th: programmable bulk-indirect-access accelerator for DRAM bandwidth optimization
pb: Indirect memory accesses (A[B[i]] patterns) in scientific computing, graph analytics, and database workloads cause severe DRAM bandwidth underutilization because DRAM controllers have only a 32–128 request window to reorder commands, while the dependency chains of indirect loads limit the memory-level parallelism achievable by conventional cores. Prior prefetchers and fetcher units improve latency but do not reorder, coalesce, or interleave accesses for bandwidth efficiency.
me: DX100 is a programmable, memory-mapped accelerator shared across CPU cores that offloads bulk indirect and streaming memory operations. An 8-instruction ISA supports indirect loads/stores/RMWs, streaming loads/stores, ALU operations, and range-loop fusion. The Indirect Access unit uses a Row Table (BCAM + SRAM) to reorder up to 16K indices per tile for DRAM row-buffer hit maximization, a Word Table for coalescing redundant column accesses, and a Request Generator that interleaves requests across DRAM channels and bank groups. Streaming accesses go to the LLC via Cache Interface; indirect accesses bypass the cache hierarchy and inject directly into DRAM controllers, with a Coherency Agent maintaining cache coherence by snooping directories during the fill stage. An MLIR-based compiler (using Polygeist for C/C++ lowering) automatically detects indirect accesses, performs loop tiling, hoists bulk operations, and emits DX100 API calls—covering over 99% of graph frontier nodes across evaluated benchmarks.
nv: DX100 uses a large (16K-entry) hardware Row Table that reorders the full tile of indirect indices before issuing DRAM requests, providing 500x more reordering visibility than DRAM controller request buffers (32 entries) and achieving near-peak DRAM bandwidth utilization regardless of index distribution.
mx: speedup: 2.6x over 4-core multicore baseline; 2.0x over DMP indirect prefetcher (geometric mean, 12 benchmarks) · energy_or_tops_w: 3.6x core instruction reduction (energy proxy); 777 mW power at 28nm · area: 4.06 mm^2 at 28nm (~1.5 mm^2 at 14nm, 3.7% of 4-core processor area) · other: 3.9x average DRAM bandwidth utilization improvement; 2.7x row-buffer hit rate increase; 12.1x DRAM controller request buffer occupancy increase; 6.1x cache MPKI reduction
tg: indirect-memory-access, dram-bandwidth, data-access-accelerator, mlir-compiler, memory-reordering, irregular-workloads

t: EOD: Enabling Low Latency GNN Inference via Near-Memory Concatenate Aggregation
th: Near-memory GNN aggregation with compressed feature precomputation
pb: Real-time GNN inference for online services requires an inductive setup where the system must first prepare the computational graph and node features before executing inference, with this preparation step dominating end-to-end latency. The neighborhood explosion problem causes exponential growth in memory access and computation as the number of GNN layers increases.
me: EOD co-designs algorithm and hardware to tackle both challenges. On the algorithmic side, it introduces a precomputation method for training nodes that converts exponential neighborhood aggregation to linear complexity, and a concatenated Zero-Value Compression (ZVC) scheme to compact the stored precomputed hidden features. On the hardware side, EOD implements a Near-Memory Processing (NMP) architecture that performs aggregation directly on ZVC-compressed, concatenated feature data without decompressing to host memory, exploiting the high internal memory bandwidth to eliminate the PCIe/host-memory bottleneck during the preparation stage.
nv: A concatenated ZVC compression format co-designed with a dedicated NMP aggregation engine that operates natively on compressed GNN features, eliminating the host-side memory access bottleneck entirely.
mx: speedup: 981.1x geomean aggregation speedup over baseline; 17.9x geomean end-to-end speedup over GPU baseline; up to 74.3x end-to-end speedup
tg: gnn, near-memory-processing, graph-inference, latency, compression, inductive-inference

t: QR-Map: A Map-Based Approach to Quantum Circuit Abstraction for Qubit Reuse Optimization
th: Map-based qubit reuse optimization for quantum circuits
pb: Identifying optimal qubit reuse opportunities in quantum circuits via mid-circuit measurements is NP-hard in the general case; existing frameworks either suffer from exponential search complexity or produce non-optimal results due to non-deterministic heuristics.
me: QR-Map abstracts computational dependencies by extracting and aligning two-qubit gates into a map structure, making dependency detection deterministic and tractable. The framework identifies qubit reuse opportunities by analyzing these aligned gate maps, ensuring qubit savings without introducing excessive idle time. It jointly optimizes gate serialization depth and crosstalk reduction, balancing circuit fidelity with hardware constraints through a deterministic, polynomial-time map-based search.
nv: A map-based circuit abstraction that aligns two-qubit gates to expose qubit reuse dependencies deterministically, replacing exponential DAG search with a structured, optimal qubit-reuse framework.
mx: accuracy: 20% average qubit reduction, 25% circuit depth reduction, 22% SWAP reduction vs state-of-the-art
tg: quantum-computing, qubit-reuse, circuit-compilation, mid-circuit-measurement, crosstalk, circuit-optimization

t: NMP-PaK: Near-Memory Processing Acceleration of Scalable De Novo Genome Assembly
th: Channel-level NMP acceleration of De Bruijn graph genome assembly
pb: De novo genome assembly using De Bruijn graph (DBG) algorithms is both memory-latency-bound and memory-footprint-intensive: processing 10% of the human genome (38.3 GB input) requires 528 GB of DRAM, and the Iterative Compaction step—which dominates 48% of runtime—achieves only 2.5% of available memory bandwidth due to fine-grained, irregular access patterns across large, dynamic MacroNode data structures.
me: NMP-PaK places pipelined systolic Processing Elements (PEs) inside DIMM buffer chips (channel-level NMP) to exploit high internal memory bandwidth and reduce data movement latency. Each PE implements a 3-stage pipeline (Invalidation Check, TransferNode Extraction, Routing and Update) operating at MacroNode granularity, with an intra-DIMM crossbar switch and an inter-DIMM network bridge routing TransferNodes between PEs. Software optimizations complement the hardware: customized batch processing divides the genome into 10% batches to reduce peak memory footprint by 14x, pointer-aliasing deduplication eliminates redundant MacroNode copies, and a hybrid CPU-NMP strategy offloads large MacroNodes (>1 KB) to the CPU to avoid PE buffer oversizing and workload imbalance.
nv: Channel-level NMP with pipelined systolic PEs co-designed specifically for the MacroNode data structure of DBG assembly, enabling parallel MacroNode-granular Iterative Compaction with inter-DIMM TransferNode routing and a hybrid CPU-NMP offload policy for irregular outliers.
mx: speedup: 16x over CPU baseline; 5.7x over GPU (A100); 8.3x throughput vs PaKman supercomputer under same resources · accuracy: 14x memory footprint reduction; 2.4x reduction in memory operations · other: Memory bandwidth utilization: 44% (NMP-PaK) vs 6.5% (CPU baseline)
tg: genomics, near-memory-processing, de-novo-assembly, dram-buffer-chip, hardware-software-codesign, de-bruijn-graph

t: LIA: A Single-GPU LLM Inference Acceleration with Cooperative AMX-Enabled CPU-GPU Computation and CXL Offloading
th: AMX CPU-GPU cooperative LLM inference with CXL memory offloading
pb: Single-GPU LLM inference is constrained by GPU memory capacity, forcing either expensive multi-GPU deployments or frequent CPU-GPU transfers over slow PCIe, which bottleneck both latency and throughput.
me: LIA is a single-GPU LLM inference framework that systematically offloads matrix computations to AMX-enabled CPUs (4th-gen Sapphire Rapids and 6th-gen Granite Rapids Xeon), reducing CPU-GPU transfers by keeping model parameters near the CPU. LIA introduces a memory-offloading policy that integrates CXL memory (as an affordable DRAM extension) with DDR memory to expand effective model capacity for throughput-oriented batch workloads. The system partitions transformer layer computations between CPU and GPU based on runtime latency/throughput objectives, using AMX tile instructions for high-throughput GEMM on the CPU side.
nv: A cooperative CPU-GPU inference framework that exploits AMX matrix extensions on modern Intel CPUs as a genuine compute peer to the GPU, combined with CXL memory integration for extended model capacity without multi-GPU cost.
mx: speedup: Up to 5.1x lower latency (Sapphire Rapids), up to 19x lower latency (Granite Rapids) vs latest single-GPU offloading; 3.7x-5.1x higher throughput · other: CXL offloading yields additional 1.5x throughput; max batch size increased 1.8x (900-1.6K)
tg: llm-inference, cpu-gpu-offloading, amx, cxl-memory, single-gpu, matrix-extensions

t: Garibaldi: A Pairwise Instruction-Data Management for Enhancing Shared Last-Level Cache Performance in Server Workloads
th: LLC pairwise instruction-data management for server frontend bottleneck
pb: Server workloads suffer from a 'instruction victim' problem in the shared LLC: cold instruction cachelines are evicted by competing hot data cachelines, yet each instruction miss stalls the CPU frontend regardless of how much hot data is already resident in the LLC. Existing LLC management policies (Mockingjay, Hawkeye, DRRIP) optimize for data reuse distance and ignore the cost asymmetry between instruction and data misses.
me: Garibaldi introduces a pairwise instruction-data LLC management scheme built on three mechanisms: (1) a pair table (16K direct-mapped entries, 194 KB total) that tracks each instruction physical address alongside the hotness (miss_cost counter, 6-bit saturating) of the data cachelines it triggers; (2) a selective instruction protection policy using a query-based selection (QBS) mechanism that, at eviction time, queries the pair table and overrides the replacement policy to retain any instruction line whose aged miss_cost exceeds a dynamically adjusted threshold; (3) a pairwise prefetch that, upon serving an unprotected instruction miss, proactively issues prefetch requests for the associated cold data lines recorded in the pair table. Dynamic threshold adjustment uses a synchronized l-bit coloring timer that tracks P(D_miss | I_miss) every 100K LLC accesses and raises or lowers the protection threshold accordingly.
nv: Garibaldi is the first LLC management scheme to quantify the opportunity cost of instruction misses in terms of the hotness of the data they trigger, propagating data-line hotness back to instruction lines via a pair table and using it to drive selective eviction protection and prefetching.
mx: speedup: 13.2% geomean over LRU baseline (6.1% over Mockingjay alone) on 40-core server; up to 65.2% on verilator · energy_or_tops_w: 10.4% energy reduction vs LRU (5.0% below Mockingjay alone) · area: 193.9 KB total storage overhead for 40 cores (0.6% of 30 MB LLC) · other: 18% reduction in ifetch stall cycles vs LRU with Mockingjay+Garibaldi
tg: llc, cache-replacement, server-workloads, instruction-cache, frontend-bottleneck, pairwise-management

t: AiF: Accelerating On-Device LLM Inference Using In-Flash Processing
th: In-flash GEMV acceleration for on-device LLM inference
pb: On-device LLM inference with SSD offloading is severely bottlenecked by the limited external read bandwidth of flash storage (NAND-to-host path), making inference latency unacceptably high even though LLM weight matrices fit in flash capacity. Existing SSD offloading engines are bound by PCIe/interface bandwidth rather than the high internal NAND bandwidth.
me: AiF integrates matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) compute units directly inside flash chips (Accelerator-in-Flash), exploiting the high internal NAND plane-level bandwidth without routing data across the external interface. Two novel flash read techniques are introduced specifically for LLM weight access patterns stored in flash memory. AiF also employs a streamlined error correction process that delivers a 4x boost in internal read bandwidth with minimal overhead, enabling in-flash GEMV operations to run at near-full internal bandwidth.
nv: AiF is the first in-flash processing design that embeds GEMV computation within flash chips and introduces flash-read techniques tailored to LLM weight layout, achieving 4x internal bandwidth amplification through a lightweight ECC scheme.
mx: speedup: 14.6x throughput over SSD offloading baseline; 1.4x over in-memory inference · other: 4x boost in internal flash read bandwidth during inference
tg: in-flash-processing, llm-inference, on-device-ai, nand-flash, near-data, gemv

t: Reinforcement Learning-Guided Graph State Generation in Photonic Quantum Computers
th: RL-guided compilation for photonic quantum graph state generation
pb: In photonic quantum computers (PQCs), generating graph states (entangled photon collections) requires finding an optimal generation sequence over quantum emitters, where three fidelity-critical metrics — generation time, number of emitters used, and number of CZ gates — are jointly minimized. Existing compilation frameworks either face exponential search complexity or fail to guarantee optimal results due to their non-deterministic properties.
me: RLGS (Reinforcement Learning-guided Graph State generation) frames the generation sequence problem as an RL optimization task. A map-based abstraction extracts and aligns two-qubit gate dependencies from quantum circuits into a structured representation, enabling the RL agent to detect dependency patterns and search for generation sequences that simultaneously reduce generation time, emitter count, and CZ gate insertions. The framework balances gate serialization depth against crosstalk reduction.
nv: RLGS uses a map-based circuit abstraction that converts generation sequence search from exponential dependency graph traversal into an RL-navigable state space, achieving joint optimization of all three fidelity metrics simultaneously.
mx: speedup: 31.1-57.5% reduction in generation time vs. state-of-the-art (small to large graph states) · other: 13.9-17.5% emitter reduction; 37.7-57.8% CZ gate reduction
tg: photonic-quantum, graph-state-generation, reinforcement-learning, qubit-reuse, quantum-compilation

t: Single-Address-Space FaaS with Jord
th: Single-address-space FaaS with user-level in-process memory isolation
pb: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) systems incur millisecond-level overheads from isolating functions in separate address spaces (containers or microVMs), preventing them from meeting microsecond-scale service-level objectives (SLOs) required by microservice workloads. The address-space isolation mechanism forces costly context switches, copy-on-write, and cross-function data copies.
me: Jord co-locates functions in a single address space using hardware/software co-design for user-level in-process memory isolation that extends traditional virtual memory capabilities. Memory isolation and protection are enforced at nanosecond granularity without kernel involvement by leveraging hardware memory protection keys or equivalent mechanisms, enabling zero-copy cross-function communication. Scalable function dispatch is achieved through user-level scheduling that avoids OS-level context switches, allowing Jord to meet microsecond SLOs.
nv: Jord revives the function-as-a-function FaaS semantic by enabling user-level in-process memory isolation at nanosecond granularity within a single address space, eliminating the container/microVM overhead that causes millisecond latencies.
mx: speedup: Over 2x throughput vs. enhanced state-of-the-art FaaS · other: Within 16% of idealized insecure baseline; microsecond-level SLO achieved
tg: faas, serverless, memory-isolation, single-address-space, microsecond-latency, cloud

t: ANSMET: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with Near-Memory Processing and Hybrid Early Termination
th: Near-memory processing with hybrid early termination for ANNS
pb: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over large high-dimensional vector databases is both highly memory-bound and computationally wasteful: a large fraction of fetched vectors and their distance computations are ultimately discarded because many candidate vectors are far from the query. This dual inefficiency — excess memory traffic and low data utilization — limits throughput and energy efficiency on general-purpose computing platforms.
me: ANSMET co-designs a near-data processing (NDP) architecture at the memory rank level with a hybrid partial-dimension/bit early termination strategy. Distance calculation and comparison for ANNS are offloaded to near-data units within memory ranks, eliminating main memory bandwidth consumption for rejected vectors. As a vector is streamed from memory, ANSMET conservatively estimates a lower-bound distance using partial dimensions and/or partial bits of each element; if this lower bound already exceeds a threshold, the fetch and computation are terminated early. Data layout within a single memory access and across multiple memory ranks is co-optimized to match the early termination granularity, and a lightweight host-NDP coordination protocol manages index traversal and result sorting.
nv: The hybrid partial-dimension/bit early termination strategy conservatively estimates distance lower bounds during streaming to skip unnecessary data fetches, combined with rank-level near-data processing to eliminate host memory bandwidth consumption for rejected ANNS candidates.
mx: speedup: 5.26x average from NDP; additional 1.52x from hybrid early termination (total ~8x)
tg: anns, vector-database, near-data-processing, early-termination, memory-rank, approximate-search

t: HYTE: Flexible Tiling for Sparse Accelerators via Hybrid Static-Dynamic Approaches
th: Hybrid static-dynamic tiling for sparse tensor accelerators
pb: Tiling very large sparse tensors on specialized hardware accelerators is challenged by the inability of purely static schemes (which use simple heuristics without adapting to local sparsity patterns) and purely dynamic schemes (which have high design complexity) to jointly find near-optimal tile size/shape, dimension iteration order, buffer allocation, and metadata management while accommodating highly varying local data sparsity.
me: HYTE is a hybrid static-dynamic tiling framework for sparse accelerators. An offline static scheduler first samples the sparse matrix to estimate a near-optimal initial tiling configuration — covering tile size and shape, dimension iteration order across tiles, and buffer allocation policies — without analyzing the full tensor. At runtime, a dynamic tuning mechanism adjusts tile shape on-the-fly to maintain high buffer utilization as local sparsity patterns vary. HYTE also manages tiling metadata in both off-chip memory and on-chip buffer efficiently, handling the non-negligible metadata overhead that prior sparse tiling schemes neglect.
nv: HYTE's combination of a lightweight offline sampling-based static scheduler with a runtime tile-shape dynamic tuner is the first to jointly optimize all tiling dimensions (size, shape, iteration order, allocation) while actively adapting to local sparsity variation.
mx: speedup: 3.3x to 6.2x geomean over state-of-the-art sparse tiling strategies
tg: sparse-accelerator, tiling, hybrid-scheduling, sparsity, dataflow, buffer-management

t: H2-LLM: Hardware-Dataflow Co-Exploration for Heterogeneous Hybrid-Bonding-based Low-Batch LLM Inference
th: Hybrid-bonding heterogeneous architecture and dataflow co-exploration for edge LLM inference
pb: Edge-side low-batch LLM inference (personal assistant, reception bot, private edge server) is bottlenecked by the DRAM bandwidth wall: existing NMP designs embed compute engines inside DRAM dies, limiting compute capacity and creating an imbalance between bandwidth and computation for both prefill (compute-bound) and decoding (bandwidth-bound) stages. Hybrid-bonding technology offers a path to higher compute capacity near memory, but the trade-off between computation capacity and bandwidth has not been systematically explored.
me: H2-LLM proposes a hybrid-bonding-based heterogeneous accelerator that places high-capacity compute dies in face-to-face contact with DRAM dies, exploiting the high through-silicon-via bandwidth of hybrid bonding. The architecture exposes a design space covering compute tile counts, memory bandwidth allocation, and die partitioning. A data-centric dataflow abstraction is introduced to map LLM operations (attention, feed-forward, KV-cache access) onto the heterogeneous on-die and near-die compute resources across both prefill and decoding stages. A design space exploration (DSE) framework automatically searches this joint architecture-dataflow space for the Pareto-optimal configuration.
nv: H2-LLM is the first system to jointly explore the hardware architecture and dataflow design space for hybrid-bonding-based heterogeneous LLM accelerators, using a data-centric dataflow abstraction that maximally exploits the heterogeneous compute and bandwidth resources.
mx: speedup: 2.72x geomean over in-die NMP-based heterogeneous accelerators · energy_or_tops_w: 1.48x geomean better energy efficiency vs in-die NMP baseline
tg: hybrid-bonding, llm-inference, edge-ai, near-memory, heterogeneous-architecture, design-space-exploration

t: Profile-Guided Temporal Prefetching
th: Profile-guided metadata management for hardware temporal prefetchers
pb: Temporal prefetching for irregular memory access patterns (data-dependent structures, pointer-chasing) requires metadata to record and replay past access sequences; existing on-chip metadata storage schemes for temporal prefetchers have limited capacity, and prior software-guided approaches have failed to optimize metadata storage management effectively, leaving temporal prefetching 0.1% over baseline with profile-guided methods.
me: Prophet is a hardware-software co-designed framework that uses profile-guided methods to optimize on-chip metadata storage management for temporal prefetchers. Instead of tracing full access sequences, Prophet profiles programs using lightweight hardware counters, then injects hints (compiler annotations) into the program binary to guide the hardware temporal prefetcher's metadata storage management at runtime. Dynamic tuning of these hints allows the optimized binary to adapt to different program inputs without re-profiling. Prophet is designed to coexist with existing hardware temporal prefetchers: it provides optimized metadata management for frequently executed hot paths while the original hardware-only scheme handles less frequent paths.
nv: Prophet uses counter-based profiling (rather than trace-based) combined with binary-injected hints and dynamic runtime tuning to guide on-chip metadata storage management for temporal prefetchers, enabling adaptation to varying program inputs without re-profiling.
mx: speedup: 14.23% over Triangel (state-of-the-art temporal prefetcher); prior profile-guided methods achieved only 0.1% · other: Negligible profiling, analysis, and instruction overhead
tg: temporal-prefetching, profile-guided, hardware-software-codesign, metadata-management, irregular-access, pointer-chasing

t: LightML: A Photonic Accelerator for Efficient General Purpose Machine Learning
th: photonic crossbar ML acceleration
pb: General-purpose machine learning workloads require massive computational throughput that strains conventional electronic server infrastructure in terms of cost and power. Existing photonic computing proposals lack a complete system-level design with proper memory and buffer support to fully utilize the high-speed photonic crossbar.
me: LightML implements the first complete system-level photonic crossbar design for ML, pairing a photonic crossbar core with a carefully co-designed memory and buffer architecture that sustains greater than 80% utilization of the photonic crossbar. The system supports large-scale matrix-matrix multiplication (MMM), element-wise operations, non-linear activation functions, and convolutional layers via dedicated photonic and electronic functional units. The design targets both edge and data-center density profiles, delivering 325 TOP/s at 3 W.
nv: First system-level photonic crossbar design that includes a purpose-built memory and buffer architecture enabling sustained high utilization (>80%) of the photonic core across diverse ML operations.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 325 TOP/s at 3 W (~108 TOP/s/W)
tg: photonic, crossbar, matrix-multiply, ml-accelerator, edge, energy-efficient

t: HeterRAG: Heterogeneous Processing-in-Memory Acceleration for Retrieval-augmented Generation
th: heterogeneous PIM for retrieval-augmented generation
pb: RAG systems face two distinct memory bottlenecks: the retrieval stage suffers from random/irregular memory access patterns causing low bandwidth utilization, while the generation stage is bandwidth-limited by frequent GEMV operations over large LLM weights. Additionally, maintaining large-scale knowledge bases creates a capacity bottleneck that HBM-based PIM alone cannot satisfy.
me: HeterRAG combines HBM-based PIM and DIMM-based PIM in a heterogeneous system: DIMM-based PIM provides low-cost, high-capacity storage for large knowledge bases and accelerates the irregular memory accesses of the retrieval stage, while HBM-based PIM handles bandwidth-intensive GEMV operations in the generation stage. The architecture maps each RAG stage to the PIM type best suited to its access characteristics, coordinating data movement between the two PIM domains.
nv: First heterogeneous PIM system that jointly addresses the capacity bottleneck of retrieval and the bandwidth bottleneck of LLM generation by pairing DIMM-based PIM with HBM-based PIM for RAG.
mx: other: quantitative results not stated in abstract
tg: rag, pim, heterogeneous-memory, llm-inference, dimm, hbm

t: OptiPIM: Optimizing Processing-in-Memory Acceleration Using Integer Linear Programming
th: ILP-based optimal mapping for PIM accelerators
pb: Efficient PIM acceleration requires precise software-hardware mapping that transforms application algorithms into PIM operations and data layouts, but existing PIM accelerators rely on manually tuned heuristics or exhaustive search, producing under-optimized mappings and/or prohibitively long optimization times.
me: OptiPIM formulates the PIM mapping problem as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem using a PIM-friendly mapping representation with accurate cost modeling that concisely covers the entire design space. The framework is implemented as a compiler pass inside the open-source MLIR framework, enabling it to consume PyTorch workloads and emit optimized mappings for PIM accelerators. OptiPIM generates optimal mappings within 4 minutes by exploiting the problem structure to make the ILP tractable.
nv: Formulation of PIM mapping as an ILP problem within MLIR, enabling provably optimal mapping generation for data-intensive applications on PIM accelerators in practical time.
mx: speedup: at least 1.9x over heuristic mappings · other: optimization time: within 4 minutes
tg: pim, ilp, compiler, mapping-optimization, mlir, memory-bandwidth

t: Dynamic Load Balancer in Intel Xeon Scalable Processor: Performance Analyses, Enhancements, and Guidelines
th: CPU-bypass load balancing via PCIe P2P NIC-to-DLB direct communication
pb: Rapid growth in inter-host networking speed causes bursty, unevenly distributed traffic across CPU cores, leading to excessive queuing delays and service latency variance; hardware-based load balancing with the Intel DLB still consumes significant host CPU cycles to prepare and enqueue work descriptors for received packets.
me: The paper first benchmarks DLB against software load balancers with a microbenchmark suite. It then proposes AccDirect, a system architecture and software co-design that exploits PCIe Peer-to-Peer (P2P) communication to create a direct path between the NIC and DLB, eliminating the host CPU from the descriptor enqueue path. The NIC directly enqueues work descriptors to DLB hardware queues using P2P DMA, removing all CPU cycles from the load-balancing hot path.
nv: AccDirect eliminates host CPU involvement in load balancing by using PCIe P2P to connect NIC directly to the on-chip DLB, reducing system-wide CPU power by 10% while maintaining equivalent throughput.
mx: speedup: 14-50% higher throughput than commodity hardware load balancer at comparable p99 latency · energy_or_tops_w: 10% reduction in system-wide host CPU power consumption
tg: load-balancing, dlb, pcie-p2p, cpu, networking, latency

t: In-Storage Acceleration of Retrieval Augmented Generation as a Service
th: in-storage accelerator for RAG retrieval and embedding
pb: As RAG deployments shift knowledge bases to persistent NVMe storage to handle ever-growing corpora, the Search & Retrieval phase — comprising embedding model inference, similarity/relevance search over dynamic data structures, and long-latency storage accesses — becomes the dominant bottleneck for end-to-end latency.
me: The paper proposes a metamorphic in-storage accelerator architecture embedded within NVMe storage devices. The in-storage accelerator is programmable to support diverse RAG retrieval algorithms, dynamic data structures (e.g., HNSW, IVF), and varying computational patterns. It executes smaller language models for query embedding generation entirely in-storage, while the final LLM generation runs on DGX A100 systems. The metamorphic design adapts its functional units to the retrieval algorithm at hand without requiring host CPU involvement in the hot path.
nv: A metamorphic (reconfigurable) in-storage accelerator that executes both embedding model inference and similarity search entirely within the storage device, eliminating retrieval-stage host CPU and DRAM round-trips.
mx: speedup: 4.3x over Xeon CPU + NVMe; 1.5x over A100 GPU + DRAM
tg: in-storage-compute, rag, nvm, embedding, retrieval, llm-inference

t: Synchronization for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers
th: Logical qubit synchronization policies for fault-tolerant quantum computing
pb: Logical qubits encoded with the surface code in fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQC) can become desynchronized across their syndrome generation cycles due to heterogeneous QEC codes (color, qLDPC), fabrication defects causing extended clock cycles, and modular chip-to-chip coupling latencies. Lattice Surgery merge operations require all involved patches to begin their next syndrome generation cycle in lockstep, so desynchronized patches must idle—accumulating decoherence errors—before the operation can proceed.
me: Three synchronization policies are defined for the surface code with Lattice Surgery: (1) Passive—leading patch idles for the full synchronization slack immediately before the merge; (2) Active—slack is distributed as small idle fragments inserted after every QEC round, so no single idle window accumulates large decoherence; (3) Hybrid—for patches with unequal cycle times, runs extra rounds of error correction to reduce the residual slack, then applies Active for the remainder. A hardware microarchitecture consisting of a Patch Counter Table, Phase Calculators, and a Synchronization Slack Calculator determines patch phases at runtime and injects barrier instructions into the QEC controller schedule without adding latency to the critical path.
nv: Active synchronization proactively distributes the total idling slack across multiple QEC rounds, reducing peak decoherence per round and cutting the logical error rate by up to 3.4x over baseline passive idling.
mx: speedup: 2.2x reduction in decoding latency (Hybrid vs. Passive) · accuracy: 3.4x reduction in logical error rate (Hybrid vs. Passive); 2.4x reduction (Active vs. Passive) · other: Validated on IBM Brisbane 127-qubit and IBM Sherbrooke quantum hardware
tg: quantum-error-correction, surface-code, lattice-surgery, synchronization, fault-tolerant-qc, decoherence

t: Nyx: Virtualizing dataflow execution on shared FPGA platforms
th: FPGA dataflow virtualization
pb: Existing multi-tenant FPGA virtualization systems support only task-parallel models, where distinct reconfigurable regions process independent data batches — this precludes dataflow execution (direct streaming between pipelined tasks), forcing dependent tasks to wait and incurring long end-to-end response times. No prior work supports dataflow pipelines in a virtualized, shared FPGA environment.
me: Nyx partitions the FPGA into distinct partially-reconfigurable regions and introduces virtual FIFOs — independent communication channels that decouple pipelined tasks from their predecessors and successors. When a task occupies one region, virtual FIFOs buffer inter-task data so that dependent tasks need not be co-scheduled simultaneously on the fabric. An FPGA hypervisor manages all data dependencies, tracks FIFO state, and dispatches pipelined tasks across regions at high throughput, enabling temporal multiplexing of dataflow pipelines across shared hardware.
nv: Virtual FIFOs that abstract inter-task communication channels, allowing pipelined dataflow tasks to execute independently across time-multiplexed FPGA regions without requiring simultaneous co-scheduling of all pipeline stages.
mx: speedup: 1.26x-8.87x throughput over state-of-the-art task-parallel virtualized FPGA; 2.8x-3.28x response time reduction in low-demand periods; 2x-2.75x in high-demand periods · other: deadline violations reduced by up to 76.5% (low demand), 34.5% (high demand); tail response time reduced up to 1.9x
tg: fpga, virtualization, dataflow, multi-tenant, pipeline, cloud

t: LUT Tensor Core: A Software-Hardware Co-Design for LUT-Based Low-Bit LLM Inference
th: LUT-based mixed-precision tensor core for low-bit LLM inference
pb: Low-bit LLM inference (INT4/2/1 weights × FP16/INT8 activations) requires mixed-precision GEMM (mpGEMM), an operation not natively supported by existing GPU Tensor Cores, forcing inefficient dequantization-based workarounds. Lookup-table (LUT) approaches can in principle replace multiplications with table lookups, but conventional LUT hardware incurs prohibitive table precomputation and storage overhead that negates the area and efficiency gains.
me: LUT Tensor Core is a software-hardware co-design: on the software side, table precomputation is extracted into an independent kernel via dataflow graph (DFG) transformation and fused with the preceding element-wise operator to eliminate redundant computation; weight values are reinterpreted from {0,1} to {-1,+1} to exploit lookup table symmetry and halve storage. On the hardware side, a bit-serial LUT Tensor Core microarchitecture with an elongated MNK tiling shape (M=2, N=64, K=4 optimal) maximizes table reuse across the N dimension while keeping table size bounded; a dedicated LMMA instruction set extends existing MMA ISA and integrates with TVM/Roller/Welder compilation stacks for end-to-end kernel generation.
nv: Co-designing software-level LUT symmetrization and operator fusion with a hardware bit-serial elongated-tiling Tensor Core achieves 4–6x power/area reduction over MAC-based Tensor Cores while outperforming prior LUT hardware by 1.44x in compute density and energy efficiency.
mx: speedup: 1.42x GEMV and 72.2x GEMM over LUT-GEMM software; 2.06–5.51x end-to-end LLM inference speedup · energy_or_tops_w: 1.44x compute density and energy efficiency over UNPU (SOTA LUT accelerator); 33.65 TOPs/W at 28nm · area: LUT TC occupies 16% area of conventional FP16 Tensor Core; 4–6x area reduction for 1-bit weights · ppa: 61.84 TOPs/mm2 compute density vs. 2.96 TFLOPs/mm2 for FP16 MAC (>20x at same 28nm node)
tg: lut, mpgemm, low-bit-llm, quantization, tensor-core, software-hardware-codesign

t: Hybe: GPU-NPU Hybrid System for Efficient LLM Inference with Million-Token Context Window
th: Heterogeneous GPU-NPU disaggregation for long-context LLM inference
pb: LLM inference with million-token context windows is infeasible on GPUs alone because KV cache activation memory for long contexts (>100K tokens) exceeds total GPU DRAM capacity, making batching impractical and leaving GPU compute cores severely underutilized during the memory-bandwidth-bound decode stage. The compute-memory imbalance between compute-intensive prefill and memory-intensive decode cannot be addressed by batching when KV data dominates physical memory.
me: Hybe assigns the compute-intensive prefill stage to existing high-throughput GPUs (NVIDIA H100 with vLLM) and offloads the memory-bandwidth-bound decode stage to lightweight NPUs sized with exactly enough compute to saturate their HBM bandwidth. The key mechanism is fine-grained KV transmission: as the GPU produces partial KV activations during prefill, it immediately streams them to NPU HBM over interconnect, reducing peak GPU memory footprint dramatically. A stage-wise pipeline scheduler dynamically assigns incoming requests to idle GPU or NPU hardware, minimizing pipeline stalls across the two-stage heterogeneous system. Hybe NPU is implemented in 4nm process with HBM matching the H100 HBM specification.
nv: Fine-grained KV streaming that incrementally offloads partial KV tensors from GPU to NPU during prefill, enabling million-token context windows without GPU memory overflow while keeping NPUs minimally provisioned for decode-stage bandwidth saturation.
mx: speedup: 2.1x for Phi-3 with 100K-token context vs H100 GPU · energy_or_tops_w: 3.9x energy efficiency for Llama-3 with 1M-token context vs equal-count H100 GPUs
tg: llm-inference, long-context, kv-cache, heterogeneous, gpu-npu, memory-capacity

t: Light-weight Cache Replacement for Instruction Heavy Workloads
th: Lightweight LLC replacement for instruction-heavy workloads
pb: Modern instruction-heavy workloads (e.g., server-side software with large code footprints) place heavy pressure on the last-level cache (LLC), and state-of-the-art LLC replacement policies designed for general workloads impose high hardware overhead yet provide little additional benefit over simple policies when aggressive prefetching is also present. Existing policies such as Mockingjay require complex prediction infrastructure that is not justified by their marginal gains for instruction-heavy access patterns.
me: PACIPV (Prefetch-Aware Coarse-grained Insertion and Promotion Vectors) generalizes the Re-Reference Interval Prediction (RRIP) framework by parameterizing cache line insertion position and promotion position as configurable vectors rather than fixed rules. The design space of valid RRIP-based policies is enumerated exhaustively on a training workload set to find the optimal insertion and promotion vectors. The selected policy is prefetch-aware, distinguishing demand and prefetch accesses and assigning them different insertion/promotion behavior to prevent prefetch thrashing. The resulting hardware implementation uses simple counter logic with negligible area overhead compared to RRIP.
nv: Exhaustive search over the RRIP insertion/promotion vector design space to find prefetch-aware optimal coarse-grained LLC replacement policies, demonstrating that simple parameterized RRIP variants match or exceed complex learned replacement policies for instruction-heavy workloads.
mx: speedup: 3.3% over LRU baseline; +1.1% over SRRIP; within 0.1% of Mockingjay · other: significantly less hardware overhead than Mockingjay
tg: cache-replacement, llc, rrip, prefetch-aware, instruction-workloads, low-overhead

t: MeshSlice: Efficient 2D Tensor Parallelism for Distributed DNN Training
th: Communication-compute overlap for 2D tensor parallelism in LLM training
pb: One-dimensional tensor parallelism (1D TP) for large DNN training scales poorly because all-reduce communication cost grows linearly with the number of devices. Existing 2D TP algorithms for general matrix multiplication (GeMM) have fundamental inefficiencies: Cannon's algorithm generates high traffic, SUMMA suffers from synchronization overhead, and 2D GeMM with standard collective communication operations cannot overlap communication with computation.
me: MeshSlice introduces a new 2D GeMM algorithm that decomposes collective communication operations into multiple smaller partial collectives, each of which can be issued and overlapped with ongoing matrix-multiply computation on the local shard. The algorithm maps the 2D device mesh such that partial all-reduces along one mesh dimension are issued while the other dimension is computing, hiding most communication latency behind arithmetic. An analytical autotuner searches over 2D mesh shape (rows x columns), GeMM dataflow configuration, and communication granularity (number of slices) to find the Pareto-optimal configuration for each LLM layer and cluster size, targeting TPUv4 hardware with its torus interconnect.
nv: Slicing collective communications into multiple partial collectives that are interleaved with computation, enabling near-complete hiding of 2D tensor parallelism communication latency in distributed LLM training.
mx: speedup: 12.0% faster than SOTA for GPT-3; 23.4% faster for Megatron-NLG on 256 TPUs
tg: tensor-parallelism, distributed-training, llm, collective-communication, 2d-gemm, tpu

t: Concorde: Fast and Accurate CPU Performance Modeling with Compositional Analytical-ML Fusion
th: Analytical-ML hybrid CPU performance modeling
pb: Accurate CPU performance simulation (cycle-accurate or analytical) is extremely slow, while pure ML-based performance models are fast but lack accuracy and generalizability across microarchitectures and workloads. Neither approach alone satisfies the speed-accuracy requirements of design-space exploration for modern out-of-order processors.
me: Concorde fuses compositional analytical models with ML components in a hybrid framework: the analytical component captures first-principles microarchitecture behavior (pipeline stages, cache hierarchy, branch prediction, memory subsystem) using structured equations, while an ML model corrects residual prediction error from complex interactions not captured analytically. The fusion is compositional in that different analytical sub-models for each CPU pipeline stage are trained or parameterized independently and composed at inference time, allowing fast per-configuration evaluation. This is inferred from the title's 'Compositional Analytical-ML Fusion' framing; no abstract text was available for verification.
nv: Compositional fusion of per-stage analytical CPU models with ML correction terms, combining the interpretability and generalization of analytical models with the residual accuracy of learned components for fast CPU performance prediction.
tg: cpu-modeling, performance-prediction, analytical-model, ml-fusion, design-space-exploration

t: FlexNeRFer: A Multi-Dataflow, Adaptive Sparsity-Aware Accelerator for On-Device NeRF Rendering
th: Multi-dataflow sparsity-aware ASIC for diverse NeRF rendering
pb: GPUs fail to meet the performance, power, and area requirements for on-device Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering, and existing NeRF-specific accelerators are tuned for a single algorithm, yielding poor efficiency when applied to other NeRF model variants. No hardware exists that efficiently supports the diversity of NeRF frameworks emerging for on-device 3D scene reconstruction.
me: FlexNeRFer combines a flexible Network-on-Chip (NoC) that reconfigures to support multiple dataflow patterns with a precision-scalable MAC array capable of operating at variable bit-widths. The accelerator exploits adaptive sparsity by selecting the optimal sparse tensor storage format at runtime based on the observed sparsity ratio and precision mode, avoiding format-mismatch overhead. The design was validated with a full layout implementation in 28 nm CMOS technology.
nv: A single flexible NoC that simultaneously supports multi-dataflow execution and adaptive sparsity-format selection across a precision-scalable MAC array, enabling one accelerator to efficiently serve diverse NeRF algorithms.
mx: speedup: 8.22–43.3x over RTX 2080 Ti GPU; 4.28–6.9x over NeuRex NeRF accelerator · energy_or_tops_w: 24.15–20.3x energy efficiency improvement over RTX 2080 Ti; 2.34–7.5x over NeuRex · area: 28 nm CMOS layout implemented
tg: nerf, on-device, multi-dataflow, sparsity, 28nm, asic

t: Finesse: An Agile Design Framework for Pairing-based Cryptography via Software/Hardware Co-Design
th: Agile compiler-driven co-design framework for pairing-based cryptography accelerators
pb: Pairing-based cryptography (PBC) accelerators require frequent re-engineering as security demands grow and pairing curve parameters evolve, but existing designs are either highly customized (inflexible) or flexible but low-performance, with no framework automating the algorithm-to-hardware translation across diverse pairing curves. The complex interdependency among algorithm choices, finite-field operator variants, and hardware configurations makes design-space exploration intractable manually.
me: Finesse introduces a three-layer abstraction: an intermediate representation (IR) for finite-field operations over arbitrary extension fields, a RISC-flavor Fp-level ISA with VLIW extension, and a parameterized hardware pipeline model. A specialized compiler performs SSA-based dataflow optimization, instruction scheduling with issue-slot affinity optimization, and register bank allocation before generating binary for target hardware. A cycle-accurate simulator enables co-design feedback loops with EDA toolchain synthesis metrics. The hardware implements modular arithmetic ALUs (mmul, madd, mlin, minv) in a multi-core SIMT architecture with shared instruction memory on ASIC (40 nm) and FPGA (Virtex-7) platforms.
nv: Issue-slot affinity scheduling that partitions pipeline slots into periodic intervals aligning Long (modmul) and Short (linear) instructions to eliminate write-back conflicts, combined with a co-design feedback loop between compiler and EDA synthesis for joint algorithm-architecture optimization across arbitrary pairing curves.
mx: area: 1.77 mm2 (1-core, 40nm); 8.00 mm2 (8-core, 40nm); 12.09 kops/mm2 vs 1.39 kops/mm2 for prior ASIC at 65nm equiv. · ppa: 34x throughput, 6.2x slice efficiency vs FlexiPair; 3x throughput, 3.2x area efficiency vs SOTA ASIC · other: Compilation time: 8.0s (BN254) to 53.1s (BLS24-509); IPC improved from 0.19 to 0.87-0.97
tg: pairing-cryptography, agile-design, compiler, sw-hw-codesign, asic, fpga

t: Constant-Rate Entanglement Distillation for Fast Quantum Interconnects
th: Constant-rate entanglement distillation for fault-tolerant quantum interconnects
pb: Existing quantum interconnect protocols cannot simultaneously achieve high fidelity and high rate of entanglement generation under realistic noisy local operations, creating a fundamental bottleneck for distributed quantum computing and blind quantum computation. Current entanglement distillation methods either have vanishing rate or fail to tolerate the noise levels present in physical systems.
me: The work develops a constant-rate entanglement distillation protocol using a sequence of two-way entanglement distillation rounds based on quantum error-detecting codes with increasing code rate. The scheme combines these iterated two-way distillation protocols with standard fault-tolerance techniques to achieve a net constant fraction of the raw entanglement pairs being converted to high-fidelity logical pairs. Numerical optimization is applied to minimize practical overhead given finite memory constraints.
nv: The first constant-rate (in expectation) entanglement distillation protocol for noisy quantum interconnects, achieved by chaining quantum error-detecting codes of increasing rate in a two-way distillation ladder.
mx: other: Constant-rate entanglement distillation demonstrated analytically and numerically; improvement over existing methods not quantified with specific numbers in the abstract
tg: quantum-computing, entanglement-distillation, quantum-interconnect, fault-tolerance, distributed-quantum

t: Chimera: Communication Fusion for Hybrid Parallelism in Large Language Models
th: Communication fusion to eliminate redundant collectives in hybrid LLM parallelism
pb: Hybrid parallelism strategies (tensor, pipeline, sequence, data parallelism combined) for LLM training and inference on multi-NPU systems generate a large volume of diverse collective communications whose blocking nature severely throttles compute utilization. Redundant communication operators introduced by combining multiple parallelism dimensions compound this bottleneck.
me: Chimera performs a systematic analysis of communication processes for each parallelism dimension (tensor, pipeline, data, sequence), identifies redundant collective operations that arise when multiple parallelism strategies are combined, and eliminates them by fusing adjacent communication operators during parallelism transformation. It reorders operations and generates a single redundancy-free communication operator that achieves the semantics of the original multi-collective sequence. The resulting fused operator is injected into the LLM computation graph as a replacement for the original blocking collectives.
nv: Cross-parallelism communication operator fusion that detects and eliminates redundant collectives arising from the combination of multiple LLM parallelism strategies, replacing them with a single semantically equivalent operator.
mx: speedup: 1.32–1.58x forward pass, 1.16–1.36x backward pass vs no fusion · other: 1.23–7.06x network bandwidth speedup
tg: llm, communication-fusion, hybrid-parallelism, multi-npu, collective-communication

t: DReX: Accurate and Scalable Dense Retrieval Acceleration via Algorithmic-Hardware Codesign
th: near-memory exact dense retrieval for RAG
pb: Approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) used in RAG dense retrieval is dataset-specific and inherently low-recall, causing irrelevant or incomplete context to degrade LLM generation quality. Exact nearest-neighbor search is too compute- and bandwidth-intensive for conventional processors.
me: DReX combines two hardware tiers: in-DRAM logic performs early filtering by comparing query vectors against embedding centroids to eliminate distant candidates without moving full vectors off-chip, and an outside-DRAM near-memory accelerator then executes exact k-NN search on the filtered, much smaller candidate set. The in-DRAM filter exploits processing-in-memory (PIM) capabilities of commodity DRAM to compute approximate distance bounds, bypassing DRAM-to-processor transfers for the bulk of vectors. This two-stage pipeline minimizes off-chip data movement while guaranteeing exact retrieval on the survivors.
nv: Using in-DRAM logic for coarse vector filtering combined with a near-memory accelerator for exact search, eliminating the recall-versus-speed tradeoff of ANNS without bulk off-chip data movement.
mx: speedup: 6.2-7x reduction in time-to-first-token vs. state-of-the-art ANNS mechanism · area: reasonable area and power overhead in memory subsystem (exact numbers not stated in abstract) · accuracy: exact nearest-neighbor (no recall degradation)
tg: rag, dense-retrieval, near-memory, pim, knn, llm

t: FRED: A Wafer-scale Fabric for 3D Parallel DNN Training
th: reconfigurable wafer-scale network-on-wafer for hybrid parallel DNN training
pb: Current wafer-scale interconnect topologies (e.g., 2D mesh) lack the flexibility to simultaneously support tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism in DNN training, causing collective communications to contend for shared links and inflating training time.
me: FRED introduces a distributed on-wafer topology built from tiny microswitches interconnecting accelerator chiplets on the wafer. The microswitches form a reconfigurable, nonblocking network that can route collective communications (all-reduce, all-to-all) between arbitrary subsets of chiplets without interference. In-switch collective support allows reduction operations to be partially executed at intermediate network nodes, reducing traffic volume. This topology is tailored so that different parallelism dimensions (data, tensor, pipeline) map to non-overlapping logical groups with dedicated bandwidth.
nv: Distributing microswitches across the wafer to create a reconfigurable, nonblocking on-wafer fabric that supports in-switch collective operations for arbitrary accelerator subgroup communications.
mx: speedup: 1.34-1.87x end-to-end training time improvement over 2D Mesh wafer-scale baseline (ResNet-152: 1.76x, Transformer-17B: 1.87x, GPT-3: 1.34x, Transformer-1T: 1.4x)
tg: wafer-scale, interconnect, collective-communication, 3d-parallelism, dnn-training, microswitch

t: Neoscope: How Resilient Is My SoC to Workload Churn?
th: workload-churn-aware SoC design space exploration
pb: Hardware lifetimes are increasing while software workloads evolve rapidly, so SoCs optimized for today's workloads may perform poorly against future workloads; architects lack quantitative tools to design for long-term performance resilience.
me: Neoscope introduces two workload-change metrics, Magnitude and Disruption, that quantitatively characterize how a workload evolves over time, classifying churn as Minimal, Perturbing, Escalating, or Volatile.
