Using these metrics, Neoscope formulates SoC design space exploration as an integer linear program (ILP) combined with job-shop scheduling concepts, enabling it to find near-globally-optimal SoC configurations for a given churn span in a single invocation rather than requiring exhaustive parameter sweeps. The framework is multi-objective and can optimize simultaneously for performance, area, energy, cost, and carbon efficiency.
nv: First multi-objective pre-silicon design space exploration framework that explicitly models workload churn using ILP-based optimization to find churn-resilient SoC configurations in one shot.
mx: other: Neoscope approaches globally optimal SoC with a single invocation; shows small SoCs require high specialization but are more vulnerable to churn
tg: soc-design, design-space-exploration, workload-churn, ilp, resilience, pre-silicon

t: Hermes: Algorithm-System Co-design for Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation At-Scale
th: Distributed hierarchical retrieval for trillion-token RAG
pb: As RAG datastores expand into the trillions of tokens, the retrieval phase dominates end-to-end latency and energy, undermining the benefits of using RAG to augment LLM outputs. Existing RAG systems lack mechanisms for efficiently routing queries to relevant subsets of a distributed datastore at scale.
me: Hermes partitions the RAG datastore across multiple nodes and uses a hierarchical search strategy that dynamically routes queries to relevant datastore subsets. A coarse-grained index tier rapidly identifies high-relevance partitions, and only those partitions are subjected to full dense retrieval (exact k-NN or approximate ANN). This co-design eliminates unnecessary retrieval computation on irrelevant partitions while maintaining retrieval quality.
nv: Hermes combines datastore partitioning with intelligent hierarchical query routing that adapts to query-to-partition relevance, reducing retrieval compute without sacrificing recall.
mx: speedup: 9.33x end-to-end latency reduction vs. state-of-the-art for trillion-token RAG · energy_or_tops_w: 2.10x energy improvement · accuracy: No sacrifice in retrieval quality
tg: rag, retrieval, llm-inference, distributed-systems, hierarchical-search, datastore

t: ATiM: Autotuning Tensor Programs for Processing-in-DRAM
th: Autotuning tensor compiler for DRAM-PIM
pb: Current software stacks for DRAM-PIM (specifically UPMEM) rely on hand-tuned libraries, lack high-level programming abstractions, and have no systematic optimization framework, making it difficult to achieve peak hardware utilization for tensor workloads including LLM layers.
me: ATiM is a search-based optimizing tensor compiler for the UPMEM DRAM-PIM architecture. It jointly searches the host-side and kernel-side tensor program space, applying PIM-aware optimizations to handle boundary conditions introduced by the banked DRAM layout. The compiler extends standard autotuning search algorithms to cover the expanded UPMEM-specific search space (e.g., tasklet counts, loop tiling, data placement across DPU banks), then generates fused, hardware-specific code without requiring manual library authoring.
nv: ATiM is the first tensor compiler to provide fully automated autotuning-integrated code generation for a DRAM-PIM system, bridging high-level tensor abstractions to UPMEM's banked-DRAM programming model.
mx: speedup: Up to 6.18x on UPMEM benchmark kernels; 8.21x on GPT-J layers
tg: pim, upmem, tensor-compiler, autotuning, llm-inference, dram

t: Precise exceptions in relaxed architectures
th: Formal specification of precise exceptions under relaxed memory
pb: The classical definition of precise exceptions assumes a sequential programmer's model and is inadequate for modern architectures like Arm-A that expose relaxed memory behavior; no formal specification exists for what exception precision means in a relaxed-memory setting.
me: The authors develop an axiomatic model for Arm-A precise exceptions in the relaxed-memory setting. They identify key phenomena—including relaxed behavior across exception boundaries, external aborts, and software-generated interrupts—that any definition must account for. A toolchain for axiomatic model execution is built, accompanied by a library of litmus tests that concretely characterize allowed and forbidden behaviors. The model is expressed in the style of existing Arm-A axiomatic memory models, extending them to cover exception entry and exit.
nv: The first formal axiomatic definition of exception precision for a real relaxed-memory architecture (Arm-A), resolving a decades-old open problem in architecture specification.
mx: other: Formal model correctness validated via litmus tests
tg: exception-handling, relaxed-memory, arm, formal-methods, axiomatic-model, architecture-specification

t: Hybrid SLC-MLC RRAM Mixed-Signal Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Transformer Acceleration via Gradient Redistribution
th: Hybrid SLC-MLC RRAM PIM with gradient redistribution for transformer inference
pb: Analog RRAM PIM using multi-level cells (MLC) can offer 2x storage density and higher compute throughput than single-level cells (SLC), but MLC's non-linearity causes catastrophic accuracy degradation (e.g., 40% drop) in Transformer models, while brute-force hybrid SLC/MLC mapping fails to move enough weights into MLC to yield meaningful efficiency gains.
me: HyFlexPIM uses a three-tier mixed-signal RRAM PIM architecture: (1) digital SLC RRAM PIM for attention Q·K^T and ×V operations that require high precision and write real-time vectors, (2) analog SLC RRAM PIM for the most critical static weight rows, and (3) analog MLC RRAM PIM (2-bit per cell) for the error-tolerant majority of static weights. A single analog PIM module is reconfigurable between SLC and MLC via a shared 6-b/7-b flexible SAR-ADC that bypasses the MSB comparison in SLC mode, adding less than 1% area/energy overhead. On the software side, gradient redistribution applies SVD to decompose each linear weight matrix, truncates to a hard threshold rank to maintain iso-computational cost, then fine-tunes for 1-3 epochs with AdamW; the fine-tuning process naturally concentrates gradient magnitude into the top 5-10% of singular values, making those rows clearly demarcated as SLC-critical while 90-95% of weights are safely mapped to MLC.
nv: Gradient redistribution via SVD truncation followed by fine-tuning actively reshapes gradient distributions to concentrate critical weight importance into 5-10% of parameters, enabling 90-95% of Transformer weights to be computed in efficient MLC RRAM while preserving less than 1% accuracy loss.
mx: speedup: 1.86x max throughput over ASADI (SoA analog-digital hybrid PIM) · energy_or_tops_w: 1.45x energy efficiency improvement over ASADI · area: 65nm technology node; <1% area overhead for SLC/MLC reconfigurability · accuracy: <1% accuracy degradation for encoder (BERT) and vision (ViT); <10% loss increase for decoder (GPT-2, Llama3) · other: 5-10% SLC protection rate sufficient for encoders; 5-20% for decoders
tg: rram, pim, mixed-signal, transformer-inference, svd, gradient-redistribution, mlc-slc

t: HardHarvest: Hardware-Supported Core Harvesting for Microservices
th: Hardware-supported core harvesting for microservice tail latency
pb: Software core harvesting—where batch 'Harvest VMs' temporarily steal idle cores from latency-critical 'Primary VMs'—incurs prohibitive overheads (hypervisor calls, TLB/cache flushes, context switches) that are acceptable for monolithic applications but intolerable for sub-millisecond microservices.
me: HardHarvest implements core harvesting entirely in hardware by adding in-hardware request scheduling logic that detects idle cores in Primary VMs and assigns them to Harvest VM tasks without hypervisor intervention. TLBs and caches are partitioned between Primary and Harvest VMs using a smart replacement algorithm that protects Primary VM working sets, enabling rapid context transfer without full TLB/cache flushes. The hardware scheduler monitors Primary VM request queues and preempts Harvest VM work before Primary VM tail latency is impacted.
nv: HardHarvest is the first hardware architecture for core harvesting in microservice environments, eliminating software overheads by combining in-hardware request scheduling with TLB/cache partitioning and a smart replacement policy.
mx: speedup: 1.8x Harvest VM throughput; 6.0x Primary VM tail latency reduction vs. software core harvesting · other: 1.5x core utilization improvement
tg: core-harvesting, microservices, virtualization, scheduling, tlb, cloud

t: DREAM: Enabling Low-Overhead Rowhammer Mitigation via Directed Refresh Management
th: DRAM Rowhammer mitigation with JEDEC DRFM
pb: JEDEC's Directed Refresh Management (DRFM) commands stall 8–32 DRAM banks simultaneously during Rowhammer mitigation, causing severe performance overheads (up to 49% slowdown) compared to the per-bank NRR assumed by prior work. Existing counter-based trackers that avoid these stalls require impractically large storage.
me: DREAM proposes two DRFM-aware variants. DREAM-R (randomized) delays issuing a DRFM after sampling an aggressor row so that other banks can also sample rows within the same window, amortizing the multi-bank stall across more mitigations per DRFM command. DREAM-C (counter-based) groups 32–256 randomly chosen rows across 32 banks into a 'gang' that shares a single counter, reducing tracker storage by 8x versus Graphene while avoiding CAM lookups and preserving DRFM compatibility.
nv: Exploiting DRFM's inherent multi-bank parallelism to either batch-amortize stalls (DREAM-R) or dramatically compress tracker storage via gang counting (DREAM-C), without requiring non-standard DRAM commands.
mx: speedup: DREAM-R reduces PARA slowdown from 12.7% to 4.24% (DRFMsb); DREAM-C reduces storage to 1 KB/bank (8x vs Graphene) with negligible slowdown at threshold 500 · other: PARA with NRR: 3.9% slowdown; with DRFMab: 49% slowdown (baselines)
tg: rowhammer, dram, refresh-management, memory-security, jedec, drfm

t: Qtenon: Towards Low-Latency Architecture Integration for Accelerating Hybrid Quantum-Classical Computing
th: Tightly coupled quantum-classical processor architecture
pb: Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms are bottlenecked by the decoupled architecture of current quantum hardware systems, which lacks low-latency communication channels and fine-grained software control for tightly coordinating quantum and classical computation. The high round-trip latency between host processor and quantum accelerator prevents real-time feedback loops required by variational algorithms.
me: Qtenon is a RISC-V extended chip implemented in Chisel that tightly couples classical and quantum processing via three hardware components: a unified memory hierarchy serving as a shared communication buffer between the host and quantum accelerators, an efficient quantum controller with dedicated data paths, and a multi-stage processing pipeline that exploits instruction-level parallelism across quantum-classical interaction phases. A custom ISA extension provides instructions for data communication, computation, fine-grained synchronization, and efficient scheduling of quantum-host interaction.
nv: Unified memory hierarchy bridging host and quantum accelerator combined with a custom RISC-V ISA extension enabling fine-grained synchronization and scheduling for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms in a tightly coupled chip.
mx: speedup: Up to 14.9x end-to-end speedup over state-of-the-art hybrid quantum-classical architectures
tg: quantum-classical, risc-v, hybrid-computing, low-latency, quantum-controller

t: ARTERY: Fast Quantum Feedback using Branch Prediction
th: Branch prediction for quantum feedback acceleration
pb: Quantum feedback in dynamic circuits introduces significant latency because each feedback branch must wait for measurement results to propagate through classical decoding and control, blocking gate execution and degrading circuit fidelity. The dynamic nature of mid-circuit measurement prevents speculative execution under current quantum control hardware.
me: ARTERY applies branch prediction to quantum feedback by combining two sources of information: historical statistics of branch outcomes and a real-time readout-pulse trajectory predictor that analyzes the in-flight pulse shape to predict the qubit state before full demodulation is complete. A reconciled branch predictor fuses these two signals to allow downstream gates to begin executing speculatively. Hardware support includes a scalable inter-FPGA backplane for feedback routing, a trigger mechanism for dynamic instruction timing, and an adaptive pulse sampling technique to maximize bandwidth.
nv: Applying classical branch prediction—fusing historical branch statistics with real-time readout-pulse trajectory analysis—to speculatively pre-execute quantum gates before mid-circuit measurement results are finalized.
mx: speedup: 2.07x feedback latency reduction vs. state-of-the-art · accuracy: Over 90% branch prediction accuracy; 1.24x fidelity improvement
tg: quantum-control, branch-prediction, dynamic-circuits, fpga, mid-circuit-measurement

t: HiPER: Hierarchically-Composed Processing for Efficient Robot Learning-Based Control
th: ASIC accelerator for robot learning-based model predictive control
pb: Learning-Based Model Predictive Control (LMPC) for robot navigation combines neural network inference with iterative MPC optimization, creating a mixed workload with rapidly varying computational patterns that neither GPUs nor simple CPU-GPU integrations can serve efficiently. The workload alternates between dense ML computation and sparse, irregular MPC solves across time steps.
me: HiPER is a 1024-PE ASIC synthesized in 16nm CMOS (16.37 mm²) built around a fractal interconnect topology that nests local systolic arrays within a hierarchical extension to handle the traffic characteristics of LMPC. A six-level pointer queue hierarchy orchestrates program composition and execution, enabling temporal and spatial mapping of workload phases at runtime. The pointer queues serve as a lightweight control mechanism that composes heterogeneous sub-programs without a complex scheduler, allowing dynamic adaptation to workload changes.
nv: Fractal interconnect topology combining local systolic arrays with hierarchical extensions, orchestrated by a multi-level pointer queue hierarchy that enables runtime temporal and spatial remapping for mixed ML+MPC workloads.
mx: speedup: 10.75x over GTX 1080; 11.6x over RoboX; 22.2x over Plasticine · energy_or_tops_w: 12.80x energy efficiency improvement over Jetson Orin Nano · area: 16.37 mm² in 16nm CMOS
tg: robotics, model-predictive-control, systolic-array, fractal-interconnect, edge-inference, asic

t: SWIPER: Minimizing Fault-Tolerant Quantum Program Latency via Speculative Window Decoding
th: Speculative window decoding for fault-tolerant quantum circuits
pb: Parallel window decoding for fault-tolerant quantum error correction requires some decoding tasks to be delayed until preceding windows complete, creating head-of-line blocking that inflates program runtime, especially during T gate teleportation where decoding latency directly extends logical circuit depth.
me: SWIPER introduces a speculative window decoder inspired by classical branch prediction. A lightweight speculation step predicts data dependencies between adjacent decoding windows, allowing multiple layers of decoding tasks to begin simultaneously rather than waiting for dependency resolution. If speculation is wrong, the decoder rolls back and re-decodes; the state-of-the-art compilation pipeline ensures that speculation opportunities are maximized. Performance is evaluated using a detailed open-source cycle-accurate simulator.
nv: Applying speculative execution—predicting inter-window data dependencies before they are resolved—to quantum error correction window decoders, eliminating blocking at window boundaries.
mx: speedup: 40% average application runtime reduction vs. prior parallel window decoders
tg: quantum-error-correction, speculative-decoding, window-decoding, fault-tolerant-quantum, branch-prediction

t: MoPAC: Efficiently Mitigating Rowhammer with Probabilistic Activation Counting
th: Probabilistic DRAM activation counting for efficient Rowhammer mitigation
pb: DDR5 JEDEC's Per-Row Activation Counters (PRAC) introduce extended DRAM timing parameters that cause 10% average performance overhead for all applications—even benign ones—because counter updates are performed on every activation regardless of actual attack likelihood.
me: MoPAC reduces counter-update frequency by performing PRAC updates probabilistically rather than on every row activation. To maintain security, the mitigation threshold is adjusted downward by the inverse of the sampling probability to ensure aggressors are still caught before exceeding the Rowhammer threshold. MoPAC-C (memory-controller side) uses two precharge command variants: a normal-latency precharge that skips counter updates and a higher-latency precharge that performs counter updates, with the controller probabilistically selecting which to issue. MoPAC-D (in-DRAM) probabilistically selects activations for counter updates within the DRAM chip and uses ALERT or REF timing to absorb the counter-update latency.
nv: Probabilistic PRAC counter updates with threshold compensation, enabling a hardware-transparent reduction in DDR5 timing overhead while preserving formal Rowhammer security guarantees.
mx: speedup: MoPAC-C: 1.7% slowdown; MoPAC-D: 0.7% slowdown at threshold 500 vs. 10% for PRAC
tg: rowhammer, dram, ddr5, prac, probabilistic-counting, memory-security

t: Process Only Where You Look: Hardware and Algorithm Co-optimization for Efficient Gaze-Tracked Foveated Rendering in Virtual Reality
th: gaze-driven foveated rendering accelerator
pb: Image rendering in VR head-mounted displays (HMDs) is computationally expensive, particularly for real-time applications where low latency is mandatory. Existing gaze-tracking and foveated rendering approaches impose high algorithmic and hardware costs that compound the overall rendering budget.
me: The paper proposes POLONet, an efficient multitask deep learning framework for real-time eye-movement tracking, co-designed with a dedicated POLO accelerator integrated as a plug-in for VR HMD SoCs. The system exploits the observation that human gaze is concentrated in a small foveal region, so full-resolution rendering is performed only where the eye is looking while peripheral regions are rendered at reduced quality. The hardware-algorithm co-optimization jointly minimizes gaze-tracking latency and rendering compute cost through a tightly coupled accelerator-SoC interface.
nv: A hardware-algorithm co-design that unifies multitask gaze tracking (POLONet) with a dedicated SoC accelerator (POLO) to achieve end-to-end foveated rendering with minimal latency overhead.
mx: speedup: 3.9x reduction in end-to-end latency vs. latest gaze tracking methods
tg: foveated-rendering, gaze-tracking, vr, co-design, soc-accelerator

t: Phi: Leveraging Pattern-based Hierarchical Sparsity for High-Efficiency Spiking Neural Networks
th: hierarchical pattern sparsity for spiking neural networks
pb: Spiking Neural Network (SNN) accelerators exploit binary activation sparsity (0-1 spikes) to skip zero computations, but they ignore the structured distribution patterns present in spike activations, leaving significant compute savings unexploited. Existing designs treat each non-zero spike independently, incurring redundant runtime multiply-accumulate operations.
me: Phi introduces a two-level hierarchical sparsity framework for SNNs. Level 1 is vector-wise sparsity: spike activations are represented using a small set of pre-defined patterns selected offline via k-means clustering, enabling offline pre-computation of pattern-weight products so that most runtime multiply-accumulates are eliminated. Level 2 is element-wise sparsity: a highly sparse residual matrix (the complement of the Level 1 approximation) handles remaining activations, further reducing computation while preserving accuracy. A pattern-aware fine-tuning technique is applied to increase Level 2 sparsity. The Phi hardware architecture processes both levels on-the-fly, with dedicated datapaths for each sparsity tier.
nv: A two-level hierarchical sparsity scheme that decomposes spike activations into pre-computable pattern vectors plus a highly sparse residual, enabling offline pattern-weight precomputation to eliminate the bulk of SNN runtime arithmetic.
mx: speedup: 3.45x over state-of-the-art SNN accelerators · energy_or_tops_w: 4.93x improvement in energy efficiency over state-of-the-art SNN accelerators
tg: snn, sparsity, pattern-based, neuromorphic, energy-efficiency

t: Assassyn: A Unified Abstraction for Architectural Simulation and Implementation
th: unified simulation and RTL generation from a single abstraction
pb: Architecture developers maintain two separate codebases—a simulation model for design-space exploration and an RTL implementation—creating coordination overhead, alignment errors, and duplicated effort that slow hardware development. Programming directly in RTL is error-prone and low-productivity, forcing teams to decouple modeling from implementation.
me: Assassyn provides a high-level, general-purpose programming framework built on asynchronous event handling—a behavioral model common to both hardware design and software engineering. Developers write a single Assassyn program; the framework compiles it to both a cycle-accurate simulator and synthesizable RTL, enforcing structural alignment by construction. The asynchronous event abstraction covers a broad class of architectures from pipeline components to out-of-order CPUs and application-specific accelerators.
nv: A single programming abstraction based on asynchronous event handling that simultaneously generates aligned cycle-accurate simulators and synthesizable RTL, eliminating the dual-codebase problem by construction.
mx: speedup: 2.2-8.1x simulation speedup over baseline simulators · area: comparable perf/area to hand-crafted RTL; 6x perf/area vs. HLS-generated RTL · other: 70% reduction in lines of code; 1.26x code overhead vs. hand-crafted RTL
tg: simulation, rtl, hls, architecture-framework, co-design, productivity

t: GPUs All Grown-Up: Fully Device-Driven SpMV Using GPU Work Graphs
th: device-driven GPU self-scheduling for sparse matrix-vector multiplication
pb: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on GPUs requires expensive host-side preprocessing to select per-row algorithms based on non-zero distribution, forcing costly CPU-GPU round-trips and limiting cache locality. This preprocessing adds latency that is particularly problematic for iterative solvers with repeated SpMV calls.
me: The paper leverages GPU Work Graphs, a novel GPU programming model originally designed for graphics, to implement fully device-driven SpMV self-scheduling. Work Graphs enable fine-grained dataflow execution of individual workgroups using emerging GPU hardware and firmware support (AMD GPUs with rocSPARSE stack). Preprocessing is fused with per-row computation: as soon as preprocessing generates sufficient work metadata, workgroups of specialized per-row SpMV kernels are self-scheduled and dispatched on-device without host interaction. This interleaving improves L1/L2 cache locality and eliminates CPU-GPU synchronization entirely. The approach uses a fixed 25 MiB device-side supporting data structure independent of matrix size, contrasting with scaling structures in rocSPARSE LRB.
nv: Applying GPU Work Graphs—a hardware/firmware-level on-device self-scheduling mechanism—to SpMV to fuse preprocessing and per-row computation on the GPU, eliminating host interaction and improving cache locality.
mx: speedup: up to 7.19x (mean 3.35x, SD 1.89) over rocSPARSE LRB for single SpMV; beats rocSPARSE CSR-Adaptive for up to 92 consecutive SpMV calls · other: 75% reduction in code complexity; fixed 25 MiB data structure vs. matrix-size-scaling rocSPARSE LRB structures
tg: spmv, gpu, work-graphs, self-scheduling, sparse-linear-algebra, hpc

t: When Mitigations Backfire: Timing Channel Attacks and Defense for PRAC-Based RowHammer Mitigations
th: timing side-channel in PRAC Rowhammer mitigation and a safe fix
pb: The JEDEC DDR5 Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC) mechanism and its Alert Back-Off (ABO) protocol and Refresh Management (RFM) commands introduce observable timing differences that create a new timing side-channel, allowing attackers to monitor memory access latencies and infer sensitive information such as cryptographic keys.
me: The paper first presents PRACLeak, a timing channel attack that exploits latency variations induced by ABO protocol and RFM commands to extract secret keys from vulnerable AES implementations by monitoring memory access timing. To counter this, the authors propose Timing-Safe PRAC (TPRAC), which replaces activity-triggered RFM commands with Timing-Based RFMs issued periodically and independently of memory activity, eliminating the observable correlation between memory access patterns and mitigation timing. TPRAC requires only a single-entry in-DRAM mitigation queue per bank and is designed to be compatible with existing DRAM standards.
nv: Identification of a timing side-channel in PRAC's ABO+RFM signaling and a defense (TPRAC) that decouples mitigation timing from memory activity using periodic, activity-independent RFM issuance.
mx: other: 3.4% performance overhead at Rowhammer threshold 1024 for TPRAC
tg: rowhammer, dram-security, timing-channel, prac, side-channel, ddr5

t: DS-TPU: Dynamical System for on-Device Lifelong Graph Learning with Nonlinear Node Interaction
th: analog dynamical system chip with native on-device graph learning
pb: Electronic Dynamical System (DS) hardware achieves orders-of-magnitude speed and energy improvements over GNNs for graph inference via natural annealing, but it (1) lacks native on-device training support—forcing reliance on slower conventional hardware for model updates—and (2) restricts node interactions to linear functions, limiting expressiveness and training accuracy.
me: DS-TPU introduces two algorithmic-architectural co-design innovations. First, an on-device lifelong learning mechanism uses feedback electric current as a native loss signal in response to observed training data, enabling electron-speed model parameter refinement directly on the DS chip without off-chip software. Second, nonlinear DS node interactions are constructed from Chebyshev polynomial expansions, making the DS hardware compatible with the richer relational structure in graph data while remaining implementable in analog hardware. The DS-TPU architecture is evaluated at a 5-Watt power envelope on six real-world graph learning benchmarks.
nv: On-device lifelong learning via feedback electric current as a loss function, combined with Chebyshev polynomial nonlinear node interactions, enabling native training on an electronic Dynamical System chip.
mx: speedup: 810x over offline DS training on A100 GPU; 640x over GNN training on A100 GPU · energy_or_tops_w: 5-Watt power envelope · accuracy: 10.8% MAE reduction over best of five GNNs on six graph learning tasks
tg: dynamical-system, graph-learning, analog, on-device-training, chebyshev, lifelong-learning

t: SpecEE: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference with Speculative Early Exiting
th: speculative early exiting for LLM inference
pb: Early exiting for LLM inference is bottlenecked by the predictor, which must search over a vocabulary of ~30,000 tokens per layer and incurs up to 20% overall inference latency overhead. Existing predictors also fail to integrate with speculative decoding token trees without exponential mapping complexity.
me: SpecEE introduces a speculative-model-based paradigm that uses a small draft model to reduce the token vocabulary search space for the early-exit predictor. It redesigns the predictor to exploit inherent data variation and GPU parallelism to cut computational complexity, uses layer-wise activation frequency profiling to weight predictor deployment non-uniformly across layers, and develops a tree-aware mapping that handles the full speculative decoding token tree without exponential blowup.
nv: Using a speculative draft model to shrink the predictor's runtime search space so that early exiting and speculative decoding compose efficiently.
mx: other: predictor overhead reduced from ~20% to lower; specific end-to-end speedup not stated in abstract
tg: early-exit, speculative-decoding, llm-inference, predictor, gpu

t: Bishop: Sparsified Bundling Spiking Transformers on Heterogeneous Cores with Error-constrained Pruning
th: heterogeneous accelerator for spiking transformers
pb: Spiking transformers combine attention mechanisms with spike-based computation, but their large size and high spatiotemporal volume of computation make efficient hardware acceleration difficult due to variable activation sparsity and the inefficiency of treating attention's binary spike operations with conventional accelerator designs.
me: Bishop introduces the Token-Time Bundle (TTB) container that groups spike data across tokens and time steps for efficient packing. A heterogeneous accelerator routes high-density TTBs to a dense core array and low-density TTBs to a sparse core array via a stratifier. BSA (Bundle Sparsity-Aware) training improves structured TTB-level firing sparsity. ECP (Error-Constrained TTB Pruning) trims spiking query/key/value activations with a provable error bound before and after attention map computation. A reconfigurable TTB spiking attention core executes attention as AND-and-Accumulate operations on binary spikes.
nv: The Token-Time Bundle abstraction that jointly packs spatial and temporal spike data to enable simultaneous dense/sparse core routing and weight reuse across both dimensions.
mx: speedup: 5.91x average speedup · energy_or_tops_w: 6x+ energy efficiency improvement (partial abstract)
tg: spiking-neural-network, spiking-transformer, neuromorphic, heterogeneous-cores, sparsity

t: DiTile-DGNN: An Efficient Accelerator for Distributed Dynamic Graph Neural Network Inference
th: distributed DGNN accelerator with redundancy elimination
pb: Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) combine GNN and RNN computations over evolving graph snapshots, creating combinatorial challenges of heterogeneous operator types, intra- and inter-snapshot data dependencies, redundant data across snapshots, and load imbalance that prevent efficient parallel scaling.
me: DiTile-DGNN uses a redundancy-free parallelism framework that analytically identifies snapshot-level data overlap and eliminates redundant computation while minimizing inter-node communication complexity. A workload-balance optimizer removes synchronization barriers between snapshots. A reconfigurable accelerator architecture with flexible interconnect dynamically adapts to support multiple DGNN dataflows (GNN aggregation, RNN recurrence, and their combination) without hardware redesign.
nv: A redundancy-free parallelism strategy that jointly eliminates inter-snapshot data redundancy and minimizes communication complexity in distributed DGNN execution.
mx: speedup: 23.2-56.1% execution time reduction vs. ReaDy, DGNN-Booster, RACE, MEGA · energy_or_tops_w: 71.4-84.0% energy efficiency improvement vs. baselines
tg: dynamic-gnn, graph-neural-network, distributed-accelerator, temporal-graphs, dataflow

t: ArtMem: Adaptive Migration in Reinforcement Learning-Enabled Tiered Memory
th: RL-driven adaptive tiered memory management
pb: Tiered memory systems struggle with three key inefficiencies: existing migration policies perform inconsistently across workloads, fail to adapt when the fast-tier access rate is low, and miss opportunities to tune migration scope dynamically based on workload patterns, causing unnecessary page migrations.
me: ArtMem is a reinforcement learning (RL)-driven tiered memory management framework that dynamically adapts migration policy to evolving workload behavior. The RL agent observes fast-tier access rates and workload access patterns at runtime to decide page placement, migration scope (which pages to migrate and how many), and when to suppress migration entirely when the fast tier is underutilized. This closed-loop control replaces static thresholds with learned policies.
nv: Using a reinforcement learning agent to jointly control migration strategy selection, scope tuning, and suppression in response to live workload evolution in tiered memory.
mx: speedup: 35-172% performance improvement over state-of-the-art tiering systems
tg: tiered-memory, reinforcement-learning, page-migration, memory-management, data-center

t: Cramming a Data Center into One Cabinet, a Co-Exploration of Computing and Hardware Architecture of Waferscale Chip
th: wafer-scale chip co-exploration for LLM data centers
pb: Current wafer-scale data center architectures waste integration density due to uncoordinated resource allocation between compute and memory dies, and lack co-optimization of system area across chiplet configurations, preventing optimal performance within physical and cost constraints.
me: The paper develops a wafer-scale single-cabinet data center model with configurable on-chip memory dies and a vertically stacked hardware architecture. On this model, Titan is an automated exploration framework that establishes parameter dependencies between intra-chip (tile sizing, SRAM capacity) and inter-chip (die-to-die interconnect, stacking) design variables. Titan integrates vertical area constraints, physical limit pre-checks, and a suite of reliability prediction models to prune infeasible configurations and accelerate the design cycle.
nv: An automated co-exploration framework (Titan) that jointly optimizes computing architecture (parallelism strategy, operator mapping) and hardware architecture (chiplet layout, memory stacking) for wafer-scale systems under physical and reliability constraints.
mx: other: integration density and cost metrics; specific numbers not given in abstract
tg: wafer-scale, chiplet, co-design, data-center, llm

t: CORD: Low-Latency, Bandwidth-Efficient and Scalable Release Consistency via Directory Ordering
th: directory-ordered release consistency for multi-PU systems
pb: In multi-processing-unit systems (CPU-GPU, multi-GPU) using write-through cache coherence with release consistency, the source processor must serialize write ordering through itself to the LLC directory, generating unnecessary round-trip communication that increases latency, interconnect traffic, and energy for producer-consumer AI/ML workloads.
me: CORD is a cache coherence protocol that relocates write-through ordering responsibility from the source processor to the LLC directory. The directory accumulates write-through operations and enforces release consistency locally, eliminating source-to-directory round-trips. Novel metadata compression mechanisms minimize the storage overhead of tracking in-flight ordered writes at the directory, and the protocol is designed to scale across multiple directories without serialization bottlenecks. Evaluation is performed on gem5.
nv: Moving release consistency enforcement of write-through accesses from the source processor to the cache directory, eliminating unnecessary source-ordering communication.
mx: speedup: 24% average performance improvement over source ordering · area: <1% storage, area, and power overheads · ppa: <1% overhead vs. source ordering · other: 13% average traffic reduction; 3% overhead vs. hand-optimized message-passing
tg: cache-coherence, release-consistency, multi-gpu, interconnect, write-through

t: PuDHammer: Experimental Analysis of Read Disturbance Effects of Processing-using-DRAM in Real DRAM Chips
th: DRAM read disturbance characterization for PuD operations
pb: Processing-using-DRAM (PuD) operations require multiple-row activation (activating multiple DRAM rows simultaneously or in quick succession), a fundamentally different access pattern from conventional single-row activation. No prior work has characterized whether this multiple-row activation exacerbates DRAM read disturbance (RowHammer-style bitflips) compared to standard single-row activation.
me: The authors conduct an experimental characterization study (PuDHammer) using 316 real DDR4 DRAM chips from four major manufacturers. They test multiple-row activation patterns (as used by PuD bulk bitwise operations) across a sweep of operational parameters: temperature, data patterns, access patterns (simultaneous vs. sequential row activation), DRAM timing parameters, and spatial variation within chips. They measure the minimum hammer count (HC_first) required to induce the first bitflip and compare to conventional single-row RowHammer.
nv: First experimental characterization of how PuD-style multiple-row activation affects DRAM read disturbance on real DDR4 chips, showing PuDHammer can reduce the bitflip threshold by up to 158.58x compared to standard RowHammer.
mx: other: HC_first (minimum hammer count to first bitflip) reduced by up to 158.58x vs. RowHammer on 316 real DDR4 chips
tg: rowhammer, dram, processing-in-memory, read-disturbance, reliability, security

t: AIM: Software and Hardware Co-design for Architecture-level IR-drop Mitigation in High-performance PIM
th: Architecture-level IR-drop mitigation for SRAM PIM via quantization-aware Hamming Rate control
pb: High-performance SRAM PIM chips operating at high frequency and density suffer severe IR-drop (up to 140 mV on a production 7nm 256-TOPS chip), which degrades performance and threatens reliability. Conventional circuit-level mitigations (power plane widening, decoupling capacitors, clock-tree slack management) are resource-intensive, compromise PPA, and are overly pessimistic because they target the signoff worst-case Rtog=100% rather than actual workload-driven IR-drop.
me: AIM introduces two architecture-level IR-drop metrics: Rtog (instantaneous toggle rate of bitstreams in a PIM bank, correlated with dynamic current) and HR (Hamming Rate — average fraction of '1' bits in quantized weights, the theoretical upper bound of Rtog). Software optimization reduces HR via (1) LHR (Lower Hamming Rate), a differentiable regularization term added to QAT loss that steers weights toward low-HR integer values; and (2) WDS (Weight Distribution Shift), which adds a constant offset delta offline to shift weights into low-HR positive ranges and corrects the numerical error via a pipelined shift compensator placed beside PIM macro banks. At runtime, IR-Booster extends DVFS with HR-aware V-f pair selection: pre-compiled HR bounds determine a safe operating level, while a hardware IR Monitor (VCO-based voltage detector embedded near LDOs) triggers IRFailure signals that drive fine-grained aggressive-level adjustment. Finally, an HR-aware simulated-annealing task mapping assigns operators to macro groups to minimize inter-group HR interference. Evaluated via post-layout simulation (RedHawk/HSPICE) on a 7nm 256-TOPS DPIM chip.
nv: First architecture-level IR-drop mitigation for SRAM PIM that correlates weight Hamming Rate to dynamic IR-drop and co-optimizes quantization, weight distribution, runtime V-f control, and task mapping to exploit real workload IR-drop margins rather than worst-case circuit signoff.
mx: speedup: 1.152x on 7nm 256-TOPS SRAM PIM chip · energy_or_tops_w: 2.29x energy efficiency improvement · area: <1% overhead from shift compensator hardware · accuracy: HR reduced 23-31% (LHR alone), up to 41-46% (LHR+WDS); accuracy loss <0.1% across ResNet18, MobileNetV2, YOLOv5, ViT, Llama3, GPT2 · other: IR-drop mitigated by up to 69.2% vs. worst-case signoff baseline
tg: sram-pim, ir-drop, quantization, dvfs, weight-distribution, sw-hw-codesign

t: IDEA-GP: Instruction-Driven Architecture with Efficient Online Workload Allocation for Geometric Perception
th: Instruction-driven FPGA accelerator for robotic geometric perception with online workload allocation
pb: Robotic geometric perception tasks (SLAM, Structure from Motion) involve diverse and dynamically varying computational operators — including point cloud registration, pose graph optimization, bundle adjustment, and feature matching — whose workload fluctuates with environment and task, preventing static mapping to specialized accelerators and causing poor resource utilization.
me: IDEA-GP is an FPGA-based instruction-driven accelerator built around an array of general-purpose computational units (PEs) optimized for spatial-positioning representations such as rotation matrices, quaternions, and homogeneous coordinates. A compiler performs online workload analysis — profiling operator types and sizes at runtime — and emits PE-targeted instructions to dynamically schedule and pipeline optimization sub-problems (e.g., least-squares solve, graph relaxation). This instruction-driven dispatch allows the same PE array to handle the varied compute patterns of SLAM (incremental pose estimation, loop closure) and SfM (bundle adjustment, triangulation) without hardware reconfiguration. The system is deployed on a Xilinx ZCU102 evaluation board.
nv: An instruction-driven online workload allocation compiler that dynamically schedules heterogeneous geometric-perception operators onto a unified PE array at runtime, achieving high resource utilization despite task and environment variability.
mx: speedup: 7.5x over Intel CPU and 19.7x over ARM CPU (SLAM); 16.4x over Intel CPU and 41.6x over ARM CPU (SfM) on Xilinx ZCU102
tg: fpga, robotics, slam, geometric-perception, instruction-driven, online-scheduling

t: SwitchQNet: Optimizing Distributed Quantum Computing for Quantum Data Centers with Switch Networks
th: Cross-layer compiler for quantum communication scheduling in optical-switch quantum data centers
pb: In quantum data centers (QDCs), quantum processor units (QPUs) in different racks are interconnected via reconfigurable optical switch networks, and cross-rack quantum communications incur both long latency and dynamic switch reconfiguration delays, significantly increasing total circuit execution time and degrading quantum state fidelity.
me: SwitchQNet introduces a compiler that co-optimizes quantum communication scheduling at both the program layer (gate decomposition and qubit routing) and the network layer (optical switch reconfiguration scheduling). The compiler models the QDC network topology and switch reconfiguration latencies, then constructs a joint schedule that batches and reorders quantum gate communications to amortize switch reconfiguration overhead across multiple operations. The approach integrates with quantum error correction (QEC) to target fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). The implementation is open-sourced at https://zenodo.org/records/15377656.
nv: A cross-layer compiler that jointly optimizes quantum gate scheduling and optical switch reconfiguration in quantum data centers, reducing end-to-end latency 8.02x over prior approaches by amortizing switch setup costs.
mx: speedup: 8.02x latency reduction over prior approaches · other: Integrates with QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing
tg: quantum-computing, distributed-quantum, optical-switch, compiler, quantum-data-center, fault-tolerant

t: RTSpMSpM: Harnessing Ray Tracing for Efficient Sparse Matrix Computations
th: Repurposing GPU ray tracing hardware for sparse matrix multiplication
pb: Sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (SpMSpM) is a critical kernel for graph analytics, GNNs, and scientific computing, but existing GPU SpMSpM libraries underutilize hardware because the irregular memory access and conditional computation patterns of sparse data do not map well to standard GPU CUDA cores and tensor units.
me: The authors first observe the algorithmic analogy between SpMSpM (identifying non-zero output positions) and ray-triangle intersection (finding ray-geometry intersections), then implement SW-RTSpMSpM — an SpMSpM algorithm mapped to the standard ray tracing API (DXR/OptiX) that uses RT core intersection units for non-zero position detection. Analysis of the differences between the two algorithms motivates RT+SpMSpM, which introduces two architectural optimizations: (1) simultaneous computation of partial products alongside RT intersection tests (not just detection), and (2) a ray mapping and scheduling strategy paired with a small row accumulation engine (RAE) that exploits Gustavson's sparse row-by-column dataflow and eliminates reliance on shader fallbacks and redundant memory operations. The RAE introduces only 0.2% area overhead on a modern high-end RT GPU.
nv: Mapping SpMSpM as a ray tracing problem and then proposing targeted architectural extensions (simultaneous multiply with intersection + row accumulation engine) that boost efficiency while adding only 0.2% area to an existing RT-equipped GPU.
mx: speedup: SW-RTSpMSpM: 1.85x over cuSPARSE; RT+SpMSpM: 3.06x over cuSPARSE; 1.66x over SW-RTSpMSpM · energy_or_tops_w: 80% performance per area vs. state-of-the-art SpMSpM accelerator · area: 0.2% area overhead added to GPU for RT+SpMSpM extensions
tg: ray-tracing, sparse-matrix, gpu, spmspM, dataflow, hardware-reuse

t: Insights into DeepSeek-V3: Scaling Challenges and Reflections on Hardware for AI Architectures
th: Hardware-software co-design analysis of a production 671B MoE LLM system with hardware architecture recommendations
pb: Training and serving 671B-parameter MoE LLMs at scale exposes critical hardware bottlenecks: HBM memory capacity growing <50%/year versus >1000%/year model memory demand, FP8 Tensor Core accumulation precision limited to 13 mantissa bits (FP22) causing numerical instability in large-scale training, NVLink bandwidth halved in H800 vs H100 (400 vs 900 GB/s) constraining tensor parallelism, and all-to-all expert parallelism (EP) communication consuming up to 20 GPU SMs for control-plane operations.
me: The paper presents DeepSeek-V3's production architecture and infrastructure as a case study, covering: (1) Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) that compresses KV cache from 516 KB/token (LLaMA-3.1-405B) to 70 KB/token via low-rank KV projection; (2) DeepSeekMoE with Node-Limited Routing constraining expert token dispatch to at most 4 of 8 nodes to exploit the 4:1 NVLink/IB bandwidth ratio, reducing inter-node IB traffic; (3) FP8 mixed-precision training with tile-wise 1x128 activation quantization and block-wise 128x128 weight quantization using DeepGEMM, requiring workarounds for FP22 accumulation precision on Hopper; (4) DualPipe overlapping MLA and MoE computation with all-to-all EP dispatch/combine via InfiniBand GPUDirect Async (IBGDA); (5) a Multi-Plane Two-Layer Fat-Tree (MPFT) network replacing a standard three-layer fat-tree, using 8 independent IB planes per node to support up to 16,384 GPUs at the same cost-per-endpoint as a two-layer topology. Experimental data includes real cluster training throughput (272.8B tokens/day, MFU 43.7%), EP bandwidth (>40 GB/s per GPU), and network latency comparisons (IB at 2.8 us same-leaf vs RoCE at 3.6 us).
nv: Systematic hardware-software co-design analysis from a production 671B MoE LLM system that quantifies the bottlenecks in FP8 accumulation precision, NVLink/IB bandwidth asymmetry, and EP control-plane SM consumption, and proposes the Multi-Plane Fat-Tree topology as a cost-equivalent path to 8x scale-out beyond single-plane two-layer fat trees.
mx: speedup: MTP module achieves 1.8x generation TPS vs. no MTP; EP dispatch/combine >40 GB/s per GPU on MPFT; TPOT theoretical upper bound 67 tokens/s on H800 IB vs ~1200 tokens/s on GB200 NVL72 · energy_or_tops_w: MFU 43.73% (non-causal) on 2048 H800 GPUs; 250 GFLOPS/token for 671B MoE vs 2448 for LLaMA-405B dense · accuracy: FP8 training relative accuracy loss <0.25% vs BF16 · other: KV cache: 70 KB/token (MLA) vs 516 KB/token (LLaMA-405B GQA); training throughput 272.8B tokens/day; 2,048 H800 GPUs for full DeepSeek-V3 training
tg: llm-training, moe, fp8, interconnect, kv-cache, multi-plane-network

t: UGPU: Dynamically Constructing Unbalanced GPUs for Enhanced Resource Efficiency
th: dynamic unbalanced GPU resource partitioning for multi-tenant efficiency
pb: Physical GPUs maintain a fixed, balanced ratio of compute and memory resources, which is inefficient when co-executing workloads have heterogeneous compute-to-memory demands. Partitioning a GPU into unbalanced slices requires accurate performance prediction under variable resource allocations and causes heavy data migration overhead when memory resources are redistributed.
me: UGPU dynamically carves a single physical GPU into unbalanced GPU slices—each with a tailored compute-SM count and HBM capacity—using a demand-aware resource partitioning algorithm that avoids complex analytical performance models. To handle memory redistribution without incurring the latency of traditional page migration, it introduces PageMove, which exploits the fact that all HBM memory channels share physical TSV connections within the DRAM stack, enabling parallel page migration between bank groups. PageMove pairs a customized memory address mapping with a Parallel Page Migration Mode (PPMM) and updated virtual memory management to move pages across memory dies at high throughput concurrently.
nv: PageMove exploits pre-existing intra-stack TSV connectivity and simultaneous multi-bank-group transfers in HBM to execute parallel page migration between memory dies, eliminating the dominant overhead of dynamic GPU slice reconfiguration.
mx: speedup: not explicitly quantified in abstract · other: PageMove reduces page migration overhead vs. traditional migration (magnitude not stated in abstract)
tg: gpu-partitioning, hbm, page-migration, multi-tenancy, resource-efficiency, cloud-gpu

t: Resource Analysis of Low-Overhead Transversal Architectures for Reconfigurable Atom Arrays
th: transversal-gate fault-tolerant quantum architecture for neutral atom arrays
pb: Fault-tolerant quantum computation on neutral atom arrays using standard lattice-surgery gate schemes requires O(d) syndrome extraction (SE) rounds per logical gate, where d is the code distance, leading to run times of years for large-scale algorithms such as 2048-bit RSA factoring. Existing resource estimates do not account for transversal gates that reduce SE overhead to O(1) rounds per gate, nor do they provide detailed architectural layouts and logical error models for such schemes.
me: The architecture decomposes target quantum algorithms (benchmarked on Shor's 2048-bit factoring) into modular functional units—magic state factories (8T-to-CCZ distillation with |T> cultivation), ripple-carry quantum adders (Cuccaro MAJ/UMA gadgets with CCZ teleportation), and quantum look-up tables (QROM via GHZ-state-assisted CNOT fan-out)—all implemented using surface-code transversal gates with O(1) SE rounds per logical operation and correlated decoding. Atom movement uses direct optical tweezer shuttling with pipelined ancilla measurement to keep moves local and bounded (≤√2·d·l per step). A heuristic logical error model calibrated against MLE decoder simulations characterizes the elevated per-gate noise from transversal CNOTs via a decoding factor α≈1/6. Space-time trade-offs (bridge qubits, time-optimal computation with reaction-time offsets) are used to parallelize circuit segments and minimize total qubit-seconds.
nv: First complete large-scale transversal architecture with detailed subroutine layouts, a calibrated logical error model, and full resource estimation showing 50x run-time reduction for 2048-bit RSA factoring using O(1) SE rounds per transversal gate via correlated decoding on neutral atom arrays.
mx: speedup: ~50x run-time reduction vs. lattice-surgery baselines (Ref. [8],[9]) for 2048-bit RSA factoring on neutral atoms · other: 19M qubits, 5.6 days at 1ms QEC cycle time; code distance d=27; up to 192 parallel magic state factories
tg: quantum-error-correction, transversal-gates, neutral-atoms, fault-tolerant-qc, resource-estimation, surface-code

t: Hardware-aware Calibration Protocol for Quantum Computers
th: hardware-aware parallel calibration protocol for quantum computers
pb: Quantum computer calibration—optimizing control parameters to ensure accurate gate implementation—does not account for physical qubit heterogeneity, and existing methods serialize calibration operations, causing excessive calibration overhead and suboptimal gate fidelity as qubit counts scale.
me: The protocol operates in two stages. First, a profiling phase evaluates qubit-pair responses to different waveform candidates, then assigns one of three calibration policies to each pair based on the profiling data (hardware-aware, fine-grained policy selection). Second, a graph-traversal algorithm identifies sets of compatible (non-interfering) calibration operations that can execute in parallel, converting the sequential calibration schedule into a parallel one. The protocol was validated on real IBM quantum hardware with up to 127 qubits.
nv: Fine-grained, per-qubit-pair waveform profiling that selects the best calibration policy per pair, combined with graph-traversal-based parallel scheduling, jointly reduces calibration time and two-qubit gate error simultaneously.
mx: accuracy: 1.84x reduction in median two-qubit gate error rate; 2.0-2.3x reduction in error per layered gate; 2x quantum volume improvement · speedup: 8-25x reduction in total calibration overhead vs. sequential calibration; 2.12x additional reduction from profiling policy · other: 1.26x reduction in pulse duration
tg: quantum-calibration, hardware-aware, parallel-calibration, qubit-heterogeneity, gate-fidelity, quantum-control

t: S-SYNC: Shuttle and Swap Co-Optimization in Quantum Charge-Coupled Devices
th: shuttle-SWAP co-optimization compiler for QCCD trapped-ion quantum processors
pb: In Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) trapped-ion architectures, coherent qubit shuttling across segmented electrode arrays increases thermal motion and consistently forces additional SWAP operations to restore qubit connectivity, significantly extending circuit execution time and degrading application success rates.
me: S-SYNC is a compiler that co-optimizes shuttle and SWAP counts simultaneously by exploiting QCCD-specific topology properties. It formulates QCCD routing as a static topology problem and incorporates generic SWAP gate insertion as a first-class operation alongside shuttle moves, rather than treating them independently. Scheduling heuristics then jointly minimize both operation types across the circuit, balancing the thermal motion cost of shuttling against the gate overhead of SWAPs. The compiler is evaluated across multiple QCCD topologies and initial qubit mapping strategies.
nv: Treating shuttle operations and SWAP insertions as co-equal, jointly-optimized variables in a static topology formulation—rather than as sequential, decoupled steps—reduces shuttling counts by 3.69x on average.
mx: speedup: 3.69x average reduction in shuttling number · accuracy: 1.73x average improvement in quantum application success rate
tg: trapped-ion, qccd, qubit-routing, shuttle-optimization, quantum-compiler, swap-insertion

t: Distributed-HISQ: A Distributed Quantum Control Architecture
th: distributed quantum control architecture with zero-overhead synchronization
pb: Distributed quantum control architectures (DQCAs) for superconducting qubits face two blockers: existing lock-step synchronization schemes incur large execution overheads (idle time or full program broadcast across controllers), and existing quantum ISAs are either too high-level or too hardware-specific to support diverse qubit technologies and gate implementation strategies on a single microarchitecture.
me: Distributed-HISQ comprises two mechanisms: (1) HISQ, a hardware instruction set built as an extension to RISC-V 32I that abstracts quantum control as 'send codeword X to port Y at time T,' decoupling instruction semantics from both quantum-operation meaning and analog electronics; and (2) BISP (Booking-based Instruction Synchronization Protocol), which exploits the deterministic duration of quantum gates to pre-book synchronization points in advance, achieving zero-cycle overhead when the deterministic tasks preceding sync are long enough to hide inter-controller communication latency. The system uses a hybrid tree+mesh network topology, with a balanced tree for region-level remote sync and mesh-like intra-layer links mirroring qubit device topology for nearest-neighbor sync. BISP hardware costs only 13 LUTs per SyncU on an FPGA.
nv: The booking-based synchronization protocol (BISP) allows controllers to pre-announce their synchronization time-points before reaching them, eliminating the round-trip latency overhead of prior on-demand sync schemes and enabling zero-cycle synchronization overhead in the common case.
mx: speedup: 22.8% reduction in average program execution time vs. lock-step baseline · accuracy: ~5x reduction in infidelity vs. lock-step baseline for long-range CNOT circuits · other: BISP SyncU costs only 13 LUTs; HISQ full control board: 4155 LUTs, 6392 FFs, 2.46 Mb BRAM
tg: quantum-control, synchronization, quantum-isa, distributed-control, fpga, superconducting-qubits

t: HiPACK: Efficient Sub-8-Bit Direct Convolution with SIMD and Bitwise Management
th: sub-8-bit SIMD convolution via packing and dual interleaved registers
pb: Sub-8-bit quantized convolutions on ARM SIMD (NEON/SVE) processors suffer from incompatibility because SIMD instructions lack native support for sub-8-bit data widths, requiring unpacking operations that conflict with parallel multiplication and negate the memory savings of quantization.
me: HiPACK introduces a packing-centric direct convolution strategy with four key techniques: (1) decoupling the unpacking phase from multiplication by pre-expanding sub-8-bit data into a packed 8-bit layout before the multiply loop; (2) optimizing caching of intermediate packed data to improve L1/L2 hit rates; (3) determining ideal segmentation of the packed layout to balance register pressure and cache reuse; and (4) a Dual Interleaved Register (DIR) mechanism that interleaves two packed-data streams in alternating SIMD registers to enable full-width SIMD multiplication without scalar fallback paths.
nv: The Dual Interleaved Register (DIR) mechanism enables parallel sub-8-bit SIMD multiplication by interleaving two data streams so that a single SIMD multiply instruction processes both without width-mismatch stalls.
mx: speedup: up to 4.6x vs. FP baseline; 1.7x vs. state-of-the-art on BCM2711 ARM
tg: sub-8-bit, quantization, simd, arm, convolution, edge-inference

t: Stratum: System-Hardware Co-Design with Tiered Monolithic 3D-Stackable DRAM for Efficient MoE Serving
th: Mono3D DRAM NMP system for MoE LLM inference with in-memory tiering
pb: MoE LLM inference is bottlenecked by the massive expert parameter volume (>95% of model size in models like Mixtral 8x7B), which overwhelms GPU HBM bandwidth and capacity; HBM-based NMP approaches are further limited by coarse-pitch TSV interconnects (~10 µm) that cap internal bandwidth.
me: Stratum integrates Mono3D DRAM with NMP logic via Cu-Cu hybrid bonding on a logic die, connected to GPU via 2.5D silicon interposer. Within the Mono3D DRAM stack, an in-memory tiering mechanism assigns expert weights to fast (low wordline-staircase latency) or slow tiers based on predicted access frequency. A lightweight topic classifier predicts which experts will be hot for a given batch of user queries and re-maps them to fast tiers before each batch via a row-swap buffer. The NMP processor on the logic die includes per-channel Processing Units (PUs) connected via a ring network, each containing near-bank PE clusters with tensor cores executing GeMM/GeMV, an intra-channel reducer, and a SIMD special-function engine for Softmax/SiLU. The prefill phase runs on the GPU (xPU) and decoding runs on Stratum NMP.
nv: In-memory tiering exploits inherent access-latency heterogeneity across Mono3D DRAM wordline layers, combined with topic-based expert usage prediction, to maximally concentrate hot expert weights in fast DRAM tiers without off-chip data movement.
mx: speedup: up to 8.29x decoding throughput improvement vs. GPU baseline · energy_or_tops_w: up to 7.66x better energy efficiency vs. GPU baseline · other: Mono3D DRAM internal bandwidth: ~5x higher vertical interconnect density than HBM (1 µm vs 10 µm TSV pitch)
tg: moe, llm-inference, near-memory-processing, 3d-dram, memory-tiering, chiplet

t: CryptoBTB: A Secure Hierarchical BTB for Diverse Instruction Footprint Workloads
th: secure hierarchical BTB with decoupled low-latency index encryption
pb: Branch Target Buffer (BTB) timing attacks allow adversaries to infer victim BTB updates and mistrain branch predictors, bypassing privilege-level isolation and secure enclave protection; existing encrypted BTB schemes either have security weaknesses or encrypt the BTB index in-pipeline, exposing high latency.
me: CryptoBTB proposes a hierarchical exclusive BTB structure where the index encryption is decoupled from the BTB set index computation. The encryption step uses a low-latency scheme that obscures the set mapping without being on the critical prediction path; the hierarchical organization (L1 BTB + L2 BTB) avoids the collision-prone flat structure of prior work (HyBP), allowing the BTB capacity to be better utilized for workloads with large instruction footprints and reducing same-thread collisions.
nv: Decoupling the index encryption from the BTB indexing path enables low-latency secure BTB access while the hierarchical exclusive design recovers the BTB utilization lost by prior schemes that only partially utilize capacity.
mx: speedup: 4.27% performance overhead (vs. 31.89% for HyBP) · area: 22.57% lower hardware overhead than HyBP
tg: security, branch-prediction, btb, side-channel, speculation, microarchitecture

t: Chasoñ: Supporting Cross HBM Channel Data Migration to Enable Efficient Sparse Algebraic Acceleration
th: HBM-aware dynamic scheduling for sparse linear algebra acceleration
pb: HBM-based sparse accelerators suffer from high resource underutilization due to static non-zero scheduling that cannot redistribute work across HBM channels when data access patterns are irregular. Existing designs like Serpens fix data-to-channel mapping, leaving processing elements idle when a channel has no work.
me: Chaso is an FPGA-based streaming HBM accelerator for SpMV that introduces Cross-HBM Channel out-of-Order Scheduling (CrHCS), which dynamically migrates non-zero data across HBM channels at runtime to balance load. When one channel's processing elements are starved, CrHCS identifies data in other channels and migrates it, enabling out-of-order execution across channel boundaries. The design is implemented on AMD Alveo U55C running at 301 MHz, targeting the SuiteSparse and SNAP matrix collections.
nv: CrHCS is the first non-zero scheduling scheme that permits out-of-order cross-channel data migration in HBM-based sparse accelerators, directly addressing per-channel load imbalance.
mx: speedup: up to 8x over Serpens, 20.33x over RTX 4090, 11.65x over RTX 6000 Ada, 2.67x over Core i9-11980HK · energy_or_tops_w: 2.03x–34.72x better energy efficiency vs. baselines · other: 301 MHz on AMD Alveo U55C
tg: sparse-accelerator, hbm, fpga, spmv, load-balancing, out-of-order-scheduling

t: Micro-MAMA: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Multicore Prefetching
th: Multi-agent RL for coordinated multicore prefetch policy learning
pb: Independent RL-based prefetchers on each core of a multicore system compete for shared memory bandwidth without coordination, causing each agent to greedily claim excessive bandwidth and converging to sub-optimal system-wide policies. This problem is an instance of the multi-agent credit assignment and non-stationarity challenge in MARL.
me: MAMA uses a two-tier architecture: distributed local multi-armed bandit agents on each core narrow the joint-action search space by selecting among local prefetch aggressiveness options, while a central supervisor agent with global bandwidth visibility learns joint policies that maximize system-wide throughput or fairness. Key local agents receive system-level perspective signals (estimated global bandwidth usage) to discourage actions that harm other cores. The supervisor uses a lightweight bandit over the local agents' reduced action space, avoiding the exponential joint-action blow-up of fully centralized control.
nv: A hierarchical supervisor that provides global bandwidth perspective to local bandit prefetchers, enabling coordinated joint policies without requiring centralized control of all per-core decisions.
mx: speedup: 2.1% throughput improvement over independent agents; 10.4% fairness improvement · other: 8-core simulated system evaluation
tg: prefetching, reinforcement-learning, multicore, multi-agent, bandwidth, fairness

t: Understanding and Mitigating Covert Channel and Side Channel Vulnerabilities Introduced by RowHammer Defenses
th: RowHammer defense-induced timing side and covert channels
pb: Modern RowHammer defenses (PRAC, RFM) introduce timing covert and side channels because their preventive refresh actions block DRAM access in ways that depend on application memory access patterns, allowing adversaries to both observe victim access behavior and establish covert communication channels. No prior work has analyzed these defense-induced timing vulnerabilities.
me: The paper introduces LeakyHammer, a class of attacks exploiting the timing latency increase caused by RowHammer preventive refresh actions. Two covert channels are built: one exploiting PRAC's per-row activation counter responses and one exploiting RFM's refresh management commands, both causing measurable DRAM latency spikes observable by a spy process. A proof-of-concept website fingerprinting attack identifies visited websites by correlating RowHammer-preventive action patterns triggered by a victim's browsing. Three countermeasures (randomized refresh scheduling, access pattern obfuscation, and noise injection) are evaluated.
nv: First systematic demonstration that RowHammer defense mechanisms themselves (PRAC and RFM) can be weaponized as covert and side channels via defense-induced DRAM bandwidth throttling.
mx: other: Covert channel capacity: 39.0 Kbps (PRAC), 48.7 Kbps (RFM)
tg: rowhammer, dram-security, covert-channel, side-channel, prac, rfm

t: LLMulator: Generalizable Cost Modeling for Dataflow Accelerators with Input-Adaptive Control Flow
th: LLM-based generalizable cost modeling for dataflow accelerators
pb: Existing performance prediction methods for dataflow-based accelerators (TPUs, NPUs, FPGAs) fail to generalize across three dimensions: unseen applications with extreme loop scales (errors exceeding 40%), input-dependent control flows where branch probabilities shift at runtime (errors up to 60%), and diverse hardware architectures with varying memory delays and loop mapping primitives. No prior method unifies all three generalization axes.
me: LLMulator uses a pre-trained LLM (LLaMA-3.2-1B fine-tuned via LoRA) as the backbone for cost prediction with three novel mechanisms: (1) Progressive numeric encoding that tokenizes each decimal digit independently and uses categorical cross-entropy rather than regression to predict performance as digit-wise classification with beam-search error correction, enabling range-agnostic estimates; (2) Dynamic Prediction Calibration (DPC) using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style reinforcement learning with a replay buffer, where the model is updated online from Verilator simulation feedback to adapt to runtime input variations in loop bounds and control-flow branching; (3) A progressive dataset synthesizer that generates multi-level training data via AST-based generation, dataflow-specific loop-tree mutation, and LLM-based augmentation, then formats data with intermediate RTL reasoning chains (via SiliconCompiler and OpenROAD) to teach the model compilation-level reasoning.
nv: Treating hardware performance values as digit-wise categorical token sequences (rather than regression targets) enables confidence-aware, range-agnostic prediction that generalizes to out-of-distribution loop scales, combined with RL-based online calibration for input-adaptive control flows.
mx: accuracy: 12.2% MAPE on ASIC scenarios; 9.7% error reduction from DPC over static; 16.7%–7.8% error reduction vs GNNHLS/TLP
tg: cost-modeling, llm-for-hardware, dataflow-accelerator, rl-calibration, design-space-exploration, numeric-tokenization

t: ρHammer: Reviving RowHammer Attacks on New Architectures via Prefetching
th: Prefetch-based RowHammer revival on modern Intel architectures
pb: Conventional load-based (MOV instruction) RowHammer attacks have become ineffective on the most recent Intel architectures (Alder Lake / Raptor Lake, 12th–14th gen), where load-based hammering produces zero bit flips, primarily because insufficient DRAM row activation rates and more aggressive out-of-order/speculative execution disrupt the attack's hammering order.
me: ρHammer introduces three coordinated techniques: (1) A layout-agnostic DRAM address mapping reverse-engineering algorithm using selective pairwise SBDR (Same-Bank Different-Row) timing measurements in a three-step Duet/Trios/Quartet structured deduction that recovers full bank functions in polynomial time without prior knowledge of bank bit counts or layouts; (2) A prefetch-based hammering paradigm exploiting the asynchronous nature of x86 PREFETCHT2/PREFETCHNTA instructions, which retire after forwarding to L1 LFB without stalling the CPU, combined with multi-bank parallelism to maximize per-tREFI activation rate while also alleviating disorder through bank-interleaving latency; (3) A counter-speculation technique using runtime control-flow obfuscation (indirect addressing) and NOP-based pseudo-barriers tuned to neutralize OoO execution and branch prediction reordering without using explicit memory barriers, which cannot order prefetch instructions per Intel SDM.
nv: A prefetch-based Rowhammer hammering paradigm that exploits the asynchronous, non-blocking nature of x86 software prefetch instructions to bypass load-based activation rate bottlenecks, enabling the first successful RowHammer attacks on Raptor Lake where all prior methods completely fail.
mx: other: flip rate: 187K/min on Comet Lake (112.4x over load baseline); 47K/min on Rocket Lake (47.1x over baseline); 2,291/min on Raptor Lake (baseline: 0); 200K+ bit flips in 2-hour fuzzing on Comet Lake
tg: rowhammer, dram-security, prefetching, speculative-execution, memory-vulnerability, reverse-engineering

t: SMX: Heterogeneous Architecture for Universal Sequence Alignment Acceleration
th: Heterogeneous ISA+coprocessor architecture for universal sequence alignment
pb: Sequence alignment accelerators are over-specialized to one alignment model (e.g., Smith-Waterman with affine gaps or simple substitution matrices) and fail to support the full variety of irregular use cases in practice (DNA, protein, ASCII text; weighted gaps; diverse substitution matrices), while general-purpose CPUs and GPUs lack the efficiency of domain-specific designs.
me: SMX is a heterogeneous architecture that integrates two components orchestrated by a general-purpose core: an ISA extension (SMX-1D) for irregular and sequential alignment tasks, and a specialized 2D coprocessor (SMX-2D) to accelerate the regular, parallel compute-intensive phases of dynamic programming. The ISA extension adds new instructions to handle variable-length sequences and edge cases, while the coprocessor accelerates the systolic-style inner-loop wavefront computation. Both components support multiple sequence types (DNA, protein, ASCII) and alignment models including weighted affine gap penalties and full substitution matrices, enabling seamless integration with state-of-the-art software alignment algorithms. Physical design targets a 22nm technology node with an area of 0.34mm², 30% of a single-issue in-order CPU core.
nv: A unified heterogeneous architecture pairing an ISA extension for irregular tasks with a dedicated 2D coprocessor for regular wavefront computation, achieving high flexibility across alignment types while delivering over 18x peak performance per area versus specialized accelerators.
mx: speedup: 256–744x over state-of-the-art software; up to 18.5x more peak performance per area vs specialized hardware accelerators · area: 0.34mm² at 22nm (30% of a single-issue in-order CPU core)
tg: sequence-alignment, genomics, heterogeneous-architecture, isa-extension, coprocessor, domain-specific

t: Interleaved Bitstream Execution for Multi-Pattern Regex Matching on GPUs
th: Interleaved bitstream execution for GPU regex pattern matching
pb: Bitparallel regex engines compile regular expressions into bitstream programs that expose fine-grained instruction-level parallelism well-suited for GPU execution, but the naive sequential (per-instruction loop-over-data) execution model suffers from poor data reuse — each data block is loaded multiple times across instructions — and high memory consumption from intermediate bitstream state, limiting GPU throughput.
me: The paper introduces an interleaved bitstream execution model in which all bitstream instructions for all patterns are fused into a single loop body executed block-wise, so each data block is loaded once and processed by all instructions before moving to the next. Three key techniques make this practical on GPUs: (1) Dependency-Aware Thread-Data Mapping that resolves cross-block data dependencies — introduced because instructions in later iterations depend on state from prior blocks — via selective recomputation of dependency chains rather than communication; (2) Shift Rebalancing that restructures dependency chains to reduce the depth of synchronization barriers needed between warp threads; and (3) Zero Block Skipping that exploits bitstream sparsity (many blocks evaluate to all-zero intermediate state) to skip computation on zero blocks, reducing total work.
nv: An interleaved execution model that fuses all bitstream regex instructions into a single data-block-wise loop, improving data reuse and eliminating intermediate memory traffic, with dependency resolution via selective recomputation instead of inter-thread communication.
mx: speedup: 19.5x geometric mean speedup over state-of-the-art GPU regex engine
tg: regex, pattern-matching, gpu-kernel, bitstream, data-analytics, kernel-fusion

t: DECA: A Near-Core LLM Decompression Accelerator Grounded on a 3D Roofline Model
th: Near-core decompression accelerator for compressed LLM inference on CPU+HBM
pb: LLM inference on CPU servers (Intel Sapphire Rapids with AMX TMUL and HBM) is bottlenecked not by memory bandwidth or matrix compute throughput, but by AVX vector decompression overhead: decompressing quantized (BF8, MXFP4) and sparsified weight tiles in software consumes over 95% of dynamic instructions per core, and even 4x more vector (AVX) throughput is insufficient to eliminate this bottleneck for highly compressed models.
me: DECA is a near-core ML model decompression accelerator placed alongside each CPU core and connected via memory-mapped interface sharing the L2 TLB. Its microarchitecture is a three-stage pipeline: (1) Dequantization using a LUT array (L parallel 256-entry LUTs) that converts low-bit quantized values (1–8 bit) to BF16; (2) Expansion that de-sparsifies data by inserting zeros at bitmask-specified positions using a crossbar (XBAR) controlled by Parallel Prefix Sum-generated expansion indices from a bitmask queue; (3) Scaling that applies per-group scale factors for group quantization. Two duplicated Loader+TOut register pairs enable hardware double buffering between DECA and the TMUL. A new ISA extension called TEPL (Tile External Preprocess and Load) eliminates per-iteration memory fences by out-of-order invocation of DECA — TEPL instructions are issued speculatively like loads, and the core is squash-safe because DECA never writes memory state. The design methodology is grounded in a novel 3D Roof-Surface analytical model extending the 2D roofline to add a vector-throughput axis (AIXV = matrix ops per vector op), which correctly predicts that highly compressed kernels are VEC-bound, not MEM-bound.
nv: A 3D Roof-Surface analytical performance model that adds a vector-throughput dimension to the traditional roofline, directly motivating and correctly sizing a near-core decompression accelerator (DECA) with an out-of-order ISA extension (TEPL) that speculatively invokes the accelerator without serializing fences.
mx: speedup: up to 4x over Intel libxsmm software kernels on compressed GeMMs; 1.6x–2.6x reduction in next-token generation time for Llama2-70B/OPT-66B vs software-only; 2.5x–5.0x vs uncompressed baseline · other: Roof-Surface model accurate to within 10% for most kernels; libxsmm BF8_5% density achieves only 1/4.94 of roofline-predicted optimal on HBM
tg: llm-inference, near-core-accelerator, decompression, quantization, sparsity, isa-extension, roofline-model

t: Quartz: A Reconfigurable, Distributed-Memory Accelerator for Sparse Applications
th: Reconfigurable sparse accelerator with distributed on-chip memory
pb: Sparse tensor and graph workloads exhibit irregular memory access patterns and variable computation densities that defeat fixed-dataflow ASIC accelerators designed for dense workloads. No single dataflow or memory organization handles the full diversity of sparse application kernels efficiently.
me: Quartz is a reconfigurable ASIC accelerator with distributed on-chip SRAM banks. The architecture exposes a programmable dataflow substrate that can be configured at runtime to match the access pattern of a given sparse kernel. Distributed memory banks reduce the bandwidth bottleneck by providing high aggregate internal bandwidth close to the compute units. A reconfigurable interconnect routes data between memory banks and processing elements according to the configured dataflow.
nv: Runtime-reconfigurable dataflow combined with distributed SRAM memory enables a single chip to efficiently serve the diverse access patterns of multiple sparse application classes.
tg: sparse-accelerator, reconfigurable, distributed-memory, dataflow, asic

t: Dissecting and Modeling the Architecture of Modern GPU Cores
th: Reverse-engineering and modeling of modern NVIDIA GPU SM microarchitecture
pb: Academic GPU microarchitecture simulators such as Accel-sim rely on pipeline models derived from NVIDIA Tesla (2006), missing 15+ years of GPU core evolution including compiler-guided dependency management, the L0 instruction cache, register file cache, and updated issue logic in Ampere-class SMs. This causes simulation inaccuracy that misleads research conclusions.
me: The authors reverse-engineer the NVIDIA Ampere (RTX A6000) SM pipeline using hand-written SASS microbenchmarks that measure cycle-precise instruction timings.
