They uncover a software-hardware co-design dependency mechanism using per-warp Stall counters and six Dependence counters (SBx) encoded as ISA control bits replacing traditional scoreboards, a Compiler-Guided Greedy-Then-Youngest (CGGTY) warp issue policy, a two-bank register file without collector units, a compiler-managed 6-entry register file cache (RFC), an L0 instruction cache with a 16-entry stream buffer prefetcher, and detailed memory pipeline queue sizing and latencies. All findings are integrated into a rebuilt Accel-sim model validated against real hardware.
nv: Complete reverse-engineering of modern NVIDIA Ampere SM pipelines revealing that dependency management is handled entirely via compiler-encoded ISA control bits (Stall/Dependence counters), eliminating hardware scoreboards and collector units.
mx: accuracy: 13.98% mean MAPE on NVIDIA RTX A6000 (Ampere); 18.24% MAPE improvement over Accel-sim baseline
tg: gpu-microarchitecture, reverse-engineering, warp-scheduling, register-file, simulation

t: A TRRIP Down Memory Lane: Temperature-Based Re-Reference Interval Prediction For Instruction Caching
th: Temperature-aware instruction cache replacement via compiler-OS-hardware co-design
pb: Modern mobile CPU workloads (interpreters, JIT compilers, UI frameworks) have large instruction footprints with long reuse distances that defeat hardware-only cache replacement policies, causing persistent L2 instruction cache miss stalls even after PGO code layout optimization.
me: TRRIP is a compiler-OS-hardware co-design cache replacement policy. The LLVM PGO compiler classifies basic blocks as hot/warm/cold by execution frequency and places them in separate ELF sections (.text.hot, .text.warm, .text.cold). The OS loader reads these ELF headers and encodes temperature (2 bits) into existing ARM PBHA bits in page table entries (PTEs), requiring no ISA changes. The MMU transfers temperature bits with every memory request to the L2 cache. The hardware replacement policy extends RRIP: hot instruction lines are inserted at Immediate re-reference priority (RRPV=0), warm lines at Near (RRPV=1), cold/data lines at Intermediate (RRPV=2) per the existing RRIP eviction scan. The variant TRRIP-2 additionally decelerates RRPV promotion for non-hot hits. No additional on-chip storage is required beyond existing PTE bits.
nv: Using existing ARM PBHA page-table bits as a zero-storage-overhead channel to pass compiler-derived hot/cold temperature to the L2 cache replacement policy without ISA modifications.
mx: speedup: 3.9% geomean over SRRIP baseline (PGO-compiled mobile benchmarks) · other: L2 instruction MPKI reduction of 26.5% (TRRIP-1) and 27.3% (TRRIP-2)
tg: instruction-cache, cache-replacement, rrip, compiler-hw-codesign, mobile-cpu

t: Pimba: A Processing-in-Memory Acceleration for Post-Transformer Large Language Model Serving
th: PIM accelerator for post-transformer LLM serving with interleaved bank sharing
pb: Post-transformer LLMs (SSMs such as Mamba-2, linear attention, RNNs) and transformer-based LLMs both become memory-bandwidth-bound during batched inference due to state update and attention operations respectively, but the diverse primitives in state updates (element-wise multiply, outer product, GEMV) make per-bank PIM acceleration area-prohibitive, and existing LLM quantization formats degrade accuracy severely on SU-LLMs due to the swamping effect.
me: Pimba implements a PIM accelerator array where each State-update Processing Unit (SPU) is shared between two DRAM banks via access interleaving: while one bank is being read, the paired bank writes its result, enabling continuous utilization of a single pipelined SPU without throughput loss. Each SPU contains a State-update Processing Engine (SPE) with custom MX8 multipliers and adders (MX format with 8-bit shared exponent and 1-bit microexponents, 16 elements per group, using stochastic rounding). The four-stage SPE pipeline executes: (1) state fetch, (2) state decay plus outer product in parallel, (3) accumulate, (4) GEMV output and write-back. KV-cache attention is accelerated by reusing the same SPU logic in an attention mode dataflow. The system offloads state update and attention to PIM during the generation phase while the GPU handles prefill and other operations.
nv: Sharing one pipelined SPU between two DRAM banks via access interleaving halves PIM area overhead compared to per-bank designs while maintaining the same throughput.
mx: speedup: up to 4.1x token generation throughput over LLM-optimized GPU; up to 2.1x over GPU+PIM baseline; 14.6x lower state-update latency vs GPU · other: Area overhead described as minimal on DRAM device; MX8 achieves near fp16 perplexity on Mamba-2/RetNet/GLA/HGRN2
tg: pim, llm-inference, ssm, mamba, quantization, mx8, post-transformer

t: CrossBit: Bitwise Computing in NAND Flash Memory with Inter-Bitline Data Communication
th: inter-bitline in-flash computation for databases and MLC ECC
pb: Existing in-flash processing (IFP) architectures can only perform bitwise operations on data sensed within the same bitline, preventing computation involving data from different bitlines. This restriction makes prior IFP designs unable to implement error correction codes (ECC) or efficiently process database query operations that require inter-bitline data interactions.
me: CrossBit extends commodity NAND flash memory with minimal additional circuitry to support both intra-bitline and inter-bitline bulk bitwise operations. It introduces inter-bitline communication pathways that allow data sensed from different bitlines to interact during in-flash compute. This enables in-flash ECC (IF-ECC) operations directly on MLC flash cells, which eliminates the prior restriction to SLC-only IFP. The same inter-bitline capability is leveraged to accelerate fundamental database selection and join queries that previously required data movement across bitlines.
nv: CrossBit is the first IFP architecture to support inter-bitline data communication during in-flash computation, enabling reliable MLC-based IFP through in-flash ECC and substantially expanding the class of operations executable within NAND flash memory.
mx: speedup: 2.1x over SOTA IFP for database queries; 1.7x on Star Schema Benchmark end-to-end · energy_or_tops_w: 2.5x energy efficiency improvement over SOTA IFP · other: 1.8x bit density increase using MLC vs SLC in prior IFP
tg: in-flash-processing, nand-flash, near-data-processing, database, mlc, bitline

t: ShadowBinding: Realizing Effective Microarchitectures for In-Core Secure Speculation Schemes
th: microarchitectural cost of in-core secure speculation
pb: Secure speculation schemes that mitigate Spectre-class speculative side-channel attacks (such as STT and NDA) lack rigorous RTL-level microarchitectural implementations and realistic performance/cost analysis, causing prior work to significantly underestimate their overhead. Specifically, STT's rename-stage taint computation creates an expensive single-cycle dependency chain that degrades performance on wider out-of-order cores.
me: ShadowBinding develops concrete RTL microarchitectures for two state-of-the-art secure speculation schemes—Speculative Taint Tracking (STT) and Non-Speculative Data Access (NDA)—implemented on the RISC-V Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). For STT, a novel variant called STT-Issue is proposed that delays taint computation from the rename stage to the issue stage, breaking the expensive single-cycle rename-stage dependency chain and improving IPC, area, and timing. RTL synthesis and cycle-accurate simulation are used to measure the combined IPC and timing impact, capturing the full performance loss including clock frequency degradation.
nv: STT-Issue delays taint propagation to the issue stage, eliminating the rename-stage dependency chain that limits performance for wide cores, and is the first RTL-backed evaluation revealing that combined IPC+timing overhead of in-core secure speculation exceeds 35% for high-performance cores.
mx: other: IPC impact ~20% for highest-performance core; combined IPC+timing loss: 35% (STT-Rename), 27% (STT-Issue), 22% (NDA)
tg: speculative-execution, side-channel, security, risc-v, out-of-order, taint-tracking

t: MX+: Pushing the Limits of Microscaling Formats for Efficient Large Language Model Serving
th: outlier-aware extension of MX block floating-point for 4-bit LLM inference
pb: The 4-bit Microscaling (MXFP4) format suffers severe accuracy degradation when applied to LLM activation tensors because activation outlier values (Block Max, BM) are encoded with only 1 mantissa bit, causing large quantization errors that also corrupt the entire 32-element block via the shared exponent scale. This makes MXFP4 impractical for production LLM inference despite its potential bandwidth and compute savings.
me: MX+ repurposes the private exponent field of the Block Max (BM) element within each MX block as additional mantissa bits, since the BM's exponent is always set to the representable maximum by definition. For MXFP4+, this converts the BM from E2M1 to an effective E0M3 encoding (3 mantissa bits instead of 1) with no change to block size or other elements. An extra 8-bit index per 32-element block identifies the BM position (5 bits for index, 3 reserved). For software integration on GPUs lacking native MX support, MX+ decomposes BM into high/low halves (BMH, BML), each representable as E2M1, enabling a standard MMA operation plus one additional sparse MMA for BMH. For hardware integration into existing MX-capable Tensor Cores (e.g., NVIDIA Blackwell), a BM Detector, Forward and Swap Units (FSUs), and a BM Compute Unit (BCU) are added outside the dot-product engine pipeline to handle BM-related multiplications in parallel with the DPE, adding 0.020mm2 area at 28nm.
nv: Repurposing the BM element's own exponent field as extended mantissa within the MX block encoding—requiring zero change to block structure, shared scale, or NBM elements—uniquely identifies and precisely represents the outlier without additional storage cost or software framework modification.
mx: accuracy: MXFP4+ vs MXFP4: up to +42.15% task accuracy improvement on Llama-3.1-8B; perplexity reduced from 27.69 to ~9.5 (WikiText-2) for Llama-3.1-8B · speedup: Hardware integration: 0.38% slowdown vs MXFP4; software integration A-MXFP4+: 1.13x slowdown max at long output lengths · area: 0.020mm2 at 28nm per Tensor Core for MX+ hardware (BM Detector + FSU + BCU) · other: 0.25 bits/element storage overhead; end-to-end vLLM speedup over BF16 close to MXFP4 at decode-dominant inference
tg: quantization, microscaling, llm-inference, block-floating-point, tensor-core, outlier

t: ORCHES: Orchestrated Test-Time-Compute-based LLM Reasoning on Collaborative GPU-PIM HEterogeneous System
th: GPU-PIM collaborative system for test-time-compute LLM reasoning
pb: Test-time compute (TTC) inference pipelines for LLM reasoning on edge devices suffer from three bottlenecks: variable parallelism due to inference-dependent dynamic control flow and varying batch sizes; branch dependencies that stall sequential reasoning steps; and branch pruning causing memory fragmentation and irregular access patterns.
me: ORCHES is a GPU-PIM collaborative system that partitions LLM reasoning workloads between a GPU and Processing-in-Memory (PIM) units. Three key mechanisms address the identified bottlenecks: (1) adaptive workload assignment dynamically balances computation between GPU and PIM based on real-time branching patterns; (2) branch-aware pipelining uses speculative execution to overlap reasoning steps and reduce inter-step pipeline stalls from branch dependencies; (3) fragmentation-aware memory structuring improves data locality through coordinated caching strategies and optimized memory layout reorganization to handle irregular access caused by branch pruning.
nv: Branch-aware pipelining with speculative execution specifically designed for TTC reasoning control flow, combined with adaptive GPU-PIM workload splitting that responds to dynamic branching at inference time.
mx: speedup: 4.16x over SOTA GPU (text-based TTC reasoning); 3.10x over SOTA GPU (vision-based TTC reasoning)
tg: test-time-compute, llm-reasoning, pim, gpu-pim, edge-inference, speculative-execution

t: SeaCache: Efficient and Adaptive Caching for Sparse Accelerators
th: adaptive on-chip caching for sparse tensor accelerators
pb: Sparse tensor accelerators suffer from poor on-chip SRAM utilization because variable-length sparse fibers (rows/columns of nonzero data) do not map cleanly into fixed-size cache blocks, wasting capacity. Theoretically optimal replacement policies (e.g., Belady OPT) require expensive on-chip metadata that consumes significant die area.
me: SeaCache combines three techniques targeting sparse on-demand caches integrated in domain-specific accelerators. First, fiber packing and splitting maps variable-length sparse fibers into fixed-size cache blocks with high utilization by splitting long fibers across multiple blocks and packing short fibers together. Second, a practical replacement policy approximates OPT-like behavior at low implementation cost by exploiting access-pattern regularities in sparse computations. Third, an adaptive space-sharing mechanism dynamically partitions the cache between actual data and replacement policy metadata using a two-phase approach that measures and adjusts the optimal partition ratio at runtime.
nv: The two-phase adaptive cache partitioning that co-locates sparse data and replacement policy metadata within the same SRAM, dynamically tuning their ratio to maximize effective capacity for variable-length sparse fibers.
mx: speedup: 2.8x over state-of-the-art sparse cache designs (average)
tg: sparse-accelerator, cache, on-chip-memory, fiber-packing, replacement-policy, memory-efficiency

t: RTGS: Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM via Multi-Level Redundancy Reduction
th: algorithm-hardware co-design for real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM on edge
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM systems cannot achieve real-time throughput (>=30 FPS) on edge devices; even the most efficient 3DGS-SLAM algorithms run at 0.78–14 FPS on a state-of-the-art edge GPU (NVIDIA ONX). The rendering and backpropagation stages dominate runtime (>80%), with severe workload imbalance across pixels and costly atomic gradient aggregation causing memory conflicts.
me: RTGS is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework targeting 3DGS-SLAM. On the algorithm side: (1) adaptive Gaussian pruning progressively removes low-importance Gaussians by reusing gradients from the backpropagation pass (no added overhead for importance scoring), and (2) dynamic downsampling reduces non-keyframe resolution from 1/16 to 1/4 of full resolution based on temporal distance to nearest keyframe, reusing keyframe identification and alpha-computing results. On the hardware side, a plug-in ASIC integrated alongside edge GPU SMs includes: (1) a Workload Scheduling Unit (WSU) combining pixel-level pairwise scheduling with subtile-level streaming, exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity to reuse scheduling patterns; (2) a Rendering & Backpropagation (R&B) Buffer that stores forward-pass intermediate values (accumulated transmittance T and per-Gaussian color contributions) to eliminate recomputation during backpropagation, reducing alpha gradient latency from 20 to 4 cycles; and (3) a Gradient Merging Unit (GMU) using a Benes network and bypass-extended reduction tree to perform pipelined sparse gradient aggregation, replacing atomic-add operations with structured in-order merging. The design is implemented at 28 nm, 500 MHz, 8.11 W, 28.41 mm2.
nv: Exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity in SLAM (where Gaussians are fixed between tracking iterations) to amortize scheduling overhead across iterations, enabling lightweight pixel-level pairwise scheduling that approaches oracle load balance with negligible cost.
mx: speedup: up to 48.8x over edge GPU baseline (ONX); real-time >=30 FPS on four datasets · energy_or_tops_w: up to 82.5x energy efficiency over edge GPU baseline · area: 28.41 mm2 at 28nm · ppa: 8.11W power at 500MHz, 28nm · accuracy: ATE and PSNR within 10% variance vs. unmodified baselines · other: Gradient merging latency reduced 68% vs. atomic ops; alpha gradient compute reduced from 20 to 4 cycles
tg: 3dgs-slam, edge-inference, algorithm-hardware-codesign, gaussian-splatting, workload-scheduling, gradient-aggregation

t: Efficient Security Support for CXL Memory through Adaptive Incremental Offloaded (Re-)Encryption
th: adaptive encryption for CXL memory in trusted execution environments
pb: CXL memory expansion devices adopted in cloud TEE environments (Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV) require XTS encryption for data confidentiality via CXL IDE, but XTS encryption's per-page latency causes significant performance overhead on memory-intensive workloads. Dynamically switching between CTR and XTS encryption modes and re-encrypting pages when access frequency changes incurs additional overhead that existing designs do not handle efficiently.
me: AIORE (Adaptive Incremental Offloaded Re-Encryption) combines CTR-mode encryption (low latency, parallelizable) for frequently accessed hot pages with XTS encryption (CXL IDE compliant) for cold pages. The framework dynamically selects the encryption scheme per page based on tracked access frequency using a lightweight monitoring mechanism. When a page's access pattern changes (cold-to-hot or hot-to-cold), AIORE performs incremental re-encryption, processing only the modified page rather than the entire memory region. Re-encryption is offloaded to computation resources within the CXL memory node itself, overlapping re-encryption with ongoing memory traffic to hide latency. The scheme is evaluated using gem5 full-system simulation across diverse benchmarks.
nv: Offloading incremental per-page re-encryption to CXL memory node compute, dynamically adapting between CTR and XTS encryption based on page access frequency to minimize both security overhead and re-encryption cost.
mx: other: Security overhead reduced by 62.8% on average; overhead within 3.7% vs. insecure baseline (gem5)
tg: cxl-memory, memory-encryption, tee, cloud-security, adaptive-security, near-data-processing

t: LEGOSim: A Unified Parallel Simulation Framework for Multi-chiplet Heterogeneous Integration
th: parallel simulation framework for heterogeneous multi-chiplet systems
pb: Simulating heterogeneous multi-chiplet systems (e.g., CPU+GPU+CIM chiplets integrated on an interposer) is not supported by existing simulators (gem5, GPGPU-Sim) because they lack modular composition of heterogeneous chiplet models and suffer from prohibitive synchronization overhead in parallel simulation—per-cycle global synchronization can waste up to 99.9% of simulation time on barrier overhead.
me: LEGOSim wraps individual chiplet simulators (open-source or proprietary) as parallel OS processes called 'simlets', each advancing independently using a PDES (parallel discrete event simulation) approach. An on-demand synchronization protocol uses adaptive time quanta and non-global fencing: synchronization only occurs when a simlet needs to send or receive a message whose timestamp falls within another simlet's current quantum, avoiding unnecessary global barriers. A Network-on-Interposer (NoI) simulator models inter-chiplet communication (latency, bandwidth, topology) and is integrated as a separate simlet. The framework was validated against SIMBA (multi-chiplet neural network accelerator) and a CiM-based accelerator, achieving average errors of 3.79% and 3.94% respectively.
nv: The on-demand, non-global synchronization protocol with adaptive time quanta that allows heterogeneous chiplet simlets to advance asynchronously and only synchronize when cross-chiplet message delivery actually requires it, reducing synchronization overhead by up to 99.9%.
mx: accuracy: 3.79% and 3.94% average simulation error vs. real hardware (SIMBA and CiM accelerator) · other: Synchronization overhead reduced by up to 99.9% vs. per-cycle sync; 66.1% reduction vs. fixed-quantum sync
tg: chiplet-simulation, parallel-simulation, heterogeneous-integration, network-on-interposer, synchronization, design-space-exploration

t: Boosting Task Scheduling Data Locality with Low-latency, HW-accelerated Label Propagation
th: hardware-accelerated locality-aware task scheduling
pb: Hardware-accelerated task schedulers dispatch ready tasks to the first available core without locality awareness, causing cache misses when dependent tasks execute on different cores. Existing locality-aware policies require static programmer hints or incur high scheduling overhead incompatible with fine-grained tasks.
me: The paper introduces Task-LP, a hardware label propagation (LP) accelerator that clusters up to 128 in-flight tasks by running a semi-synchronous graph clustering algorithm on the dynamic task dependency graph built by Picos. Task-LP uses a bitmask adjacency matrix, color-iteration parallelism (First-Fit online graph coloring), and bitwise popcount to compute label popularity; it converges in under 300 cycles for typical inputs. A Task Placement Engine (TPE) combines LP cluster labels with core-idleness signals via a tunable relaxation policy (cycle-length parameter R_len) to balance locality and core utilization. The full system is prototyped on a 24-core RISC-V (Rocket Chip) mapped to an Alveo U55C FPGA, interfaced via custom RoCC instructions and the Phentos task scheduling API.
nv: A hardware label-propagation accelerator that clusters dynamic task dependency graphs in under 300 cycles (up to 581x faster than software), enabling runtime data-locality-aware task placement with negligible scheduling overhead.
mx: speedup: up to 1.50x program execution time improvement on 24 cores · area: 0.313 mm2 at GF 12 nm for 128-node Task-LP configuration · ppa: 600+ MHz timing met in ASIC synthesis · accuracy: clustering modularity statistically indistinguishable from software LP · other: LP accelerator 581x faster than equivalent software LP; task size reduction up to 1.81x
tg: task-scheduling, data-locality, graph-clustering, label-propagation, risc-v, fpga

t: Accurate Leakage Speculation for Quantum Error Correction
th: accurate leakage speculation for quantum error correction
pb: Physical qubits in quantum error correction (QEC) can leak into higher energy states (e.g., |2>), corrupting syndrome measurements and spreading errors to neighboring qubits; detecting leakage on data qubits is especially hard because they are never directly measured during QEC cycles.
me: GLADIATOR frames leakage detection as a graph labeling problem. Offline, it constructs a code-aware error-propagation graph whose nodes are syndrome patterns and weighted directed edges represent transition probabilities under leakage vs. non-leakage errors, calibrated to device characterization data. Each node accumulates incoming leakage-edge weights (W_L) and non-leakage-edge weights (W_NL); nodes where W_L > W_NL by a threshold factor are labeled as leakage patterns and compiled into a lookup table. Online, a parity-adjacency generator extracts a 5-bit syndrome pattern per data qubit each QEC cycle and a combinational sequence checker (at most 10 LUTs per data qubit) classifies it in under 1 ns, triggering an LRC only for patterns flagged as leakage-dominated. GLADIATOR-D extends the design to a two-round sliding window of syndrome history for further accuracy. The method generalizes to surface codes, color codes, and qLDPC codes.
nv: A probabilistic graph-labeling framework that distinguishes leakage-induced syndrome patterns from standard Pauli-error patterns using calibrated transition probabilities, enabling code-agnostic, low-overhead leakage speculation that requires at most 10 LUTs per data qubit versus 177-5393 LUTs for prior work.
mx: speedup: 1.7x-3.9x QEC cycle speedup vs. always-LRC baseline · area: <0.1% LUTs at code distance 25 on Kintex UltraScale+ FPGA; 10 LUTs per data qubit · accuracy: 16% reduction in logical error rate; 1.91x lower false-positive rate vs. eraser · other: 17x-63x FPGA LUT reduction vs. eraser across code distances 5-25; combinational logic evaluates in <1 ns
tg: quantum-error-correction, leakage-detection, syndrome-classification, fault-tolerant-qc, fpga, surface-code

t: Empowering Vector Architectures for ML: The CAMP Architecture for Matrix Multiplication
th: quantized GEMM acceleration in vector/SIMD architectures
pb: Existing vector architectures (VAs) and SIMD units—including ARM SVE and RISC-V SIMD—cannot efficiently execute quantized neural network (QNN) matrix multiplication at 4-bit and 8-bit integer precisions because their datapaths are designed for wider, fixed-width computations.
me: CAMP (Cartesian Accumulative Matrix Pipeline) introduces a hybrid multiplier that hierarchically decomposes quantized integer multiplication into a two-level Cartesian product structure. The architecture natively handles multiple integer precisions (focus on INT4 and INT8) within the same datapath by exploiting structural regularity of quantized GEMM. CAMP is integrated as a micro-architecture extension to ARM A64FX (ARMv8 SVE, synthesized at TSMC 7 nm with Synopsys ICC2) and a RISC-V edge SoC (GlobalFoundries 22 nm, Cadence Innovus), adding 1% and 4% area overhead respectively.
nv: A hierarchical hybrid multiplier (Cartesian Accumulative Matrix Pipeline) that enables vector architectures to natively support multi-precision quantized integer matrix multiplication with minimal area overhead.
mx: speedup: up to 17x over ARM A64FX; up to 23x over RISC-V SoC for quantized matrix multiply · area: 1% overhead at TSMC 7nm (ARM); 4% overhead at GF22nm (RISC-V)
tg: quantization, vector-architecture, simd, integer-gemm, arm-sve, risc-v

t: A. Delegato: Locality-Aware Atomic Memory Operations on Chiplets
th: locality-aware atomic memory operation execution on chiplet architectures
pb: Chiplet-based architectures impose high, non-uniform memory access latencies across chiplet boundaries, severely degrading the performance of atomic memory operations (AMOs) used for fine-grained synchronization; existing solutions (near AMOs and centralized AMOs) either cause expensive cache-line ping-pong across chiplets or introduce coherence misses and require ALUs at the directory.
me: The paper introduces two new coherence transactions for far AMOs beyond centralized: (1) Delegated AMOs, which forward the RMW operation via a new SnpAMO snoop to the current cache-line owner, executing the operation locally without cache-line transfer; (2) Migrating AMOs, which transfer cache-line ownership to the requester using an AtomicLoad request (distinguishing it from a ReadUnique for smarter directory tracking). Five static directory AMO policies (All-Central, All-Migrate, Present-Central, Pinned-Owner, Unowned-Central) and a Chiplet-Aware policy are defined based on cache-line state and chiplet location. On top of this, Delegato is a tracing mechanism where the L2 private cache sets a one-bit reuse_bit in every SnpAMO response; the directory's Predictor Table transitions between Pinned-Owner, Present-Central, and Chiplet-Aware states based on this reuse feedback. Evaluated using gem5 23.1 with AMBA 5 CHI protocol, 32 OoO cores (dual 16-core chiplets), and HeteroGarnet NoC.
nv: Delegated and Migrating AMO coherence transactions that enable the directory to execute AMOs at the cache-line owner without invalidation or cache-line transfer, combined with a one-bit reuse tracing mechanism (Delegato) that transports private-cache locality information to the directory predictor.
mx: speedup: 1.07x over centralized AMOs; 1.13x over DynAMO (state-of-the-art AMO predictor) · area: atomic ALU extension: 2894 um2 at TSMC 7nm (0.11% of Neoverse V1 core tile) · other: Delegated AMOs reduce critical-path inter-chiplet messages from 4 to 2 in pathological cases
tg: atomic-memory-operations, chiplet, coherence-protocol, numa, cache-locality, chi-protocol

t: Symbiotic Task Scheduling and Data Prefetching
th: symbiotic task-seeded prefetching and scheduling for hardware task-parallel systems
pb: Hardware task-parallel systems that operate with fine-grained tasks (approx. 100-cycle execution time) cannot benefit from conventional hardware prefetchers because tasks are too short for prefetches to complete before the task finishes, leaving DRAM latency fully exposed and undermining the performance gains of hardware task management.
me: The Task-Seeded Prefetcher (TSP) learns the data-access pattern of each task function type and issues prefetches as soon as a task descriptor is queued by the hardware task scheduler, using the descriptor as a seed to identify which memory addresses the task will access. The Memory Response Task Scheduler (MRS) augments the baseline task-to-core dispatch policy by monitoring prefetch completion status from TSP: when a task's prefetches are done, MRS preferentially dispatches it to a ready core, maximizing prefetch utilization without stalling the pipeline. Together, TSP and MRS form a symbiotic pair where scheduling drives prefetching and prefetch status informs scheduling.
nv: A symbiotic co-design of a function-aware task-seeded prefetcher (TSP) and a prefetch-status-aware task scheduler (MRS) that together exploit the task descriptor queue as an early prefetch trigger in hardware task-parallel systems.
mx: speedup: up to 3.1x; geometric mean up to 1.4x across 13 benchmarks on 256-core systems
tg: task-parallelism, prefetching, scheduling, many-core, data-locality, irregular-workloads

t: Flexing RISC-V Instruction Subset Processors to Extreme Edge
th: automated RISC-V instruction-subset processor generation for flexible extreme-edge electronics
pb: Extreme edge applications (smart labels, wearable healthcare, smart textiles) require processors that are ultra-low area, ultra-low power, conformable, and low-cost—properties that conventional silicon RISC-V processors and existing smallest designs like Serv cannot meet—while still supporting programmability for occasional firmware updates.
me: The paper proposes RISC-V Instruction Subset Processors (RISSPs), generated by an automated methodology that (1) compiles applications to the full RV32E ISA to identify the required instruction subset (typically 24-86% of the ISA), (2) pulls formally pre-verified instruction hardware blocks from a library where each RISC-V instruction is implemented as a standalone, fully verified RTL block, (3) stitches them into a Modular Execution Unit (ModularEX) via a case-statement switch, and (4) synthesizes the result with commercial EDA tools (Synopsys ICC2 or Cadence Innovus) on Pragmatic Semiconductor's 0.6-um IGZO FlexIC process, where synthesis tools automatically eliminate redundant gates. A single-cycle non-pipelined microarchitecture suffices for kHz-range extreme edge performance requirements. For long-lasting applications needing firmware updates, a generative AI tool rewrites instructions not in the subset using equivalent subset instructions.
nv: A bottom-up RISSP generation methodology built on a library of formally pre-verified instruction-granularity RTL blocks, enabling automated generation of minimal-area FlexIC processors without conventional design-and-verify cycles for each new application.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: ~40x more energy-efficient per instruction than Serv · area: 8-43% area reduction vs. full RV32E processor (synthesis); up to 42% reduction in FlexIC physical implementation · ppa: 3-30% power reduction vs. full RISC-V; up to 21% in physical FlexIC; max frequency 1500-1850 kHz on 0.6-um IGZO process · other: Applications use only 24-86% of full RV32E ISA (9-32 distinct instructions at -O2)
tg: risc-v, instruction-subset, flexible-electronics, extreme-edge, flexic, low-power

t: OmniSim: Simulating Hardware with C Speed and RTL Accuracy for High-Level Synthesis Designs
th: C-speed RTL-accurate simulation for complex HLS dataflow designs
pb: High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools cannot correctly simulate complex dataflow designs at the C level—particularly those with non-blocking FIFO accesses (read_nb/write_nb), infinite loops, and cyclic module dependencies—because the OS-level scheduling of software threads does not correspond to hardware timing, leading to incorrect functional results and inaccurate cycle counts; falling back to C/RTL co-simulation takes hours to days.
me: OmniSim introduces a multi-threaded simulation framework operating at the LLVM IR level. It classifies dataflow designs into three types (A: blocking-only/acyclic; B: non-blocking or cyclic but single-behavior; C: non-blocking with behavior depending on FIFO access outcome) and applies different simulation strategies accordingly. Key mechanisms: (1) one software thread per active dataflow module (Func Sim threads) plus a dedicated Performance Simulation thread (Perf Sim thread); (2) FIFO read/write timing tables that explicitly record the hardware cycle at which each FIFO event occurs, independent of OS thread scheduling; (3) a Query Pool where Func Sim threads pause on non-blocking FIFO accesses until the Perf Sim thread resolves the query by comparing hardware-cycle timestamps; (4) flexibly overlapped execution where Func Sim and Perf Sim threads run concurrently rather than in strict phases, yielding additional speedup. An LLVM pass instruments the IR to track basic block execution traces and rewrites dataflow functions to launch concurrent threads. Incremental simulation is supported to avoid full restarts when FIFO sizes change.
nv: A tightly coupled, flexibly overlapped multi-thread simulation framework where a dedicated performance simulation thread synchronizes non-blocking FIFO events using hardware-cycle timestamps stored in FIFO tables, enabling correct simulation of previously unsupported Type B and C HLS dataflow designs at near-C speed.
mx: speedup: up to 35.9x over C/RTL co-simulation; up to 6.61x over LightningSim · accuracy: near-RTL accuracy (99.9% cycle accuracy maintained for Type A, functionally correct for Types B and C) · other: Incremental FIFO-size DSE: 4 orders of magnitude speedup over full simulation; correctly simulates 11 designs previously unsupported by any HLS tool
tg: hls, simulation, dataflow, llvm, fifo, design-space-exploration

t: Citadel: Rethinking Memory Allocation to Safeguard Against Inter-Domain Rowhammer Exploits
th: memory allocator for Rowhammer security via physical domain isolation
pb: Rowhammer attacks exploit DRAM's physical row-adjacency to corrupt memory rows belonging to different security domains; hardware mitigations are costly, slow to adopt, and repeatedly circumvented, while software mitigations incur large performance and memory capacity overheads or provide only partial protection.
me: Citadel is a software-based memory allocator that prevents inter-domain Rowhammer by introducing flexible security domains and physically isolating them in disjoint DRAM regions—ensuring no two domains share physically adjacent rows. The allocator tracks DRAM physical row topology and partitions the address space so that domain boundaries are always separated by guard rows or page-aligned gaps. The design supports thousands of simultaneous security domains on server systems with a 7.2% average memory overhead and no measurable performance loss, without requiring hardware changes and remaining deployable on legacy, current, and future DRAM platforms.
nv: A memory allocator that prevents Rowhammer cross-domain exploits by design through physical domain isolation in disjoint DRAM row regions, achieving security without hardware modifications, performance loss, or the excessive overhead of prior software schemes.
mx: speedup: no performance loss (0% overhead) · other: 7.2% average memory overhead; 4-6x lower overhead vs. recent domain isolation schemes; supports thousands of security domains
tg: rowhammer, dram-security, memory-allocator, domain-isolation, security, server

t: A Probabilistic Perspective on Tiling Sparse Tensor Algebra
th: probabilistic tiling optimization for sparse tensor algebra
pb: Tiling sparse tensor algebra computations for cache efficiency is challenging because the effective tile size and cache behavior depend on the sparse data distribution, which varies across inputs and is not known at compile time.
me: The paper takes a probabilistic approach to sparse tensor tiling, modeling the sparsity pattern probabilistically to predict cache behavior and guide tile-size selection. Specific mechanism details are not available from the abstract alone.
nv: A probabilistic framework for analyzing and selecting tile sizes in sparse tensor algebra that accounts for input-dependent sparsity patterns.
tg: sparse-tensor, tiling, probabilistic-modeling, cache, compiler, sparse-algebra

t: FALA: Locality-Aware PIM-Host Cooperation for Graph Processing with Fine-Grained Column Access
th: locality-aware PIM-host cooperation for graph processing with fine-grained DRAM column access
pb: Graph processing exhibits irregular memory access patterns that cause significant memory bandwidth waste on DRAM architectures: cache-based graph tiling suffers from overfetching due to the mismatch between DRAM burst size and the sparse data actually needed, while PIM-based approaches fail to exploit cache locality for high-reuse workloads.
me: FALA is a hybrid architecture integrating PIM and cache-based acceleration. It introduces a fine-grained column access mechanism within DRAM memory banks that allows selective access to individual columns (vertices) rather than fetching full DRAM rows, eliminating overfetching for sparse graph accesses. A locality-aware PIM architecture is designed to route accesses: high-reuse vertex data is served through the host CPU cache hierarchy, while low-reuse, irregular accesses are processed near-memory via PIM. The design minimizes unnecessary memory traffic while fully utilizing both internal DRAM bandwidth and on-chip caches.
nv: A fine-grained column access mechanism within DRAM banks that enables PIM to process individual graph vertices without loading full DRAM rows, combined with a locality-aware policy that routes reused data through host caches and irregular accesses through PIM.
mx: speedup: 1.56x geometric mean speedup vs. prior art · energy_or_tops_w: 35.3% energy reduction vs. prior art
tg: graph-processing, pim, near-data-processing, dram, cache-locality, fine-grained-access

t: Drishti: Do Not Forget Slicing While Designing Last-Level Cache Replacement Policies for Many-Core Systems
th: sliced-LLC-aware last-level cache replacement policy design
pb: State-of-the-art LLC replacement policies (Hawkeye, Mockingjay) use a per-slice sampled cache and a per-slice reuse predictor that make myopic decisions based only on accesses to a single slice, unaware of global reuse behavior across all LLC slices in many-core systems; additionally, per-slice sampled cache sets receive insufficient LLC misses to drive accurate replacement decisions.
me: Drishti proposes two enhancements to existing LLC replacement policies for sliced LLCs: (1) a per-core global reuse predictor where each core's predictor is trained on all accesses by that core across all LLC slices—achieving global reuse awareness without centralized inter-slice interconnect traffic—combined with a local (per-slice) sampled cache that remains slice-local; (2) a per-slice dynamic sampled cache that adaptively expands the set of LLC sets used for sampling to improve the sample quality and ensure adequate miss coverage per slice. Evaluated by augmenting Hawkeye and Mockingjay on 4, 16, and 32-core systems with 8, 32, and 64 MB sliced LLCs.
nv: Decoupling the reuse predictor (per-core, globally aware) from the sampled cache (per-slice, local) in sliced LLC replacement policies, enabling global reuse inference without centralized interconnect traffic.
mx: speedup: 5.6% IPC improvement (Hawkeye+Drishti) and 13.2% (Mockingjay+Drishti) over LRU on 32-core system · other: Without Drishti: Hawkeye 3.3%, Mockingjay 6.7% over LRU; Drishti roughly doubles the gain
tg: llc-replacement, cache-slicing, many-core, reuse-prediction, hawkeye, mockingjay

t: MCBP: A Memory-Compute Efficient LLM Inference Accelerator Leveraging Bit-Slice-enabled Sparsity and Repetitiveness
th: bit-slice-level compute-memory co-optimization for LLM inference acceleration
pb: LLM inference faces three simultaneous bottlenecks—GEMM computation in the prefill stage, weight loading during decoding (52.4% of short-prompt latency for LLaMA-7B), and KV cache loading for long contexts—which existing Transformer accelerators address in isolation at value granularity, missing fine-grained bit-level optimization opportunities.
me: MCBP is an algorithm-hardware co-design operating at bit-slice (BS) granularity. Three key techniques: (1) BS-Repetitiveness-enabled Computation Reduction (BRCR): decomposes a k-bit weight matrix into k BS matrices, groups m rows into a Group matrix, identifies repeated column vectors via a Content Addressable Memory (CAM) unit, computes a Merged Activation Vector (MAV) for repeated activations (H*(1-bs) additions), and reconstructs output via an Enumeration matrix (m*2^(m-1) additions), achieving up to 12.1x computation reduction vs. value-sparsity. (2) BS-Sparsity-enabled Two-State Coding (BSTC): stores weights in sign-magnitude format; high-order bit-slice matrices (bits 3-7 in INT8) exhibit >65% sparsity and are encoded with two states ({0} for zeros, {1,m-bit data} for non-zeros) at the same group granularity m as BRCR, achieving positive compression without requiring bit reordering for computation; low-order bits (1,2,8) remain uncompressed. (3) Bit-grained Progressive Prediction (BGPP): estimates attention scores MSB-to-LSB across multiple rounds; a radius-scaled filter (threshold = max(A_hat) - alpha * radius) eliminates Keys whose partial score falls below the threshold after each round, enabling early termination that reduces KV cache accesses by up to 50%. Hardware: CAM-based BRCR unit, lightweight parallel BSTC encoder/decoder, clock-gated BGPP prediction module, on-chip SRAM hierarchy (384KB token, 768KB weight, 96KB temp), and external HBM.
nv: A unified bit-slice-granularity co-design that simultaneously exploits bit-level repetitiveness (via CAM-based grouped matching), bit-level sparsity in high-order weight planes (via two-state coding), and progressive bit-by-bit KV cache filtering (BGPP) to jointly address all three LLM inference bottlenecks at a finer granularity than any prior accelerator.
mx: speedup: 9.43x vs. NVIDIA A100 GPU · energy_or_tops_w: 22740 GOPS/W average energy efficiency; 31.1x vs. A100 GPU; 35x vs. Spatten; 5.2x vs. FACT; 3.2x vs. SOFA · other: BGPP reduces KV cache accesses by up to 50%; BRCR achieves 5.1x group-wise computation reduction vs. full-size merge across 5 LLMs
tg: llm-inference, bit-serial, sparsity, quantization, transformer-accelerator, kv-cache

t: REACT3D: Real-time Edge Accelerator for Incremental Training in 3D Gaussian Splatting based SLAM Systems
th: Real-time 3DGS SLAM edge acceleration
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM requires incremental training and rendering at over 30 FPS on edge devices, but existing GPU-based solutions and prior accelerators fall short due to redundant training computation, unnecessary loss computation, and irregular memory access patterns. The combination of continuous camera streaming, per-Gaussian gradient accumulation, and sparse activated Gaussian sets creates severe compute and memory irregularity.
me: REACT3D introduces two algorithmic optimizations: (1) spatial consistency and convergence-aware sparsification that predicts under-optimized Gaussians based on spatial coherence and convergence dynamics, eliminating redundant forward/backward rendering passes; and (2) a pixel block-wise fine-grained dataflow that fuses loss computation into the rendering pipeline, removing explicit loss storage. At the architectural level, a Content Addressable Memory (CAM)-based Dual-index Gaussian Buffer resolves discontinuous memory accesses by maintaining two parallel indices into the Gaussian buffer, avoiding computation conflicts during gradient merging across scattered Gaussian-to-pixel mappings.
nv: The CAM-based Dual-index Gaussian Buffer that resolves the irregular memory access and gradient-merging conflict problem inherent to 3DGS training on sparse, streaming SLAM data.
mx: speedup: 12.10x over NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin · energy_or_tops_w: 33.69x energy efficiency improvement over NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin · other: Achieves >30 FPS real-time 3DGS SLAM threshold
tg: 3d-gaussian-splatting, slam, edge-accelerator, sparse-training, irregular-memory

t: MUSS-TI: Multi-level Shuttle Scheduling for Large-Scale Entanglement Module Linked Trapped-Ion
th: Zone-aware quantum circuit compilation for modular trapped-ion systems
pb: Compiling quantum circuits for Entanglement Module Linked Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (EML-QCCD) trapped-ion architectures is inefficient because existing compilers do not account for the distinct functional zones (storage, operation, optical/entanglement) within each QCCD module, leading to excessive ion shuttle operations and reduced circuit fidelity. Cross-module nonlocal gates via photonic fiber links further complicate qubit routing.
me: MUSS-TI constructs a dependency graph (DAG) of the quantum circuit and applies a multi-level scheduling strategy analogous to classical memory scheduling: storage zones map to L0 (disk), operation zones to L1 (memory), and optical zones to L2 (CPU). Gate selection prioritizes immediately executable gates; qubit routing assigns each qubit to the nearest-level available zone; conflict handling uses an LRU eviction policy to relocate the least-recently-used qubit to a lower-level zone. A look-ahead SWAP insertion algorithm (k=8 layers) strategically inserts SWAP gates between different QCCD modules to reduce long-range shuttle counts; a SABRE-inspired bidirectional initial mapping further reduces overhead.
nv: Applying the multi-level cache scheduling abstraction (LRU replacement, zone-level hierarchy) to trapped-ion qubit routing, where storage/operation/optical zones are treated as memory levels and qubit eviction mimics page replacement.
mx: speedup: 58.9% shorter execution time vs. baseline for small-scale circuits · other: Shuttle operation reduction: 41.74% (30-32 qubits), 73.38% (117-128 qubits), 59.82% (256-299 qubits)
tg: trapped-ion, quantum-computing, qubit-routing, shuttle-scheduling, compiler

t: LLM.265: Video Codecs are Secretly Tensor Codecs
th: GPU video codec hardware repurposed as LLM tensor compressor
pb: LLM training and inference are increasingly bottlenecked by memory footprint and communication bandwidth for weights, activations, gradients, and KV cache, but existing tensor-compression methods are specialized for only one type of tensor and require custom hardware or software stacks. A unified, bandwidth-efficient compression mechanism applicable across all LLM tensor types is missing.
me: LLM.265 repurposes existing GPU hardware video encoders/decoders (H.265/HEVC engines) as general-purpose tensor codecs. The key insight is that LLM tensors expose spatial and temporal statistical structure (smooth weight manifolds, slowly changing activations, correlated KV cache vectors) that codec stages — inter-frame prediction, DCT/transform coding, scalar quantization, and entropy coding via context-adaptive arithmetic coding — can exploit directly. The system maps tensor layouts to frame formats, applies intra/inter prediction to exploit tensor correlations, and uses entropy coding to compress residuals. Custom hardware extensions to the existing video engine improve tensor encoding/decoding throughput without major GPU architecture changes.
nv: Reusing commodity GPU video codec hardware engines as unified tensor compressors for all LLM data types (weights, activations, gradients, KV cache), eliminating the need for specialized compression accelerators.
mx: other: Compression effectiveness for weights, activations, gradients, KV cache not stated in abstract; throughput vs. baseline not stated
tg: video-codec, tensor-compression, llm, kv-cache, gpu-video-engine

t: ReGate: Enabling Power Gating in Neural Processing Units
th: Fine-grained NPU power gating via hardware-software co-design
pb: Modern NPU chips (e.g., Google TPU generations) waste 30-72% of their active energy on static (leakage) power because they lack fine-grained power management support; conventional CPU/GPU power-gating techniques do not transfer directly because NPUs use large systolic arrays with deterministic dataflows, software-managed SRAM scratchpads, in-order VLIW pipelines, and no dynamic instruction scheduling.
me: ReGate uses hardware-software co-design differentiated by component. For systolic arrays (SAs): non-zero weight detection generates row/column bitmaps (col_nz, row_nz), and a prefix-sum circuit derives which rows/columns should be powered off; PE-level power gating then follows the diagonal weight-stationary dataflow — the PE_on signal propagates diagonally from the SA input, overlapping wake-up with computation to expose only single-PE wake-up latency. For ICI and HBM controllers: a lightweight hardware-based idle-detection state machine gates these units between collective operators (AllReduce, AllGather). For vector units and SRAM: a new NPU ISA extension adds setpm instructions with three modes (on/auto/off) that let the ML compiler insert power-management instructions at statically-known idle boundaries — the compiler determines VU idle gaps from instruction scheduling and SRAM capacity from tile-size analysis.
nv: Diagonal-dataflow-aware cycle-level PE power gating in systolic arrays, where the PE_on signal propagates through the array following the inherent weight-stationary diagonal dataflow, enabling fine-grained power gating with only single-PE wake-up latency overhead.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: 8.5%-32.8% energy reduction (15.5% average) vs. no power gating · other: <0.5% performance degradation; <3.3% area overhead; 31.1%-62.9% carbon emission reduction at fleet scale
tg: power-gating, npu, tpu, systolic-array, leakage-power, isa-extension

t: Bootes: Boosting the Efficiency of Sparse Accelerators Using Spectral Clustering
th: Spectral clustering row reordering to minimize SpGEMM off-chip memory traffic
pb: Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication (SpGEMM) accelerators using row-wise product dataflow suffer from poor off-chip memory traffic because row reordering — the primary technique to improve data reuse — is either suboptimal, slow to compute, or fails to detect when reordering is counterproductive for certain sparsity patterns.
me: Bootes applies spectral clustering to reorder rows of the input matrix A before feeding them into a row-wise SpGEMM accelerator. A similarity matrix capturing structural properties of A's row sparsity patterns guides the clustering; similar rows are placed adjacent so that their accesses into B have high overlap, maximizing data reuse. The spectral clustering algorithm itself is optimized to reduce preprocessing time to a geometric mean of 11.61x faster than existing reordering techniques. A decision tree model trained on real-world sparse matrices predicts whether reordering will be beneficial before executing it, enabling cost-aware preprocessing that avoids overhead when reordering would increase traffic.
nv: Using spectral clustering on a row-similarity matrix to optimally reorder SpGEMM inputs for maximum off-chip data reuse, combined with a decision tree gating mechanism to skip reordering when it is counterproductive.
mx: other: Off-chip traffic reduction: 2.31x (Flexagon), 1.67x (GAMMA), 1.38x (Trapezoid); preprocessing speedup: 11.61x geomean over prior reordering
tg: spgemm, sparse-matrix, row-reordering, spectral-clustering, off-chip-traffic

t: Misam: Machine Learning Assisted Dataflow Selection in Accelerators for Sparse Matrix Multiplication
th: ML-guided FPGA reconfiguration for adaptive SpGEMM dataflow selection
pb: SpGEMM accelerators that support multiple dataflows (e.g., row-wise, column-wise, inner-product) face two critical problems: (1) no fast principled mechanism exists for selecting the optimal dataflow at runtime given input matrix sparsity patterns, and (2) providing hardware flexibility for multiple dataflows incurs area overhead and underutilization when one dataflow is locked in.
me: Misam uses a lightweight decision tree classifier to dynamically predict the optimal SpGEMM hardware configuration from matrix structural features (sparsity density, distribution, pattern statistics) extracted at runtime. To overcome hardware underutilization from multi-dataflow support, Misam targets FPGAs and exploits FPGA partial reconfigurability to deploy specialized, resource-efficient bitstreams tailored to specific sparsity regimes on demand. A reconfiguration engine evaluates whether the anticipated performance gain from switching bitstreams exceeds the reconfiguration overhead before triggering a reconfiguration.
nv: Using FPGA partial reconfiguration guided by a runtime ML decision tree to deploy sparsity-regime-specialized bitstreams on demand, achieving the efficiency of a fixed-dataflow accelerator with the adaptability of a flexible one.
mx: speedup: Up to 10.76x speedup via adaptive reconfiguration
tg: spgemm, sparse-matrix, fpga-reconfiguration, dataflow-selection, adaptive-accelerator

t: StreamTensor: Make Tensors Stream in Dataflow Accelerators for LLMs
th: Automated dataflow compiler for stream-based LLM acceleration on FPGAs
pb: Dataflow accelerators for LLMs (e.g., AMD Versal, SambaNova SN40L, IBM AIU) require manual effort to wire together kernels via on-chip FIFOs, manage external DMA access patterns, size FIFOs to prevent deadlock, and fuse kernels with compatible stream layouts — problems that compound across inter-kernel, multi-DMA, and large context-length LLM workloads, preventing end-to-end optimization.
me: StreamTensor is an MLIR-based compiler that introduces an iterative tensor (itensor) type encoding element shape, iteration space, and iteration map to uniquely capture a kernel's stream access order. The compilation pipeline proceeds through: (1) Linalg tiling and conversion to dataflow IR with itensor-typed kernel boundaries; (2) stream-based kernel fusion that compares producer/consumer itensor types — matching types are connected by FIFOs directly, mismatched types get minimal ping-pong buffer layout converters sized analytically from itensor types; (3) itensor folding to merge adjacent producer-consumer buffers; (4) iterative tensor vectorization to align FIFO bandwidth with kernel parallelism; (5) LP-based FIFO sizing that formulates token flow as a scheduling problem and solves it with linear programming to minimize FIFO depth while preventing deadlock; and (6) ILP graph partitioning for resource allocation. Three hierarchical design spaces (Linalg tiling, kernel fusion, resource allocation) are explored with Optuna blackbox optimization, intensity-aware unrolling, and heuristic permutation.
nv: The iterative tensor (itensor) type system that explicitly encodes streaming access order (iteration space + iteration map), enabling automated correctness-verified stream-based kernel fusion, minimal layout converter generation, and LP-based FIFO sizing for dataflow accelerators.
mx: speedup: Up to 0.76x lower latency than state-of-the-art FPGA LLM accelerators; 0.64x lower latency than GPUs · energy_or_tops_w: Up to 1.99x higher energy efficiency compared to GPUs
tg: dataflow-compiler, fpga, llm, kernel-fusion, streaming, mlir

t: ColumnDisturb: Understanding Column-based Read Disturbance in Real DRAM Chips and Implications for Future Systems
th: New DRAM column-based read disturbance phenomenon characterization
pb: A newly discovered DRAM read disturbance phenomenon called ColumnDisturb allows a single aggressor row activation to disturb DRAM cells through bitlines (columns), inducing bitflips in rows sharing the same columns across multiple subarrays — up to 3072 rows simultaneously in DDR4 — which is fundamentally different from RowHammer/RowPress that affect only a few adjacent rows in a single subarray.
me: The paper conducts a rigorous experimental characterization of ColumnDisturb on 216 DDR4 chips and 4 HBM2 chips from three major DRAM manufacturers. Experiments vary temperature, data patterns, DRAM timing parameters (tRCD, tRAS, tRP), average bitline voltage, memory access patterns, and spatial variation across chips. The study measures minimum time to first bitflip, affected row count, and bitflip counts under nominal 63.6ms DDR4 refresh windows. The authors compare ColumnDisturb severity against DRAM retention failures and perform cycle-level simulation to quantify the impact on retention-aware refresh mechanisms that propose to skip refreshes for cells with long retention times.
nv: First experimental demonstration and comprehensive characterization of ColumnDisturb — a column/bitline-mediated read disturbance affecting up to 3 subarrays simultaneously from a single aggressor row, fundamentally broader in spatial scope than RowHammer.
mx: other: First-bitflip time reduces by up to 5.06x (2.96x average) with smaller DRAM node; affects up to 3072 rows simultaneously; induces bitflips within 63.6ms DDR4 refresh window on real chips; up to 198x more affected rows than retention failures
tg: dram, rowhammer, read-disturbance, reliability, memory-scaling, column-disturb

t: TransFusion: End-to-End Transformer Acceleration via Graph Fusion and Pipelining
th: End-to-end Transformer layer fusion and pipelining via Einsum Cascades
pb: Transformer acceleration has focused on fusing individual submodules (MHA, softmax) in isolation, but as models grow in depth and context length, inter-layer data movement, buffer fragmentation, and scheduling inefficiencies across the full encoder/decoder stack (QKV projections, MHA, LayerNorm, FFN) dominate end-to-end latency and cannot be addressed by fragmented per-module optimizations.
me: TransFusion represents the full Transformer layer stack as Einsum Cascades — a structured DAG of Einsum operations capturing precise data dependencies and execution order. The DPipe scheduler partitions this Einsum DAG and applies latency-aware inter-layer pipelining across hardware memory hierarchies using dynamic programming to balance FFN and attention stages. TileSeek, a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based tiling search algorithm, explores the tile configuration space to balance buffer reuse against on-chip memory constraints at both cloud and edge scales.
nv: Modeling the complete Transformer encoder/decoder stack as Einsum Cascades and using dynamic programming (DPipe) with MCTS-based tile search (TileSeek) to co-optimize inter-layer data reuse, intra-layer pipelining, and operator scheduling end-to-end.
mx: speedup: Average 1.6x on cloud, 2.2x on edge over FuseMax
tg: transformer, end-to-end-fusion, pipelining, einsum, tiling, mcts

t: Towards Closing the Performance Gap for Cryptographic Kernels Between CPUs and Specialized Hardware
th: Closing CPU-to-ASIC performance gap for cryptographic kernels via SIMD and minimal ISA extension
pb: Achieving near-ASIC performance for cryptographic kernels (Number Theoretic Transform, NTT; and large-integer BLAS operations) on commodity x86 CPUs remains an open challenge; current CPU baselines lag ASICs by orders of magnitude for these workloads, which are foundational to post-quantum cryptography and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE).
me: The paper develops optimized scalar x86-64 implementations of NTT and large-integer BLAS at the per-core level, then applies SIMD vectorization using AVX2 and AVX-512 to achieve 38x and 62x speedup over state-of-the-art CPU baselines for NTT and BLAS respectively. To narrow the remaining gap, the authors propose a small x86 ISA extension called MQX (multi-word extension) that adds three new instructions targeting multi-precision modular arithmetic patterns common in NTT and BLAS. MQX cuts the slowdown relative to ASICs to as low as 35x per core; a roofline analysis of multi-core scaling shows that top-tier server CPUs with MQX can approach ASIC-level throughput.
nv: The MQX (multi-word extension) ISA extension — just three new AVX-512 instructions targeting multi-precision modular arithmetic — that closes much of the remaining gap between x86 CPUs and cryptographic ASICs for NTT and large-integer BLAS.
mx: speedup: 38x over CPU baseline for NTT; 62x for BLAS (with AVX-512); ASIC slowdown reduced to 35x per core with MQX
tg: cryptography, ntt, homomorphic-encryption, isa-extension, avx-512, cpu-optimization

t: Characterizing and Optimizing Realistic Workloads on a Commercial Compute-in-SRAM Device
th: Real-hardware compute-in-SRAM characterization and optimization for RAG
pb: Prior compute-in-SRAM evaluations rely on simulators or small prototypes, so the real-world performance and energy efficiency of commercial devices under realistic AI workloads (particularly retrieval-augmented generation over large corpora) is not well understood, and programming principles for exploiting the architecture's 2-million bit-processor parallelism are largely unknown.
me: The paper characterizes the commercial GSI APU (2M 1-bit processors at 500 MHz, 25 TOPS, 26 TB/s on-chip bandwidth, 12MB L1 / 64KB L2 / 1MB L3 / 16GB DDR) using the Phoenix benchmark suite and matrix multiplication microbenchmarks, and develops a Python-based analytical framework modeling non-uniform data movement costs across 4 memory levels (L1-L4) and intra-VR vs. inter-VR operations. Three optimizations are proposed and validated on real hardware: (1) communication-aware reduction mapping that maps the reduction axis temporally to cheaper inter-VR operations (scalar-vector product) rather than costly intra-VR spatial reduction; (2) DMA coalescing via subgroup copy to eliminate redundant off-chip data duplication across loop iterations; and (3) broadcast-friendly data layouts that reduce L3 lookup table sizes from K*N to N elements to cut broadcast latency. These optimizations are applied to RAG retrieval over 10-200GB corpora.
nv: First comprehensive real-hardware evaluation of a commercial compute-in-SRAM device (GSI APU) under realistic AI workloads, revealing that even compute-in-SRAM can be bandwidth-bound without careful data layout optimization, and demonstrating three concrete optimizations that approach the compute roofline.
mx: speedup: 4.8x-6.6x retrieval speedup over optimized CPU; 1.1x-1.8x end-to-end RAG latency improvement; matches NVIDIA A6000 GPU latency for RAG · energy_or_tops_w: 54.4x-117.9x energy reduction vs. NVIDIA A6000 GPU for RAG; 41.8x speedup over CPU on Phoenix benchmarks
tg: compute-in-sram, gsi-apu, rag, energy-efficiency, characterization, data-layout

t: FlashInfer: Efficient and Customizable Attention Engine for LLM Inference Serving
th: attention-kernel-optimization
pb: LLM inference serving requires attention kernels that simultaneously handle heterogeneous KV-cache storage layouts (ragged, paged, tree-structured), diverse attention variants (GQA, MLA, sliding-window), and dynamic request batching, while remaining compatible with static CUDAGraph capture.
me: FlashInfer introduces: (1) Block-Sparse Row (BSR) format as a unified KV-cache representation that encodes ragged, paged, and prefix-tree layouts via a single sparse block structure; (2) composable format decomposition that splits shared-prefix attention from unique-suffix attention and merges partial softmax accumulators; (3) a JIT compiler that instantiates CUDA attention templates per attention variant at first use, reusing compiled binaries across requests; (4) a load-balanced scheduler that uses a priority queue to assign work tiles to thread blocks while preserving CUDAGraph compatibility via a static wrapper that hides dynamic dispatch.
nv: BSR as a single unifying KV-cache abstraction that collapses paged, ragged, and tree-structured layouts into one kernel path; CUDAGraph-compatible dynamic load balancing via a static-size priority queue indirection layer.
mx: ITL_reduction_vs_triton: 29-69% inter-token latency reduction vs compiler backends on LLM serving benchmarks · long_context_latency: 28-30% latency reduction for long-context inference · parallel_generation_speedup: 13-17% speedup for LLM serving with parallel generation
tg: attention, KV-cache, BSR, JIT, CUDAGraph, LLM-serving, FlashInfer, load-balancing

t: FLStore: Efficient Federated Learning Storage for non-training workloads
th: distributed-systems
pb: Federated learning non-training workloads (scheduling, personalization, clustering, debugging, incentivization) impose high latency and cost because they access large volumes of metadata (model weights, hyperparameters, aggregated updates) stored in remote cloud object stores or in-memory caches without data locality.
me: FLStore is a serverless cache framework that co-locates compute and data on the same cache tier. A Cache Engine (hash-table-based) routes requests to the cache node holding the relevant data based on a locality-aware key hashing. A Request Tracker maintains per-client access history to identify hot data. Four caching policies (P1-P4) are derived from a taxonomy of FL non-training workload types: P1 caches client model updates by round; P2 caches aggregated models; P3 caches derived metadata (gradients, loss) across rounds; P4 implements prefetching for predictable access patterns.
nv: Unified data+compute serverless cache tier with a four-policy taxonomy derived from a systematic analysis of FL non-training workload access patterns, enabling locality-aware execution without a central aggregator bottleneck.
mx: latency_vs_objstore_agg: 71% average latency reduction vs cloud object store aggregator; 99.7% peak · cost_vs_objstore_agg: 92.45% cost reduction; 98.8% peak · latency_vs_cache_agg: 64.6% average latency reduction vs in-memory cloud cache aggregator · cost_vs_cache_agg: 98.83% cost reduction vs in-memory cache aggregator
tg: federated-learning, caching, serverless, non-training-workloads, storage, FL

t: TileLink: Generating Efficient Compute-Communication Overlapping Kernels using Tile-Centric Primitives
th: distributed-compute-communication-overlap
pb: Distributed LLM training and inference require overlapping compute with inter-GPU communication (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter) to hide network latency. Operator decomposition is easy but leaves performance on the table; fusing communication into compute kernels is effective but requires expert CUDA/NVSHMEM code that is error-prone and non-portable.
me: TileLink has a frontend and a backend. The frontend exposes tile-centric primitives: producer_tile_notify/consumer_tile_wait synchronize tile-level data readiness; peer_tile_notify/peer_tile_wait coordinate cross-rank tile dependencies; tile_push_data/tile_pull_data transfer tiles between devices; rank_copy_data/rank_notify/rank_wait handle rank-level collective coordination. The backend performs tile-centric mapping in three stages: (1) shape mapping assigns tile dimensions to compute and communication workloads; (2) rank mapping determines which GPU rank computes/receives each tile via affine transforms (static) or runtime lookup tables (dynamic); (3) channel mapping assigns each tile to an NVLink/InfiniBand channel. The backend compiles these mappings to PTX via Triton extended with NVSHMEM primitives, producing fused kernels that interleave compute threads and communication threads within a single CUDA kernel.
nv: Tile-centric primitive abstraction that decouples compute and communication design spaces at the tile granularity, compiled to overlapping kernels via shape/rank/channel mapping; achieves expert-level overlap with ~10x less code than handwritten CUDA.
mx: speedup_vs_non_overlapping: 1.17x to 20.76x speedup vs non-overlapping baseline · vs_flux: Performance comparable to FLUX (expert-written library) with ~200 Python lines vs ~2000 CUDA lines · code_reduction: ~10x less code than equivalent FLUX implementation
tg: compute-communication-overlap, tile-centric, kernel-fusion, NVSHMEM, distributed, tensor-parallelism, compiler

t: QServe: W4A8KV4 Quantization and System Co-design for Efficient LLM Serving
th: quantization-for-serving
pb: INT4 weight quantization methods targeting edge/single-batch inference do not translate to throughput gains in cloud LLM serving because dequantizing INT4 weights or partial sums on CUDA cores introduces 20-90% runtime overhead that erases memory bandwidth savings at large batch sizes.
me: QoQ (quattuor-octo-quattuor, 4-8-4) algorithm with three components: (1) Progressive group quantization: first applies INT8 per-channel quantization to weights, then applies INT4 per-group quantization with a protective range of [-119, 119] that guarantees INT4 values, when scaled back to INT8, remain within safe INT8 range for Tensor Core matmul without overflow. (2) SmoothAttention: applies a per-channel scale lambda to Key tensors to suppress outliers, then absorbs this scale into the preceding linear layer weights; exploits RoPE commutativity to apply the scale before positional encoding, enabling 4-bit KV quantization without accuracy loss. (3) Compute-aware weight reordering: stores INT4 weights in the order they are accessed during GEMM computation (not the order of the weight matrix), enabling 128-bit/thread memory transactions rather than scattered accesses. Fast dequantization: performs subtraction before multiplication (reverses typical order) to keep values in INT8 range, uses 4-way register-level parallelism via vadd4 instruction to dequantize 4 weights per instruction. KV4 attention: replaces FP32 CUDA core accumulation in attention decoding with FP16 Tensor Core ops; bit manipulation tricks reduce dequantization from 5 to 2 ops per element.
nv: Progressive group quantization with protective range enabling W4A8 Tensor Core GEMM without overflow; SmoothAttention absorbing per-channel Key scales into weights via RoPE commutativity; compute-aware weight reordering enabling 128-bit/thread memory access patterns.
mx: llama3_8b_throughput_a100: 1.2x Llama-3-8B max serving throughput on A100 vs TensorRT-LLM · llama3_8b_throughput_l40s: 1.4x Llama-3-8B max serving throughput on L40S vs TensorRT-LLM · qwen15_72b_throughput_a100: 2.4x Qwen1.5-72B throughput on A100 vs TensorRT-LLM · qwen15_72b_throughput_l40s: 3.5x Qwen1.5-72B throughput on L40S vs TensorRT-LLM · l40s_vs_a100: QServe on L40S achieves higher throughput than TensorRT-LLM FP16 on A100
tg: quantization, W4A8KV4, QoQ, SmoothAttention, progressive-quantization, GEMM, vadd4, LLM-serving

t: Marconi: Prefix Caching for the Era of Hybrid LLMs
th: kv-cache-management
pb: Hybrid LLMs combining Attention and SSM (State Space Model / Mamba) recurrent layers cannot use standard prefix caching because SSM layers use in-place state updates that preclude rolling back to partial sequence states; only exact-match cache hits are possible, causing an explosion in cache entries with low reuse, wasting memory and compute.
me: Marconi maintains a unified radix tree storing both KV-cache blocks (for attention layers) and SSM state checkpoints (for recurrent layers) per sequence. Two key policies: (1) Admission: speculative insertion before prefill execution identifies branch points in the radix tree where SSM state checkpointing is needed; admits only entries in two reuse classes - (a) purely-input shared prefixes (system prompts, shared context) and (b) input+output prefixes (multi-turn conversation history). Entries not in these classes are rejected at admission time. (2) FLOP-aware eviction: utility score S(n) = recency(n) + alpha * flop_efficiency(n), where flop_efficiency(n) = FLOPs_saved_by_hit / bytes_of_cache_entry; alpha is tuned via grid search on a bootstrap period. Only leaf nodes and single-child intermediate nodes are eligible for eviction (evicting a branching node would invalidate its subtree). This prevents eviction cascades while prioritizing high-FLOP-return entries.
nv: First prefix caching system for hybrid Attention+SSM LLMs; FLOP-aware eviction metric (FLOPs saved per cache byte) that jointly considers compute savings and memory cost of cached states; speculative admission before prefill that identifies SSM checkpointing points without executing the model.
mx: token_hit_rate: up to 34.4x higher token hit rates vs state-of-the-art prefix caching (vLLM+) · ttft_reduction_pct: 71.1% lower P95 Time-To-First-Token vs vLLM+ · ttft_reduction_abs: 617 ms lower P95 TTFT vs vLLM+
tg: prefix-caching, hybrid-LLM, SSM, Mamba, FLOP-aware-eviction, radix-tree, KV-cache

t: Supply-Chain Attacks in Machine Learning Frameworks
th: ml-security
pb: ML frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, HuggingFace) have a larger dependency attack surface than comparable non-ML software, yet the ML community has no higher security awareness than non-ML communities, leaving ML-specific supply-chain vulnerabilities unaddressed by existing defenses.
me: Two contributions: (1) Attack demonstration - introduces ML-specific supply-chain attacks using two Python mechanisms: (a) global variable overwriting where a compromised upstream package directly mutates PyTorch/TorchVision globals (e.g., interpolation mode enums, softmax functions, model forward methods) at import time; (b) local variable overwriting using Python's inspect module and undocumented PyFrame_LocalsToFast C API to modify in-scope variables in downstream function call stacks. Three attack types demonstrated: backdoor injection via forward function hijacking, pipeline vulnerability injection via interpolation mode swap, and model weight stealing via steganographic encoding in inference outputs. (2) Security awareness analysis - LLM-assisted analysis of 549,635 GitHub issues/PRs from Top-50 ML repositories using GPT-3.5 for coarse filtering (97.8% recall) then GPT-4 for fine-grained safeguard classification (78.9% precision, 0.85 Cohen's kappa). Compared against Top-50 Linux repositories.
nv: First systematic demonstration that Python's shared memory model enables ML-specific supply-chain attacks that manipulate model behavior (not just OS security) while evading all conventional detection; LLM-assisted large-scale security awareness study across 549k GitHub issues.
mx: llm_pipeline_recall: 97.8% recall vs manual annotations (0.85 Cohen's kappa) · llm_pipeline_precision: 78.9% precision vs manual annotations · ml_repos_analyzed: 549,635 issues/PRs from Top-50 ML repositories · security_pr_acceptance_pytorch: 64.20% security PR acceptance at PyTorch (lower than most ML repos) · ml_vs_linux_distribution: Similar security awareness distribution between ML and Linux communities
tg: security, supply-chain, Python, adversarial-ML, backdoor, model-stealing, GitHub-analysis

t: ProtoRAIL: A Risk-cognizant Imitation Agent for Adaptive vCPU Oversubscription In the Cloud
th: cloud-resource-management
pb: Cloud vCPU oversubscription policies must jointly minimize overloading risk (hot nodes) and maximize utilization (stranded resource recovery), but demand patterns vary dynamically across VM types and time, making static heuristic policies either too conservative (waste capacity) or too aggressive (cause overload).
me: ProtoRAIL has three components: (1) Prototypical Imitation Learning - a trajectory encoder (LSTM or Transformer) maps CPU usage trajectories to embeddings; K prototype embeddings represent equivalence classes of usage patterns; policy is a linear layer over similarities to prototypes. Loss has four terms: Lrep (representativeness: L2 distance to nearest prototype), Ldiv (diversity: repel close prototypes), Lint (interpretability: anchor each prototype to a real trajectory), and LIMloss (imitation learning via behavior cloning or adversarial IL). (2) Active Knowledge-in-the-Loop (KITL) - identifies uncertain prototypes (high cluster entropy) and risky predictions (predicted oversubscription rate below actual usage) via a query framework; solicits feedback from domain experts (or LLMs) as up/down votes on prototypes and actions, plus merge/split operations on prototype clusters; feedback is applied via advice potential gates (exponential scaling of loss components) to steer training without explicit prior design. (3) Query scheduling - minimizes feedback budget by only querying at uncertain or risky stages.
nv: Prototypical imitation learning for sequential decision-making with explicit interpretable pattern classes; active knowledge-in-the-loop with prototype-level feedback (merge/split/vote) to de-risk policies with minimal expert queries.
mx: hot_node_rate: 0% hot node rate (vs 0.89-1.47% for baselines including Coop-MARL, GAIL, BC, DDPG) · remain_core_benefit: 8161 remain cores vs 7938 for best baseline (Dagger with 20 human steps) · deployment_utilization: 9.4% vCPU utilization improvement on Microsoft internal cloud · deployment_hot_nodes: 0% hot node rate on 300 deployed clusters · kitl_query_budget: <=10 total feedback queries to reach stable performance · benefit_risk_ratio: BRR 31.34 vs 18.95 for heuristics and 7.79 for manual
tg: cloud-oversubscription, vCPU, imitation-learning, prototypical, active-learning, KITL, resource-management

t: Rethinking Key-Value Cache Compression Techniques for Large Language Model Serving
th: kv-cache-compression-evaluation
pb: KV cache compression algorithms are evaluated on naive transformer library (TRL) benchmarks with fixed response lengths, hiding three critical problems that prevent production deployment: suboptimal throughput under real serving frameworks (FlashAttention + PagedAttention), increased end-to-end latency due to compression-induced response length growth, and per-sample accuracy fragility on specific task types.
me: Empirical study evaluating four representative KV cache compression methods (KIVI for quantization, GEAR for quantization with error correction, StreamingLLM for structured sparsity, H2O for dynamic attention-score-based sparsity) under three missing evaluation dimensions: (1) Throughput analysis - benchmarks on LMDeploy (with PagedAttention+FlashAttention) and TRL across batch sizes, prompt lengths, and tensor parallelism degrees for LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-70B; (2) Length distribution analysis - measures response length shift D = (Lun - Lcs)/Lun across 1000 ShareGPT samples; (3) Negative sample analysis - defines negative samples as benign inputs where compression causes >10% accuracy drop on LongBench tasks; categorizes by task type (summarization, QA, code, few-shot, synthetic). Additionally provides three tools: throughput predictor (attention-layer profiling + Vidur runtime), length predictor (BERT-based classifier predicting response length given compression algorithm), and negative sample benchmark dataset.
nv: Identification of three overlooked production deployment dimensions (throughput under serving frameworks, response length distribution, per-sample accuracy fragility) for KV compression evaluation; suite of tools (throughput predictor, length predictor, negative sample benchmark) for practical deployment.
