mx: throughput_under_serving_frameworks: Compression speedup vanishes or turns negative at batch size >4 and KV length >=1024 when PagedAttention+FlashAttention are enabled · length_increase: More than 20% of samples show >=1.5x response length increase from lossy compression · negative_samples_kivi: 400-600 negative samples out of ~2000 evaluated at 10% threshold · negative_samples_h2o: 600-800 negative samples at 10% threshold · throughput_predictor_accuracy: >85% across all four compression methods · length_predictor_accuracy: >85% across all four compression methods · tensor_parallelism_effect: Compression speedup decreases or goes negative under tensor parallelism (TP=2,4) due to reduced memory bandwidth contention per GPU
tg: KV-cache, compression, quantization, sparsity, benchmarking, FlashAttention, PagedAttention, production-serving, negative-samples

t: DiffServe: Efficiently Serving Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Query-Aware Model Scaling
th: diffusion-model-serving
pb: Text-to-image diffusion model serving faces two simultaneous challenges: high-quality models (e.g., SDv1.5 at 50 steps) are 4.6-18x slower than lightweight variants (SD-Turbo, SDXS), limiting throughput; and query demand fluctuates, causing static resource provisioning to either waste capacity during off-peak or fail SLOs during peak.
me: DiffServe uses query-aware model cascades with two technical innovations: (1) Discriminator design - EfficientNet-V2 trained on binary real/fake classification (real = MSCOCO ground truth images, fake = generated images from both light and heavy models). At inference, confidence score (softmax output for 'real' class) determines if lightweight model output is accepted or deferred to heavyweight model. Counterintuitive finding: using heavyweight model outputs as 'real' training labels hurts performance; ground-truth images as 'real' labels produce the best discriminator. (2) Resource allocation via MILP - Controller periodically solves a Mixed Integer Linear Program maximizing confidence threshold (proxy for quality) subject to latency constraints (execution time + Little's Law queuing delay) and throughput constraints (device counts x per-device throughput >= demand). Variables: x1, x2 (device counts for light/heavy models), b1, b2 (batch sizes), t (confidence threshold). Demand estimated via exponentially weighted moving average with 5% over-provisioning factor. MILP solved asynchronously (~10ms overhead) off critical path.
nv: EfficientNet-V2 discriminator repurposed from real/fake classification to route diffusion model queries; MILP formulation co-optimizing confidence threshold, batch sizes, and device allocation for cascaded diffusion serving under dynamic demand.
mx: quality_vs_proteus: Up to 20% FID improvement vs Proteus (random query-agnostic routing) · quality_vs_static: Up to 24% FID improvement vs static configurations · slo_violations_vs_static: 19-70% lower SLO violation rate vs static provisioning · slo_violations_vs_clipper_heavy: Up to 52x lower SLO violation vs Clipper-Heavy · milp_runtime: ~10ms MILP solver runtime (off critical path)
tg: diffusion-models, model-serving, cascaded-inference, MILP, resource-allocation, text-to-image, SLO, query-routing

t: SparseTransX: Efficient Training of Translation-Based Knowledge Graph Embeddings Using Sparse Matrix Operations
th: sparse-computation-for-graph-ml
pb: Training translational knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models (TransE, TransR, TransH, TorusE) is bottlenecked by fine-grained scatter/gather operations during gradient computation (up to 40% of CPU training time), causing irregular memory access patterns, high backpropagation overhead, and large intermediate memory allocations.
me: SparseTransX reformulates translational KGE training by constructing a sparse incidence matrix A from training triplets: each row represents one triplet, with +1 in the head entity column and -1 in the tail entity column (for ht expression) or additionally +1 in the relation column offset by entity count (for hrt expression). Multiplying A (sparse, M x (N+R)) by the embedding matrix E (dense, (N+R) x d) directly computes batched (head - tail) or (head + relation - tail) expressions via a single SpMM call. Both forward and backward pass benefit: backward reduces to SpMM on the transpose A^T. Four models implemented: TransE (hrt computation, L2 norm), TransR (ht computation + per-relation projection matrix Mr applied separately), TransH (two ht computations with hyperplane projections), TorusE (hrt with torus distance). Framework uses iSpLib (CSR format, SIMD vectorized, auto-tuned) for CPU and DGL g-SpMM (COO format) for GPU. PyTorch DDP/FSDP wrappers support distributed training.
nv: First application of SpMM to replace scatter-gather in translational KGE training; sparse incidence matrix formulation that unifies head-tail-relation embedding extraction into a single matrix multiplication enabling high-performance sparse library acceleration.
mx: cpu_speedup_transe: up to 5.3x speedup on CPU vs TorchKGE (across 7 datasets including BioKG 4.8M triplets) · gpu_speedup_transe: up to 4.2x speedup on GPU vs TorchKGE · gpu_memory_transe: 5.61 GB vs 13.55 GB (TorchKGE) for TransE · gpu_memory_transh: 0.28 GB vs 3.1 GB (TorchKGE) for TransH (11x reduction) · flops_reduction_transe: 220 vs 483.87 billion FLOPs (TorchKGE) for TransE · cache_miss_improvement: 26.54% vs 29.37% (TorchKGE) for TransE
tg: knowledge-graph, SpMM, sparse-matrix, TransE, TransR, graph-ml, training-optimization, GPU-memory

t: PipeFill: Using GPUs During Bubbles in Pipeline-Parallel LLM Training
th: training-efficiency
pb: Pipeline-parallel LLM training leaves substantial GPU idle time (pipeline bubbles) that represents wasted compute capacity at scale.
me: PipeFill schedules independent fill jobs (batch inference, small model training) into pipeline bubble slots using a Pipeline Bubble Instruction (PBI) abstraction, a Fill Job Executor that maps fill work to idle GPU time, and a Fill Job Scheduler that tracks bubble windows and dispatches work. Implemented on DeepSpeed with GPipe and 1F1B schedules.
nv: First system to systematically characterize and exploit pipeline bubble structure for productive secondary workloads, introducing the PBI abstraction that expresses fill work independently of the primary schedule.
mx: speedup: 1.63x GPU utilization increase (63% improvement) at 8K GPUs · accuracy: <2% slowdown on primary LLM training job · other: Fill job throughput scales with pipeline depth and bubble ratio
tg: pipeline-parallelism, GPU-utilization, LLM-training, scheduling, bubble-filling, DeepSpeed, distributed-training

t: Uncertainty Disentanglement for Multimodal Foundation Models in Robotic Systems
th: reliability-and-safety
pb: Multimodal foundation models used in robotic systems conflate perception uncertainty (sensor/input noise) and decision uncertainty (model ambiguity), making it impossible to reason about or mitigate each type independently.
me: Conformal prediction quantifies perception uncertainty by constructing calibrated prediction sets for multimodal inputs. Decision uncertainty is modeled via Formally-specified Markov Decision Processes (FMDP) using Kripke structures and temporal logic specifications, enabling formal verification of behavioral compliance. Active sensing triggers additional observations when perception uncertainty is high; automated model refinement is triggered when decision uncertainty is high. Evaluated on LLaVA-1.5-7B and CLIP on the Carla simulator and real-world driving data.
nv: First framework to formally disentangle perception uncertainty (conformal prediction) from decision uncertainty (FMDP + temporal logic) in multimodal robotic systems, enabling targeted mitigation strategies for each uncertainty type.
mx: accuracy: 40% reduction in output variability; 5% improvement in specification satisfaction; 95%+ temporal logic compliance
tg: uncertainty-quantification, conformal-prediction, formal-methods, robotics, multimodal, LLaVA, CLIP, autonomous-driving, temporal-logic

t: Distributed Submodular Subset Selection at Billion Scale
th: data-efficiency
pb: Submodular subset selection for dataset pruning requires materializing all candidate points in a central machine's memory, making it infeasible at billion-point scale.
me: A distributed bounding algorithm partitions data across workers; each worker computes local upper/lower bounds on marginal gains using grow/shrink steps based on min/max utilities without requiring point-to-point communication. A multi-round partition-based greedy scheme with adaptive repartitioning aggregates global selections. Implemented on Apache Beam for large-scale distributed execution.
nv: Bounding algorithm that avoids centralizing data by computing provably tight bounds on submodular marginal gains in a distributed manner, enabling selection quality approaching centralized greedy without a central memory bottleneck.
mx: accuracy: 98% of centralized greedy quality at 32 communication rounds · other: Scales to 13 billion points; adaptive partitioning reduces rounds needed
tg: submodular-optimization, data-selection, dataset-pruning, distributed-systems, Apache-Beam, scalability, billion-scale

t: AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
th: systems-evaluation
pb: There is no standardized evaluation framework for AI agents tasked with cloud operations (AIOps), making it impossible to rigorously compare agent capabilities for real-world fault detection, localization, root-cause analysis, and mitigation.
me: AIOpsLab defines an Agent-Cloud Interface (ACI) through which agents interact with a live microservice testbed (DeathStarBench) instrumented with ChaosMesh for fault injection, Prometheus for metrics, and Jaeger for distributed tracing. A 100-problem benchmark spans a 4-level task taxonomy: detect, localize, root-cause-analyze (RCA), and mitigate. Faults are categorized as symptomatic (observable but not causally specified) or functional (specified by root cause). Best-performing agent FLASH achieves 59.32% accuracy.
nv: First holistic AIOps benchmark combining a standardized Agent-Cloud Interface, realistic microservice fault injection, and a hierarchical 4-level task taxonomy that covers the full incident management lifecycle.
mx: accuracy: FLASH: 59.32% task accuracy; GPT-4-W-Shell: 49.15% task accuracy · other: 100-problem benchmark; 4-level task taxonomy; Kubernetes/DeathStarBench testbed
tg: AIOps, cloud-operations, AI-agents, benchmark, fault-injection, microservices, Kubernetes, incident-management, LLM-agents

t: N:M Sparse DNN Kernels for RISC-V MCUs via Custom ISA Extension
th: hardware-efficiency
pb: N:M semi-structured sparsity cannot be efficiently exploited on RISC-V microcontrollers (MCUs) because standard ISAs lack the hardware primitives to accelerate structured sparse operations without prohibitive overhead.
me: A custom xDecimate ISA instruction is added to a RISC-V core that performs hardware-accelerated N:M sparse selection and MAC in a single operation. Decimate Im2col reformulates convolution to enable xDecimate on im2col-transformed feature maps. The MATCH compiler generates xDecimate-aware kernels. Synthesized at 22nm targeting the Vega PULP SoC (basis for commercial GAP9). Evaluated on ResNet-18 and ViT at 1:4, 1:8, and 1:16 sparsity ratios.
nv: xDecimate: first RISC-V ISA extension specifically designed for N:M semi-structured sparsity, enabling hardware-level acceleration of 1:4 through 1:16 sparse patterns at only 5% area overhead on a commercial-grade SoC.
mx: speedup: 3.21x (ResNet-18) and 1.81x (ViT) at 1:16 sparsity vs dense baseline · area: 5% area overhead for xDecimate unit on 22nm RISC-V core · accuracy: Accuracy maintained within standard N:M sparsity training tolerances · other: 1:4 and 1:8 sparsity also evaluated with proportionally lower speedups
tg: RISC-V, ISA-extension, N:M-sparsity, MCU, edge-inference, PULP, GAP9, compiler, hardware-acceleration, semi-structured-sparsity

t: FlexAttention: A Programming Model for Generating Optimized Attention Kernels
th: kernel-optimization
pb: Every attention variant (causal, sliding window, document masking, ALiBi, paged, etc.) requires a bespoke hand-written CUDA/Triton kernel, creating an O(variants x hardware) maintenance burden and blocking rapid research iteration.
me: Users express attention variants via two Python callables: score_mod (modifies attention logits, e.g., ALiBi bias) and mask_mod (defines which token pairs to attend to). A BlockMask data structure precomputes block-level sparsity from mask_mod, enabling block-sparse FlashAttention. torch.compile lowers score_mod and mask_mod into a Triton kernel template, fusing them into a single tiled GEMM+softmax+GEMM pass. Tile-level masking avoids computing fully-masked blocks.
nv: BlockMask + score_mod/mask_mod composable API that reduces any attention variant to a Triton template instantiation, achieving near-FlashAttention-2 performance for standard variants and large gains for unsupported variants, with <1% overhead for paged attention vs. 20-26% in vLLM.
mx: speedup: 0.68-1.43x vs FAv2 (standard); 5.49-8x vs SDPA (unsupported variants); 2.04x inference; 2.4x training · accuracy: Numerically equivalent to reference implementations · other: <1% paged attention overhead vs 20-26% in vLLM; evaluated on H100 and A100
tg: attention, FlashAttention, kernel-fusion, Triton, compiler, torch.compile, block-sparsity, LLM-inference, programming-model, GPU

t: XGrammar: Flexible and Efficient Structured Generation Engine for Large Language Models
th: inference-efficiency
pb: Context-free grammar (CFG) constrained decoding for LLMs is slow because every token generation step requires recomputing token masks from scratch, dominating inference latency for structured output generation.
me: XGrammar splits the token vocabulary into context-independent tokens (whose acceptance can be precomputed offline once per grammar) and context-dependent tokens (requiring runtime evaluation). For Llama-3.1 with JSON grammar, only 1,134 of 128k tokens are context-dependent (<1%). A persistent pushdown automaton stack tracks parser state. Context expansion reduces context-dependent tokens further (to ~120, a 90% reduction). An adaptive token mask cache stores masks per parser state, with 0.2% memory overhead. CPU-GPU overlap hides remaining mask computation behind GPU attention.
nv: Context-independent/context-dependent token split that precomputes >99% of token masks offline, combined with a persistent pushdown automaton and adaptive token mask cache, achieving near-zero constrained decoding overhead.
mx: speedup: Up to 100x per-token speedup; 80x end-to-end serving throughput vs vLLM+Outlines · accuracy: Exact grammar compliance; no accuracy loss vs unconstrained sampling within grammar · other: Context-dependent tokens: <1% of vocabulary (1134/128k for Llama-3.1); mask cache 0.46MB vs 160MB naive
tg: constrained-decoding, structured-generation, context-free-grammar, pushdown-automaton, LLM-inference, token-masking, JSON-generation, serving, MLC-LLM

t: Dynamic Input Pruning for Efficient LLM Inference on Mobile Devices
th: inference-efficiency
pb: SwiGLU-based LLM MLP layers on mobile devices are memory-bandwidth bound, with all weight matrices (up, gate, down projections) fully loaded from DRAM for every token, causing excessive energy consumption and low throughput.
me: Dynamic Input Pruning (DIP) applies predictor-free top-K selection on MLP input activation magnitudes, selecting only the K largest input elements and pruning corresponding columns of the up, gate, and down projection matrices. No separate predictor network is needed. LoRA adapters can be added for fine-tuning recovery. DIP-CA (cache-aware variant) uses a gamma multiplier (gamma=0.2) to bias selection toward cached weight columns, reducing DRAM refetch. Evaluated via simulation of Apple A18 (60 GB/s DRAM, 1 GB/s Flash) on Phi-3-Medium, LLaMA models.
nv: Predictor-free input-magnitude-based dynamic pruning of all three SwiGLU MLP matrices simultaneously, with a cache-aware variant (DIP-CA) that coordinates column selection with hardware memory hierarchy to maximize DRAM reduction.
mx: speedup: 40% throughput increase on Phi-3-Medium on Apple A18 simulation · accuracy: <0.1 perplexity increase at optimal sparsity ratio · other: 46% DRAM reduction; evaluated on Apple A18 simulation (60 GB/s DRAM, 1 GB/s Flash)
tg: dynamic-pruning, SwiGLU, mobile-inference, DRAM-reduction, activation-sparsity, cache-aware, LoRA, Phi-3, on-device-LLM, Apple-A18

t: SOLA: Optimizing SLO Attainment for Large Language Model Serving with State-Aware Scheduling
th: inference-efficiency
pb: Existing LLM serving systems apply coarse-grained, fixed scheduling policies (prefill-prioritized or decode-prioritized) that cause significant latency distribution bias between TTFT and TPOT and high inter-request variance, resulting in poor SLO attainment.
me: SOLA models scheduling as a constrained optimization problem over a design space parameterized by request execution order (Fi), number of requests per iteration (ni), and tokens per iteration (ki). A State Monitor tracks per-request TTFT/TPOT, output length distribution, and system memory usage. A Strategy Generator solves one of two constrained optimization problems at each iteration: (1) minimize max TPOT subject to TTFT SLO, or (2) minimize max TTFT subject to TPOT SLO. Hierarchical prioritization (phase-level then request-level) implements the derived strategy. A polynomial cost model (Cp for prefill, Cd for decode) predicts latency and is tuned online via a scaling ratio. Implemented on vLLM v0.4.2.
nv: First serving system to formalize LLM scheduling as a per-iteration constrained optimization with real-time SLO state awareness, enabling dynamic switching between TTFT-optimal and TPOT-optimal strategies based on monitored request and system states.
mx: speedup: 1.04-1.27x more requests served than state-of-the-art at 90% SLO attainment; 1.04-1.11x at 99% attainment · accuracy: SLO attainment improved from 45.5% to 99.4% (Llama3-70B, ShareGPT, 4 A100s) · other: Scheduling overhead: 0.40-0.45% additional latency; evaluated on 8x A100 80GB SXM4
tg: LLM-serving, SLO, scheduling, TTFT, TPOT, constrained-optimization, vLLM, continuous-batching, state-aware, goodput

t: Efficient On-Device Machine Learning with a Biologically-Plausible Forward-Only Algorithm
th: training-efficiency
pb: Backpropagation-based DNN training on IoT and wearable edge devices is infeasible due to excessive memory (activations must be stored), energy consumption, and biologically implausible requirements (weight transport, non-locality, update locking, frozen activities).
me: Bio-FO trains each layer independently using only forward passes. For each hidden layer l, an auxiliary classifier with a fixed random matrix Bl projects layer activations hl to class predictions, computing local cross-entropy loss and gradient without backpropagating through other layers. Weight updates use only local activations (hl-1 and hl), avoiding weight transport (no symmetric backward weights), non-locality (no inter-layer error signals), update locking (updates proceed as activations arrive), and frozen activities (no activation storage required). A sparsity mask Sl enables locally connected (LC) and CNN extensions. Implemented in PyTorch; evaluated on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, medical EEG/ECG datasets, and mini-ImageNet on NVIDIA Jetson Nano.
nv: First forward-only algorithm to simultaneously and fully address all four biological implausibility issues of BP (weight transport, non-locality, update locking, frozen activities) while outperforming prior forward-only methods (FF, PEPITA, DRTP) in accuracy and achieving 3x memory reduction and up to 19.8x energy reduction.
mx: energy_or_tops_w: Up to 19.8x energy reduction vs FF (CIFAR-100: 37.9 Wh vs 753.5 Wh for FF); evaluated at 5W power on Jetson Nano · accuracy: CIFAR-100: 74.57% error (vs 76.16% PEPITA, 85.76% FF); mini-ImageNet: 67.39% error (vs 74.58% CaFo, 91.23% PEPITA); 3x memory reduction vs BP · other: Fastest convergence: MNIST slowness 0.156 (vs 0.541 FF, 1.494 DRTP); hardware: NVIDIA Jetson Nano (128-core Maxwell GPU, 5-10W)

t: Interference-Aware Edge Runtime Prediction with Conformal Matrix Completion
th: scheduling
pb: Predicting workload runtime on heterogeneous edge computing platforms under multi-tenant interference, where observation data is sparse and platforms vary widely in architecture.
me: Pitot: a two-tower MLP-based matrix factorization system with side information (opcode-count feature vectors for workloads, hardware specs for platforms). Adds a low-rank bilinear interference term F_j embedded in the latent space to model multi-tenancy effects. Trained with a log-residual objective. Uncertainty quantification via conformalized quantile regression (CQR) with optimal quantile selection and per-platform calibration pools.
nv: First runtime prediction system to integrate interference modeling directly into the matrix factorization embedding space via a low-rank bilinear interference term, enabling joint completion of the runtime matrix and interference estimation from sparse observations.
mx: accuracy: 5.2% MAPE; up to 48% lower error and 44% tighter prediction intervals vs next-best baseline · other: 2x improvement over naive matrix factorization baseline
tg: edge-inference, runtime-prediction, matrix-completion, conformal-prediction, multi-tenancy, heterogeneous-hardware

t: MiLo: Efficient Quantized MoE Inference with Mixture of Low-Rank Compensators
th: quantization
pb: MoE LLMs suffer large accuracy degradation at INT3 weight quantization; existing calibration-free methods yield poor accuracy and existing INT3 kernels lack measured throughput gains at batch size > 1.
me: Calibration-free HQQ-based INT3 quantization combined with a mixture of adaptive low-rank compensators (SVD-based residual reconstruction). Compensator rank is selected per-layer based on: (1) dense vs sparse layer type, (2) weight kurtosis, (3) expert activation frequency. Iterative joint optimization of quantized weights and compensators. Both weights and compensators are INT3-packed. Custom W3A16 Tensor Core GeMM kernel with zero-bit-waste INT3 packing, binary manipulation I2F dequantization, async global weight loading, and support for batch size > 1.
nv: First W3A16 Tensor Core kernel with demonstrated throughput speedup at batch size > 1 for MoE models, combined with calibration-free adaptive low-rank compensation that recovers accuracy without calibration data.
mx: speedup: 1.2x over MARLIN backend for Mixtral-8x7B; 3x faster quantization vs GPTQ · accuracy: Recovers 87%+ accuracy at 22% compression ratio; MiLo-s2 surpasses GPTQ by 17% on Wikitext2 PPL
tg: MoE, INT3, quantization, low-rank, tensor-core, LLM-inference, Mixtral

t: Enabling Unstructured Sparse Acceleration on Structured Sparse Accelerators
th: sparsity
pb: Unstructured sparse DNN models cannot be accelerated on structured sparse hardware (e.g., 2:4 NVIDIA sparse Tensor Cores), and structured sparse models require hardware-specific fine-tuning making them non-portable.
me: TASD (Tensor Approximation via Structured Decomposition): decomposes any sparse tensor into a series of N:M structured sparse tensors using the distributive property of tensor algebra. TASD-W performs offline weight decomposition via greedy layer-wise search minimizing dropped non-zeros while maintaining 99% model quality. TASD-A handles dynamic runtime activation decomposition with sparsity-degree-based pattern selection attached to accelerator input. TTC (TASD Tensor Core) extends VEGETA/STC to support multiple N:M patterns simultaneously. Decomposition-aware dataflow keeps B/C tiles stationary to amortize the decomposition overhead.
nv: First method enabling unstructured sparse DNNs to run on structured sparse hardware without fine-tuning, via tensor series decomposition exploiting the distributive property of matrix algebra.
mx: speedup: 39% speedup on NVIDIA RTX 3080 (2:4 sparse Tensor Cores) · energy_or_tops_w: EDP improvement up to 83% (dense DNNs), 74% (sparse DNNs) · accuracy: Maintains 99% model quality target with greedy decomposition · other: Computation reduction up to 40%
tg: sparsity, N:M-sparsity, structured-sparse, tensor-decomposition, ASIC, GPU, ResNet, BERT

t: ThunderServe: High-performance and Cost-efficient LLM Serving in Cloud Environments
th: scheduling
pb: LLM serving on heterogeneous cloud GPU clusters with diverse GPU types and limited/heterogeneous network bandwidth (PCIe/Ethernet rather than NVLink/InfiniBand) suffers poor throughput and high latency.
me: Two-level hierarchical scheduling: (1) Upper-level tabu search partitions GPU pool into model-serving groups, designating each group as prefill-phase or decode-phase. (2) Lower-level deduces optimal tensor/pipeline parallelism per group and orchestrates request routing via a two-stage transportation problem solved as linear programming. Phase splitting assigns prefill to high-FLOPS GPUs (e.g., A40) and decode to high-HBM-bandwidth GPUs (e.g., 3090Ti). 4-bit KV cache quantization for inter-phase transfer; dequantized before use. Lightweight rescheduling adjusts phase designation and orchestration without model reload when load changes.
nv: First system integrating prefill-decode phase splitting with heterogeneous GPU assignment in cloud environments with low-bandwidth interconnects, using tabu search for upper-level partition and LP for lower-level routing.
mx: speedup: Up to 2.1x, avg 1.7x throughput vs SOTA; up to 2.5x, avg 1.5x latency reduction · other: Rescheduling completes in ~13s vs ~157s for full reschedule
tg: LLM-serving, heterogeneous-GPU, prefill-decode-disaggregation, cloud, scheduling, KV-cache-quantization

t: NEO: Saving GPU Memory Crisis with CPU Offloading for Online LLM Inference
th: memory-system
pb: GPU memory limits LLM inference batch size, wasting GPU compute; existing CPU offloading systems either hurt latency (symmetric pipelining bubbles) or require expensive dedicated CPUs.
me: NEO asymmetric GPU-CPU pipelining: each iteration splits into two sub-batches. Batch-0 (all prefill requests + most decode requests) runs a long linear projection stage on GPU. Batch-1 (CPU-assigned decode requests) runs a long attention stage on CPU — both overlap. KV cache split into GPU-cache (HBM) and CPU-cache (DRAM). Layer-wise KV swap overlaps PCIe transfer with GPU compute. Load-aware scheduler uses offline-profiled time models + linear interpolation to greedily assign requests per iteration, comparing GPU-only vs asymmetric pipelining and choosing higher throughput. ISPC-compiled SPMD CPU attention kernels (PACPU) with paged attention, SIMD loads, and Flash Decoding-style parallelism across cores.
nv: Asymmetric sub-batch design that integrates prefill into the GPU batch to extend GPU-stage duration, hiding CPU attention latency and eliminating symmetric pipelining bubbles.
mx: speedup: Up to 7.5x throughput on T4, 26% on A10G, 14% on H100 vs GPU-only; up to 79.3% with higher-bandwidth CPUs
tg: LLM-inference, CPU-offloading, GPU-CPU-pipelining, KV-cache, attention, throughput

t: TurboAttention: Efficient Attention Approximation for High Throughput LLMs
th: quantization
pb: LLM attention is a dominant inference bottleneck at long context lengths: KV cache consumes massive memory, FlashAttention requires FP16/FP32 (using slow CUDA cores for softmax exponentiation), and existing KV cache compression methods still dequantize to FP16 before attention, negating latency benefits.
me: TurboAttention combines two innovations: (1) FlashQ — blockwise progressive quantization (BPQ) of Q/K/V to INT8 for FlashAttention-compatible quantized MatMuls, then channel-wise asymmetric INT4/INT2 compression of K/V for cache storage; headwise mixed precision assigns 2-bit quantization to the lowest-priority heads (based on a gap×std priority metric) and 4-bit to the rest. An enhanced KV buffer defers progressive compression every nb=64 steps. (2) SAS (Sparse Activated Softmax) — approximates exponentiation via LUT (integer part) + degree-3 polynomial (decimal part), runs entirely on Tensor Cores in FP16, and sparsifies near-zero attention scores to zero. Together these enable fully INT8 MatMul + FP16 softmax on Tensor Cores.
nv: First unified approach bridging FlashAttention's tiled dataflow with quantization algorithms, enabling fully quantized attention execution (both MatMul and softmax) on GPU Tensor Cores without FP32 CUDA core softmax.
mx: speedup: Up to 1.8x prefill speedup, 1.7x decode speedup vs FlashAttention FP16; up to 2.37x maximum throughput · accuracy: Near-lossless: avg 60.27% vs 61.89% FP16 baseline on GSM8k/AQuA/BBH across Llama3/Qwen2/Phi-3 · other: KV cache size reduced by over 4.4x; enables 32k context where FP16 OOMs at 4k
tg: attention, quantization, KV-cache, FlashAttention, softmax-approximation, LLM-inference, Tensor-Core, INT8

t: Lumos: Efficient Performance Modeling and Estimation for Large-Scale LLM Training
th: parallelism
pb: Existing performance models for distributed LLM training fail to accurately capture complex inter-stream dependencies (computation-communication overlap), leading to large prediction errors (dPRO averages 14% error) and preventing reliable what-if analysis for configuration exploration.
me: Lumos: a trace-driven performance modeling and estimation toolkit. Uses PyTorch Kineto profiler (only ~10 lines of hook code) to collect CPU operator traces, CUDA runtime events, and GPU kernel traces. Constructs a task-level execution graph with four dependency types: CPU-to-CPU (intra/inter-thread via cudaLaunchKernel), CPU-to-GPU (correlation IDs), GPU-to-CPU (cudaStreamSync), GPU-to-GPU (intra/inter-stream via cudaEventRecord/cudaStreamWaitEvent). Graph manipulation supports adjusting data parallelism (update communication times), pipeline parallelism (repartition layers, insert communication tasks, update schedule), and model architecture (adjust tensor dimensions for GEMM kernels, duplicate layers). Simulation runs a dependency-respecting event-driven scheduler producing replayed traces.
nv: First trace-driven performance model to accurately capture LLM inter-stream compute-communication dependencies (via cudaEventRecord/cudaStreamWaitEvent), enabling both accurate replay (3.3% avg error) and flexible what-if estimation for parallelism and architecture changes.
mx: accuracy: 3.3% average replay error across GPT-3 15B to 175B, 16 to 512 H100 GPUs; 4.2% for scale-out what-if · other: dPRO baseline achieves 14% average error; Lumos faithfully replays SM utilization
tg: LLM-training, performance-modeling, simulation, distributed-training, 3D-parallelism, trace-driven, H100

t: LAVA: Lifetime-Aware VM Allocation with Learned Distributions and Adaptation to Mispredictions
th: scheduling
pb: VM scheduling in hyperscale cloud data centers is NP-hard with incomplete lifetime information; one-shot lifetime predictions accumulate mispredictions over time, causing host fragmentation and wasted capacity.
me: LAVA: three lifetime-aware algorithms using distribution-based VM lifetime prediction. ML model: GBDT trained on VM features (zone, family, shape, SSD, project metadata) to predict E(Tr|Tu) — conditional expected remaining lifetime given observed uptime. Multiple training examples per VM by augmenting with Tu quantiles. Model compiled into Borg scheduler binary (<10us latency, 780x faster than LA-Binary's inference server). Three algorithms: (1) NILAS — non-invasive reprediction tie-breaker using max repredicted exit time of co-scheduled VMs; (2) LAVA — lifetime-class based host state machine (open/recycling) placing shorter-lived VMs in gaps of longer-lived hosts, upgrading/downgrading host lifetime class on mispredictions; (3) LARS — lifetime-guided migration ordering for defragmentation, migrating longest-lived VMs first to let shorter VMs exit naturally.
nv: First production VM scheduler to use distribution-based lifetime reprediction (conditional expectation updated via uptime) and adapt scheduling decisions on misprediction detection, demonstrating that reprediction is theoretically and practically superior to one-shot prediction.
mx: accuracy: 3% stranded compute reduction, 2% stranded memory reduction; 2.3-9.2 pp increase in empty hosts; 4.5% reduction in VM migrations · other: Model latency <10us (780x faster than LA-Binary); fleet-wide production deployment
tg: VM-scheduling, cloud, lifetime-prediction, GBDT, bin-packing, defragmentation, Google-Borg, production

t: Venn: Resource Management for Collaborative Learning Jobs
th: scheduling
pb: Multiple concurrent collaborative learning (federated learning) jobs compete for ephemeral, heterogeneous edge devices with overlapping eligibility requirements; existing schedulers use random device-to-job matching, causing high scheduling delays and poor job completion time.
me: Venn: a centralized CL resource manager with two algorithms. (1) Intersection Resource Scheduling (IRS): groups jobs by device requirements into Resource-Homogeneous Job Groups. Within each group, sorts jobs by ascending remaining demand (shortest-first). Across groups, greedily allocates intersected resources to the group with the longer queue-to-resource ratio, prioritizing groups with scarce resources. Algorithm runs in O(max(m log m, n^2)) time. (2) Resource-aware tier-based device matching: partitions eligible devices into V tiers by hardware capability; assigns randomly-selected tier to each job. Triggers tier-based matching only when JCT reduction condition holds (1 + c > V + c*g). Fairness extension adjusts demand weights to prevent starvation.
nv: First CL resource manager to formalize and solve the Intersection Resource Scheduling problem — where job resource demands may overlap, contain, or be nested — with a contention-aware heuristic that jointly optimizes scheduling delay and response collection time.
mx: speedup: Up to 1.88x JCT improvement vs random matching baseline · accuracy: No impact on final model accuracy vs random matching · other: O(max(m log m, n^2)) scheduling complexity; negligible overhead at scale
tg: federated-learning, collaborative-learning, edge-scheduling, resource-management, contention, device-heterogeneity

t: Optimizing LLM Queries in Relational Data Analytics Workloads
th: memory-system
pb: LLM batch inference over relational tables is extremely slow and expensive because naive row-order invocation achieves low KV cache prefix hit rates, wasting prefill computation on repeated data patterns.
me: Two algorithms for row and field reordering to maximize KV cache prefix hit count (PHC). PHC is defined as the sum of squared prefix lengths reused from the previous row. (1) OPHR (Optimal Prefix Hit Recursion): recursively splits table by distinct values in each field, selecting the split maximizing total PHC; provably optimal but exponential complexity. (2) GGR (Greedy Group Recursion): greedy approximation selecting the highest-hit-count value/field at each step; uses functional dependencies (primary/foreign keys) to group correlated fields together in prefixes and skip redundant recursion; uses cardinality and average value length statistics for early stopping. GGR runs in under 15s for tables up to 30K rows and 57 fields. Implemented as a PySpark UDF with vLLM as the serving backend.
nv: First approach exploiting relational data structure (functional dependencies, field cardinality) to reorder rows and per-row field orderings for maximum KV cache prefix sharing in LLM batch analytics workloads.
mx: speedup: 1.5-3.4x end-to-end query latency speedup vs Cache (Original); 1.8-3.8x vs No Cache · accuracy: Within 5% accuracy of original ordering (except FEVER+Llama3-8B where GGR is +14.2% better) · other: 32% cost savings on OpenAI GPT-4o-mini; up to 79% estimated savings with Anthropic auto-prefix caching; GGR runs in <15s for 30K rows x 57 fields
tg: LLM-inference, KV-cache, prompt-caching, relational-analytics, batch-inference, query-optimization, prefix-sharing, Spark, vLLM

t: ReaL: Efficient RLHF Training of Large Language Models with Parameter Reallocation
th: LLM training systems
pb: RLHF training of LLMs involves multiple model function calls (actor, critic, reference, reward) with fundamentally different compute and memory profiles, yet existing systems apply static parallelization strategies that leave GPU resources severely underutilized.
me: Parameter reallocation: model weights are redistributed across GPUs between function calls so each stage uses an optimal parallelization strategy. An MCMC-based search finds the best execution plan (parallelization configs + scheduling order) over the combined search space of all model functions.
nv: First system to dynamically reallocate model parameters between RLHF pipeline stages rather than holding a fixed replica layout, paired with an MCMC planner that searches the discrete plan space efficiently.
mx: speedup: 3.58x over DeepSpeed-Chat/OpenRLHF/NeMo-Aligner/veRL; 81% over Megatron-LM heuristic at 8192 context on H100 128-GPU cluster · accuracy: No degradation in reward model quality vs baselines
tg: rlhf, parameter-reallocation, parallelism, mcmc, llm-training, scheduling

t: MEADOW: Memory Efficient Adaptable Dataflow for On-Device LLM Workloads
th: Edge ML acceleration
pb: Running LLM inference on edge FPGAs is severely constrained by the FPGA's limited on-chip SRAM and external DRAM bandwidth, making naive GEMM-based attention execution impractical at the bandwidth envelope of sub-10W devices.
me: Token-Parallel Head-Sequential (TPHS) dataflow partitions attention across token dimension in parallel while sequencing across heads to fit SRAM; weight packing extracts unique chunks from weight tensors, applies packet-specific encoding precision, and uses frequency-aware reindexing to minimize DRAM traffic. W8A8 quantization applied throughout.
nv: Combined TPHS dataflow and three-level weight packing (unique-chunk extraction + per-packet precision + frequency-aware reindexing) co-designed for sub-10W FPGA inference, achieving 1.5-2.5x latency reduction over GEMM baseline.
mx: speedup: 1.5x decode latency, 2.5x prefill latency vs GEMM baseline; >40% improvement vs CTA/FlightLLM · energy_or_tops_w: Sub-10W device (Xilinx ZCU102) · accuracy: W8A8 quantization with accuracy preserved
tg: fpga, edge-inference, attention, quantization, dataflow, weight-compression

t: SwiftVI: Faster Value Iteration via Heap-Based Action Elimination
th: Reinforcement learning algorithms
pb: Standard value iteration (VI) for large Markov Decision Processes is computationally expensive because it updates all state-action pairs every iteration, even when most actions can be provably pruned.
me: Maintains a max-heap of action upper bounds per state; after each value update, eliminates actions whose upper bounds fall below the current best lower bound. Combines four algorithmic variants: VIH (heap only), VIAE (asynchronous elimination), VIAEH (hybrid), VIAEHL (with lookahead), all exploiting monotone value function structure.
nv: Heap-based action elimination that leverages monotonicity of the value function to prune dominated actions incrementally during VI, without requiring offline precomputation of the action space structure.
mx: speedup: VIH consistently best on random and real-world MDPs vs VI/IVI/BAO/AncVI; exact ratios depend on MDP structure · accuracy: Exact (not approximate) value iteration results
tg: value-iteration, mdp, action-elimination, reinforcement-learning, scheduling, heap

t: FlexInfer: A Flexible CPU-GPU Collaborative Framework for DNN Inference
th: LLM inference systems
pb: LLM inference on commodity servers with limited GPU memory forces weight offloading to CPU, but existing offloading systems (FlexGen, SplitGen) use static policies that either underutilize the GPU or overspend PCIe bandwidth on unnecessary transfers.
me: FlexInfer employs an analytical policy estimator that, given current hardware state (GPU memory available, PCIe bandwidth, CPU compute), selects per-layer execution policy: CPU-only, GPU-offload, or SplitGen (split computation between CPU and GPU). Policy decisions are made at runtime without profiling overhead.
nv: First system to apply phase-aware and layer-aware dynamic policy selection between CPU-only, GPU-offload, and hybrid (SplitGen) modes for LLM inference, using an analytical model rather than learned or exhaustive search.
mx: speedup: 75% (Server1) and 76% (Server2) end-to-end latency reduction vs FlexGen · accuracy: No accuracy loss (exact computation) · other: 96-98% of FlexGen time is PCIe transfer; FlexInfer reduces this bottleneck significantly
tg: cpu-gpu-offload, llm-inference, pcie-bottleneck, policy-selection, scheduling, memory-offload

t: FastTree: Optimizing Attention Computation for Tree-Structured LLM Inference
th: LLM serving and attention kernels
pb: LLM serving systems that share KV cache via radix trees (prefix sharing) waste compute by running separate GEMV attention for each query even when many queries share a large common KV prefix, failing to exploit the tree structure for hardware-efficient GEMM.
me: Binary edge assignment algorithm greedily partitions the radix tree into context groups (shared prefix) and query groups (independent queries). A FlashAttention-style tiled attention kernel reuses the shared KV prefix across all queries in a group, transforming per-query GEMV into batched GEMM via query aggregation.
nv: Greedy binary edge assignment on the radix tree KV-cache graph that maximizes query aggregation opportunities, enabling GEMV-to-GEMM conversion and shared KV reuse within a single fused attention kernel.
mx: speedup: 2.2x system throughput over SGLang+FlashInfer; kernel: 5.1x over FlashAttention, 4.2x over FlashInfer, 10.6x over DeFT · accuracy: Exact attention (no approximation) · other: Hardware: H100 GPU
tg: attention, kv-cache, radix-tree, prefix-sharing, gemm, llm-serving

t: GSplit: Scaling Graph Neural Network Training on Large Graphs via Probabilistic Splitting
th: GNN training systems
pb: Mini-batch GNN training with data parallelism causes significant redundant feature loading and computation because the same graph vertices appear in multiple GPU micro-batches, limiting scalability to large graphs.
me: Split parallelism: each mini-batch is sampled once and non-overlappingly partitioned (split) on-the-fly among GPUs using an offline probabilistic splitting algorithm. The offline phase uses pre-sampling to weight graph vertices and edges by expected sampling frequency, then applies weighted min-edge-cut partitioning (METIS) to find a global vertex-to-GPU assignment. Online splitting maps each sampled vertex to its pre-assigned GPU in constant time. Inter-GPU feature shuffles at each GNN layer exchange only required features.
nv: Online probabilistic splitting that reduces NP-hard per-mini-batch partitioning to a constant-time lookup by leveraging an offline pre-sampled weighted graph partition, providing provable expected communication minimization and load balancing.
mx: speedup: Up to 4.4x over DGL (2.5x average), 4.1x over P3 (2.4x average), 1.9x over Quiver (1.4x average) on Orkut/Papers100M/Friendster graphs · accuracy: No accuracy loss vs data-parallel training (verified on Papers100M) · other: Hardware: AWS EC2 p3.8xlarge with 4x NVIDIA V100 GPUs
tg: gnn, graph-neural-network, data-parallelism, split-parallelism, mini-batch, large-graph

t: Photon: Federated LLM Pre-Training
th: Distributed LLM training
pb: LLM pre-training is constrained to high-bandwidth data centers because standard distributed training (3D parallelism) requires AllReduce at every step, making cross-region or internet-scale collaboration impractical due to low inter-datacenter bandwidth.
me: Photon is a federated LLM pre-training system using cross-silo FL with LocalSGD. Each client performs many local gradient steps before synchronizing. The system exploits federated averaging's robustness to enable small local batch sizes with high learning rates—a combination that improves generalization via noise injection. Architecture includes an Aggregator (central server), LLM Clients (local training nodes), and Data Sources. Communication uses parameter server, AllReduce, or Ring-AllReduce depending on network topology. Adaptive local parallelism selects DDP/FSDP vs sub-federation based on client connectivity.
nv: First complete system for federated LLM pre-training at billion-parameter scale that trains models matching or exceeding centralized training quality, exploiting federated averaging's robustness to combine small batch sizes with high learning rates for 2x faster convergence than DiLoCo.
mx: speedup: 35% wall-time reduction vs centralized for 7B model (95.6h vs 147.9h at 10Gbps with Ring-AllReduce) · accuracy: 7B model: 13.8 perplexity vs 16.6 centralized (-16.9%); 3B: 15.7 vs 18.2 (-13.7%) · other: Communication reduced 500x for 7B model; 64-512x less overall
tg: federated-learning, llm-training, low-bandwidth, distributed-training, localsgd, pre-training

t: LeanAttention: Hardware-Aware Scalable Attention Mechanism for the Decode-Phase of Transformers
th: Attention kernel optimization
pb: During LLM decode-phase, attention computation suffers critically low GPU SM occupancy because FlashAttention-2 only parallelizes over batch and heads (Nq=1 for decode), leaving most SMs idle; FlashDecoding's fixed-split partitioning causes imbalanced loads and quantization inefficiencies.
me: LeanAttention applies a Stream-K style decomposition to attention: the context length dimension is linearized into LeanTiles (fixed-size KV blocks optimal per hardware), then total LeanTiles are divided equally among all CTAs regardless of head or batch boundaries. Partial attention outputs from CTAs spanning head boundaries are reduced using the associativity property of the softmax re-scaling operator, enabling exact attention with near-100% SM occupancy for any problem size.
nv: Proves and exploits the associativity of the softmax re-scaling operator to enable Stream-K style arbitrary work partitioning in attention, achieving near-100% GPU occupancy for all context lengths and batch sizes, unlike fixed-split which fails at many configurations.
mx: speedup: Average 1.73x over FlashDecoding on A100 (max 2.18x at 256k context, 56 heads, BS=2); average 1.52x on H100 (max 2.53x at 64k context); 3.5x at 128k context for head_dim=128 · energy_or_tops_w: More energy-efficient than FlashDecoding at context lengths >128k (lower SM idle time) · accuracy: Exact attention (no approximation); maintains bit-exact parity with FlashAttention-2 · other: End-to-end: 1.73x speedup on Phi-3 Medium for >16k output tokens
tg: attention, decode-phase, stream-k, gpu-occupancy, softmax, llm-inference

t: MAS-Attention: Memory-Aware Stream Processing for Attention Acceleration on Resource-Constrained Edge Devices
th: Edge attention acceleration
pb: On resource-constrained edge neural accelerators (e.g., smartphone NPUs), attention acceleration methods like FLAT execute MatMul and softmax sequentially on separate MAC and VEC compute units, leaving one unit idle at all times and achieving suboptimal latency.
me: MAS-Attention schedules two streams of tiled tasks: tiled MatMul on MAC units and tiled softmax on VEC units, in a semi-synchronous pipelined fashion. A multi-tiered tiling scheme (sub-matrix tiling for MatMul, row-granularity for softmax) is optimized via MCTS + Genetic Algorithm offline. A proactive buffer overwrite strategy prevents cache overflow by selectively overwriting K or V matrix tiles and reloading as needed, prioritizing softmax completion.
nv: First attention acceleration method for edge accelerators to exploit MAC-VEC heterogeneous parallelism via semi-synchronous stream processing, combined with a proactive cache overwrite strategy that prevents pipeline stalls under constrained on-chip memory.
mx: speedup: Up to 2.75x over FLAT (simulated edge, geomean 1.70x); up to 1.76x on real Huawei MatePad Pro 13.2 DaVinci NPU (geomean 1.42x vs FLAT); 8.50x over Layer-Wise baseline · energy_or_tops_w: 54% energy reduction vs FLAT (simulated); geomean 18.55% energy savings vs FLAT across all networks · accuracy: Exact attention (golden data validation on all workloads) · other: Evaluated on BERT, LLaMA3-8B, T5, ViT, XLM; 6% end-to-end latency reduction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 UNet
tg: edge-inference, attention, npu, mac-vec-parallelism, dataflow, memory-management

t: AdaParse: An Adaptive Parallel PDF Parsing and Resource Scaling Engine
th: ML data infrastructure
pb: Building trillion-token scientific text datasets for LLM pre-training requires parsing millions of PDFs, but state-of-the-art high-quality parsers (e.g., Nougat) can only process 1-2 PDFs/second on a 4-A100 node, while lightweight parsers produce poor quality on complex documents.
me: AdaParse implements a hierarchical three-stage classifier pipeline: CLS I (rule-based validity check on PyMuPDF-extracted text features), CLS II (metadata-driven regression predicting if improvement is likely), CLS III (LLM-based multi-class parser selection). Human preferences are collected from 23 domain experts and incorporated via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to fine-tune the SciBERT-based classifier. Parsl orchestrates parallel execution on HPC (Polaris), batching PDFs, warm-starting ML parsers, and distributing tasks across nodes.
nv: DPO-aligned adaptive PDF parser routing that combines a fast text extraction first-pass with hierarchical ML classifiers, aligned to expert human preferences, achieving 17x throughput improvement over Nougat alone with 0.2% better BLEU accuracy.
mx: speedup: 17x throughput improvement vs Nougat (state-of-the-art parser); ~78 PDF/sec at 128 nodes vs ~8 PDF/sec for Nougat · accuracy: BLEU 52.1 vs Nougat 48.1 (+0.2% better); 76.9% accepted token rate vs 69.8% Nougat · other: Evaluated on Polaris HPC (560 nodes, 4x A100 per node); 1000-document held-out benchmark
tg: pdf-parsing, data-curation, dpo, adaptive-routing, hpc, llm-training-data

t: Seesaw: High-throughput LLM Inference via Model Re-sharding
hw: NVIDIA A10, L4, A100 GPUs; multi-GPU server nodes
wl: LLM inference (prefill + decode), Throughput-oriented serving with mixed request batches
th: LLM Inference & Serving
pb: A single static parallelization strategy (tensor parallelism or pipeline parallelism) cannot optimally serve both the prefill and decode stages of LLM inference, leaving throughput on the table.
me: Seesaw dynamically re-shards the model between TP for prefill and PP for decode at every stage boundary. KV cache is moved via a tiered buffering scheme: GPU VRAM for active batches and CPU DRAM as an auxiliary store, with asynchronous swap-in/swap-out pipelines. A transition-minimizing scheduler batches multiple requests together so re-sharding occurs less frequently, amortizing the overhead.
nv: Dynamic mid-inference model re-sharding combined with CPU-backed tiered KV cache buffering and a transition-minimizing request scheduler that jointly minimizes resharding frequency and maximizes batch utilization.
tg: llm-inference, parallelism, tensor-parallelism, pipeline-parallelism, kv-cache, scheduling, dynamic-resharding

t: FedProphet: Memory-Efficient Federated Adversarial Training via Robust and Consistent Cascade Learning
hw: Memory-constrained edge devices (federated); server-side coordination node
wl: Federated adversarial training on image classification (CIFAR-10, Caltech-256), VGG16, ResNet34 model families
th: Training Efficiency & Memory
pb: Federated Adversarial Training (FAT) requires large models to attain high accuracy and robustness, but memory-constrained edge devices cannot fit full-model training; existing memory-efficient FL methods sacrifice accuracy or robustness through objective inconsistency between local and global models.
me: FedProphet uses adversarial cascade learning: the full model is split into small sequential modules, each trained on one class of devices. Strong convexity regularization on each module's loss ensures local module objectives remain consistent with the global adversarial loss. A server-side coordinator performs Adaptive Perturbation Adjustment (APA) to balance utility vs. robustness trade-off dynamically, and Differentiated Module Assignment (DMA) to assign modules to heterogeneous devices, mitigating objective inconsistency across rounds.
nv: Cascade learning with strong convexity regularization that simultaneously achieves memory efficiency and adversarial robustness in federated settings, proven to imply low objective inconsistency, combined with APA and DMA coordinators on the server.
tg: federated-learning, adversarial-training, memory-efficiency, cascade-learning, edge-ai, robustness

t: Self-Data Distillation for Recovering Quality in Pruned Large Language Models
hw: GPU inference (A100-class); edge deployment of pruned models
wl: LLM instruction following, HuggingFace OpenLLM Leaderboard v1 benchmarks, Speculative decoding inference
th: Model Compression & Pruning
pb: Structured depth pruning of LLMs removes decoder blocks and reduces compute, but post-pruning SFT causes catastrophic forgetting by shifting the data distribution away from the original model's knowledge.
me: Angular cosine distance between adjacent block outputs is used to identify which layers are most redundant (lowest angular distance = most similar outputs = best pruning candidates). The unpruned model then rewrites the fine-tuning dataset: for each prompt, the unpruned model generates a 'distilled' response that preserves semantic richness. Conditional selection keeps original responses for prompts where the pruned model already performs acceptably. SLERP model merging blends pruned and distilled model checkpoints. The pruned model is also used as a speculative decoding draft model paired with the full model as verifier.
nv: Using the unpruned model to regenerate a semantically-aligned distillation dataset for post-pruning SFT, preventing catastrophic forgetting while maintaining the efficiency of depth pruning; plus SLERP merging and speculative decoding as downstream applications.
tg: model-compression, structured-pruning, knowledge-distillation, llm, speculative-decoding, model-merging, catastrophic-forgetting

t: HyC-LoRA: Memory Efficient LoRA Fine-tuning with Hybrid Activation Compression
hw: GPU (NVIDIA; Triton-compatible); targets on-device fine-tuning scenarios
wl: LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs (Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B), Downstream NLP tasks (commonsense reasoning, instruction following)
th: Training Efficiency & Memory
pb: LoRA fine-tuning dramatically reduces trainable weight count but the buffered activations needed for backpropagation still dominate memory—69.7% of total in Llama-2-7B—and non-linear operator activations (RMSNorm, RoPE) are the hardest to compress due to outliers.
me: HyC-LoRA introduces two compression tiers. Intra-operator: for RMSNorm activations, calibrate which channels contain extreme outliers, store those at full precision (FP16), quantize the rest to INT2; for attention Q/K, quantize before RoPE application (pre-RoPE quantization) where values are smoother. Inter-operator: LoRA Reorder Computing reorders the quantization and LoRA adapter application so that XA (activation times LoRA A matrix) is retained while the main branch quantizes YW separately, allowing YAB to be recomputed during backward pass rather than stored; Triton-based kernel fusion merges quantization and dequantization with adjacent ops to reduce kernel launch overhead.
nv: Hybrid two-tier compression combining structured per-channel outlier extraction for non-linear activations (intra-operator) with LoRA-aware reordering of quantization to enable recomputation instead of storage (inter-operator), plus kernel fusion—achieving near-2-bit across all operators.
tg: lora, fine-tuning, activation-compression, quantization, memory-efficiency, kernel-fusion, llm, triton

t: VoLUT: Efficient Volumetric streaming enhanced by LUT-based super-resolution
hw: Commodity mobile devices (receiver-side); server-side encoding; edge streaming
wl: 3D volumetric video streaming and super-resolution, Point cloud upsampling
th: Efficient Inference on Edge/Mobile
pb: 3D volumetric video streaming requires extremely high bandwidth; downsampling before transmission and upsampling via super-resolution at the receiver is needed, but existing 3D SR algorithms are too slow for real-time use on commodity mobile devices.
me: VoLUT has a two-stage SR pipeline. Stage 1 (dilated kNN interpolation): broader spatial context via dilated k-nearest neighbor search for initial upsampling; octree parallelism accelerates the kNN computation; neighbor relationships are reused across upsampling steps. Stage 2 (LUT refinement): coordinates of upsampled points are normalized to [0,1], quantized into b discrete bins per axis (bin=128 by default), and looked up in a precomputed 3D LUT that stores high-resolution position offsets (RF=4 receptive field, bin=128 yields 1.6GB LUT). The LUT is built offline from a trained NN model. MPC (Model Predictive Control)-based adaptive bitrate algorithm dynamically selects downsampling rate based on network conditions, streaming a continuous range of quality levels.
nv: First system to run high-quality 3D point cloud super-resolution on commodity mobile devices at line-rate, using offline NN-to-LUT conversion with position encoding quantization and dilated kNN interpolation, combined with MPC-based continuous ABR streaming.

t: Scaling Deep Learning Training with MPMD Pipeline Parallelism

wl: GPT-3 175B training (BF16), Llama-2 70B training (BF16), Large-scale distributed training
th: Distributed Training & Parallelism
pb: GSPMD/SPMD-based pipeline parallelism in JAX can only encode GPipe-style schedules; it cannot express MPMD schedules like 1F1B or Interleaved 1F1B that improve memory efficiency and throughput, and it forces homogeneous stages with poor scalability over low-bandwidth (DCN) inter-node links.
me: JaxPP extends JAX with a MPMD pipeline parallelism runtime. Users annotate model code with pipeline_yield calls that mark stage boundaries; JaxPP infers stages from data dependencies. An accumulate_grads API implements the gradient accumulation loop with user-specified schedules (1F1B, Interleaved 1F1B). A single-controller driver process traces the JAX computation to a task graph, assigns tasks to SPMD actors (each actor manages one or more devices with a local SPMD mesh), and infers send/receive pairs using topological ordering to avoid deadlocks. Buffer deletion is handled by a liveness pass. All task dispatches are fused into a single RPC per actor. A loop commuting pass handles weight sharing (tied embeddings) efficiently.

t: AI Metropolis: Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Simulation with Out-of-order Execution
hw: NVIDIA L4 GPUs (GCP G2), NVIDIA A100 GPUs; LLM inference served via SGLang
wl: LLM multi-agent social simulation (GenAgent, SmallVille 25 agents, LargeVille up to 1000 agents), Llama-3 8B, Llama-3 70B, Mixtral 8x7B inference
th: LLM Inference & Serving
pb: LLM-powered multi-agent simulations use global step-wise synchronization (borrowed from RL frameworks) that creates false dependencies between agents who are spatially distant and have no actual interaction, severely limiting parallelism and LLM inference batch sizes.
me: AI Metropolis introduces out-of-order execution for multi-agent simulation. A spatiotemporal dependency graph tracks real read-after-write dependencies: agent A is blocked by agent B only if their spatial distance is within reach over the step difference (radius_p + |StepA - StepB - 1| * max_vel). Agents that are coupled (within interaction range at same step) form clusters. A controller process uses geo-clustering to form ready clusters and dispatches them to worker processes via a priority queue sorted by step number (earlier steps = higher priority). Workers update the dependency graph in parallel using an in-memory Redis database with transactional updates. The critical path is C++ for low-latency controller logic.
nv: Out-of-order execution scheduling for LLM multi-agent simulation based on spatial-temporal dependency tracking, eliminating false dependencies while preserving temporal causality, enabling near-optimal parallelism as agent count scales.

wl: Long-sequence LLM serving (64k-512k tokens), Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Minitron-4B inference, NIAH, LongBench, RULER benchmarks
th: LLM Inference & Serving
pb: Serving LLMs on long sequences (>64k tokens) is bottlenecked by attention: quadratic complexity during prefill and linear KV cache memory pressure during decode. No existing system addresses both stages simultaneously in a unified framework.
me: LServe unifies structured block-sparse attention patterns in a single framework. For static sparsity: half of attention heads are designated as streaming heads (attend only to sink tokens and recent local window, Λ-shaped mask) identified offline via DuoAttention's optimization-based gating. A fused CUDA kernel handles both streaming and dense heads in one pass for both prefill and decode. For dynamic sparsity (decode only): hierarchical paging introduces a two-level abstraction where logical pages (fine-grained, NL tokens) are used for importance scoring while physical pages (NP = g*NL tokens) hold the actual quantized KV data. Page importance is max-pooled from logical page scores (query dot product with per-logical-page kmax/kmin statistics). Reusable page selection exploits temporal locality: the same page selection result is shared across a chunk of consecutive decode steps. All sparsity patterns are unified in block-sparse attention kernels with W4A8KV4 quantization.

wl: Shuffle jobs in distributed data processing frameworks (Apache Beam-like) at Google, Video processing, ML, database query workloads on 10 production clusters
th: ML for Systems
pb: ML-based storage tiering (SSD vs HDD placement) cannot be practically deployed at Google-scale because a monolithic model in the storage layer must be retrained whenever any workload changes, breaks separation of concerns, and becomes a single point of failure across heterogeneous workloads.
me: Bring-Your-Own-Model (BYOM): each workload trains its own lightweight gradient-boosted trees model at the application layer, not in the storage layer. The model predicts an 'importance' ranking category for each shuffle job based on application-level features (execution metadata, allocated resources, historical I/O metrics, timestamps). Importance categories are designed by analyzing oracle placement decisions under varying SSD capacities: category 0 = negative TCO savings, categories 1-N = I/O density quantiles. At the storage layer, an Adaptive Category Selection (ACS) algorithm uses a sliding admission threshold driven by real-time SSD spillover TCIO feedback, dynamically adjusting which importance categories are admitted to SSD without needing to retrain the model.

wl: ST-DiT video generation inference (OpenSora 1.1B), 1080p 8-64s, 2K 8-16s, 4K 8-16s video generation, Distributed multi-machine inference

pb: Existing sequence parallelism techniques (DeepSpeed-Ulysses, RingAttention, DSP) for distributed ST-DiT inference incur 34-44% communication overhead when crossing machine boundaries, preventing efficient strong scaling beyond a single server.
me: ScaleFusion exploits spatial-temporal independence: spatial attention is independent along the temporal dimension, and temporal attention is independent along the spatial dimension. This allows slicing each layer execution into NT temporal slices (spatial layers) or NS spatial slices (temporal layers). Intra-layer scheduling: execute all-to-all for slice i+1 asynchronously while computing slice i (pipelining communication and computation within a layer). Inter-layer scheduling: further decompose the first slice's all-to-all into LT or LS sub-partitions, and lift 2/3 of them to overlap with the last-slice computation of the previous layer, eliminating the head and tail of the pipeline that can't be overlapped by intra-layer alone. Two CUDA streams (compute and communication) are used. Hyperparameters NT=NS=4, LT=1, LS=3 are used by default.

th: Gradient Compression / Communication Reduction for LLM Training

th: Memory-Efficient LLM Optimizer / Training Efficiency
pb: AdamW optimizer for LLM training maintains first and second moments, tripling memory requirements over model weights alone (28 GB optimizer states for LLaMA-7B). This forces smaller batch sizes, more GPUs, or lower-end models.
me: APOLLO identifies that AdamW's element-wise learning rate adaptation can be coarsened to channel-wise or tensor-wise scaling without performance loss. It approximates channel-wise gradient scaling factors using an auxiliary low-rank optimizer state in a random-projected space (not SVD). Algorithm: (1) project full gradient to low-rank space via random Gaussian matrix; (2) apply AdamW on the low-rank gradient to get low-rank moments; (3) extract channel-wise scaling factors from low-rank moments; (4) apply scaling to full gradient for weight update. APOLLO-Mini uses tensor-wise (rank-1) scaling for SGD-level memory. The random projection matrix is resampled every T=200 steps. A Norm-growth Limiter stabilizes training.

t: SampleAttention: Near-Lossless Acceleration of Long Context LLM Inference with Adaptive Structured Sparse Attention
th: adaptive structured sparse attention for long-context LLM prefill
pb: Long-context LLM prefill (TTFT) latency scales quadratically with sequence length due to dense attention computation; existing sparse attention methods use either static sparse patterns or fixed sparsity budgets, failing to adapt to per-head, per-input, and per-model variability in sparsity ratio and pattern. Both dimensions—optimal sparsity ratio and the exact structure of important tokens—must be determined dynamically at runtime to avoid accuracy loss.
me: SampleAttention introduces a two-stage query-guided key-value filtering algorithm driven by a new accuracy proxy called Cumulative Residual Attention (CRA), defined as the minimum fraction of attention probability mass retained per query after sparsification. Stage 1 (Query-Guided Chunked Sampling) partitions queries into chunkn equal segments, computes full attention scores for a small query block at the tail of each chunk, then reduces these token-level scores at block granularity (block size 128) along both column and slash directions. Stage 2 (Score-Based Key-Value Filtering) independently selects the minimum number of column-strip blocks and slash-strip blocks needed to satisfy separate CRA thresholds (αc, αs) via cumulative-sum top-k, extends the selected block indices to cover the full attention matrix, merges them into a binary block-sparse mask, and executes sparse FlashAttention2 on the result. Hardware efficiency is achieved by kernel-fusing the sampling pipeline (bmm, mask_fill, softmax, reduction) and by operator fusion for sequences >256K. Hyperparameters are tuned offline per model and per sequence-length range on a small RULER subset.
nv: The CRA metric—minimum per-query retained attention probability—provides a principled, runtime-computable proxy that tightly correlates with downstream task accuracy across models and tasks, enabling fully adaptive (per-head, per-input) sparsity ratio and pattern selection without retraining.
